I've read other reviews about this game and having viewed a lot of the flack the game as got I felt obliged to weigh in.  I've bought every FM since I can remember and put A LOT of time into each version.  Yes the graphics in the match engine could be better, the press conferences are a drag and the new social media tab is repetitive, but overall the game is great.  It hasn't brought in hundreds of new additions from last year, but as the old adage goes 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it'.  It is still a wondrously in depth game that requires thought and attention rather than button mashing and luck.  I get the frustration with results when having 20+ shots yet losing 1-0, but this happens in real life not just FM.  I don't understand complaints about the game being just a database update when FIFA has barely changed a thing in 10 years yet charges £50 every year without fail for the same game with an updated database.  At least FM is only £35, with a far larger database, far more realistic and often available on offers during either sales or reduced as part of a loyalty deal.   In conclusion, if you want a more realistic experience then it's FM every time.  If you're happy watching David Alaba join Juventus for £30 million on deadline day (without fail) then play FIFA.  Both games have their place.  Personally I feel SI are doing a great job.

Wow. This is really something. Its in a completely different league from Civ or any of those space games, and not (just) because its super polished, bug free, and has awesome replayability. It has a story that drives the gameplay and factions that are unique in ways that go beyond "+5% construction bonus" and "+10 army morale bonus".
The AI is really good. Like, really good. You will be able to win on normal, but it won't be because you're roflstomping the AI into doing stupid things like sending its armies into baitstacks and declaring wars it can't win. And the difference between when you first play and when you know what you're doing will be day and night.
The bonuses in this game stack in a positive feedback kind of way--if you have enough money to buy that extra resource, you will more than make your money back, allowing you to buy that other resource to increase diplo point production so you can get that more advanced empire plan and have more money.....etc.
1. Each faction really plays differently. Especially the cultists. You could win almost any kind of victory with almost any faction, but you definitely have tools available to you to make one way much easier than others. This is all draped in some really good lore that you're rewarded with by completing quests.
2. The winter mechanic really drives home the whole "end of times is coming" theme.
3. Battles are amazing. There is a lot of awesome character animations, tons of units, and lots of different strategies to try. Why? Because battles don't just take place on one hex, they take place on a unique battlefield every time that is drawn from the terrain of the surrounding squares. You can look up on youtube what that means, but in gameplay terms it means your units getting caught in a narrow bottleneck, archers firing down death from cliffs, armies being hemmed in so tight they can't reinforce, and flying units getting into your rear to wreck your archers are all things that can happen.
Battles are also on a timer, so a smaller high quality force can definitely give a larger army some trouble. Said larger army can also then counterattack on their turn and wipe them out if they're not careful.
4. Army customization is awesome and based on resource acquisition. Proper planning to get said resources, research appropriate techs, and balance costs/benefits of more expensive units are much more important than in other games. You could try to just make an army of all juggernaut titans, but it may not be the best thing to do, as they may be too slow to destroy any units in battle.
Bad Things:
A. The endings are pretty hollow. Its like the ending of a paradox game, there's a screen that says you won and then a score screen, and thats it. I'd like at least a recap screen like civ had where it shows you how the game went over all the turns or some kind of reward, like additional lore being revealed depending on how you win. Something like WH: Dark Crusade, for example.
B. The UI is good, but not excellent. Not really a bad thing, but its definitely not the smoothest interface I've ever seen.
C. Thats it! I can't think of anything else bad about this game.

Well I recently bought this game, and I have got to say it is absolutely hilarious. This is because the nature of the game is to insult your opponent (online, couch co-op or online multiplayer) by linking  phrases into an insult from a selection of choices presented to you in a typical duel between two characters in a scene where the argument takes place. This game does have a bit of a strategy element with how you link phrases togeather and figure out each characters weak points are by playing the game in a way to score as many points as possible and deplete your opponents health bar. The game does have alot of british humor and jokes from old sitcoms and movies, so I can see there being problems for some people to fully appreciate the humor if they have not watched similar stuff prior but believe me you will be laughing regardless. Now with all these positive points come some negatives. Well for starters once you have got the hang of how the game works the quickplay and tournament options are really straighforward (only 5 stages for tournament) as the computer does not pose much of a challenge once you've figured out each characters weakness and are able to string togeather more complex word combos. I also noticed that there is alot of repatition in the phrases used, so this did dissapoint me a bit, however hopefully this will be addressed in upcoming patches or DLC which will hopefully add more phrases, characters and stages. I had a go at the multiplayer portion and from what I played I experienced no problems and I feel that this is where the game shines. When playing multiplayer there is a lot more strategy involved when people are playing against each other, as it is more of a challenge, instead of playing against the CPU that spews out gibberish the majority of the time. However with this in mind the game is highly recommendable in its current state justnow, so if your looking for something to play for short periods of time between other games or for playing with a group of friends this is an instant buy.

You have to form sentences and insult your opponent as best to your possibilities, and take into account their weaknesses. However, the scarce choice of words often result in an insult that makes little sense, adding to the hilarity. Don't expect a groundbreaking story here though, or extensive amounts of gameplay.
Thanks for reading and take care!

Influent is a simple application for learning household vocabulary for the languages it sports, there are many languages available, such as Korean, Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese, European Portuguese, Norwegian, Finnish, Latin, and so on. The game sees you take control of Andrew Cross, an inventor who, after getting his invented handheld language device's prototype stolen, decides to prove it was his all along by learning 100 words from a foreign language. In the game, you play as Cross and learn common household words using the device in the languages provided as DLC. That's Influent, and while there are more than 100 words in each of the languages, there's a few things you should know.
1:
This isn't Duolingo or Memrise, this isn't a full language-learning application as much as it is a vocabulary aid, you aren't going to learn grammar in this game, so don't buy, say, the Bulgarian language pack and expect to be be able to get into intense ideological debates in Burgas come the next week or month, Influent serves to normalize household worlds to people already learning the language. For example, I'm taking a Latin class outside of my using of Influent to help me with my Latin, Influent doesn't teach grammar, it helps teach and normalize common household objects and on occasion those objects' adjectives depending on the object, getting you to more easily learn vocabulary.
And 2:
The in-game user interface is only available in English, Japanese, Russian, German, Swedish, French, Spanish, Italian, European Portuguese, and Brazilian Portuguese. What this means is if you speak, say, French, there will be an option for you in any of the language packs to boot up and play the game in French, even if you're planning to learn Latin or Korean. You'll learn the languages but the in-game interface (mostly text and menus) will be in French, save of course for the languages you're planning on sharpening up on.
Now that those three points are out of the way, I'll go deeper into the review.
So Influent is, as described above, a language application/game to help you with household vocab for a foreign language, literally, as the game takes place in Cross' apartment, complete with hundreds of objects and their names to learn. The game can be played in first or third person, the former locking the mouse to the reticule. You go around Cross' apartment collecting words to be put on a future vocab test, tests you get every 10 new objects/objects' adjectives or otherwise you find, the tests will then see you moving around the apartment to find the objects as the game tells you their names in the language you're learning, with a total score out of ten at the end. If you get a word wrong, the game tells you the correct answer and you have to take the test again in order to have incorrect words "mastered",
"mastered" words being words that you don't have difficulty remembering anymore, and the game's algorithm for determining if you truly know the word isn't butchered or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it serves as a great language learning vocab app and does its job damn well. The game isn't limited to objects lying around the main space of Cross' room, either, the map, although small, can mostly entirely be interacted with, you can open doors, closets, your fridge, and select objects in the rooms, closets, and your fridge to be on the next vocab test, from milk in Cross' fridge to the conditioner in his shower.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. It's a great language aid and a great tool to help learn basic vocabulary for a foreign language, it does its job amazingly and smoothly, and is overall a great application for foreign language vocab.

This game is a great way to assist you with learning to speak another language. It won't teach you syntax or anything like that, but it does give you a way to learn and practice a good number of common words.

Sachi is your typical one-eyed girl next door that you've always had a crush on...
Wait, one-eyed girl?
This short visual novel describes a slice of life scenario where a young man, Mamoru, falls in love with the moderately-bruised Sachi, who only longs to have a smile worthy of the name her parents gave her (sorry Grisaia!) There really is nothing that stands out too much in this VN:  Boy falls in love with girl, girl reciprocates, they date, she meets his friends, he meets her relative, girl learns to stand up for herself... everything here is something anyone over 15-18 has already seen or experienced, whether first hand experience or through an entertainment medium.
The story doesn't overstay its welcome, though it'd have been worthwhile if we could have had more unique scenarios. Backgrounds are heavily reused, there aren't a lot of variety to sprites, characters are not voiced.  BUT despite these flaws (if you would call them that), the entire story is a warm, feel-good experience.  Characters have well-defined, one-dimensionsal personalities, but Sachi especially exhibits some growth, which is nice to see.  Though initially weak and spineless, Sachi is likeable and it's fun seeing her mature overly the course of the story.  Sachi's eye is initially viewed as something to be embarassed about, but Mamoru is not repulsed, or even attracted, by this unique aspect.  The eye isn't a big problem; very little about the story would be changed even if Sachi had two eyes. It differentiates Sachi but doesn't define her.  -------> [Good moral to glean]
To sum it up, the story/art is pretty generic, but it'll make you feel good inside.  It's worth a read or two.
I'd recommend this to anyone with a few hours to kill, or as an intro to a VN rookie.

The good things about LEGO Batman 3: Beyond Gotham are the things that are good about the whole LEGO series: relatively easy puzzle play, drop in/drop out coop, lots of collectibles, and a general lack of angst and drama. Beyond Gotham goes even farther with tons of post-storyline quests and locations, different fight animations for different characters, and an amazing amount of voice-over recording.
For me, though, my favorite thing about LEGO games is the humor, and I didn't find as much as usual in Beyond Gotham. Maybe it's just that I missed all the inside jokes (I'm less familiar with the DC universe than with other LEGO game topics). Normally, I find myself laughing out loud frequently, and wanting to show all the silly bits to friends. But my snickers-per-minute ratio was far below standard with this particular LEGO game.
So, if you want hours of gameplay, especially co-op with a less-skilled friend, Beyond Gotham is a fine choice. If you want silly humor, there are better LEGO games to start with.

Aside with the random & interesting glitches, Star Wars: KOTOR is a terrific game. Not only is the plot fleshed out and the cast & dialogue well-written, but the game gives you a lot of replay value. There's so much to do in KOTOR 1, it's a shame that the sequel had to be rushed.
As for the MMO, it was fun at first but got old fast. Sure, it allowed your character to be portrayed with a voice and a personality, but it wasn't what many people expected it to be. No matter who you played as, what you chose to be and how you handled situations, the outcomes were almost ALWAYS the same. Very little differences. Very little diversity. Very little thought put into it.
They removed the classic RPG elements of the main games and replaced them with overused MMO standards. If only they made it a game with many different ways of completing the quests, the unforgiving consequences like most old RPG's (though not as harsh as FOnline 2238) and combined them with original & balanced MMO mechanics, would they have made a worthy replacement of Star Wars Galaxies.
Star Wars: The Old Republic was, in short, a World of Warcraft game set in the Star Wars Universe with Mass Effect dialogue. Shortly after finding out about Mass Effect 3, I realized BioWare's true beliefs and views on its players & subscribers. I quickly left SW:TOR and vowed never to give them another penny out of my wallet!

You may have heard of the new MMORPG, Star Wars: The Old Republic. If you are a huge SW fan like myself, skip over that for now and consider buying this game. Even though it has many flaws, it's quite fun.
What separates this game from the rest? Simple: you are directly responsible for how your characters acts towards others, deals with situations, and evolves to meet your own personal taste. The game is styled quite similarly to Neverwinter Nights or Dungeons and Dragons- you pick a class, advance levels, and choose abilities and skills you yourself are interested in. Will you be a valiant Jedi knight? A grey Jedi? Or perhaps a Sith Lord? It's all up to you.
As far as the story goes, good God- it has everything. Over 40 hours of gameplay is crammed with interesting and vibrant characters, from Bastila, the nagging stereotypical Jedi, to HK-47, the homicidal droid obsessed with killing everything that moves. There's a little bit of everything for everyone- mystery, intrigue, conspiracy, romance, you name it, SW:KOTOR has it.
Now, what do I have to complain about? A few problems occur when playing this game. The original release was from 2003, and somewhere between then and now, a few rough spots cropped up in the game's ability to work at 100%. The screen resolution won't perfectly fit, and leads to you being forced to play in a black frame around the game itself. It's a little distracting at first, but not too bad. However, one HUGE problem I encountered was the frequent crashing of my game. Every half hour or so, it'd freeze and shut down, leading to some paranoid saving antics. It was incredibly frustrating, especially when you were forced to go through a long cut scene...again. I think an attempt was made to fix it, and towards the end of my run it wasn't as frequent, but the crashes never really stopped.
In game problems are sparse as far as the plot and characters go. Everyone is fleshed out quite well, and you learn quite a lot about everyone in your personal entourage. There is, however, one thing that bugged me a lot. The romances. Jesus. I don't know WHY they picked the two most unlikeable and whiny characters as the main romance options- they're both ridiculously obnoxious, and as soon as I realized who my character was supposed to end up with, I started leaving the guy behind all. The. Time. You have the option to turn down their advances (thank God), because otherwise, this complaint would be a heck of a lot longer.
All in all, this game is really an enjoyable experience. The plot moves forward and engages you constantly, culminating in an awesome revelation I didn't see coming. The characters are all believable and the banter between everyone is often hilarious. Would I recommend this? If you have a lot of patience for a few technical difficulties, then yes, I would. This game is less of an homage to several adventure games and RPGs from the past and more a shoehorning of A Link to the Past into Final Fantasy VII with a few character names barely obscured.  Speaking of shoehorning, the plot goes from boilerplate JRPG to essentially ripping off the most major scenes from FFVII without context or emotion in the last hour.
That said, it does add some of its own character through the "evolution" of the graphics, sound and gameplay; it's a naturally flowing romp through all your favorite visuals in the first half with a rather pleasing visceral effect on someone that grew up at the same time.
Unfortunately, the second half is almost entirely everything about FFVII battles that were tedious; constant, irritating, overly showy, slow turn-based battles with literally the same 4 or 5 enemies for all but two short sections.
Pros:
- Smooth gameplay
- Amusing "upgrade" system for the graphics, sound, UI, and character gameplay
- High on nostalgia if you're into that
Cons:
- Far, far too short (6 hours for me)
- Gameplay padded by irritating, repetitive battles with the same enemies (fewer than 20 in game)
- Not at all challenging, other than collection side quests
Verdict:
I don't feel cheated at the $2.50 price point I paid during a Steam sale.  I would have at the $10 regular price.  If you want a short trip down memory lane, you could do worse than Evoland; just wait until it goes on sale.

This might be a bit of a difficult sell. You've probably heard by now that this is essentially a paid demo for the upcoming MGS5: Phantom Pain. This, regrettably, is true. You're essentially paying for a small taste of what's to come in September of this year. I honestly can't recommend this at full price. However, if you can get it for between $5-$10, then I think you'll get you're money's worth.
I do suggest buying it either on a sale or when the price drops because it's actually a pretty good game. The game is very well optomized. My gaming rig isn't exactly the best, but I was able to run this with almost all the settings up to High, and with a decent framerate.
Gameplay wise, it's insanely good. It's a third-person stealth game with a lot of the marks that let you know it was done right. On all but the hardest setting, the enemies don't immediately turn hostile upon seeing you, giving you time to get out of their range of sight. And there are plenty of high spots to mark enemy locations so you can see them through walls once you head back to ground level. You can also interrogate enemies you sneak up on and grab in order to learn the location of collectibles, weapons, and prisoners that can be saved in order to increase your rank at the end of the mission.
Overall, good game with an asking price that's just a bit too high. Like I said, wait for it to go on sale and pick it up. Plus, if you complete this, you'll get an exclusive mission in the full release of Phantom Pain, as well as some other bonuses. So if you're huge Metal Gear fan, you'll probably want to pick this up.

You take the role of an unfortunate young man unable to leave his apartment, seemingly stuck in time. The only other living things with him being his cat who never wakes from her slumber, and a few plants, one of which is neglected through lack of watering. A quick look at the clock in the kitchen reveals that time stands still. It becomes apparent that you're stuck in some sort of time loop, or that time has somehow frozen. The outside tempts you through pictures of the protagonist and a young woman whom I assume is his girlfriend. Various posters and books strewn around tease the existence of a world outside. Forms of communication like your computer and television do nothing. The television looping the same video over and over, the "portatil" and "ordenador" stuck on the same webpage, a phamplet pushed through a mail slot...it's all a reminder to his predicament.
Stuck, the young man does what any sane person would do. Learn a new language. There are 420 words to be learned, and you must help him learn them. Lindo, Techo, Muro, he learns these new words. Portatil, pelota; the man keeps going. You know its all futile in the end, but you must keep going. I'm about 100 words away from 420 (great reference there BTW), but I fear I might think "now what..." when I get there.
There's a silver lining to all this for you the player. In alternate versions, you learn new words like: "cama", "寝床", and "lit." Words you can use with the beautiful women of this world (warning: you might get slapped). That said, this is a WONDERFUL language reference in my opinion. Team it up with a good education, the "Duolingo" app, or a nice girlfriend (or bf, or both) if you're into multicultrual dating. It's a great supplement to your language learning arsenal. I try to keep my PC library efficent by getting rid of games I've finished, and files I don't need any longer. But this "game" Influent...It's going to stay on my hardrive for a loong time.
My version is Spanish, and any additional version is USD 4,99. Unless you're Jason Bourne, a linguistic professor, or a robot, I would not recommend buying more than a few in a short time span. The price tag of USD 9.99 is very well worth it IMHO. A good tip to help out: change UI language settings to whichever one you're trying to learn.

This game accomplishes what it sets out to do, for the most part. I, however, purchased the Japanese version. Don't buy the Japanese version.
Here's a simplified version of how the game works: Walk around a house and look at things. Learn how to read and speak these things. Increase your vocabulary for your language of choice. You'd be surprised just how many words you can learn by walking around an ordinary house pointing at things and saying "What's that?"
Here's the problem though; the house is the same in each language. So when you go into the Japanese version, for instance, and see...let's say a bed, you learn that a bed is called...a bed (technically bedo) in Japanese. So essentially you're just walking around a house learning how to pronounce things you already know with kana.
Maybe further down the line they will release some DLC that provides a more personalized environment for each language; but as it stands, this is a big problem.
Do I recommend it? Yes....if you are studying a language without many borrowed words/cognates. Don't get the Japanese version.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic is a game I had mixed feelings about going into. On the one hand, it's a Star Wars game with all the baggage that brings. On the other hand it's a Star Wars game that's set in an era where nobody from the movies can ruin things with a cameo. I eventually ended up getting with the deciding factor being that it's a Bioware game and back then Bioware still made a good RPG.
To start you off Knights of the Old Republic is nothing revolutionary, in fact it's a step backwards in a lot of places. It's real time but with behind the screens turn based combat as played in third person and while the third person camera does add more action to the combat it also makes any semblance of strategy feel distant and uninvolved.
As you start off the game you are a seemingly unimportant Republican soldier that survives an attack on your ship by the evil Sith empire. You then set about gathering companions, finding loot and solving everybody's random problems in a usual RPG fashion. As you progress through the storyline things quickly become more than they seem and you eventually end up having to save the galaxy.
The storyline and the interaction with the various characters are one of the main points of the game and this is also where one of the game's major flaws become apparent.
Bioware has never been good at writing grey, they always tend to stick with the ultimate black and white scenario, either you stop and help every kitten down from every tree or you stop to kill every kitten in every tree with the only neutral option being not accepting the quest in the first place. Normally they can get away with it through the storyline placing the player as some form of superhuman on a quest so epic that it probably needs 1812 as it's theme music. Although this also happens here the black and white writing of Bioware is combined with the natural black and white of the Star Wars universe and it becomes rather jarring at times being forced to take such extreme positions on every little issue with the only option for neutrality being to decline any story/experience/loot that might be on the table and say "Gotta go save the galaxy, bye!" to the quest givers.
The storyline is not Bioware's greatest in general but the various interesting characters you meet along the way does a lot to make up for it, even if some of the lesser ones are just Bioware archetypes.
The gameplay is not terrible, it just isn't that impressive either, while the occasional boss fight might force you to do more than click attack and sit back and wait for your enemy to die that is the default position even on the highest difficulty. This I suspect is to compensate for how cumbersome it feels to use any sort of strategy beyond setting up which AI type your companions should use.
If you have heard about this game, chances are you have heard about the by now famous plot twist. For all it's hype however it is not particularly surprising nor particularly plausible. The story is not bad mind you, and the game throws so half-decent choice and consequence your way every once in a while even if it's marred by the game's poor morality system.
All in all Knights of the Old Republic is a solid piece of RPG, it might have some technical issue, it might have some poor combat and it might have some less than stellar story writing but none of this is enough to detract from the overall quality of the game. It might not be the RPG classic we were hoping for but it does give you many, many hours of entertainment.

I enjoyed this game quite a bit. Yes, it's a wee bit cheesy at times, and can definitely get a bit repetitive if you reach the point I did of being determined to get all the endings, but it's still very replayable and takes a looooong time to reach that point. It's basically a visual novel of a retelling of Cinderella, but with it's own twists on the story. The graphics are very pretty, and the overall art style is really enjoyable. While there's very little animation, because it's a visual novel you don't really expect much either. The story (and all it's variations) is very well done, and it's a lot of fun to try and figure out different endings, and how different actions impact things. Like I said, it can eventually get a bit repetitive, but only if you're at that point where you're just bound and determined to get those last few endings.
Now, that being said, once you've gotten all the endings and achievements, it's unlikely you'll play it again, or at least not for a good long while. This is the same experience I had with a different visual novel (based on Pride & Prejudice) I played elsewhere, however, so I sort of expected that once I finally completed everything. If you enjoy reading, making choices in books (sort of like a more interactive choose-your-own-adventure), fairy tale variations, or just visual novel type games, definitely buy this one. I would totally buy another visual novel from this developer, and sincerely hope they make more like this (with a different story, of course) in the future.

Somehow a highly intelligent, socially fluid, doctorate-level philosopher finds herself under the thumb of an overbearing taskmistress stepmother whose power over Cinders, our protagonist, lies in the ability to not feed her if she doesn't clean up the mansion like she's supposed to.
Cinders injects agency into the on-rails plot of the fairytale narrative Cinderella by offering four major ending types and enough sub-endings to make it feel like you've gotten what you wanted - on the game's terms, of course. You have three romance options, only one of which is worthy of Cinders's hand. The conversations with Sophia and Gloria, the "evil stepsisters," are charming and at times vigorous rounds of badminton repartee. You can choose to warm up to either or both of them, as well as the opposite.
The events of the story play out like any soap opera would. You have a limited amount of freedom in choosing the order of the scenes and how they unfold. The dialogue is pleasant enough although the stylized "ruffian" speech of the top hat-wearing Obligatory Shady Person was a bit annoying to read through.
If I had my druthers, I would have left town with Sophia; I ended up leaving town on my own, thinking that this represented independence. The epilogue then presented me with an outcome that hand-waved away the panache with which Cinders had handled the entirety of the story. Apparently the independent ending requires you to administer a noble house as opposed to leaving a place that disliked you to start up your own life somewhere else.
I didn't buy the premise or the variable representations of Cinders's intelligence, but it's a nice little romp through the fairy-filled forest.
Overall, 7/10. Buy it on sale.

It was a really tough decision, but I can't recommend this game.
I think the fault doesn't lie in the game itself, but in it's rating - I think the game got pretty much overrated by people saying that this "is a new approach to the classic fairy tale with a lot of different paths to take". Also that "it's one of the best visual novels". One thing I can agree with is that the art is really stunning. It was something new to see a visual novel made in this style and I think it really fits the game.
Okay, now the not-so-great-things:
1) They said it's not like a fairy tale... well okay, maybe they didn't, but I thought they would at least change the plot slightly so that e.g. you don't have to go to the prince in every route. Also I thought it fairly discouraging that you can't choose a lot of things...
Well, I pretty much think that it is still the fairy tale...
2) I felt that the plot was really rushed. You didn't have time to learn about the characters and you didn't have time to explore the environment. Also, I didn't quite like the pacing of the romance paths. The guard was a stranger to you, but you willingly chose to trust him
... And my, I think it's really naive... I wished there was more story... Also with the prince...
3) There was the feeling that they pretty much copy pasted, whenever they could, so at particular moments in the story the personality of the main and the other character just changes without reason....
Do you still want to buy this game?
Well, I'm not a jerk, so let's talk about the good points..
1) The art is really amazing, like I said
2) The character are well done, expecially this is the reason, why I finished the game. Besides Cinders, who I found is a bit Mary Sue (idk, just my opinion), I really liked the description and the interaction with the other characters in the game. It is clearly visible that whoever wrote this, must have dealt with the human psyche a lot and succeeds in describing realistic characters, who are either nor good or bad and nor strong or weak. They have all their respectable opinions and struggle to live. My favorite was Sophia, who clearly shows that she can be a strong-willed woman, who has wits and who is trying to change her life little by little.
For my part, if you really want to play this game, buy it, when it's on sale. I got one route done in 3h, so I think it'll be 3-4h more to get everything else.
And before you start judging: I DON'T THINK THE GAME IS BAD! I THINK THAT THE PEOPLE ARE TOO MUCH RECOMMENDING IT HERE, SO THAT YOU ARE DISSAPOINTED, WHEN ACTUALLY PLAYING IT!

This is an unfortunately sloppy port of what is normally a good game.
When I originally tried to play this game, I... well, couldn't. Despite greatly exceeding the minimum system requirements needed to run the game, every single race was plagued by massive stuttering. Sometimes I would wonder if the game itself had frozen, because it would suddenly stop for more than a full second in the middle of race for no reason whatsoever. It made the game totally unplayable on every single level, and there was nothing I could do to fix it. Reading up online, I was not alone in having this issue, and the game's developers apparently made a statement that it was a "shader caching" bug effecting certain graphics cards (primarily the AMD Radeon brand) and it was somehow impossible to fix.
A couple months ago, I rebuilt my entire PC, and a friend provided me with a hand-me-down graphics card that, when it debuted in 2012, originally cost $450. Not exactly top-brass in 2016, but more than capable to get the job done. It's also an AMD Radeon card, but for whatever reason, the stuttering bug I originally experienced when I first bought the game was not present on my brand new, rebuilt system. Instead, I was greeted with errors rendering environment shadows, missing effects, flickering particles, and occasionally corrupted textures. The game runs fine otherwise -- a solid, unflinching 60fps. But the rest of the visual presentation leaves a little bit to be desired.

Evoland is a game about games. It's not a good game on it's own merit, but taking it for what it is, (being a game that is meant to take you through the Action/Adventure/RPG genres) it delivers a sense of nostalgia that can only be appreciated if you have played any of the games it constantly references or jokes about.
The game borrows almost every aspect of itself from successful RPG's of the past and incorporates them into this journey through the evolution of games. Although the overall idea of the game is good, the delivery of things is a little underwhelming and it leaves the game with a sense of emptiness about it. Puzzles are simple, enemies are lifeless, areas are bland and empty, and collectibles require almost no work to get. Yes, Evoland certainly does take you through the Action/Adventure/RPG genre, but don't expect it to compete with the games it borrows from. Evoland is NOT a good RPG, but it IS a good experience.
If you like RPG's, you'll like Evoland.
If you're looking for an engrossing, original game, Evoland is not for you.
All in all, I enjoyed it, but it's not a game I'll ever revisit or feel the need to play again.

For a game made in 2 months this's fairly impressive, but for a game on Steam with an asking price of  $10 it's very underwhelming.
I understand the constraints the dev was under to get this game ready in time for a convention he wished to sell it at, but there's no reason why afterwards, when the pressure was gone, that he couldn't have revisited the title and expanded upon it before putting it onto a larger market, such as Steam.
As it stands the story is decent, but nothing spectacular. More than once there were times you'd expect there to be more shown, but he just ends up alluding to events and then skipping right over them (presumably cuts made to get the game done on time). The story with the main antagonist ended in a very unsatisfactory manner, though I will refrain from expanding on that any further to avoid spoilers. Most of the side characters also didn't really get as much time as I would have liked in order to get to know them better. Also - unless you share in some of the creator's fetishes for things like injuries - a lot of the dialog will seem forced, weird or unnecessary as they are mainly tacked on to serve his own indulgences.
The art style is nice and the main selling point that drew me to this title. Though as with everything else about this game, it would have been nice to have had more of it, for instance there was very little by way of CG stills/cutscenes. However, it does have a far more coherent and enjoyable aesthetic than most other amateur VN offerings and deserves a fair bit of praise for that alone.
Sound was just so-so. Some of the music could use a bit of work, there were some grating off key notes thrown in inexpertly throughout a few of the tracks that detracted from my enjoyment, but otherwise the soundtrack was ok and fit the story well enough.
Overall, I enjoyed it, but the creator really should put another 2-4 months into completing this, then this would be well worth the asking price and a highly recommended title for those who enjoy quirky VNs. But as it stands I can't recommend it unless you find it on a pretty decent sale, as you just wont get your money's worth otherwise.

However, they end up seeing eye-to-eye on many things, and their relationship is magnified as a result.
Since this is a kinetic VN, most of the story is told through one point of view, and the exploration of themes is a bit near-sighted because of its short length, but for what it's worth, this is a pretty decent feel-good game that doesn't lose focus on its artistic vision. Because of that, I can turn a blind eye on its faults and recommend it.

Ok, this is my first review, where I try to keep some structure to my review because it's gonna be a longer one.
First of all: I haven't played the game all that long by now (6 hours maybe) including the tutorial and I have the feeling I still barely scrachted the surface of things this game has to offer. Second is very similar to the first: The diversity in general. Not only in mechanics and win possibilities but also in the playable and non-playable races. I have tested 3 of the existing 9 (I think) and each one was unique and made me play them a lot different although they were still "similar" races. Haven't played any of the more war focused races so far and I still had a lot of diversity.
Another thing I really like is the "love to the detail in this game". This game really hooks me and I always end up playing longer than I intended to. Even when not playing I often think about this game and theorize about good strategies, that I want to test. I guess that's mostly because I'm still learning how to play this game "good" but as said before, this game offers so many different ways leading to the same result and even more different results, that you will be busy with truly understanding this game long enough to make it worth your money. It's just fun in general and that's all what matters when it comes to games, right?
It's all about the fun you have with it and for me this game was and will be a lot of fun, so I can recommend it without any cons (so far, as said before: still learning; but I doubt, that I will meet any big cons, if they would exist I would have already stumbled into them)

Having played almost every edition since 07, I'd like to believe I know a thing or two about the Football Manager series. Prior to my purchase I had a few doubts looking at some of the reviews and the 'Mostly Negative' overall score. But I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised.
I know a lot of people say, don't buy it, nothing has really changed from last year... but the same can be said about FIFA, and yet, millions of people continue to buy it year after year. So, what to make of this year's addition....
I know in previous versions of FM, there have been some very noticable issues with the match engine, but this year's version seems to perform very well. While the game hasn't had a revolutionary overhaul, I have already noticed a lot of subtle improvements (both in terms of the match engine and the UI) that make the game feel much more polished than previous editions. If you're a FM tragic like me, I'm sure you will appreciate them. Is it worth the $60 price tag?? Yes and no.
If you're new to FM and keen to know what all the fuss is about, I would say "go ahead", once you've chalked up 500+ hours you won't be phased by the $60 price tag. For those of you thinking about upgrading from FM15 or 16, if you're indecisive like I was, perhaps get it on sale (I got it for $30). There are definitely enough improvements to warrant the $30.
Overall, as a standalone FM game I would rate it 4.5 stars and certainly don't think its worthy of its 'mostly negative' rating.

I've been using Influent to learn Mandarin, and it has been one of the most helpful vocabulary tools I have found. It provides a very clear UI for gamification (although the controls are wonky) and reads words out loud, which is super important trying to learn a tonal language, coming from English. It is a little disappointing with the limited environment, although that environment does contain a massive amount of objects, so it's less of a problem then it could be, and I respect the developer increasing the breadth of languages rather than the depth of each.
I would reccomend looking at this game after looking at other free or cheap language learning tools. It may be you will find one that works very well for you and you won't need to spend money on this game. However, very few free Mandarin sites provided me with the pronunciations I wanted, and the gamification here makes me feel very intensely about wanting to get a random list of 10 words correct.

This game is great for practicing and learning new vocabulary for languages.
Expect an interactive flash card game experience in 3D. This is not a game for someone trying to learn the language, but rather someone that is already in the process, and is using this to increase or practice their word comprehesion/vocabulary.

[Note: this is actually a review of "Stronghold Crusader Extreme" which is bundled with "Stronghold Crusader HD". I honestly don't remember the distinguishing factors between the base "HD" game and the "extreme" edition, or if I even played the former. But I know that if u buy the "HD", u get "extreme" bundled with it, so at the very least, you are guaranteed every bit of entertainment described in the review below, and then some!]
Stronghold Crusader Extreme will go down in history as one of the most epic RTS games and one of my favorites, for the simple fact of:
One of the missions on the crusader trail, was like a 7v1, and over the course of a multi-hour mission of shoring up my castle, building my econ, and eventually building a good enough army to go on the offensive, I killed over 100,000 attacking enemies.
O . O
I have played a lot of TD, a lot of RTS, a lot of twin-stick shooters, and "horde survival" FPSes, and I honestly can't think of another game that comes even close to that kind of number.
The enemies just kept sending waves and my archer/crossbowmen towers just kept munching them like a woodchipper. It was beautiful! :D
There are other qualities to the game, of course, but the above is why this is a "hall of fame" game for me.
One other thing I always really liked about the stronghold games is what I'd call the "No Abstraction Economy": i.e. if a farmer puts a basket of apples in your granary, you're going to have a basket of apples sitting in your granary. It doesn't just turn it into some abstract number like "Food: 30". If u want to build 5 macemen, then u need 5 maces, 5 leather armors, 5
, and a little bit of gold to cover the "administrative cost" I guess ;P. U don't just magically turn "10 iron, 5 wood, 20 food, 5 gold" into a maceman. Etc. (Unfortunately from Stronghold 2 onward they diminished this system to be more like a traditional RTS where sometimes things do just turn into abstract numbers.) (Edit: and btw I'm certainly not saying this makes the difference between a "good" RTS and "bad" RTS -- far from it! -- but I'm just saying, I always found this aspect of Stronghold to be quirky and fun.)
Bottom line: If u like RTS, u should give it a shot. It is different from the typical RTS in many ways and anyone who is a lover of the RTS genre deserves to experience Stronghold "just cuz".

First thing to know about this game when you find yourself wondering "Are the graphics in the game as good as I think it is from the videos?". The answer is a resounding YES, and better. I found myself just drooling over the vistas and the art of this title. It never gets tiring. The game is relatively short if you consider play time vs other titles but you need to think of this title in a slightly different way. It's being part of Gladiator the movie instead of just watching it, and it's more intense. The whole game is a rollercoaster ride of intense twists, memorable characters, beautiful scenes and testosterone wall to wall. You really appreciate how well they've done the facial animations and voice acting. It brings the characters alive and they tell the story in a deep and engrossing manner. When you're done playing through this game you don't think "Oh, is that all? Why so short?", you think "Wow, i need a break to bring my heart rate down, that was fun". If you think it was short it's only because you would actually like more of the game to play because it was fun to play, but that feeling would have been there no matter how long the title if it kept up the quality all the way through.
As for the negatives, well don't take it too seriously. If there was a star rating in these reviews I would maybe subtract half a star (maybe a full star, maybe) out of 5 for these negatives. The combat is fairly basic. You can draw comparisons to Batman Arkham games but Batman has more variety in the moves and the mobs you fight against. The combat is still engaging however but if you're a keen eye you'll pick up the types of enemies you're dealing with and it won't take you long to master how to kick butt without breaking a sweat. You kinda feel like you're some superman with how good your skills become, so I reckon a bit more variety and difficulty would have made this feeling harder to obtain and feel more worthwhile once achieved. Again, with the mobs there isn't a lot of variety in the types of guys you tend to fight with. They copy paste the foes all the time and don't really have much of a progression through the game where you'll encounter something new. Basically same enemies, different environment and you'll destroy them all fairly easily. Granted, I have yet to play on the Legendary difficulty but I always play a game first on normal mode as I figure that was the mode you're intended to play first.
Final word there are some EPIC death scenes in this game and I won't spoil it for you but you're gonna love the final cut scene.

This is one of my favorite games I have found on Steam thus far. I love surrealism, and if you share that interest, then this game is for you. The two very different game pathways provide a strength to the game through variation of objectives and gameplay. While this game shows all the telltale signs of a still-learning developer, I do not hold that against it. This game refuses to be straightforward, relying on trial and error to advance through either scenario. There are minor adjustments that need to be made in the future, including being able to skip dialogue and cutscenes when we fail an objective. The transitions are interesting and stylish, but after the umpteenth time, I just want to get back to hopping around Immensity again. The Basement is a fun level, but it is entirely too dark. Let me have the flashlight before I need to stack boxes. I skip this level most of the time during my replays because of it. The achievements won't unlock, but who cares about that anyway. The sights on the pistol are useless, and I want that tommygun earlier in the game than the last level. This game captures imagination, and holds attention with its visual displays.
Edit: One last thing, what's with the dancing technicolor frogs at the end of Immensity?

Characters with motorcycles are by far the best in the game, they handle nearly as well as most other vehicles and the get to preform "ground tricks" which is basically a wheelie which if preformed uninterrupted gives a boost. This is a kinetic visual novel about falling in love with a cyclops. I found the characters likable, the story enjoyable, despite being completely predictable, and the art decent. As far as dialogue is concerned, it fit and made sense, yet I still found it slightly dull somehow, with exceptions for all of the puns and reoccuring themes.
In the extras the developer said that he rushed the game for a release date and procrastinated for some time. This is evident in a few places, which are not that horrible, and for which I was surprised for him to site as examples of this. The greatest effect of this though is actually the limitation of certain characters in regards to their presence, the scope of their personalities, the amount of scenes that they are in, their actual appearance in the game, and segments of story that would make sense to include, or would have been nice to have in it.
For some reason despite wondering why the affection object character, Sachi Usui, was depicted as being constantly injured and wearing bandages in screenshots before buying it, I didn't realize how much of a fetish game this is. It contains no nudity or purely sexual content, however Sachi is almost entirely based on fetish fufilment, and fetish interests are very heavy throughout the story. It didn't bother me, however it did catch me off guard. The fetish themes are:
Beneath the fetish fulfillment there is a very sweet and endearing story which I will remember and am glad that I experienced.

You could change out any mention of her being a cyclops to her being ugly / purple skinned / a reptilian and the story would be the same.

Do you like RPGs?  Do you enjoy irony, wit and win?  Try Evoland.
I'm not sure which wall Evoland breaks when the game has you unlock gaming elements but it makes for an outstanding experience.    Players start with Gameboy-like graphics and a serious lack of options.  Both can be remedied by bumping into chests that unlock things like 16-bit graphics (which improve!) and save points.  Some more recognizable RPG elements included are FF6, Diablo, Ocarina of Time as well as similar game mechanics.
I would like the game more if any mechanic you unlocked stayed available throughout.  One early dungeon can be frustrating due to the inability to use healing potions or companion characters even if both are unlocked.
Thankfully the game does not include 16-character "save codes" ala Metroid or Goonies II.  Some RPG elements should stay buried.

This game is truly awesome! In the short time I've played so far, it has reminded me of old NES style RPG's, through the 16-bit era and on to full blown 3D.
Covering Adventure and RPG style games, the game draws heavily from the Zelda series and the early Final Fantasy games. At certain points in the game, it plays out as a Zelda-like dungeon crawler/puzzle adventure game, and almost seamlessly transforms itself into an RPG with Active Time Battle systems!
The artstyle is beautifully reminiscent of early 8-bit games, all the way through to late DS style Zelda Phantom Hourglass/Spirit Tracks animation, and the music evolves with the graphics.
All in all, I'd say this is a must-buy for any Zelda or Final Fantasy fan(boy/girl). Just like me!

Evoland is a great trip through the nostalgia of gaming. It may be short, and the story may be lacking, but all in all it is a great journey through time. The bottom line is that this game really shines as a tribute to the evolution of gaming, and serves as a somewhat makeshift history lesson to younger generations.

Ok, this is my first review, where I try to keep some structure to my review because it's gonna be a longer one.
First of all: I haven't played the game all that long by now (6 hours maybe) including the tutorial and I have the feeling I still barely scrachted the surface of things this game has to offer. That's my first pro argument. This game got lots of content and lots of different ways to win the game including complete peaceful ways for the pacifists :)
Second is very similar to the first: The diversity in general. Not only in mechanics and win possibilities but also in the playable and non-playable races. I have tested 3 of the existing 9 (I think) and each one was unique and made me play them a lot different although they were still "similar" races. Haven't played any of the more war focused races so far and I still had a lot of diversity.
Another thing I really like is the "love to the detail in this game". So many small things that wouldn't be necesary to understand the game but I absolutly adore this little details, although some people might not care about them all that much because they mean reading a lot :D (in summary, the single things are not much to read)
This game really hooks me and I always end up playing longer than I intended to. Even when not playing I often think about this game and theorize about good strategies, that I want to test. I guess that's mostly because I'm still learning how to play this game "good" but as said before, this game offers so many different ways leading to the same result and even more different results, that you will be busy with truly understanding this game long enough to make it worth your money. It's just fun in general and that's all what matters when it comes to games, right?
It's all about the fun you have with it and for me this game was and will be a lot of fun, so I can recommend it without any cons (so far, as said before: still learning; but I doubt, that I will meet any big cons, if they would exist I would have already stumbled into them)

The game has a long learning curve - hundreds of hours in, I'm still improving. I absolutely love this about the game, though some may find it overwhelming. Every turn presents choices, and every choice feels important. Mistakes are punished harshly, and can make or break your early game. To play well, you must pay close attention to every detail. You must be aggressive but careful at the same time, and most of all, you must be thorough.
Manual combat is very difficult, and can be frustrating. Checking each unit's initiative and minding the terrain are essential. Even then, things will not go as planned. That being said, I don't see this as a weakness - just a challenge. Keep in mind, most 4x games do not feature anything close to this. And if you don't like it, you can just use auto-combat (which works quite well).
Once you learn the ins and outs, you realize that Endless Legend has one major weakness: Endgame. The problem is with pacing, scaling, AI, and the lack of an effective "limiter".
The pace of the game accelarates as certain empires start to dominate the map, and the numbers get out of control. The victory conditions are reached too quickly, and feel anticlimactic. By the time you reach the final tier of technologies and get the best gear, the game is pretty much over and you don't get to use any of it. This is extremely disappointing after a very long game of building up to that point.
Additionally, the AI does not function well in endgame. They don't upgrade their equipment all the way, and you can crush them easily in every fight. Even on higher difficulty settings, they just pump out lots of weak armies.
Basically, endgame needs a serious rebalancing, and it needs something that slows the game down (especially victory conditions) and limits the exponential growth of empires. Approval rating (the equivalent to happiness in Civ) should be the limiting factor, but it is too easily overcome.
If the devs pulled off a serious endgame overhaul, I can say confidently that Endless Legend would be the greatest 4x game ever made. As it stands today, it's still a great game, but the disappointing endgame is a real buzz-kill.

Influent is sold as a “Language Learning Game” focusing on vocabulary and and pronunciation. I was the lucky winner of the Japanese pack and I’ve played around with it for quite a while, so let’s explore it a little, shall we?
I already had (a very low) background in learning Japanese when I got this game, so my experiences may vary from someone who has never touched the language before.
Believe it or not, Influent has a sort of ‘story’ behind it. It’s not overly… special, but a story is something you don’t necessarily expect in something like a Language Learning software - game or not.
In Influent you take the role of Andrew Cross. He’s spent three years developing a device that would allow people to interact with their surroundings by providing them the item’s names in different languages. However, this device is stolen and sold under the thieves’ branding, and so Andrew’s response to this was to improve on the device and launch a campaign, swearing to learn 300 words in a foreign language to prove how evil those thieves are.
Just how precisely that works, I have no idea. The story makes no sense, hence it gets a low rating, however, the fact that they even thought as far as to give it a bit of a backstory besides “randomly get words in another language” deserves cookie points in my book.
The graphics aren’t out of this world, but I think they’re sufficiently good in their cartoonish way, and fit the quirky story of the game. I actually really like the art and the style of it. It’s simple, it does the job, and, more importantly, it makes it more approachable as you don’t need a super computer to run it.
That said, I don’t feel this is neither a language learning software, nor all it could be. Don’t get me wrong, I do love this game, but it lacks something. Before I get into that, though, let’s get on with the more technical aspects:
You can play this in first or third person. All of the game (so far) happens inside Andrew’s apartment, so it’s a tad limited in that sense, however, there is good depth of detail on the words you can learn; for instance, you can point at the door to get that word in Japanese, but if you point at the door frame, you will actually get “door frame” and not just “door”. You can open things (drawers, closets and cabinets, fridge, etc) and look at the things inside.
Basically, you move around the house and press a button to have the name of the item you’re looking (pointing with the mouse) at appear in the target language. The user interface is already available in various languages, and there are several target language DLCs you can choose from, in my case, since it was Japanese, you got all the necessary information: romaji, kana and kanji (along with pronunciation). You can select which of all this to see, you can see alternate words for the item, you can choose to add it to lists, and as you progress through your lists achievements you will be able to unlock more things: you start with simple words for objects, then you move on to adjectives and the like.
You have various lists, all of 10 items, which you can then test yourself on. When you play this mini-game, you will be given or told a word, and you will have to find the item and press a button again to mark it. Depending on how fast you are, you might even earn stars. Complete enough lists or achieve a certain speed and you will start ticking off achievements in the game. It also has small goals with their corresponding achievements.
Now, here we reach part 1 of what bothers me: This isn’t really so much a Language Learning game as just a tool to aid in Language Learning. There is a difference, as with a language learning programs you can expect to get some basic structure so that you can start speaking with, at the very least, short, broken sentences; Influent, however, only gives you words. There are no connectors, no real actions (even in you have some verbs), and no further information on how to put a sentence together. That’s fine, but it’s what makes it only an aid tool. It’s basically just an interactive flashcard system and a great help to expand on your basic and not so basic everyday vocabulary, but it’s not the only tool you’ll need if you actually want to learn the language.
It can, however, also be used as a starting point to gain some vocabulary before you go into basic sentences.
The second thing that… not so much bothers me, but just disappoints me, is how limited it is. Since everything happens within his house, then that is all you get to learn about. I would really, truly adore to see the game be expanded on (as default, and not as DLCs!) by include the outside world. The idea of being able to take my character out into the world and see the items at a park, or buildings, or houses, enter a shop and see what they sell… it could be so much more, and it feels like the game doesn’t reach its full potential. I feel like they could even include very basic dialogue with NPCs (for instance, talking to a neighbor and saying “Nice weather” or entering a shop, picking an item, and being able to choose between “how much is this” and “I’ll take 5 of this”). So at the end of the day, it feels rather bland.
The game controls aren’t too difficult, but they aren’t overly comfortable either. The replayability is both high and non-existent depending on your level with the target language. it’s high while you’re learning and reinforcing the basics, but once you’re past the basic household items level, you really have nothing else to do with the game other than an occasional revision.
All in all, Influent is a very nice tool to help with your language learning, and I would highly recommend it as that, but I don’t think I would recommend it if you’ve never touched the language before OR are way past beginner level.

Cinders is a story-rich fantasy visual novel developed and published by MoaCube. A horrible stepmother and two unlikeable stepsisters...sounds familiar as it should because Cinders pays homage to "Cinderella", one of the most popular and beloved fairytales of all time. Cinders is a lovely young woman living out a quite mundane existence with her overbearing stepmother and two rude and constantly bickering stepsisters often wondering if life has something "more" in store for her. Tiring of the status quo of her current situation, she soon comes to a decision to make some changes...drastic changes that could possibly affect her entire life from this point forward forever. How will this fairytale end? This intriguing visual novel cleverly gives you the choices to shape Cinders personality while also determining how the story unfolds.
Visually, this title is beautiful with a palette of bright colors and fantastic lighting that also compliments the gorgeous artstyle which I'm happy to report is not anime inspired considering that most of the visual novels that I've read on Steam to date have been. The characters themselves are wonderfully animated in that their eyes and mouths move during dialogue and the facial expressions vary accordingly to mood. Something else of note about Cinders that I've yet to see in any other V.N. is the animation applied to static objects in the backgrounds. For example, if a scene is taking place in a house, the fireplace is ablaze with flame while outside the window you can see trees and shrubery fluttering in the wind. Likewise in town, you'll notice birds flying about overhead as the lanterns on lamposts are gently swaying to and fro from a light breeze flowing through. This use of animation on normally still objects like this really serves well to immerse you within the story so my compliments to the developers for applying this terrific mechanic to the V.N.. The U.I. in this title is also quite impressive whether you're selecting choices in game or options in the menu screens. The sound effect, colors and animation used on something as simple as the selection process just looks and sounds excellent with beautiful sparkle effects attached. Speaking of sound, the original soundtrack by Rob Westwood is absolutely fantastic in this visual novel. I have no doubt that you will find many of these tracks quite memorable like myself. In short, the outstanding graphical and aural presentation of Cinders very much compliments the wonderful narrative of this great visual novel.
As "Cinderella" is one of my favorite fairytales I was extremely anxious to experience this unique take on the classic title. I very much enjoyed my read of Cinders from start to finish with it's compelling storyline and choices that actually matter and shape the narrative as you progress. I found myself connecting and really caring about what happens to her so it's always great when a V.N. can make you feel that way for a main character. I also thoroughly enjoyed many of the conversations between Cinders, her sisters and a few of the other N.P.C.'s in this title as they had some really thought provoking and hilarious dialogue. With over 120 decision points and multiple endings this visual novel has very high replayability. There are also a number of in-game trophies to be obtained but you'll have to discover for yourself how to unlock them as that is a total secret which is a nice additional feature. Option-wise, there are the basics for music, sound and text speed. There are a limited number of Steam Achievements to hunt down and Steam Trading Cards to collect as well. In conclusion, this V.N. takes a story that you've heard before and probably love but manages to add a unique and intriguing interactive spin to the narrative so Cinders is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to visual novel, fairytale and fantasy fans.

It's impressive in some intriguing and vastly immersive ways, but perhaps lacks content to justify it being a stand-alone title. Other reviewers mock this a bit as being a tech demo - which isn't entirely unjustified. I think I could see this being part of the upcoming Phantom Pain instead. For it's current price tag you get some solid yet a bit short-lived stealth action. The motion capturing looks fantasic and Kiefer Sutherland sounds great even though he hasn't got that many events to comment. This and Phantom Pain may be the most adult - or "wise" - and thoughtful Metal Gear games I'll be playing. All of Kojima's games seem to have a certain overarching theme, in Ground Zeroes he apparently wanted to criticize the U.S. and imprisonment facilities such as Guantanamo Bay. You infiltrate some U.S. outpost in Cuba during the Cold War era rescuing certain VIPs and, if you want to, random PoWs. The main mission can be completed very quickly or within some hours depending on what style of play you prefer. There are some collectiables but really aren't that many, and their content can easily be looked up on YouTube or the sorts. Some of them one may already know from Peace Walker as they seem to have been copied from that game (audio tapes). Your actions are rated when the mission debriefs, rewarding you with additional gear or collectiables if you do well enough. There are side-missions and time trial challenges (with online leaderboards) too but while they may happen at different times of day and weather it's always the very same base you are infiltrating, making efforts to give different feelings and interestingly changing objectives and obstacles to overcome but ultimatively recycling things you've already seen in one way or another. So, if one wants to see if he can run Kojima's Fox Engine on his machine (Ground Zeroes runs very smoothly on mine throttling down some specific graphic opions and even keyboard controls feel as if a good amount of thoughts went into them), get a taste for the upcoming Phantom Pain and loves going for any kind of collectiables or hunting for highscores this is a good buy. If someone is seeking a full-length stealth action title better look elsewhere or go for Phantom Pain right away once that is released.

Sweet, unusual and heartwarming. I will try to keep this completely spoiler-free, which means I will probably not talk much about it story-wise.
- Story and Characters
You must have noticed that the heroine of this VN isn't your mainstream moe heroine, she's way more cute and interesting. I won't say anything else about her, because I found out that actually getting to know her through the story is what made this such a great experience for me.
The story is short and the cast small, but I loved every part of it, even the slightly strange ones.
You have two very likeable characters as your support casting, who are not just filling up the space, but instead have their own things going on. Their personalities are also built very clear, so that the way they act and interact with you and the other characters feels very natural.
Also, don't forget to check the Extras after you finish. There are a few extra scenes there.
- VN
Now, for the technical stuff.
This is a linear visual novel with a single route. Which means it's more like a digital book than a game itself, and to be fair most visual novels are exactly that. I would say the greatest selling point of this kind of product is that you get an experience similar to those you would get from reading books, comics or manga, but with the extras allowed by the medium used to convey the story.
A story can be conveyed in many different forms. A linear visual novel allows you to attach shifting scenes to every piece of dialogue, with characters in different poses over backgrounds. You are also allowed to place pictures drawn for special events, and in this game's case, even small cutscenes for every chapter title. And finally, wrap it all up with music fitting for every moment. This is an experience that is most close to reading a novel, with many additionals you'd only get from it being digital.
If this is what you came here looking for, then Love at First Sight is indeed what you want.
- Art

A surprisingly great racing game featuring Sega characters.
When I first saw this game, I thought it was Sega's poor attempt at a Mario Kart rip-off. Boy, was I wrong! This game is a blast to play! The visuals are nice, the soundtrack is fantastic, the selection of characters is good, and the tracks are well designed.
This game debuted sometime in 2010. Even so, with its crisp HD textures, soft particles, motion blur, shadows, and good models, the visuals hold up even to today's standards. No complaints here.
The sound effects are nothing special, but get the job done. Where the audio really shines is in its soundtracks. Man, they are fantastic! Most (if not all) of them are ripped or remixed from past Sega games, but they all sound great. I like listening to the Billy Hatcher soundtracks, and I especially love the Samba de Amigo tracks!
There's the Sonic staples: Sonic, Amy, Knuckles, Tails, Eggman, and Big, but there's also Billy Hatcher, Aiai, Jet Set Radio people, and more. Sega did an outstanding job at really offering a diversified ensemble of characters to choose from.
Just like with the characters, the race tracks include vistas from Sonic, Billy Hatcher, Jet Set Radio, Samba de Amigo, and more. Being a big Billy Hatcher fan myself, I was overjoyed to be able to race through Dino Mountain and Blizzard Castle (I'm still waiting for a Billy Hatcher sequel, Sega!).
The kart selection, compared to games like Mario Kart, is underwhelming. You do not win or unlock new vehicles (though you do win/unlock an in-game currency and new stages); you have only one vehicle per character. This is not bad, as each character has a vehicle that handles differently from the last, but it would still have been nice to select from different kart variants. Oh well.
For a game that debuted so many years ago, it is surprising just how poorly optimized it is. At times I encountered random stuttering and frame drops. It plays almost as smooth as butter on low settings, but hiccups here and there on anything else.
This is an outstanding racing game that offers crisp visuals, a fantastic sound track, a great selection of characters and tracks, and includes wonderful gamepad support and smooth controls. There is an overwhelming amount of replay value here, what with grand prix, missions, multiplayer, single races, challenges, and more. Perhaps the only negative is the lack of wireless multiplayer (it's local only). It would have been a blast to race with others around the world! Final thoughts: this is a great racing game.
