Endless Legend has the feel of old-school turn-based strategy games, with modern graphics, a great soundtrack and a great variety of factions to play with, most of which *actually* require different playstyles. I've played through all the expansions and I've enjoyed it immensely. It's definately worth your money if you're a fan of turn-based strategy games like Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic. If it's on sale, you should absolutely pick it up!
Choosing a faction in Endless Legend is more than just choosing bonus stats, there are actual gameplay differences between them. There's a faction that only can build one city, but spread its influence through neutral civilizations, a faction that don't use food, but buy everything with gold, and a faction that can close out others from the marketplace but who can't declare any wars. I found the gameplay to be varied enough to warrant several playthroughs, atleast once with each of the factions.
It does feel like the factions are focused on a specific win condition, so if you play with just one then the game can feel imbalanced. Play with several win conditions and the game balance evens out significantly.
The ambience in Endless Legend is amazing as well! The soundtrack blows other games in this genre out of the water, Civ doesn't hold a candle to it. Graphically, I also think Endless Legend outclasses Civ. The game looks great and feels alive and thriving. There's a lot of information on the screen to digest, which takes a while to get used to, but most of it feels pretty relevant.
You've got incredible replayability with the customability of gameplay. You can change almost everything concerning the world, you can create your own factions, you can change difficulty and do tons of tweaks in timed turns, timed battles and number of opponents. Actual customability that changed how I experienced the game.
When it comes to DLC and expansions, the price quickly racks up fast as each individual piece has a pretty steep price. If you feel like buying one, I'd recommend the Guardians, Shadows and Shifters, in that order. They all ad something significant, but since I don't like spies, Shadows comes in second with its addition of spying. Shifters is priceworthy on sale, I'd say 33% off or more.
It's not without flaws, though. There are situations where your quest victory conditions can become unachievable, like when you need to talk to a neutral town and it's been conquered. There's not much to do in these situations, except starting a new game, which can definately become annoying. Especially so if you come upon this problem more than once.
The game also tends to slow down over time. However, for me it never got bad enough to actually warrant a restart. For me, it just slowed down enough to be noticable. Not a deal breaker, just something to keep in mind.
Finally, and this is purely personal preference, the manual fighting can become an exercise in frustration. You don't have full control of your units, so they can sometimes freak out and run around completely randomly, causing you to miss out on their turn as well as miss out on the turn of the unit who's space the first unit randomly walked to. I'm sure there's a lot of possible strategy and skill involved, but after a while I just started to do auto battles, just like I did in every Total War game to date. The actual battles, to me, become very repetetive very fast, so being able to reliably auto battle was nice.
Endless Legend is a good turn-based strategy game. It's got some issues, but seriously solid gameplay, great replayability, nice graphics and a soundtrack you could listen to even outside of the game. It suffers from lots of DLC as well as expensive DLC, even though they all add to the game significantly.
If you're looking for a turn-based game like Civ, why not pick up Endless Legend? I think it's more than worth its price. If it's on sale, definately pick it up!

The factions are played extremely differently with their different traits that hard to find in other games. The Necrophage is driven for combat and thrive on blood spilled, the Broken lord is supreme lord of dust that can only grow with its power; each faction represents different mechanic of the game and make them fun to play. This make EL stands apart from its brethen that rely on minor trait different to different factions.
Unit customization is better than most games (the only game that allow you to customize more than this in 4X is probably Galactic civilization series). You can equip weapon, shield, armor, helmet, greaves, and accessories on each unit. Each piece grants your unit with ability. With better tech, more options can be explored and diverse you design to counter specific tactic in late game.
Each DLC gives you more mechanic to explore - Guardian gives you chance to create Golem that roam the battlefield, Shadow open espoinage gameplay, Shifter plays with winter mechanic and add pearl to your resource list. I dare say that EL's DLCs are worth the money because of this reason.
But be warned that the learning can be steeped in certain factions and require understanding of the game's multiple mechanics in order to fully enjoy them.

I came away from this game irritated and insulted. It's preachy, pretentious, and worst of all, it's bad at it. The art is gorgeous, and the level of polish makes this game a pleasure to look at, but the writing is absolutely awful:
Every character speaks with the same tone, style and vocabularly--a flat, boring style that is NOT fun to read.
What's worse, though, is that the majority of the characters spend the entire game spewing faux-philosophical thoughts, narrating their own motivations and introspection, and reminding each other that everyone should have compassion because everyone else has problems too.
is that the writer treats the player like an idiot, and spells out everything--and I do mean
--over and over again. There were at least 10 different times that the game reminded me that the stepmother has had it rough and deserves a little credit. There is not a single thing that the game lets you figure out for yourself, or at the very least, muse over for a bit before the game reveals it to you. The game actually starts by telling you that the stepmother and stepsisters aren't all that bad and that you need to have compassion for them--something that the player should have been able to figure out for him- or her-self.
As a huge fan of visual novels, I bought this game with the intention of playing it through multiple times to explore all the possible endings--but after suffering through it once, I'm never going to touch it again. Don't waste your money.

An excellent Third Person, Hack-And-Slash RPG that excels in every aspect but fall short on the gameplay and content. I bought this game solely for the graphics and I was not dissapointed. The were great together with the sound effects, voice acting, animation, story and plot. They really manage to capture the pinnacle of the great Roman empire which enthralls the player.
The gameplay however gets really repetitive with hacking and slashing with some first person shooting action occasionally, till the end. Generally the gameplay is simply a series of quick time events. There are no skills to learn or other weapons to wield. The upgrades available simply gives you addtional health, focus or more execution moves (solely for eye candy and does not affect gameplay).
Interacting with objects in-game can be frustrating because most of the time I am taunting them rather than interacting as indicated in the screen. I was standing in front the gate and the screen prompts for me to knock them down by right clicking mouse button but instead I am just making silly gestures.
The game does not allows you to explore to collect the collectibles because most of the time, taking the wrong step or too close to the intended area takes you to the next chapter in the story. You have no way to collect them other than replaying the entire Act.
So if you are into a game that offers good story and graphics, then you are in for a treat. Apart from that, Ryse is still a decent hack-and-slash game and you will have a blast playing with a friend.

+Choice between Light Side and Dark Side with every decision made within the story.

+Non-linear story; both in terms of moral choices and the effects of some side missions.
+Some cool mini-games, from Swoop racing to Pazaak (card game).
+Endless REPLAY VALUE.
CONS:
-6th gen (PS2 era) graphics will annoy graphics snobs.
-No multiplayer.
-No Steam Achievements (yet).

A wonderful take on the 4X genre. Though victory can be achieved many ways, it's always a race against time. A limited-turn game, it doesn't end arbitrarily like Civ 5. The planet is dying. I was a little shocked and uncomfortable at first with the fact that "Winter is Coming," but it helps keep the late game fresh. Your empire could figurativley be bleeding out by the end, but as long as your enemies are doing worse, victory will be yours.
I also want to take a moment to appreciate Privateers. You can hire an army of mercenaries to wreck opponents, but the allegiance of these mercenaries stays hidden, and you don't have to declare war. It works great, very realistic, and is another way to fight dirty.
I'll keep the rest of the review brief:
-Cold war: border skirmishes with other civs, without having to formally declare war
-More real-feeling, nuanced diplomacy than Civ 5
-Lots of ways to win
-Every faction is super unique-feeling
-You can make your custom factions
-Turn-based, tactical hex-grid combat resolutions

I've played many games and bought many games over the past few years but none of them have really 'clicked' for me. I'd buy them and then play them for a few hours and probably never touch them again.
This was the case with Endless Legend when I bought it shortly after it first came out. I played half the tutorial and didn't touch it again. Jump to 2016 and I thought - "You know what? I feel like getting into that Endless Legend game I've had for a while now." and oh boy am I glad I gave it another shot. I'm enjoying it a lot more than CIV 5.
The key features I like about it are as follows:

Fairly simple, very aesthetically pleasing game that's fun with friends.
This game revolves around insulting your partner, who has crossed you in some way or another. You must combine words and phrases to hit your opponent's weak spots. Sipping your tea also gives you a spark of inspiration for new words.
The actual gameplay, is, again, very simplistic in nature. It really is just a game of luck most of the time, since most of the huge point combos come from insulting your opponents specific weak spots with certain phrases. If you don't get lucky enough to get one of those key phrases: Tough luck buddy, you're out.
Forming actual insults won't give you more points in this game, as stringing random bits of garbage together is more fruitful. This can be frustrating for long term gameplay, as the only true strategy revolves around knowing your opponents weakness, and praying you get the correct phrases you need to win.
Overall I'd say this game is worth the price, and is good for a few short laughs and giggles, but can get frustrating and boring quickly.

An absolute must-buy for any fantasy (or even sci-fi) lovers out there. If you enjoy a beautiful world with a rich story then buy this game.

It has a scifi/fantasy theme. I think it is vastly better than Civ5 if you buy all of the expansions.
I will address the biggest complaints I see most people talking about
The UI can be a bit strange to new players but the things that seem clunky happen for a reason for the most part, such as the units being put in a garrison instead of outside a city. Units stack, so it's pretty much pointless to have units outside of a garrison unless they are in a group together. Garrisons also give units passive xp.
As for the game being "boring" and having nothing to do, I really don't get people who say that.
A core part of the gameplay is about exploring and questing. I feel like a lot of people are playing this like Civ5 and ignoring minor factions, quests, and ruins. Of course if you ignore a huge part of the game you won't find much to do. If you are spam clicking end turn up till turn 50 waiting for buildings to finish you aren't properly experiencing what the game has to offer.
You need to be exploring to find quests and missions from ruins and minor factions. Exploring is also important for finding resources. A huge part of this game is finding strategic and luxury resources and settling regions in a correct location. A think a lot of people are confused about how founding cities work. You are not just founding a city, you are actually taking control of an entire region with your city. Your cities borders will never expand. The way you make your cities larger is by building extractors within the region, and building borough streets to expand what your city can exploit.
Now for the combat
A lot of people hate the combat system, and I can understand why to some extent. I feel like most people hate it because it is slow though, which can easily be fixed by changing the combat speed option. I think the planning and attack system is actually pretty good personally, but I think that is mostly a subjective thing. Doing auto combat pretty much functions like stack attacking in Civ4 but much better so I don’t see a huge problem with that either.
A big downside is that you pretty much need all of the expansions to properly experience the game as a mentioned above. Do not just buy the base game. That is like buying base Civ5 and expecting it to be the same game people talk about and love when they play Gods & Kings and Brave new World. If you play only in MP all DLC including expansions are shared if one person has them.
Overall I think this game is far more unique, fun, and interesting than Civ5. It looks way better and has incredibly good music as well. I feel like it is entirely worth 60 dollars for the collection edition, which is also the only version you should buy due to what I mentioned above, unless you only want to play MP with someone who owns everything.

This was easily one of the best games I've ever played. I've enjoyed this game so much that I've finished it roughly in 3 days, spending each evening playing this title.
It is fairly short (around 8 hours, but I imagine you could finish it in 5-7 hours) but has many incredible things to offer.
In short, if you love great story, great, original characters, wonderful and long cinematics, cool soundtrack and amazing visuals - this is your game! If you are a fan of history, even more so!
The combat system is in some aspects less creative and elaborate then in some games, but it is definitely not different from Batman games and can be very fun and rewarding if you let some flaws go past you. I did so myself and I've been having tons and tons of fun on the combat alone.
In terms of art design, it is one of the best, if not the best game I've ever encountered. I've spent some time on looking in awe on all the incredible details, textures, lights, facial expressions, enviroment atmosphere. The character design was again, one of the best out there. I really felt connection with Marius, who was portraied as a ordinary man driven by extraordinary lust for vengence. And all the other characters - loved their faces, voices - energy in them! In most games, you can feel that the characters has been programmed, but not here.. Here you feel that everything is alive. That your character breathes, feels pain, grief.. I loved that feeling that was kept during the entire game.
So all in all, this is in my opinion highly underrated game  (61 on metascore? That's really really sad... I can't understand how Tomb Raider can have higher score. This game is worth so much more!) that definitely deserves your attention and money. Believe me, it is worth it!

Overall, if you are just looking for a game to play for a little while while enjoying a good fiction story set in Ancient Rome, then I would completely recommend this game; however, if you are looking for a game to sit down and and play for a long while then I would recommend either waiting for this game to go on sale (what I did) or look for a game with more content. But in conclusion, I had a blast playing this game and with the amazing graphics, great story, fun combat, and cool leveling system, I would recommend this game to almsot anyone that like 3rd person action/story telling games.

I enjoyed this game and got a number of hours out of it between multiple ending playthroughs (free flow and some with a guide to finish a few missed options).  My one caveat is that you should snag this game on sale or as part of a bundle, as I'm not sure most people will find it justifies its full price.
First, you should know that this game is a lot of reading relative to the interaction time.  As the game warns you about in the begining, this is more like a book where you can make some choices to change the ending, rather than a typical point-n-click story where you are making choices constantly.  Luckily, it has a very nice "fast forward" option for skipping dialgoue you've already seen on playthroughs, which is something that is lacking in many similar games and is amazingly wonderful if you're hunting down other endings.
I like the concept of this game; building my own Cinders' personality and making my own choices and creating my own ending.  I also liked the take on the stepsisters as more than just evil sadists, and actually was fond of Sophie in particular.  It is a nice retake on a fairy tale in a less black & white perspective, especially since you can deivate significantly from the classic tale by making Cinders "bad" or reject the prince, etc.
The art is also beautiful, although I wish there had been more than a few backdrops, and a few characters whose faces and arms where animated.  I do like that there was some movement and facial expression over static art, just to keep things interesting through a lot of dialgoues boxes with otherwise identical visuals.  But like anything good, I want more than just a small taste of it!
The dialgue can be repetative, cliche, and predictible, but I didn't think it was totally awful (there was even a joke about the Captain's belts that genuinely made me laugh out loud).  Could it have been better?  Sure.  Did I find it turn me off from the game?  Nah.  Another review also complained that the writing was too blatant and the foreshadowing too obvious, but I find this preferrable in these types of games, otherwise it is too challenging and uninuititive to guide the story in the direction you desire.  While the choices are not always clear how they will affect the ending and you don't always get exactly what you were aiming for in this game, some opacity makes the gameplay more interesting.  There is a fine balance and I think the game gets it decently well.
The one change I would have made to this game would have been to add more frequent interactions with more choices.  They could have been additional conversation selections that were meaningless as far as the outcomes were concerned but valuable in terms of increasing replayability and creating more dynamic character personalities.  I think adding a number of trivial dialogue choices in between the "important" decisions would make players feel more engaged, break up the large amounts of reading, and make Cinders feel more realistic to each individual's vision of her.  There are already a huge amount of possibilities in terms of the endings, so I'm hesitant to wishlist for anything that increases those, but it would have been nice to have more options to influence the fates of more people in more ways.
Overall, I quite liked this game and am glad I bought and played it.  It might not be the most amazing game ever but it was some hours of enjoyment, which is all I wanted or expected out of it.

I got the spanish pack with the Humble Bundle.
I've gotten to about 170 words so far. Pretty enjoyable pace. You have the option of hearing a word as well as reading, or you can disanle one and use the other.
The real game side of things is the ten question quiz, which has you going around via walking or flying a space ship toy and finding the objects it names (or another word attached to said object).
Having never taken a Spanish class the thing I found so surprising is that plenty of words are so similar!
The word for newspaper sounds like periodical. The word for spatula is espatula. The word for skateboard is skateboard, the word for CD is CD. The word for poster is poster.  THE WORD FOR SANDWICH IS SANDWICH! It really blew my mind.
A window sounds like a vent (ventana). So many words that are easy to pick up because they sound similar. It's great!
If I had to make a complaint, it's that not all the audio recordings are very clear (MOST OF THEM ARE) so there's a few words where is feels like they started recording a quarter second too late: a V will sound like a B,  an R will sound like a D.
Some suffer noise pollution: ruedecilla (stove knob) for example has an odd beep in front of it.
But on the whole, the game is worth getting. It's a pretty entertaining approach and I think I'll spend some more time on it.

Main quests, side quests, research quests and more - competition, that can be felt, even though you might not have even encountered your enemy on the map yet, and have searched your region only.
And the design, man, the design - there are so many beautiful things I would want to say to people who designed the universe of this game. Even if you do not like such strategies, The game is worth to play just for the story. Every element in the game has it's own story.
Because they are the children of Auriga.
And the tale of Auriga is the Legend that is Endless.

Endless Legends is a marvelous piece of a strategy game. It is beautiful, by its graphics and by its sound and music. When I first launched the game, I had to stop and listen the theme it was equipped with as it had a very beautiful tone.

The in-game graphics are very pretty. Animations look smooth for the most part, though some units look a bit sluggish and some attack animations aren’t that impressive though I guess it’s better that the animations aren’t that long in a turn based combat.
The gameplay is very similar to Civilization-series. In my eyes, this is a fantasy-civilization and I think it was intended that way. So, if you’re familiar with that game series, jumping into this won’t be a trouble.
What sets this apart from CiV-series in my eyes, is that each race has its own story quest to follow. You also get quests from small villages and caves from time to time, if you want to have their support either in the form of units or treasure. I have to admit though, I don’t recall if CiV had a similar system.
The game also has seasons. Well, just two, summer and winter. Summer time, everything is nice and pretty, don’t have to work so much… But then, Winter came. Your units move slower on the map, you’ll gain less resources from resource tiles and food consumption in your cities go up, you’ll research slows down as well... You have to manage resources differently on winters. As the game progresses, the winters get longer and longer. This is an interesting system, though at times annoying since the winter just lasts on and on and on…
I have noticed that the game pushes you to focus on army upgrades quite fast. In some of my games that if I don’t upgrade my army fast enough, the enemy AI or players will just crush my armies very easily. This might frustrate some of the players who prefer to be more diplomatic in these types of games. This applies to the roaming random AI enemies as well.
If you’re not familiar to these types of games, prepare to do some reading in-game. While the system is fairly simple and you don’t have to rush anywhere as this game is turn based, it takes time to read and understand some things. So I recommend to play a few single player campaigns before joining multiplayer, so your fellow players won’t have to wait so long for you to do your turn.
So far this game has been a very pleasant time for me. I heartily recommend this for everyone who has an interest in strategy games!

You can level them up in there own skill trees. And lastly, your units (and heros) have a tab where you can customize their armor and weapons to do different things. All in all, this game is awesome and I highly recomend it.

And, of course, everyone's all-time favourite:

Should you presently find yourself soiling your pants with laughter, then I would advise you buy this game AT ONCE. What starts out pulling at the heartstrings of you childhood, ends in nothing but disappointment and disgust. The first hour or so of Evoland brings such hope and expectations only for them to be completely destroyed. It's worth it if its on heavy sale, but game has a total playtime of roughly 4 hours (full completion) so not worth paying full price.
The concept is that as you progress through the game, you progress through the history of video game evolution, so I guess given the quality of most games today compared to the 'old' days, Evoland holds true to it's aim. It goes from dragging you in with aspects of the early FF and Breath of Fire like games, and ends simply mocking FF7 and FF8 from everything from names to events. Overall it gives the feeling that the developers were heavily interested in the game at start and by about the halfway point they just wanted to be done with it all.

It's...not a good game. It would have worked better as a flash animation or Youtube video. It has some laughs. The transitions between the eras look good. The nostalgia factor is there. But its major failing is that it's the sort of game that thinks simply mentioning a trope and winking is enough.
The hero's a Cloud/Link mash-up named Clink. He meets a healer girl named Kaerith (spoiler). The bad guy's named...Zephyroth? Something like that. You start off as a kid. You get a huge sword. You meet a guy with an airship named Sid. You end up in a village where everyone's afraid of some nearby environment that's begun to show signs of corruption. And the list goes on and on. It never does anything interesting with these tropes, or comments on the bygone era beyond, "That was silly, eh?"
Evoland features basic versions of turn-based, adventure and ARPG combat and lasts longer than it should. In the end, it feels like an exercise more than anything. As in, if it wasn't about 3 hours long, I would have quit an hour into it.
Know what game's actually successful at what Evoland tries? Half-Minute Hero. That game actually manages to be a nostalgia trip and a very interesting and enjoyable new experience at the same time. Evoland's more of a slog.

I'm not quite sure what most people were expecting going in to this from some of the reviews that I have seen. This is not a AAA title by any means, and doesn't try to be, so please do not expect that. No it doesn't have the best graphics... But the game delivers on every level that it promises:
Does it have constant bear puns? - Yes
Does the story represent bears taking over the world and a lumberjack saving humanity? - Yes
Do you get to punch bears? - Yes
Does it pay tribute to Streets of Rage, Double Dragon and Final fight? - Yes
Would this be enjoyed more by people with/or that admire beards? - Quite possibly
Yes it does get very repetitive, but for anyone who enjoyed these types of games in the 80s and early 90s this was a gameplay staple. It may lack the special police car attack from Streets of Rage, but it improves upon the somewhat one note (but favored classic) Double Dragon in terms of controls, gameplay and in my opinion story as well. The game also features an interesting health mechanic of auto healing. Being a fan of the games I have mentioned previously I did not approve of this choice initially. However I came to welcome this feature due to the constant barrage of enemies, and with that the rapidly expanding enemy health bars. The XP gain and upgrade system is also a nice little addition and adds more flavor, but does not seem critical.
In closing, I do really enjoy this game. The otherwise mind numbing, repetitive beat em up genre offers just enough bear puns and beard fanaticism to entertain. Please also keep in mind that back in the day for a game like Final Fight you would expect to pay $50+ to own it on Super Nintendo... I was able to purchase this as part of a Humble Bundle for $1, and in all fairness I believe it is worth more.
For what it is (and for what it wants to be) I give it 3 beards and a soul patch out of 5.

Cinders is one of my all-time favorites.  I've played it a few times over the past couple years - whenever I feel like being whisked away into this magical, yet very realistic, fairytale world, and it never fails to make me smile.  It's always the first game I recommend to my friends that like choice driven VNs or fairytales.
The scenes are beautifully drawn in a sort of pastel style with vibrant colors to help set the mood.  The music is good too and very immersive.  Most importantly, the story is well-written.  The language can be a bit over-wrought at times, but that just adds to the old fairytale/literature feel.
There are quite a few ways the story can go, depending on your choices, and it's not always clear which choice made the diffference, but that's part of the charm for me.  It's not necessarily about where you wind up (it's definitely possible to get an unsatisfying ending), but about the journey of how you got there.  Each time I play, I feel like I learn something new about the characters and the world.  There were actually whole storylines I didn't even know existed on my first playthrough that made it pretty fun to play again.  Most of the characters are pretty intricate and more than willing to give you their soliliquy on life if you prod them the right way... or offer you a brutally scathing retort if you don't.  A few of them are really funny too!  Best of all, Cinders, herself, is a pretty relatable and empowering character with her own quirks and insecurities.  I could definitely see myself in her shoes (or glass slippers) if I lived in her fairy world.  Thanks to this game, I can imagine that I really am for a little while.

The characters have great depth (depending on how you play the game), and there's several differnet paths and combinations you can take that maximize the playthrough value.
One aspect that might be frustrating is that the game does not make obvious what the different personality choices are coded as. For example, is the choice you picked "good," "bad," or "naive?" The lack of labelling makes the game a bit more challenging to get all the endings. If you are looking for a quick playthrough for 100% completion, you may have to go online if you don't want to do it through trial and error.
Overall amazing game with great relationships, story, and visuals. Highly recommended for those who like VNs or those who are looking to get into the VNs.

Despite being built upon the old fairy tale, Cinders really went past the original in terms of storyline and setting (won't spoil it), I feel- while still being very faithful to the setting of the original, I feel. Or rather, Cinders established a believeable universe in which Cinderella would have occured, explained and went into detail on the otherwise normally supporting characters (the stepmother and sisters, the prince, the fairy godmother(s)), making them all not just believeable but very real and alive in the story itself. For such a short average playthrough (guesstimating 2~ hrs on the first run) everything really just fit in place so well.
The characters, as mentioned already, are exceptional. Even the typical villain (the stepmother and sisters) has complex motivations or reasoning- not to say they are morally ambiguous as I feel is a common flaw in such themes, but that their origins, their personal feelings whether right or wrong, their ambitions, etc... drive them. They're humans and they're inherently flawed, I guess. It seems like you really can reason, if you pursue it far enough, with any of them, really- even befriend them and mend the relationship. And the controlling family dynamic and how it affected each sister I also found a really unique take on such an environment. I found myself not really hating anyone in particular,
All in all:
+Excellent storyline and believeable, relateable characters. Just really well put together overall
+Great art, personally enjoy the stylistic approach taken as well if that counts for anything
+Some decent form of replayablity, I feel- I think I'll be coming back to this one

I could make several jokes about this game's name, but I won't. I will start this review off instead by getting to the heart of the matter. If you want my opinion in a single sentence, here it is: Only If is one of the worst games I have ever played. If you want it in multiple sentences, by all means, keep reading.
Let me clarify that I have played some great walking simulator games. I like the genre when it is done well. It can be difficult to find good ones, but when they shine, they really shine. There are some people who argue that they aren't video games. I don't agree, yet that's neither here nor there. The point is that I am not biased against Only If because of its genre. It is also called a horror game, but the only thing horrifying about it is how bad it is, so I'm not counting that. I guess the "tense atmosphere" is why it's labeled as a horror game, but in my eyes, it doesn't qualify as horror.
So let's start with some basics. The graphics are okay. A couple of scenes look pretty. I don't know how many of the models are stock assets or not. This game is unfortunately made in Unity, but I'll discuss that in a second. Whether they are stock or not, the game is fine from a visual perspective. The music is nothing special. There isn't always music, but when it pops up, it tends to be quickly forgotten.
I would usually talk about characterization and plot next. However, that is going to be a lengthy topic, and I am aware some people would rather know about the gameplay first. Let me get the technical bits out of the way to show that this is terrible for many different reasons. This part right here is damning enough, let alone when I get to the story.
Controls can't be rebound. I normally don't care about this, but having to use WASD to move was troublesome. I usually use the arrow keys, and while WASD works fine most of the time, this game has all the necessary keys tucked into a small space. This isn't too bad when you're just walking around. You can stop, press E on its own, jump with Space if needed, and run along while holding Shift. But there are parts in Only If that are timed. There are parts that are platforming-based. These controls don't work well in those situations.
Yes, you heard me right. They used Unity and had the gall to put in timed events and platforming sections. The times Unity has worked well for physics are few and far between. This only happens when a developer knows what they are doing with the system. This developer did not. The random jumping segment includes a gun. The controls there are slippery and unresponsive. I fell to my death many times thanks to these atrocious controls. Add in the lack of knowing where to go and you have an extremely frustrating area. As for the timed sections, pray you don't get caught on an edge or you'll be shot down by invisible guns.
I also got stuck on a gear once and had to reset the game. That was great. By the way, to get back to a part in the game, you have to type in the name of the location you were in from the main menu. It's a weird and unwieldy system. Save files would have been vastly preferred. That, and the ability to flipping pause, since that evidently wasn't seen as important.
There's also a really bad bug with achievements. If you tab out of the game with Steam overlay, then you have to go through a tedious process of verifying the game's files every time you load it up again. Otherwise, you don't get achievements at all. The ten achievements have a couple of obscure ones with others being straightforward. Nothing special there. No trading cards, there's nothing to buy in the game itself.
Speaking of obscure, finding out where to go half the time is bloody ridiculous. There is a difference between avoiding hand-holding and being obnoxiously secretive. This falls in the latter. The rules of the game change on a dime. I have particularly "fond" memories of the part where I had to mash E like mad to survive in a burning landscape. It required me to almost break my keyboard, and the way to get through the area changed in the middle of it. Ah, good times.
But enough about the actual gameplay, let's get to the story parts! First off, the voice acting is gold. The one bit of enjoyment I got out of Only If is from how cheesy the characters sound. You're mostly only going to hear two of them, but "the guy on the radio" really hams it up, and it is a riot. The character you play as is also hilariously over-the-top on several occasions. Basically, it's so bad that it's good.
Note that I was praising the goofiness of the voice acting. The dialogue, on the other hand, is garbage. If you actually listen to what the characters say, it's absurd. About half the script can be summarized as the two main characters insulting each other's sexual preferences and genitals. Rivoting. If I wanted that, I could've gone to a high school.
That's if you can even hear the characters. As funny as the voice acting is, oftentimes the words are difficult to make out. Subtitles are desperately needed here, and Only If doesn't have them. Instead, the developer posted a game script in the "Guides" section on Steam. I don't know what stopped the developer from putting subtitles instead of posting the script, but imagine if you went to watch a movie, couldn't hear anything in it, and had to go look up what was being said later. That would be absurd. This game is not excused from this flaw because the developer put up the script. To add insult to injury, it has grammar and spelling errors all over the place, so it's a pain to read anyway.
Then we get to the story. Walking simulators need a strong story to remain interesting. Only If decides to take this "hangover/drugs" concept and make it some "deep" tale about the character you play as coming to moving realizations about himself. Or something. Frankly, I am sick of coming across these "deep" games that feel they can get away with throwing any weird concept at you because the main character is dreaming/high/almost dead. When a game is properly executed and a lot of care and thought is given to it, then it works wonders. But it is so easy to slap together a bunch of randomness and pawn it off as a life lesson. A life lesson I took from it is "don't do this." I greatly dislike the story. It's too heavy-handed and ambiguous at the same time, and in the end, it all feels pointless.
With that in mind, consider this. In the "Guides" section, the developer put a guide about what the story meant. Let that sink in. The DEVELOPER felt they had to EXPLAIN the story in an ENTIRELY. SEPARATE. GUIDE. You know what that sounds like? "Oh sorry you weren't smart enough to figure out my really meaningful and artistic game, here's a dumbed-down explanation for you!" You know what else? I read that guide after I finished, curious as to what might be said in it. I was left in disbelief at how pretentious it is. It is so self-righteous and condescending that it made me hate this game even more than I already did. Maybe it wasn't meant to come off that way, but again, that's how it sounded to me, and thus that is the message I got from it. To top it off, this guide is also loaded with spelling and grammar errors. I guess the guide's too deep for a proofreader to make sense of.
"But Only If is free! You can't be too mad at it!" Well congrats to it for being a free game, because that is one of the few saving graces it has. I still feel like I got robbed. I sunk over seven hours into this game. A good 3/4ths of them were related to segments being poorly programmed. It probably could've been beaten in less than an hour if it didn't handle so badly. I went through this entire game in hopes of finding something redeeming, and instead, it got worse and worse.
Only If angers me as both a gamer and a writer. Its gameplay is infuriating and its story is appalling. Don't waste your time on it. It's not worth it. It's really not worth it.

Despite the time-limited development of 2 months of serious work, and the 2-man dev team of Ray-Kbys and kyou1110 (kyou helping with most of the music, Ray-K doing everything else), this visual novel manages to produce a touching-yet-refreshing story, with a cast of 6 underused-stereotype characters and more than decent writing in plot and character development. As a personal fan of Ray-Kbys' artwork, this piece displays some of his most inspired 2-D animations, which are short, but are used to astounding effect. This being a fairly short piece (I finished all content within 5 hours), hearing that this may have been a full-blown dating sim game with a branching story (if Ray-K hadn't procrastinated until 2 moths before) raises my hopes that Ray-Kbys may try his more determined hand at a full-blown dating sim one day.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes vanilla romance visual novels, people who like cute anime games, people who like unique artwork, people who are into injury/cyclops girls/sickeningly sweet romance fetishes, and just people with good humor, as this VN displays all these qualities and more. Just enough character development is placed into the story to entice veteran 2D romance enthusiasts and critics of the genre alike. As an added benefit, the cards for this game sell for nearly as much as the game itself on 50% off atm, assuming you don't wish to collect them for the rare adorable-cyclops-girl Steam backgrounds, so buy away!
Well worth $5, still worth $10 for VN enthusiasts. You're supporting an excellent and unique artist, after all.

Oh my god.
This game is hilarious.
Nearly everything is this game is done WRONG. COMICALLY WRONG.
Oh where do I start? How about basic controls?
Press spacebar to jump. Jump once and you fall twice, the second time being gravity kicking in after the preset fall animation.
Hold spacebar to do your impression of a rabbit on meth. Boingboingboingboingboingboing. Careful though, you can get fall damage from jumping too much. Seriously.
Press M1 to bring up a mutated, paralyzed left hand, completed with an elongated pinkie finger and a stretched texture.
Press M2 to bring up another mutated, paralyzed arm with a tapered, shrunken hand holding a pebble. It reels back, unmovingly, as if made of wood, then quickly forward again, throwing the pebble...which gently floats to the ground. Physics!
There is no crouch or run button (shift does nothing).
There is no map ('M' changes the mouse sensitivity) and no hints or aids in finding quest items. Now, I'm all for a little open-world exploration. Not every game needs a big old Bioshock arrow pointing at anything of interest. But this is the polar opposite. Here, there first level is a castle full of winding, identical corridors, and the first mission in that level is to find a sword and some keys. I managed to find one of the keys through blind explortion. It was difficult, though because it was the same color as everything else: greyish brown, and had nothing indicating its presence. No outline, no environmental context, not even so much as a reaction from the character when looking right at it.
Press Escape to see the tiny, 200x200 pixel menu. The itty-bitty options are mostly miscellaneous graphical options, like blood decals. If TotalBiscuit ever did a WTF on DS-AoE, he might have to start playing the game BEFORE the ten minute mark, since there's not much twiddling to be done with a menu like this.
As for me, I ended my game after I jumped on even terrain and the fall damage killed me. Then the game crashed. Yup.
This is a walking simulator for insomniacs. Or, alternatively, comedy gold for people who love to laugh at terrible games. Either way, it's too bad to pass up. I recommend it.

Similar concept to Civilization, but set in a very well-executed fantasy/sci-fi world
(TL;DR: Take civilization, but set in a much more interesting setting, with a better UI, much more interesting gameplay and factions. Highly recommend this game.)
Setting: Pre-apocalytpic dying fantasy/sci-fi world, where increasingly long winters plague the planet. The planet itself seems to have some sort of consciousness, and each of the different factions have a different relationship with the planet and different long-term victory goals.
Combat: When army stacks fight, the campaign map turns morphs into a smaller combat map, where the armies enter a turn-based combat system, with magic and leveling hero units.
Factions: The various fantasy races play very differently from each other and adds a ton of replayability. For example, one race must complete a story-driven questline which contradicts the interests of other factions. Another faction is unable to declare war, but can periodically "force peace" on an aggressor.
UI: The User Interface is fantastic in this game, all the menus blend and flow seamlessly. A right click at any time takes you back and everything is laid out neatly. A lot of information is sorted nicely and easy to get to.
Visuals: The game map and world  are very nice to look at, just look at the screenshots. Zooming out morphs the map into a colorized world map, which is very nice. Unit models look good too.
Soundtrack: Also a gem. The ambient music is very nice to listen to. Check it out on Youtube, don't take my word for it.
All in all, highly recommend this game if you're into turn based 4X. I would recommend this game over Civilization by a long shot.
Great addition to the fantasy and turn based genres

You start with a field of view zoomed in way to far to actually see much at all, and when you figure out the controls (J and K keys) to zoom out, you'll see your own two sadly deformed looking arms which much more closely resemble "tentacles" then they do arms. All I can say is "Wow". I didn't have particularly high expectations going into this game, but after playing it, I can say with certainty that this is my GOTY.
The characters and rich background really add to the atmosphere of the game. When I heard that not only the gold, taxes AND WEAPONS were being held by the monsters (Spoilers: They are only in disguise), I shed a tear. And then to discover that Katarina, with whom I am in love, is also in danger... I spent 5 minutes sobbing uncontrollably before getting into the game proper. The fact that the entire kingdom had fallen to a group of monsters who aren't really monsters while I was off chasing a runaway horse (which the intro character brilliantly mispronounces) only adds another layer of depth to the gripping narrative, which truly ponders the nature of the human condition.
Now for the gameplay. The main character's snail-like movement speed (even while sprinting) adds a level of tension one could find in inferior games such as The Last of Us or Dead Space, but then takes it to the next level. By making the player character's hands see-through and seemingly boneless, we are given a glimpse into the soul, the very essence of mankind. A true work of artistic brilliance.
I experienced my first death after jumping on the stairs and then glitching out for several seconds. Upon my death, maniacal laughter could be heard. Truly gripping stuff.
It also has a dog in it.
11/10 would chase horse again.

This game was good - great infact. It combined 4x gameplay as seen in games such as Civilization but much more focused and varied in all the right areas. But...
True to form, this developer (They make any game with "Endless" in it) Endlessly (pun intended) faffed around with the mechanics. First they added Guardians; huge creatures with great powers... which wasn't too bad since everyone could use them but was a bit of a facepalm moment in the sense of how easily they lay waste to enemies.
They then added a new faction called "The Forgotten" and with them espionage gameplay. "Cool! I love spy crafting in games!" I hear you cry. "No, you don't understand." I reason. "This game is made by Amplitude Studios and they are notorious for making great games which are then broken with new mechanics." And that's exactly what happened. I had a Forgotten spy in my capital city who killed 2 units of population every few turns until there was no one left and I could do nothing about it. 2 units of population - that's more that the Spanish flu, Bubonic Plague, AIDS and 3rd wave Feminism combined. Why is there even a spy skill that allows you to destroy huge swathes of population at a time in a game? Idiotic!
Then came the latest expansion. Though the new Yin Yang faction was fairly interesting, with them came new winter effects: now when winter comes, you can pick up a new resource and build shiny new things. Sounds great right? More content! Steady on there, ducky... have you not listened to anything I've said in this review? These shiny new things that you can unlock are ONLY there to negate the NEW crippling effects of winter that came with it. As if winter wasn't hard enough. It's like throwing a turd into someone's living room and bragging that it's okay that it stinks because you have also thrown some tissue paper in there for them to pick it up with.
I don't recommend this game anymore, sorry. The game has been Amplitude Studio'd up, just like they Amplitude Studio up everything that they make, sooner or later. It happened to Endless Space with the addition of fighters and troops, now it's happened to Endless Legends with Espionage and even nastier winter effects (despite complaints about "endless winter" in the first place). *Slow clap*
To Amplitude Studios: Stop breaking your games please!

This game is centered around learning vocabulary and that is it.  Gameplay centers around exploration of your limited environment in order to pick out objects that you come across.  It then gives fun little quizzes that ask you to find the objects in your environment.  For its intended task, it is great and works well.

From my experience, it does not introduce verbs, sentence structure, etc.  If someone goes into the game thinking it will be a full language course, then they will be dissappointed.  If they go in looking at Influent from the perspective of a fun tool to help master some common objects, they will be very happy with their purchase.
I can't wait to see how the game evolves.  I can see the game expanding into explorations outside of the small aparment and into the world with further exploration of items.  Then expanding further to have the user build sentences to interact with the environment or even order food at restaurants.  If the developer takes it that far, they will be in a full league/class of their own for interactive linguistic education.  Great start to a product with loads of oppurtunity to expand.

This will teach you 420 words (mostly household items) of a foreign language, with no conjugation lessons or anything like that.  Your average six year old knows about 4000 words and how to put them into actual sentences, so don't expect to actually understand a foreign language if all you use to learn it is this one game.
The game has potential, but it's nowhere near the expectations you might get from the opening video.  I think it was a mistake for them to release it in this alpha-ish incarnation because some other language-learning software house with more resources will now probably execute the concept in a more complete form - and I hate to see real innovators get ripped off before they can realize their full vision.
In it's current state, I wouldn't recommend buying this unless you catch a really good sale and were going use it as a tiny suppliment to a real language program.  It will take maybe 8 hours to complete everything in this game as it is today, and there's not much satisfation in completing it by itself.

You can tell by my hours played that I didn't play this game that long. This isn't just because I didn't want to play anymore, but because I was skeptical that I'd further my education by doing so.
To begin with, the game environment is uncomfortable. You're confined to an extremely small apartment, with 400 objects you can learn to say in one of twelve languages. The amount of stuff cramped into such a tiny area makes it feel even more claustrophobic than it would as just an unfurnished area, which makes me feel like shutting off the game right from the beginning. This is especially true if you're playing in third person, which means your character model is added to it all. I don't know much about what can and can't be patched, but I'd like to suggest to the dev if it's possible to edit the map so that the 3 rooms are at least a few feet wider, and have some of the furniture spaced out a bit as well.
The actual objects themselves aren't very fun to look at either (except for the Cowboy Bebop reference in one of the posters!). Everything is completely static, and the only interaction available with them is to find out the word for them in your chosen language. This might seem like all that you'd need, but with the actual quizzing being so basic, it makes things really boring when you literally can do nothing else. It'd be cool if some objects had animations (especially the doors, which I desperately wanted to open for some more space), or even physics that let you drag them around.
One small complaint to add before moving on to my biggest one: while the one track available is actually very enjoyable, there needs to be more songs added. I think I'd go crazy if I had to listen to that same song over and over for more than an hour.
Now my biggest problem of all isn't really relevant for people who aren't learning Japanese: There's no focus on the Kanji. In the Japanese language, Kanji is /VERY/ crucial to being able to read or write anything. Yes, it is included in the game, but there's nothing to help you remember the details of it, let alone the stroke order for writing it. Without that, it's fairly pointless to play the game at all for anything besides listening practice, but even for that you'd be better off watching anime and/or Japanese films, and listening to Japanese music and podcasts.
For vocabularly, I personally would suggest downloading a free language learning program called "Anki", and then dowloading (also free) both the Heisig Kanji card pack, and the Japanese Core 2k pack. Some untranslated mangas are decent practice as well.
The developer for this game obviously had great intentions, and on paper his concept is great. But in execution, not so much.

Evoland is a walk down memory lane for anyone who has played a flurry of early adventure and rpg games. The game mimics styles of black and white, limited color, turn based battle, & real time battle games. It cycles you through these game types in an attempt to display a timeline of the evolution of these games. Through style or substance you may find Evoland "winking at you" and reminding you of past gaming experiences. Near the end of the game you may find yourself searching through the various evolutions of gameplay in order to achieve a higher completion level of the game.
Evoland offers real time battles and turn based battles. The real time battles can be frustrating at times and the turn based battles seem lackluster in a game with so few items and so little to gain from turn based combat. The game is fairly short but can be adequately drawn out by collecting all the cards and stars. All in all Evoland offers a unique experience but may end up making you yearn for a more complete version of one of its styles of gameplay rather than the game itself as a whole.

Evoland is a charming tribute to the history of RPGs. Obviously influenced by The Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, and Diablo, there's a lot to love in this indie gem. You'll traverse the annals of video game history as you move from early 8-bit games through 16-bit and 3D, gaining little bonuses along the way that poke fun at RPG stereotypes. I smiled on more than one occasion at the humor in the game, and I was always looking forward to the next technological progression of my character.
In a way, Evoland presents as a haphazard combination of themes. On the one hand, you have the excellent unlockable tributes to video game history. You unlock the ability to enter houses, you gain the ability to fight, and you'll be able to fight random enemies. All good, and all evenly and comically presented. However, the game eventually becomes a casual RPG with a light story that features frequent testaments to the major moments in RPG classics. While it is a little jarring to have your little world suddenly begin to be fleshed out, it makes sense mechanically and keeps the game moving.
As you journey on through this adventure, you'll play a collectible card game, solve Zelda-style puzzles, find optional collectible items, and enjoy many different modes of play. Evoland is something special, and anyone who looks upon the roots of RPGs fondly will enjoy this nostalgic love letter.

Overall I had a great time with Fist Of Awesome. I laughed and tapped my foot through every level, and immediately started my second play through on a higher difficulty after finishing the game. This game has the perfect blend of great art and music style, humor and fluid game play, and one of the best credit theme songs of all time. Fist Of Awesome is priced perfectly and left me with a smile on my face and nostalgia in my heart. This is a great indie title and has earned 7.5 out of 10 from me.
STORY
The story of Fist Of Awesome is a timeless tale about a lumberjack called Tim Burr, who must fight his way to the truth, and set right the timeline that has seen his home destroyed and his family taken from him. Tim is empowered with the mighty Fist Of Awesome, a talking hand that guides his travels through the damaged timelines searching for the cause of the temporal disturbance. Along his journey Tim must face off against super advanced bears, deer and buffalo who due to the timeline alterations have risen to be the dominant power on Earth.
Fist Of Awesome's story is silly, but that is what I fight Bears was aiming for, and each funny one liner, pop culture reference or throw back to old school gaming is so perfectly delivered that the player will have a great time and laugh right through to the end. The fist play through of the story will take the average gamer no more than an hour to complete but with this in mind I was not disappointed by the playtime, and instead finished the game feeling that I had a great bit of fun getting there.
GAMEPLAY
Fist Of Awesome's controls will be instantly familiar to anyone who has spent some time playing side scrolling fighting games and are easy to get the hang of. The combat is basic in concept but as enemies become more resilient in the higher levels a degree of strategy is required to progress. Each time zone Tim progresses through culminates in a boss fight which is started off with some funny dialogue and are a decent challenge to the player.
Tim gains points and levels up throughout the stages depending on the combos the player can land, and is able to allocate one point to life, strength, speed or special per level. I had a great time with the general game play and leveling system, with the only let down being that enemy types were a bit too samey, and didn’t use their type specific attacks often enough.
VISUALS & MUSIC
The 8-bit art and music style of Fist Of Awesome is brilliant, and further enhances the comedy of the game. I found each level to be entertaining and beautiful in its own way, and enjoyed the well paced soundtrack throughout this crazy adventure.

Love the art style and unique take on Cinderella. If you like fairy tales and visual novels, give this a go.

Is the classic Cinderella a victim of her stepmother and step sisters, or is she a victim of her own inability to change her circumstances? Do faries steal people's agency in a literary sense as well as literally? Is the self immutable, or can it change in response to circumstance? If it changes in order to better survive difficult times, is that an improvement, or the shameful death of something precious? Is a democratic government merely an excuse for people to lie to each other all the time?
In addition to offering a chance to ponder the above questions, Cinders is a fantastic exploration of both self-empowerment and self-destructive tendencies within the context of a classic fairy tale. It also has some fantastically witty lines and some good meditations on romantic love and its strengths and limitations.
For its message of empowerment, ambtitous themes, and fascinating characters, 10/10, cannot wait to play again.
Like the premise, wish there was more replay value for sure.

I wish there were a complete walkthrough for each of the endings, but unfortunately I haven't found one yet.
Before I bought the game I had no idea just how many endings there were; there are four main ways to end the story, but each one of those endings has four or five different endings as well. It's incredible how easy it is to get sucked into the game. And, fortunately, if you've encountered a line of conversation before, the game will let you skip all the dialogue until you hit something new.
I love the art style and although there isn't any voice acting involved, the music is soothing (and can be turned off if you're not into it). The game developers have done a great job with the characters as well. Cinders herself can be incredibly devious or a pushover, depending on how you play her.
All in all, an excellent way to spend many, many hours on your computer.

Similar concept to Civilization, but set in a very well-executed fantasy/sci-fi world
(TL;DR: Take civilization, but set in a much more interesting setting, with a better UI, much more interesting gameplay and factions. Highly recommend this game.)
Setting: Pre-apocalytpic dying fantasy/sci-fi world, where increasingly long winters plague the planet. The planet itself seems to have some sort of consciousness, and each of the different factions have a different relationship with the planet and different long-term victory goals.
Combat: When army stacks fight, the campaign map turns morphs into a smaller combat map, where the armies enter a turn-based combat system, with magic and leveling hero units.
Factions: The various fantasy races play very differently from each other and adds a ton of replayability. For example, one race must complete a story-driven questline which contradicts the interests of other factions. Another faction is unable to declare war, but can periodically "force peace" on an aggressor.
UI: The User Interface is fantastic in this game, all the menus blend and flow seamlessly. A right click at any time takes you back and everything is laid out neatly. A lot of information is sorted nicely and easy to get to.
Visuals: The game map and world  are very nice to look at, just look at the screenshots. Zooming out morphs the map into a colorized world map, which is very nice. Unit models look good too.
Soundtrack: Also a gem. The ambient music is very nice to listen to. Check it out on Youtube, don't take my word for it.
All in all, highly recommend this game if you're into turn based 4X. I would recommend this game over Civilization by a long shot.
Great addition to the fantasy and turn based genres

This game was good - great infact. It combined 4x gameplay as seen in games such as Civilization but much more focused and varied in all the right areas. But...
True to form, this developer (They make any game with "Endless" in it) Endlessly (pun intended) faffed around with the mechanics. First they added Guardians; huge creatures with great powers... which wasn't too bad since everyone could use them but was a bit of a facepalm moment in the sense of how easily they lay waste to enemies.
They then added a new faction called "The Forgotten" and with them espionage gameplay. "Cool! I love spy crafting in games!" I hear you cry. "No, you don't understand." I reason. "This game is made by Amplitude Studios and they are notorious for making great games which are then broken with new mechanics." And that's exactly what happened. I had a Forgotten spy in my capital city who killed 2 units of population every few turns until there was no one left and I could do nothing about it. 2 units of population - that's more that the Spanish flu, Bubonic Plague, AIDS and 3rd wave Feminism combined. Why is there even a spy skill that allows you to destroy huge swathes of population at a time in a game? Idiotic!
Then came the latest expansion. Though the new Yin Yang faction was fairly interesting, with them came new winter effects: now when winter comes, you can pick up a new resource and build shiny new things. Sounds great right? More content! Steady on there, ducky... have you not listened to anything I've said in this review? These shiny new things that you can unlock are ONLY there to negate the NEW crippling effects of winter that came with it. As if winter wasn't hard enough. It's like throwing a turd into someone's living room and bragging that it's okay that it stinks because you have also thrown some tissue paper in there for them to pick it up with.
I don't recommend this game anymore, sorry. The game has been Amplitude Studio'd up, just like they Amplitude Studio up everything that they make, sooner or later. It happened to Endless Space with the addition of fighters and troops, now it's happened to Endless Legends with Espionage and even nastier winter effects (despite complaints about "endless winter" in the first place). *Slow clap*
To Amplitude Studios: Stop breaking your games please!

I couldn't get into this game.  I had trouble becoming invested in matches. To compare it to my experience with other games like Civilization, generally from turn 1, or at most the first 10-20 turns, you can have a strategy developed for how you want to play a map based on available resources, nearby civs, terrain, etc.  This may change as the game progresses, but its based on what you find around you and your surrounding opponents.
In Endless Legend, I wasn't able to conceptualize that strategy, or my strategy was almost purely based on my chosen race's victory condition.  Mostly, I just ended up empire building for the sake of empire building, and without that purity of focus from working towards a real long term strategy, that just felt empty and pointless even as I progressed to new eras and built larger cities and bigger armies.
The combat system is an interesting quirk, but ultimately didn't hook me - often I found myself either wishing I had a larger "map" to maneuver around, or found the map too constrictive with too many units trying to use the limited space.
There are interesting ideas and mechanics in EL - from its specific way of city growing, to villages and secondary races, army equipment, resources, quests, etc. But In the end, whether it was a failure of translation of more advanced game concepts to me the player, or lack thereof, the game simply lacked the ability to hold my interest.
Much like civilization beyond earth, for me the game looked pretty and initially seemed to have what it would take to hold my interest for hundreds of hours, like previous games in this genre, but ultimately proved too shallow or hard to approach to hold my interest.

I don't understand how the developer thought it made sense that you have to walk along a ledge on a wall, with your character basically floating above the ground, to get to the top of a cabinet that holds the oil you are looking for.
After you finish the first level, you watch yet another poorly rendered movie, and then on to the second level, which is just about as bad. The problem these levels really have is that they are almost like mazes. You are required to endure a very slow trek through levels with no sense of direction to them. It would make sense if the levels followed some form of logic, or had a graphical quality to them that helped point you in the right direction, but you will find no such thing here.
The combat is hard to read, as you aren't sure just how much damage your strikes are doing, or if they're hitting at all. Meanwhile, you are moving backwards after every strike to not be hit, while lunging forward to do a hit. It requires little skill at all, and isn't fun.
I hate to harp on a game that from what I have heard, has very few developers, to the potential of only 1 developer. I find it hard to believe one man did all the programming, music design, graphical design, and whatever else went into making this game, but if that is the case, it is impressive it reached a finished product. It just seems pointless, however, to make such a flawed product. I can only hope the game gets better with time, but I feel that simply isn't possible without a complete overhaul to this game, from the engine, to the controls, to the levels and graphics themselves.
I'm sorry, but I simply cannot recommend this game. I was lucky to receive it as part of a bundle, with the luck falling on the part of paying a low sum for multiple games, and not having this game as part of the bundle received.

Castlevania is old-school. Zelda 64 is old-school. Doom is old-school. This game's graphics, on the other hand, just look like they were♥♥♥♥♥♥out by the leftovers from Morrowind, which in my admitedly unpopular opinion, has not aged well at all.
Second, let's talk about the controls. You can't keybind anything. You can make some adjustments to mouse sensitivity, and invert the mouse's Y axis, but that's it. Don't like the layout? Well, ♥♥♥♥ you. Your character's movement, too, is just weird in general. Movement is very sluggish. Everything seems a bit zoomed in, but if you zoom out, it still just feels nauseating. Combat, if you've got the patience to even get to it (I'll get back to that), is painfully bare. There's no strategy involved whatsoever. Hit your enemy, pull back, then go back in for another hit. Third, let's talk about the story. What's the story? A bunch of monsters and/or people in scary get-up have been ravaging the land, and got into the castle. They killed all the guards, and took all the money, taxes (yes, taxes), and swords. Also, they took this guy's sister, and you better save her, because you're in love with her. The only image we see of said woman is awkwardly animated, with flailing arms and a grand total of one facial expression. And all of it is separated between different rooms in this quite large castle.
All this makes the game seem REALLY bad. It is. But the worst thing about this game, I repeat, the WORST thing about this game is nothing I have mentioned thus far. When you look past the strange heroine,
is a pretty straightforward high school romance VN. There's no ero in the game itself, but it has a few ero-guro undertones that might be off-putting for some. Even so, there's a certain soft grace to it all; Ray-K's painterly style brings warmth and tenderness to every scene, catching the restrained giddiness of young love in a way that might be lost with cleaner, flatter designs. It is, in a word, comfy.
The characters are likeable, for the most part, with Sachi standing head and shoulders over any run-of-the-mill moeblob love interest. She invites sympathy and the urge to protect, but her vulnerability never really grates. The music doesn't stand out by any means, but its gentleness supports the cozy atmosphere well.
There is very little beyond the story's single path, unfortunately — about two hours of content in all. Even the most casual reader will chew through it quickly, and depending on their tastes, they'll probably be left wanting more. It's perhaps not enough to warrant the full $10. But if it's on sale and you have five bucks to spare, time spent on crisp autumn back-streets with a cute cyclops girl is time well invested.
Admittedly, I might be biased here; that wide, bottomless eye will ease open your chest and grope the scars. But isn't that the point?
Pick this up if you enjoy cutely macabre aesthetics, monster girls, romance, and if you see it on sale.
---
+ Cute monster girl heroine
+ Cozy autumn setting
+ Warm, comfy art style
+ The extra features serve as a fun little epilogue and development backstory
+ When you're done with the story and extras, check the creator's Pixiv for a bit more
- Only one story path
- That one path is a little bare-bones and straightforward
- At 2-3 hours, the VN is extremely short — perhaps too short to justify a $10 price tag

Can't decide if you want this game, or Transformed? I'll make it easy. Buy them both. Wait till they're on sale and get them both. Why? Because both this and Transformed are excellent games.
Ok, so now that we got that outa the way, here's why I recommend this game. I actually started off playing Transformed first when I first got into PC gaming. I absolutely love Transformed which is why I was kinda scared to buy this installment. I had looked up video footage and it didn't appear to be worth my while. Well I had some extra Steam money and had nothing else to spend it on so I finally just bought this game. As many have complained about there is no online multiplayer. Boo hoo......I don't care. I buy games for their single player experiences. What I've always liked about Transformed is that it is a REAL racing game, unlike Mario Kart which feels like dodge ball on wheels. Sonic and Sega All Star Racing is no exception. Even though it is not as fast as Transformed, it is still a balls to the wall racing game. The A.I. DOES NOT rubberband on you like Mario Kart does and the weapons slow you down, but not so bad that your chances of winning are ruined by a few unlucky hits. If I had one complaint about the game, it would be the weapons. They're kinda boring (like Mario Kart) but that's to be expected because this was Sega's first crack at a kart racer. However to me the racing is important, and the drift and stunt boosting are still here though it's not as elaborate as Tranformed is. I love the tranforming dynamic in Transformed, but I don't miss it in this game. What I'm trying to say is that this is an excellent kart racer than stands on it's own and I still like it 10 times better than any recent release of Mario Kart. It still does everything right, and the best reason buying this game as well as Transformed is that all of the tracks are different from the second installment. I bought this game because I wanted more Sonic All Star Racing after I completed Transformed.
Lastly this game is not coded as well as Transformed is so don't be surprised if the game drops a few frames here and there. You won't see the drops in your frame rate counter, but you'll notice the slight stutters. They are not even close to game breaking, but just know that there's nothing wrong with your computer.

This game is a really clever and charming tool for basic vocabulary. There's  not conversation or grammar included, and the words are all pretty 'Unit 1,' but at $10 for the base game plus one language pack, and $5 each per language pack, the price is right. Are you going to achieve fluency in any given language with this game? No. Will you achieve fluency in any language for ten dollars? Probably not, but if you find a way please let me know.
TL;DR: Good vocab tool to supplement other, more intense, language learning programs. Inexpensive and charming.

TL:DR summary:
This game is not fun and won't help you learn a language.
I'm interested in language learning and so I was really excited to try this "game" and see what it brings to the table. I knew about that game for a long time, but with the recent humble bundle, I spent a buck to find out. This is what I think:
- I can hardly call this a game. While I really like the "intro-story", the game doesn't build up on the story at all. The whole "game" consists of you running around in your flat and clicking things. Your character isn't talking at all and the only objectives are getting the achievements and/or completing an ingame todo list, which groups certain words thematically. While the latter kept me motivated for a while, but also got me frustrated, since the list contains the "to be learned"-words in target language. So you have no real clue what to look for
- You only learn vocabulary. While I'm not a big fan of grammar rules in the form of equations or conjugation tables, this game doesn't contain a single sentence! Only words! Mainly nouns, but later on adjectives and verbs as well. But no sentences!
- You don't really learn any vocabulary. I have to major issues. First, the game tells you that you "mastered" a word after several successful training units. However the game doesn't contain any concept about long-term memory. After you learn words in a language, you have to repeat them in growing intervals. Repeat after 1 minute, 15 minutes, an hour, 5 hours, a day, 5 days, a month and so on... this game thinks you "mastered" a word in 3 min. That is not how memory works :( Second: The way the game teaches you is: it shows or tells you a word and you have to find the corresponding object in your flat and click it. However this only builds your passive vocabulary. If you were given a word in your mother tongue and you should translate it to the language you are learning, this game won't really help you
So all in all the "TL:DR summary" is very black and white (in this case black). This software gives you some motivation to learn/repeat words and you might indeed learn a thing or two. If you are just planning to fool around with some vocabulary of a language and spend 2 or 3 hours, this game is fine. For anything else it is really ill fitted. You definetely won't learn a language and I can hardly believe that anyone will build a real vocabulary with this. Rather pick up
courses or get anki for vocab training,

Wow... I bought this game a while ago and only recently got around to playing and have to say i'm impressed. Having played copious amounts of VNs in the past (and present, they are a guilty pleasure of mine, afterall), I was surprised with how many options and endings were available to the player to affect the story. Usually there are a couple of options with some rather than others being the more 'important' ones that affect the story but here, it seems as if almost every option branches the story in another direction. You help guide Cinders and with the choices you pick, her personality changes and so does the outcomeof the tale. The 'evil' stepmother and stepsisters aren't as black or white in this case - everyone has a reason for doing what they do and the characters are humanized. You're forced to take into account not only the actions but the setting the characters are in; whether they do things considered good or bad, most of the times they're just trying to do the best they can do in that situation.
Okay so basically what I'm trying to say is yes you should get the game and try it out because its worth the money. They put a lot of time and efforst into this one and it shows :)
