TL;DR: This game builds upon Lego Batman and DC Super Heroes. It improves controls and visuals, and offers a new, unique story. Combine this with a change of scenery, and you’ve got yourself a hit.
I’m not going to say much that others haven’t already said. But to sum it all up, this game is like “Lego Batman 2: DC Super Heroes” on steroids. All the classic features that made people love this game are present. That “Batman: Arkham City” style free roam. The “brain friendly” (detect sarcasm here) puzzles that made “Lego Indiana Jones” a hit. The powers of all your favorite childhood super heroes. And now, a story worthy of the game! If you’re like me, and have played any (or all) of these titles, you’ll get a major de ja vous.
The last two Lego Batman games were astounding, but this ramps up everything to a new level. As mentioned above (in other reviews), the graphics in this game are improved. And when I say improved, I don't mean a tiny bit, I mean A LOT. I know this might not be the best comparison to make here, but if any of you have ever played Minecraft with the R3DCraft resource pack and/or Shaders (SEUS) mod enabled, you might have an idea as to what I mean. For those that haven’t played Minecraft (haven’t played it seriously, I mean) try googling images of the Shaders mod. It’s a night and day difference between the standard shader pack. While the difference between “Beyond Gotham” and “DC Super Heroes” might not be quite THAT drastic, I think my example gives an accurate portrayal of how much better the game not only looks, but feels. And keep in mind, Lego Batman 2 was NOT a bad looking game. The change of scenery doesn’t hurt either. I love the fact that this game takes you places you don’t often get to go in the DC universe. It’s really quite refreshing. Honestly, I think that this game rivals even “Arkham City” in terms of the best Batman game. Well, that might be pushing it. But one thing’s certain: It’s certainly a great deal better thank “Lego Marvel Super Heroes”! :D
It sometimes boggles my mind; why make such a great title a Lego game? But in actuality, I think it’s that fact that makes the game as enjoyable as it is. For any newbies, don’t let the fact that it’s a Lego game discourage you; this game is definitely worth the play. I know as well as anyone that the constant sales sometimes, or often, make us want to spend no more than the price of a sandwich on a game. But this is one worth full price. Honestly guys, you should have picked up the Premium Edition yesterday!
P.S.  “Lego Batman 4: Justice League” anyone? XD

Amazing game, and I say that as someone who doesn't normally play visual novels because: a) they are usually drawn in the style of anime, and b) they are usually dating sims -- I find neither of those two things particularly appealing. This game, however, is not even close to being a dating sim (although there are different romance options you can choose to pursue) and the art style is miles away from anime and very beautiful.
The story is a retelling of the Cinderella fairytale with a lot more depth, featuring well-rounded characters, complicated familial relations and meaningful choices. It emphasizes the extent to which characters' personal choices are limited by/the product of their circumstances and surroundings. The wicked stepmother and stepsisters are not simple archetypal chracters but complex figures with motivations and agendas that arise from their life circumstances. The main character Cinders, the young woman who lives as a servant in her own house, is trying to take destiny in her own hands and break free from her current circumstances, but cannot do so without outside help. The game makes a point: despite her desire to be independent and have agency, her available options are nevertheless to some extent the product of particular conditions that are outside of her influence (of her father marrying as he did, of her mother ensuring Cinders gets help when she needs it, etc).
The writting is very good and the choices in the game are meaningful; I found replaying the game to explore different results very interesting. The first playthrough takes about 3 hours, while subsequent playthroughs can be made a lot shorter as there's an option to skip through dialogues that you've read in previous playthroughs.
Definitely recommended for people who love good stories and don't mind reading a bunch.

Cinders is very interesting take on the classic story everyone knows, and so far it is absolutely my favourite adaptation of the story.

You may even end up sympathizing them when you know what are the motivations behind their actions, which you don't actually see much in some other Cinderella stories - where the step family is just mean because potatoes.
Also the art in this game is just amazing, backgrounds are like atmospheric paintings... character art is nice too but sometimes the anatomy is maybe a bit awkward. But that is just nitpicking.
Another thing what I liked about in the game is that it has few different endings, and none of them are actually truly happy endings... well maybe one could be counted as almost perfectly happy ending. But others, well, they are not actually that good when you think about them.
Overall, I do recommend you to play this game. It may not be very long, but at least to me it was nice experience. If you are fairytale lover like me, I am quite sure you will enjoy this game as well.

This is what kept me playing during my first hours. I did not have to read guides, or to worry about my build - i was just having fun playing this little game. In a few hours only I had understood the basic mechanics of the game.
Jump, shoot, drop, drop, shoot, oh damn there's someone needing help !
Take the jump pad, dash towards the enemies, thus saving your mate, and then drop down to jungle and escape. Woosh, you nearly died, but you just saved your mate.
Ok, your two buddies are right there in top lane, and you see the 3 enemies standing there. Time to initiate ! You dash, your mates follow, you prevent them from escaping by bodyblocking them while nado'ing.. One is about to espape, you are about to die, but your friend Nibbs just launched her Orb, teleports, and the guy is dead. It's a wipeout. Time to push !
And that's basically what the entire game is like. You have no time to rest. You always have something to do, always on your nerves. The slightest mistake might turn the fate of the game.. But you keep playing, you keep pushing. Until victory (or defeat) is achieved.
After more than 600 hours in this game, I still did not master 100% of the game.
Each one of the 23 characters has a completely different gameplay. That's 23 playstyles to master.  Out of these 23, I think I'm mastering 8 of them. I still have 15 characters to continue learning.. And that's what keeps me playing, even after 600 hours.
Be it when you kill someone in air battle, or when you barely escape a gank and manage nevertheless to kill one of them, resulting in a wipeout (all 3 of the enemy team dead) because your team supported you - or when both of your team mates died, but all 3 enemies have low health, and you manage to take them all out..

Awesomenauts is a 3v3 MOBA-style 2D platformer where each player takes control of one unique Awesomenaut and battle with the other team to push their turrets, destroy them, and ultimately destroy their base.
The gameplay is your typical MOBA with a twist in that it's a platformer as well, making it a pretty interesting combination. Besides your typical knowledge about characters, their specializations and skills, you will also need some platforming experience as well, especially that certain characters have different movement abilities than others (certain are even capable of flight). It's action-packed and fun, but very hard to grasp and often turns into an unreadable chaotic mess due to the sheer amount of stuff that is going on at the same time.
Graphic-wise, the special effects look nice, and all the characters have their own general style, though they all are pretty cartoonish and sometimes a little cheesy. It does add a bit to their charm, however.
The music is, for the lack of better wording, awesome. Each character has their own musical theme (which also plays if you get a killstreak) and all of them are a good listen, especially that they cover a lot od different styles and genres, like Clunk's metal or Voltar's classical orchestra.
So, on the surface the game feels nice, but the problems begin piling up when you go play online.
The first thing is the horrible supposedly skill-based matchmaking. I say supposedly as it only operates on a league system, with each player being given a number, 1 being the highest, and 9 being the lowest in skill. The main two flaws are the fact that leagues reset every two months, so the first one or two weeks after the reset newbies are very likely to encounter skilled players who will absolutely stomp them to the ground, and the other is that the matchmaker has no problem teaming you up with a premade team consisting of Prestige 10 players (who reset and regained their levels a total of ten times) when you're new to the game, which, unless some kind of a miracle happens, will most likely result in a complete steamroll.
It also doesn't help that the balance changes are made on a constant basis and while this is good in general, it also makes most user-made guides outdated pretty fast, so you're effectively stuck with the general description of character's role and abilities, and maybe a friend's help when it comes to learning the game, and considering it's a MOBA platformer, it's not only pretty harsh at the start, but also very easy to lose against veterans.
The game does put up a certain "Difficulty" rating on each 'Naut, either Easy, Medium or Hard, but it's honestly far from correct. For example, it labels Coco as "Easy" even though she relies very heavily on mobility and correct use of her abilities instead of just whacking things in the head with your weapon, while at the same time calling Swiggins "Hard" despite his abilities being rather straightforward and generally easy to use.
There are also certain Starstorm-exclusive 'Nauts where I can barely stop myself from calling them "pay to win" (mostly looking at Nibbs), so I am going to use a more generally accepted term of "horribly skill-gated and not fun to play against unless you know the exact way to counter them".
When it comes to the expansion itself, it kind of does not help my opinion about the developer when they already begin to collect preorders for the next expansion, Overdrive, when they didn't even release everything associated with the Starstorm expansion (namely its exclusive map). Generally speaking you should finish the content people already paid for before moving on to create content for a separate purchase, unless you want people to look at you a bit shadily. Doesn't help that despite the beta the new heroes were overpowered as hell and often relied on cheap tactics, and the promised matchmaker rebalance still matches up newbies versus veterans. To the developer's credit, however, they do release some free updates for everyone every few months.
Overall, this is a fun at its core, but very difficult to master and incredibly demotivating at start game. Personally, I just can't get myself into it big-time. Badly-designed matchmaker, a lot of things being far from obvious at first, and certain characters being just way too tricky to counter effectively while being generally easy to use if you're new to the game, and newly-released ones being overpowered or even P2W if they're DLC, are some of the factors that kill it for me. It's not a bad game, just one that's ridiculously difficult to learn at start and where the high skill ceiling makes it pretty much impossible to play casually unless you restrict yourself to bot matches.

This game offers a lot of opportunities to expand your vocabulary through fun challenges. If you purchased a few languages, you must select which one you want to start with first; I started with Korean and will later pick up more. Once you select the language (Korean) for example, you have the choice to also select Hangul. Once the game starts you are in an apartment, with lots of household items and the learning begins.
As you move around (Limited interaction with the items) you can select items and learn the name in the language you purchased. There you can see the English translation, pronunciation, image, spelling, noun and verb versions of the word. Once you have found a few words you are comfortable with you can start adding them to your list, you can then play these challenges like "time attack" which test you in your ability to locate the items; either they are said to you, you read them without assistance of pronunciation of the software meanwhile you are being "tested" in speed/accuracy.
There is a lot more this game has to offer through these challenges and I recommend getting comfortable with a few set of words before adding more to your list. There is no rush and after each challenge you get a percentage but no penalization for failing. There is also a "To do list" which makes it easier for you to know what challenges you need to complete and they are not meant to be done in any particular order.
Overall I have played this game for only a few hours and am enjoying it. It is a relaxed, straightforward, fun way to learn a set of words in a new language. The price is good and the only thing I would want added is the chance to explore more areas (more locations) this would allow me to expand on my vocabulary besides household items.
Next Phase of Influent?
An added software in conjunction with this one; Once we have the words learned take us to the next "Learning phase" Learning how to use them in a sentence, this would help us with the ability to actually use the words and have a conversation. The price is good for what this game offers. An added sweet bonus would be steam trading cards even though it is educational software.
Final thoughts
It is not meant to teach you a whole new language but help you expand on your vocabulary. It does make the learning process of learning new vocabulary fun and I would recommend this game. Will be adding screenshots soon!

I absolutely love this game.
Let me start by saying that I picked this up for the German version.  I've been learning German with Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, and German television shows for a few months, but wanted something that I could sit down and play when I want to change up my learning style.
This game should not be purchased if you want to learn grammar or phrases.  In the German version you learn mostly vocabulary words (I say mostly because I still haven't found every word, and who knows... maybe there's something else out there).
Now, one of the most important things for learning words in a foreign language is having a memory to place with the word.  A game like this provides this SIGNIFICANTLY better than a memory based card game.  Why?  Because you're remembering a word based on not only its graphic visualisation, but you're remembering it within the context of the home.  In this game, if you have to find the "pfeffer", you not only have to remember the word for pepper, but WHERE the pepper is.  It's helped me remember words extremely easily.
Don't buy this as your primary way to learn a language.  Buy it as a way to help you build vocabulary alongside a few other language learning classes or programs.  That's what I bought it for, and that's what it does best.
If duolingo ever releases bulgarian, I'll definitely be picking up another version of this game.  I highly recommend it.

My first contact with Influend was weird. I was like "oh, another learning game, probably not interesting". though I tried it anyway and it turned out to be something better than "just a learning game". First of all - it is not boring. It even has a plot, you know. You are an independent inventor whose prototype machine named Senjun...dammit, the name of that prototype is too hard to write. So yeah, in order to prove it he wants to learn 300 words in one of the languages. You can buy the game with one language and then buy the rest of languages as cheaper DLCs - I like the idea.
Let's get to the real action. You are in your flat, filled with 420 (blaze it) things. Basically the goal is to walk around and interact with things to see their name. It's a good system in my opinion, since when you look at the thing you know what it is and you get the name in the other language. But not only that, you can also get synonyms and adjectives for some of those too (and in case of Japaneese - how the things I written. I felt good with romaji)! You can see that hard work was put into that, because there's also a native speaker saying the word out loud too! Anyway, after getting to know names of stuff int he room you can try Time Attack mode - it's all about "mastering the words" and choosing the right things. After you master 50 words - SURPRISE, YOU CAN FLY AROUND THE ROOM AND SHOOT STUFF WITH LAZERS! So it's not only learning after all.
Now, a few words about graphics - game doesn't look bad, I like its art style. It is kinda like in comics, so that's a plus. Some of the texutes are less detailed, but that's only things that you can do much with. And they're usually placed in some corners and places normal human doesn't usually visit (unless he's a nerdy RPG player that has to visit every corner).
Other stuff - you will probably spend more time looking at numerous references that are hidden withing the game. I really liked book on the table. Get the game (it's not that expensive, especially when you see the amount of content and educational value of it. Really, educational games can be damn good and this one is the example of it) and see it.
BUT - every rose has its thorns. It took me some time to get used to controls. You can switch in this game between TPP and FPP modes, but when in FPP zooming in has to be with mouse wheel instead of good ol' FPS right-click (it is assigned for different function). Apart from getting to know controls, rest is good. Even tutorial (you can skip it and get to know controls by yourself - not suggested).
To sum up, I loved that game since 10 minutes after launching it. And I actually learned that pillow in japaneese is "makura".And yeah, this thing is definitely worth getting.
Rating: 9+/10 - grab it, grab

For an in-depth review, tune into the video below:
Otherwise, here’s a summarized write up.

Aztez’s story is almost non-existent. The campaign has you pushing the Spanish out of your cities and the missions just depict the process in which you do that. These serve more as descriptions of the mission rather than a main plot line throughout the experience. There are no narrative cutscenes and as such, almost nothing to get attached to story wise.
Aztez is Team Colorblind’s attempt at a unique hybrid between a beat em-up and a turn based strategy title, so the rating of this review is going to hinge on how satisfying the brawling is and how well it’s incorporated into the game’s strategic elements.
As a brawler it sticks to the core concept of a single character fighting multiple enemies, each of which fall into 8-9 types of foes that all have different move sets and weapons. I’m going to be making a few comparisons to Bayonetta and DMC since the devs have stated that their intention was to be more like those games.
With that in mind, Aztez incorporates most of the expected mechanics of the genre, so that includes multiple weapons, switching between those weapons in the middle of combos, dashes with invincibility frames, and blocks that allow for counter attacked if timed precisely enough. However, where the game disappoints is in its execution of its actual attacks.
You know how most beat em up games have light and heavy attacks and combining something like L-L-H-H-H results in a different combo to L-L-L-L-H? Aztez doesn’t have much of that combat variety. Instead you have a 5 string combo with your square attack and another 5 string one with your triangle attack (or your xbox counterpart). Mixing between them with S-S-T-T-T just gives you the first two attack animations of the former string and the three last attack animations of the latter string.
I also don’t call them light and heavy attacks since they do the exact same amount of damage per hit, making combos using them utterly redundant in conjunction with the earlier issue. It’s a far cry from the sheer amount of combinations offered by Bayonetta which utilizes even holding down buttons or pausing between two inputs to engage different move sets.
The only thing that really allows for move variation is when you swap between weapons in the middle of attacks since doing this allows you to restart the hit counter, making it very easy to put your foes in an endless stagger state. Once you get 2 weapons, you’ll very often be knocking enemies up into the air and spamming them to death since not many foes hit upwards frequently.
While other games like DMC have this air juggle feature with weapon swapping, executing it isn’t nearly as simple as the single button input that’s required in Aztez. The fact that newer weapons introduce different move sets doesn’t really matter when the game never gives you a compelling enough reason to divert from its spammy playstyle.
What combat does do well however is the enemy variety since they their moves match their associated weapons. You get notification prompts on when they’re about to attack but since they have 2-3 different moves, you’ll need to pay close attention to which one they telegraph since each of them has a different parry window. Besides this, dealing enough damage also puts enemies into a “broken” state in which grabbing them and hitting the attack button will lead to a LOT of blood spurting out of their bodies. You can absorb this blood to fill up a vial which, when full, can be spent to deal out a god attack.
In terms of the turn based campaign, it centers around a large map with many cities to conquer. You start with owning 4 of them and you gain resources and the end of every turn for every location under your control. Each turn has you deploying soldiers to missions for completion rewards that you can use to further expand your control. Besides that you can also use items and Agents (at the cost of resources) to do things like secure areas or ensure that a town that’s yours will never dissent as there is a random chance of that happening to a neutral town and that dissent status can spread to your own cities.
I never thought that dissent was particularly harmful though since you’re very capable of keeping it from spreading to all your cities before the big Spanish boss comes. Since beating the Spanish is all you need to win the campaign, I’ve always found the difficulty of their fights to be a much more present threat than that of my cities dissenting against me.
Overall, the turn based strategy neat addition to the otherwise monotonous gameplay but it’s not much more than a basic element. Once you realize that the winning condition depends on succeeding the last few fights, something that is achievable regardless of how little cities you have, the lack of priority for the missions becomes a lot more apparent. I found myself just going for missions based on the benefits I wanted but having to go through the same core gameplay loop in each mission constantly reminded me of the title’s repetitive nature.

1) Neat strategy element
2) Good audio queue for when an attack is coming or when an enemy is “Broken” (missed this out in the video review, apologies)
3) Decent background variation
1) Repetitive and spammy nature – combo mixing is unsatisfyingly little
2) very exploitable juggling with the simple mechanic of swapping weapons
Aztez has some of the makings of a compelling brawler like the ability to cancel jumps or transition from hits to blocks very quickly but it fails to provide enjoyable gameplay in its fundamental mechanics. Its repetitive nature takes a lot of the replay value out of the product and that’s something that isn’t outshined by the few good things it accomplishes. As such, I’d recommend getting it at 10 to maybe 12 dollars instead of at full price.
A 15th century Actraiser with stylish visuals, Aztez is a great addition to the many fantastic releases of 2017.

I want to love Paradox games for their deep historical ambientation and some interesting mechanics. And I have played many hours (a few hundred) to this and other games that I have.
But I can not recommend this game because of its very important flaws:
The AI is A but not I. It is not very smart and do not offer any challenge to the player. You may be at war with the AI in one side of the continent, but it sends its army to attack you territories in the other side of the continent. Not very interesting at all.
The military and battle system is really bad and makes no sense. It does not allow you either to make any strategy.  I remember old MS-DOS games that were much better.
Most of the game consist in clicking a lot of buttons in the right time. This can be very annoying.
I had actually much more fun modding and changing the things in the game that I find wrong than actually playing. But Some things I can not change like the dumb AI behavior.
Maybe Paradox will improve and eliminate some of these flaws in the future, and will make great games to enjoy. Until them, I can not completely recommend this game.

KOTOR (as the cool kids call it) is; put simply; a classic. If you've enjoyed newer BioWare titles such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age, you will enjoy Knights of the Old Republic.
Following a battle system very similar to Dragon Age, KOTOR puts you in the shoes of a force sensitive character trying to survive, find his (or her) place in the universe, and deciding between the call of the light side or the pull of the dark side. Of course you've got to save the universe somewhere along the way.
This game shines in always giving you the option to CHOOSE how to do things. Will you help that troubled person, or destroy them? Will you show charity, or rob the helpless of what little they have? Whether you are a Star Wars fan or not, this is a must play. Very few games give you an experience like this.
The gameplay is no slouch either, with deep customization, party choices, and force powers to train and use. If you're a fan of RPGs, Star Wars, or video games in general, get this!

I purchased Ark Evolved and played this game through the custom games menu long before it was standalone. Ark Survival of the Fittest more fun and lasting than Ark Survival Evolved, and it is free.
SOTF is 35-minute matches similar to the Hunger Games. Last man standing, everyone starts naked in the middle and gets forced back to middle by the end of the match. This is an eSport game and the top 10 ladder players each month win cash prizes, up to $3500 for being rank #1 and $700 for rank #10 in *each ladder*. There is no cash shop *at all*. It is meant to compete, not to make friends and build a community. It is a "rinse and repeat" game - you start over at level 1 and naked each match.
Ark: Survival Evolvedis similar to Rust but with Dinosaurs, however the official servers will never be wiped and there are no plans for new servers anytime soon. This means playing Ark: Survival Evolved is playing at the mercy of the Alpha Tribe who has invested thousands of combined hours to make their bases and their dinosaurs 100% invulnerable to you. The only way to succeed in Evolved as a new player is to farm thousands of cementing paste and buy your way into the Alpha Tribe.
Unless you are a core member of an existing Alpha Tribe I doubt you will play Evolved for more than two weeks. It takes this much time to build the basics, have some fun and realize that everything you do is futile when a single Giga destroys your entire base in seconds.
Survival of the fittest however has no futile efforts. It is really just a quick competition of your combat prowess and building rotation. I have won as a dino tamer. I have won as a marksman with guns or arrows. I have won games by default because everyone else died. I have won with explosives and with narcotic tripwire. And I have lost many more times again.
I will play Evolved again one day, when more official servers are released. There is no reason to be a slave for an Alpha Tribe when you can carve your own glory, gaining rank and prize money in SOTF.

"Love at First Sight" is a short yet extremely charming visual novel,  set within typical school life, but with atypical characters.
The characters are few, but they all endearing and all contribute to the flavour of the story
Sachi, the heroine, is a timid and quiet girl that is "ocularly challenged".
Mamoru, the protagonist, is a transfer student who happens to be easy going, kind and is immediately, yet inexplicably, drawn to Sachi.
Tomoyori and Akemi are Mamoru's friends, both individually unique in personality, yet caring and accepting of each other and those around them.
Lesser of the cast of characters is Sachi's aunt, Mayumi, and of course, the bully Rui. However, these two offer support to and insight into Sachi's character and condition.
The graphics are refreshingly unique in style, working well within the context of the story and create a captivating atmosphere. Creepy cute.....
Although basic and synthed, the soundtrack works well, adding texture to the unvoiced story and supporting the unique atmosphere. I feel it possibly has more variety than some titles that have higher production budgets or larger support staff in spite of the DIY nature of the music.
Although a short and unvoiced story, it is nonetheless captivating and character attachment develops easily. The protagonist isn't a complete imbecile, and stays true to the name, Mamoru  (Japanese for "protect"). The heroine, Sachi, may be "ocularly challenged", but is a very cute character that is easily loved.
Even though the author makes apologies for his creations shortcomings within the extras, I find no need to criticise the work.
Rather, Love at First Sight is a new favourite of mine, was time well and enjoyably spent, with a pittance of an investment required.
Don't hesitate. Buy it. Enjoy it. Love it (at first sight)!

A short kinetic visual novel, Love at First Sight: Hitomebore is a solo project by the artist Ray-K.
The plot is a fairly standard high school love-story/drama with an unusual character; Usui Satsi (or Sachi, as this official release has localized her name as). The story is warm for the most part, and touches on typical subjects in high school that come with being an "odd one out".
That being said, there isn't a whole lot to get out of this read if you aren't already predisposed to a few things:
A) Liking Ray-K's cute and macabre artwork.
B) Finding cyclops girls to be the most precious thing in the world (who doesn't?).
C) You don't have stupidly high expectations because you've actually read (or tried to read) more than just the popular, cream of the crop VNs (with even some of those not actually being that good).
I'll be frank, $10 is a steep price for this short read. There's nothing new or unprecedented here, just a small solo project that's well put-together for the most part. Ray-K is responsible for everything except some of the music and of course, the Ren'py engine.
However, as a fan of Ray-K's art and general curiosity after skipping through an untranslated demo he released a while back, I was pleasantly surprised to see it translated and released here. I didn't hesitate at all to purchase it.
The game actually includes some nice extras: character profiles, stages of development, and some bonus scenes, but some are left untranslated at the moment. Hopefully that will be changed in the future.
The creator, Ray-K, admits it wasn't ultimately near his original vision in an Afterword that's included, but is very satisfied he was able to make a game featuring his character, Usui Satsi.
But yeah, buy this game so you can learn to love cyclops girls if for some reason you already don't and earn some cute trading cards.

I'll preface with: I think the idea of this game is golden. I would love to play a game and learn a new language while having some level of fun and immersion.
This isn't that, but it's a good start.

But it certainly doesn't get you to conversational level and for someone brand-new to their language, it's just... not good. But if you know how to conjugate a verb and what articles to use for which nouns, then it's a pretty o.k. tool for an incredibly limited amount of words. It isn't really worth the price right now- You can pick up a children's book from the native country for cheaper and probably get about the same experience.
tl;dr: love the medium. hopeful of more places to go in the future, until then, overpriced and underwhelming.

Honestly, this is the fantasy-flavored Civilization/4X game that I've always wanted.
In a nutshell, you're building a civilization on a dying planet on which winters are getting longer and harsher. You have the usual supremacy/extermination/diplomacy victory conditions that you expect, but you also have access to some RPG elements. Each faction has a lore quest that leads to a victory. And along the way, you also have the opportunity to take on other lore based quests, and outfit your heroes and armies as you see fit.
The heroes are another interesting mechanic. Apart from leading your armies (think generals in Civ, or hero units in Warcraft III), they can also be assigned as governors to your cities, with a skill tree specific to governance.
The lore and worldbuilding is, in my opinion, some of the best in the fantasy genre I've seen in quite some time. Each faction is unique beyond their unit designs/builds, and each gives you specific goals to work toward.
THe only caveat - if you're coming from or prefer straight 4X games like Civ or Master of Orion, you may be put off by the focus on questing and lore.
Also - the devs are pretty great, with another upcoming faction expansion. Definitely a buy.

The prototype was already a blast, and what it lacked in features it made up for with a hilarious setting and a fantastic, fresh, original gameplay.

So what is this about, you ask?
The game title already gives you a hint: It's an insult simulator (DUH)
Think Monkey Island's sword fights, but with silly Monty Python dialogue.
Two characters start a sort of wang measuring contest over a silly situation (originally inspired by Monty Python - Nudge, nudge, wink, wink). You take turns to select a sentence fragment out of a pool, and when you are done or can't choose more fragments, you speak your insult. This will hurt the other person to a greater or lesser degree (think getting hit by your enemy in a Beat 'em Up) until your health bar is gone.
Make the insults as silly as you want (don't be
goofy or you may not hit hard - see below), but take care not to make a nonsense sentence, or else your character will stutter and loose the insult.
All characters have a weak spot you can exploit (for example, the old lady is susceptible to death related insults), and repeatedly hitting the same target (Your son / your mother / your country) results in bonus points.
How the score (or the "damage") for an insult is computed is a bit of a mystery (beyond the mentioned combos and weak spots), and there
an RNG element to the game's fragment pool (you are sometimes painfully missing "and" to continue adding insults, for example) but that's part of the fun, so roll with it you nitpicky fop.

Here's a game that shows promise, only to fall flat on its face at the end. The game's beginning is unbelievably charming, with a simple mechanic: gameplay evolves, bit-by-bit, slowly adding color/music/new mechanics, changing how the game looks and plays every few minutes. However, the last two hours or so, the game suddenly runs out of new things to try and just tries to be Final Fantasy 7, including unavoidable, uninspired JRPG battles (where your characters have only three or four abilities at most) that never really lead to any sense of progression, making them feel more like a chore than a core part of the gameplay. Somehow, this four-hour game (being generous) manages to feel longer and more drawn-out than many console RPGs I've played, simply due to changing its mind what kind of game it wants to be partway through.
This game could have been great, but in the end all it can do is imitate what came before and hope greatness ensues from referential humor and "classic" gameplay. It doesn't, because the game fails to understand what made old games appealing and doesn't capitalize on its few original ideas as well as it could've. One of the greatest disappointments in my Steam library.

Influent is a relatively interesting style of "game" to aid in the building of vocabulary.  By associating what is familair with the foreign language, it speeds up the memorization of the new words.  By looking around and highlighting a given item, you can get the name for it in the requested language.  The learning is context based, so it helps bridge the gap that having the translation often leads in learning.
Like most vocabulary programs/books/tapes, it is no substitute for a qualified teacher, but if you have one, then this makes an excellent supplement.
Overall, I would reccomend this game to aid students of a foreign language, but I cannot reccomend any game that does not allow key remapping.

Though I will reccomended this game from a gameplay standpoint, this review is a critical look at MGSV as a product. While I certainly enjoy the gameplay Ground Zeroes offers, there is no reason this game was not offered as a free demo as opposed to a paid product. There is only one story mission, and it will take you a little over an hour to complete. I always assumed the complaints about the games runtime were an exaggeration; but they are far from it. This is essentially a 15$ demo with some quick and cheap side content plastered on to make it feel like less of a rip off.
The major defense thrown up by most fans is that there is content outside the main mission, which is only somewhat true. The side missions, while fun, can hardly be considered "content." Each of the 6 side missions take place in the same map the main mission does, but with a different objective.  One has you destroy anti-air emplacements, another has you identify and assasinate two targets. In other words, there is nothing these missions have to offer that the main one doesn't. Ground Zeroes is essentially the same mission in the same place 6 times, each with slight differences.
These minor distractions are better than nothing, sure, but the design philosophy of Ground Zeroes seems to be in allowing players to complete the game in whatever way they please. No two playthroughs of the main mission are really the same; in my first attempt I snuck into the main base through a side entrance, but in another I hopped into the back of a truck and entered the Admin complex that way. Sometimes my plans follow through flawlessly, other times I find myself dodging enemy fire and desperately hoping the escape helicopter won't be gunned down.
It's this same non-linear design that makes the side missions feel spectacularly pointless. The side missions offer nothing that the main mission doesn't. They only really exist to create the illusion of meaningful content and to make the purchase feel more worthwhile when it really isn't. This problem is amplified by the fact that  some of the side missions completely fail to maintain the high level of freedom that the main mission offers. The perfect example of this is the mission where you have to destroy the Anti-Air emplacements so the base can be bombed. When the C4 is detonated, the alarm is sounded, forcing the base to be under alert. I attempted to get around thisby stealthily placing C4 on each of the turrets and then waiting until the evac helicopter arrived outside the base to detonate them. As it turns out, the player is still required to destroy the tank that spawns after the turrets are destroyed, so rather than flying away from the base and allowing me to complete the mission stealthily, the helicopter proceeded to fly aimlessly over the base and be shot at by the tank and the soldiers in the base.  For a game that seems to pride itself on how non-linear it is, I find these sorts of things to be highly unacceptable.
These complaints will probably seem quite nitpicky to someone who hasn't played the game, but given both the design of the game and the small amount of content it provides, the only way to get your money's worth is to play the game over and over again. And through repeat playings, it can become obvious how flawed Ground Zeroes is. The decision to sell and package Ground Zeroes as it's own game has only served to hurt it. If Ground Zeroes were released as a free demo without all the extra bells and whistles, the controversy behind this title would be non-existent. But instead it's made Metal Gear fans skeptical towards the future of the franchise, made consumers skeptical towards the future of the video game industry, and has given detractors of the series more ammunition.
The gaming industry is still young. There are many different ideas and philosophies as to what makes a game worth paying for and many publishers are attempting to push boundaries to see what they can get away with. Even if this game were merely a means of gathering money for the development of Phantom Pain, this practice still feels incredibly dishonest. In capitalism we vote with our money, and by buying games like Ground Zeroes and attempting to defend them as products we are telling publishers like Konami that we are okay with them selling tech demos for exorbitant prices. The fact that so many Metal Gear fans were hurt and upset by the runtime shows exactly how dishonest this practice is. When the game was released it was 40$, and when you buy a 40$ game, you expect a certain amount of content. Many of the people who paid that much for this game were tricked into thinking it would be something more, something worthy of having the legendary Metal Gear name on the box and something the developers deemed worthy of 40$, but instead what they got was a tech demo with a few collectibles and little more.
I can only really reccomend this game if you are a hardcore fan of the series and want to support the development of The Phantom Pain.The story is great, the gameplay is great, the graphics and animations are great but the package it's presented in is not. I don't regret my purchase. I've played it for 9 hours now and intend to continue playing it, but it just seems so ridiculous to ask anyone to spend money on it, even if the current 15$ asking price isn't nearly as bad as it was. Wait for a drastic sale to pick this one up, unless you just want to support Kojima and encourage him to continue porting his games to PC -- which he has done an excellent job with thus far. I really want to love this game, and to some extent I do, but I still can't shake the feeling that I've been ripped off by whoever decided to sell the game this way.

What makes Endless Legend stick out in my mind from any 4X game I've ever played is the wide differences between each playable race. Most 4X games have each playable race/nation/faction able to achieve victory with some adjustments to compensate for their "unique" characteritics, which comed down to some +/- modifiers to stats. In Endless Legend the races have some entire features of the game unavailable to them, like the use of diplomacy or use of more than one resource type. Each time you play with a different race you have to play by their own rules.
On the downside the AI is pretty dumb. Winning becomes less of a challenge once you figure out how to best use the idiosyncrasies of the race you're using. Aside from that, the sheer novelty of having such a wide gulf in playstyles is enough to sell me on the game.

As a big fan of the Star Wars Franchise I’ve delved into the expanded universe through reading some of the novel’s watching the movies and television shows and of course playing the games. As with the other Star Wars games I was very excited to try this one out. The title ‘Knights of the Old Republic’ just brought up fantasies of fighting with a lightsabers and force powers, exploring galaxies, and enjoying a deep and captivating narrative. I am happy to say that all of these fantasies came true. SWKOTOR is not only one of the most enjoyable Star Wars videogames, but it lands in my top five of videogames of all time.
From start to finish the player is just captured by the World, characters and gameplay systems implemented in this RPG. You start off as a soldier, scout or scoundrel and end as a guardian, sentinel or a consular of the light side, dark side or even somewhere in between that. The story has a good twist near the end of it and is perfectly paced. The other characters in the game are fully realized, having their own backstories and missions, making this Star Wars experience so satisfying and engrossing.
The combat system is smart and allows for a wide variety of strategies that will have to be thought out by you to emerge victorious. You are almost always allowed to have two other characters with you in a party as you explore the planets in the galaxy. You’re allowed to save your progress at any time and can talk to pretty much anybody. There are also two other side activities to do that are actually quite fun in addition to the side missions. The first of these side activities involves a card game called pazaak where you can win, or lose some credits. The second comes in the form of land speeder racing circuits which are available on three of the planets. You can also win a considerable amount of credits doing this. These credits can be spent at different stores and cantinas on weapon mods, armor enhancements and such. You can upgrade your weapons and armor via workbenches found around the world and on your ship, yes that’s right you get a ship, how else would you travel the galaxy at will? They thought of everything for this game and implemented it in the best way possible. If you love role playing games you should definitely set aside some time to play this, I have played this three to five times on the original Xbox and plan to play it some more on the PC, I strongly advise you to do the same on the PC since you’re reading this.
This is my favourite RPG to Date, and possibly the best Star Wars game ever created.

Oh, this brings me back to the days of Super Puzzle Fighter. It revived the idea beautifully, with Powerful satirical (and generally respectful) Plays on Precursor comic icons and tropes for the flavour. My interest was Piqued Past the Proverbial face of the game, especially by the varied character mechanics that were more than just counter-block Pattern differences. The addition of specials and supers, abilities available after generating enough Points from block-breaking, compelled me to test out more than just one or two characters. The abilities were unique enough; some options had similar use, but the difference in implementation was enough so that nothing felt redundant.
I'd recommend this to almost anyone, from casual Players to those experienced in the genre. Good times, good design, and it isn't even done yet!

Let's not beat around the bush here.
It IS a Super Puzzle Fighter Clone, with power ups, based in a superhero universe. Plays well, controller compatibility is a plus for a title like this, and the music and graphics will take you back with nostalgia thrills. But in all honesty, for a puzzle title like this, the retro arcade graphics probably work better than something brushed up and smoothed with complex textures. This makes the game feel more raw and likable, and five or ten years from now could still be enjoyed without cringing a little.
The Normal setting was a bit of a cakewalk, so I'm yet to try my luck with the hard setting.
The "superpowers" that are character specific is a very neat touch to the gameplay. Instead of generic power-ups for everyone, each person gets their own power that is best used in certian situations over others. Professor Puzzler's power is by far one of the most annoying personally.
Online and local multiplayer is a plus and overall; if you like drop style puzzle games that have or have the potential to be competitive, this is a definite buy. An absolute MUST if it's on sale.

The stealth sandbox that I always wanted. Gameplaywise, it's pretty much the best MGS has ever been. However, the alert system feels like a step down from previous games in the series: whereas from MGS2 onwards guards would have to contact their base with the radio (which you could shoot down) to trigger an alert, in this game everyone in the base will know about you the moment a guard says "Huh?". This is mitigated by the reflex mode which triggers a slow motion when you are spotted, but it feels like a cheap clutch.
Storywise, it's hard to judge this game without knowing what TPP has in store, but it does have some moments of dialogue that are a bit cringe-worthy.
Graphically, this game is a technical wonder. It runs on a huge variety of systems and looks absolutely amazing in any modern system.
Finally, regarding content, this is a demo that already sucked 10 hours of my life. The main story mission will take you an hour or two to complete, but there are 5 additional missions, all taking place in the same map, which add a few hours to the game if you enjoy the gameplay. Even if you're in it just for the story, you owe it to yourself to at least collect all the cassette tapes.

Someone else has said that only Hideo Kojima could get away with charging money for a Tech-Demo and they were absolutely right. Hideo Kojima did this game right and further more, he did the port right too. :) If you are a fan of the MGS games or of Tactical Espionage games in general, then pull up a chair and plop down your money for you will not regret buying this.
I personally love how you can choose to focus on just the objectives or rescue everyone and you get to choose how you do it too. Be it full on stealth (I hope you're better at it than I am) or going full "Loud and Proud" you won't go wrong either way. As for the story, it is very nicely done. Like VERY nicely done. Complete with a backstory.

A very well written take on the classic Cinderella tale. Part of what made the game for me was how three dimensional the characters are. In the original tale the step mother and sisters were such evil caricatures that they are as realistic as any pantomime villian (i.e not at all). In Cinders, while still mostly despicable, they are fleshed out and given realistic motivations for their actions and that helps the whole tale resonate much more. There are quite a few paths through based on what descisions you make during conversations so there is some replay value, though you will have to sit through quite a bit of the same text and dialogue if you wish to see them all, as often the variations aren't major until the end. All in all a fantastic visual novel with a story that will continually surprise you with the turns it takes while at the same time making you laugh with its witty dialogue and gentle pokes at traditional fairy tales.
Pros:
Excellent writing
Full of twists and surprises
Well realized characters
Awesome soundtrack
Multiple endings
Cons:
Getting all the endings can be a bit of a chore

Most 4X games have each playable race/nation/faction able to achieve victory with some adjustments to compensate for their "unique" characteritics, which comed down to some +/- modifiers to stats. In Endless Legend the races have some entire features of the game unavailable to them, like the use of diplomacy or use of more than one resource type. Each time you play with a different race you have to play by their own rules.
On the downside the AI is pretty dumb. Winning becomes less of a challenge once you figure out how to best use the idiosyncrasies of the race you're using. Aside from that, the sheer novelty of having such a wide gulf in playstyles is enough to sell me on the game.

This game proves that Civilization isn't the last word in civilization-building strategy games.
The game excels at coming up with new ideas and gameplay mechanics that manage to make it play quite differently from the aforementioned game while still having the same general premise.
While the game obviously takes place in a fantasy world but it goes to great lengths to bring life to clichés while still including them among more unique creations. In fact they incorporated this into the same universe as Endless Space, using many of the same elements in the lore providing for an excuse to re-use many of the same natural resources from the other game, which also facilitated some of the incorporation of gameplay elements from the other game such as population assignment.
On game play you are not only competing against the other AIs, who on normal difficulty are basically no threat, but against time as the planet is dying, manifesting in increasingly cruel winters which apply cumulative random effects and last for longer and longer each summer/winter cycle.
The combat is innovative if infuriating at times, not having total control of your own units during battle, however I would rather have the developers experiment than rehash something more conventional.
The research tree is balanced, as you have to prioritize things you need as by the time you have researched everything you could have already won or lost.
The city building is quite interesting, having one city per region and that city having jurisdiction over everything in the region is one thing that really makes Endless Legend different from Civilization and it works quite well.
The quest system is quite annoying however, you can randomly get un-researchable technologies form them which can give you a large advantage in a particular area, however they are random and it is quite vexing to try and get them, the rewards are random so if you want to you can just save scum again and again till you get the reward you want. Most quests are just a pain in the neck and I try to avoid them.
Diplomacy is a bit underpowered. With enough influence points to spend you can go from allied to war in a single turn without any kind of consequence. And it is not like you can even coordinate with your allies making it more like, if you happen to be there at the right time you can team up…
While there are some things about this game I don't like, a few bugs technical bugs, some annoying game play, I like this game quite a lot. I like it more because it promises even more innovative games in the future.

Como mencionamos en una nota anterior, los Kickstarter son un buen método de inversión para comenzar y desarrollar un proyecto. Uno de los focos principales son los videojuegos. ¿Qué pasa si esto lo juntamos con otro tema popular hoy en día que son los super héroes? Podemos conseguir cosas como Heroes Never Lose: Professor Puzzler’s Perplexing Ploy, si, ese es el nombre.
Heroes Never Lose comenzó como un proyecto en Kickstarter que luego fue creciendo hasta lograr su objetivo (cosa que es difícil en éste mercado) y así poder salir a la luz con ese extraño y largo nombre. Desarrollado por Magic Pants y publicado por Spearhead, Heroes Never Lose salió al mercado el 23 de Noviembre de éste año, llevándose una muy buena recepción del público.
Te nombré superheroes y si, podríamos decir que el juego tiene algo de temática estilo fighting, pero no es como te lo estás imaginando. Si tuvieramos que describir la temática podríamos decir que es un juego casual, de esos con puzzles. Para hacerla fácil, es similar al tetris.
Exísten varias opciones de juego. Podemos jugar el modo Arcade, Versus, y también Online. En cada uno de los modos tenemos una amplia selección de personajes, lo cual es lo mas distintivo del juego. El diseño de personajes es algo a destacar, al igual que la descripción de los mismos. Muchos son personajes bastante estereotipados pero con una vuelta de tuerca. Claramente, todos son una especie de super-héroe o villano con distintas cualidades y stats. Algunos te van a recordar a personajes de cómics muy vistos.
Una vez tenemos nuestro personaje elegido podemos jugar contra la máquina, contra otro jugador que se encuentre con nosotros si es que lo jugamos en consola, o contra otro jugador online. Todos los modos se componen del mismo puzzle, un tipo de Tetris en el que tenés que ir alineando cuadritos de colores para formar combos o cadenas que te darán puntos. Esos puntos son recolectables y sirven para conseguir poderes que podrás usar contra tu adversario. Cuantos más puntos juntes mayor será el daño que hagas luego. La barra de poder se va llenando en tres instancias, siendo la última una especie de super combo que le hará casi imposible ganar a tu contrincante.
Otro detalle que se destaca en éste juego son los diálogos. Si, tiene dialogos. Claramente no muchos porque se basa en otra cosa, pero usualmente a lo alrgo del juego los personajes tiran comentarios divertidos que hacen de la experiencia de juego mucho más dinámica.
La música es otro factor a favor ya que al no ser el mejor juego indie del mundo, le aporta mucho, además de ser muy pegadiza. (Acordate de mi cuando estés tarareándola todo el día). El estilo chiptune definitivamente es lo que mejor encaja en estos juegos.
Si bien no es una recomendación absoluta, definitivamente es algo que hay que jugar ya que no es un puzzle típico como la mayoría, tiene sus vueltas y es bastante divertido. Ideal para pasar una tarde con amigos y reírse un rato con los comentarios tan inteligentes de nuestros personajes.
Puede conseguirse en Steam y también está disponible para WiiU.

In fact it goes really well with Duolingo, which is much stronger on grammar but weak on a lot of very basic, everyday vocabulary that is present here. It's also a little bit less of a game than a gamified study tool, because how well you do really depends on how much you put into it. If you just fly through the time attacks and gather up words, your retention won't be that good. If you have the patience to limit yourself to, say, 20 words per session, 10 nouns and 10 verbs/adjectives, and replay the Time Attacks with various options on and off, it's a great way to learn the vocabulary in a visual context.
This is an extremely effective tool.

I want to make it clear before I go on that I
recommend this game,
only as a supplement to other language learning avenues.
This game is great for helping you memorize the common words for common objects you might find around a household. I was playing for only about an hour and I could already walk around the apartment and 100% a time attack challenge for my first vocab list in Swedish. However it's not going to teach you a language. It doesn't teach you sentence structure or grammar, it doesn't explain inflections or even usage in a pre-built sentence.
This game is purely a game of memory. See an item, learn the word for that item, with no additional context. It would be excellent for a person trying to sharpen up their vocabulary recollection on a language they're already at least partially familiar with, but as a tool for teaching you a whole new language it's absolutely not an option.
Clearly a lot of hard work has gone into this game and hopefully it continues to receive updates to make it more useful, broaden the scope of its teaching and address some issues with spelling in some of the other language packs. For now I think I need to go and find an actual teacher to learn this new language and at best I'll use this to help me along the way once I've already grasped the basics.

There are very, very few games that ever make me want to say: "Even if you don't like or care about {X}, play this game anyway." As someone who thinks deeply about game mechanics and play styles, I understand not everyone will enjoy certain games.
That said: even if you don't like or care about visual novels, play this game anyway.
Cinders retells the fairy tale we are all familiar with -- and walks a fine line betwen the lighthearted enchanted Disney version or the dark, sadistic Brothers Grimm. Well rounded, fleshed out characters (even for the "evil" and minor characters) gives this a vibrant color and tone that is often missing, both from fairy tales or from games. Rather than giving certain endings an official seal of approval, Cinders uses this potential ambiguity to allow players to ask themselves what the "best" ending should look like.
All in all, this results in a thoughtful and "political" game -- not through design choices or the author's intent to make a specific statement, but merely by reflecting the player's choices back to them in a realistic and candid fashion.

The game is really replaying and roleplaying - all your choices have their consequences that may not appear now, but take place later, when you almost forgot about them, so chose wisely. You have many possibilities to turn story in your favor, every ending has many variants and sometimes its change the tone of an ending completely. Your Cinders can be kind and modest, wise and bold, egoistic and rude - all this changes the story that you'll see. I really recomend you to try and play, especially if you fan of visual novels or choices and consequences games. Cinders really worth a shot. First note this is after completing all paths, and alternate endings/etc. So this is a full review on the entire game and my personal opinion/s.
I'd suggest the game to others but I have played better VN's for the same price with artwork that was just as well done, which had voice acting and a longer story. Cinders feels short but it does have a good story/alternate endings.
Artwork - 9.5/10.
* Cinders' facial anatomy is uneven in an unnattractive way and some expressions make her eyes rotate which uh they don't do in real life. Also the prince has a lazy eye.
* Overall graphically the game looks great. It really does, it has a french painting type feel to the entire game, and it has wonderful coloring/shading
Story/Gameplay - 8/10.
* The story does change depending on what choice you make, but without looking up the wikia page of Cinders, there's  no way of knowing what skill you gain or didn't gain by choosing that option. It isn't always obvious what the smart/bad/good choices were.
* Having a meter on the left side of the page would be super helpful as there's a lot of unused space there. (Spoiler following.)
* Half point loss for me is lacking the ability to go back and see moments such as the (spoiler)
. For me collecting the extra scenes/memories is half the fun in VN's. Cinders lacks this.
* Half point loss also goes to the fact that the game controls are NOT the same as -most- other VN's, Having skip be keybound to left CTRL is a major annoyance, as the windows key is right beside it for my computer. :/  plus due to the location of the windows key on a US based keyboard. left control is not optimal.[/spoiler]
Music - 6/10.
* The music does not loop seamlessly and it is quite noticeable, not to mention there is NO IN GAME VOLUME ADJUSTMENT OPTION. The game's music by default is -too loud.- This game lacks voice acting, so I did expect more out of the music in the game.
Possible Bugs and updates to think about? -
* When in the options menu, right clicking in attempt to return back to the game. causes the screen resolution of the game in windowed mode to switch resolution, which might be intentional but is very annoying especially to those of us who play many other VN's and right click normally exits menus/enters them no matter which page you're on.
* The steam overlay is missing the ability to resize itself to the size of the window, meaning that it's rendered entirely useless the user is playing in full screen, which some may do, but I personally dislike doing as I often have friends in other chat clients, and as such may need to alt-tab to a different window. There's a fix for this although I'm not sure how, I do know that it does resize in other games however.
* The text speed is uneven at times or lags and suddenly slingshot-text superspeeds across the UI screen, which made me skip several lines while on autoplay in Normal. AND I could not scroll back far enough to re-read/ There's no actual Script page with the full scene. As such - had I not already played Cinders once, I would have been entirely lost on the story. There's a limit to how fast a person can read, even on the Normal speed it would randomly speed up. This isn't new to the steam release either. It's been there since I purchased the game originally. Pleeaaaase at the very least fix this.
* If you attempt to skip text by pressing control once or twice the dialogue box disappears entirely, which obviously skipping text so whatever. But - when doing so sometimes the UI text box would be -gone- which also made the text-skip for that part of the game super quick. Bug methinks.

This was a hard game to get people into, especially if one has a bad taste from the MOBA-genre in general, but now it's damn near impossible to get newer folks to play. I love the characters, abilities, graphic style, and the flow of the fight especially in a team of friends, but some recent updates have marred the former image of Awesomenauts.
For players from the pre-XP system era, like myself, some are able to work past the changes but almost all of us dislike the system for a number of reasons. Notice though how I said "work." The shorter game span and snowballing was really not necessary since there already was a leveling system in place before (Solar currency and maxing items on a character).
But now that system is still in effect... with an additional layer of HP and damage % upgrades doled out instantly for player kills and droid/creep kills. There's no strategy involved with that; it's merely a grind to see who is a better farmer. Making this not only like "other MOBA games" but also causing players to play more selfishly, stealing health creeps for XP instead saving for a heal, or ignoring a push and focusing on kills.
I still recommend this game because it's near and dear to me - but it has a steeper learning curve than it previously had without any real value added, unfortunately.

Do not buy this game.
The Playerbase is openly hostile, fueled by issues plagueing it since its release.
The Multerplayer-Servers are actually peer-to-peer, so lagging is commonplace.
But being a lagger actually has an advantage, since the enemy can barely hit you teleporting all over the place, especially if they are playing a character requiring precise aim.
These issues have lead to many new players fleeing the game and therefore a stretched-thin playerbase.
Matchmaking is terrible and commonly matches you with players of insanely deviating skill-level.
The difference in the upper ranks is staggering, with singular people being able to shift the entire game, while in the lower leagues you tend to be paired with incapable people, therefore losing you rank and keeping you stuck in their group.
The only way out is being in a premade group of people you know.
Solo-Qers are heavily disadvantaged since there is no solo-q-only matchmaking.
There is also no unranked matchmaking, therefore you HAVE to play with people who are either not as competetive if you or hyper-competetive while you maybe just want to try out some new characters.
This has led to an insanely hostile playerbase, with many being frustrated by the perceived injustices that exist since its release.
Many prematurely leave games because it can be economical to leave a game that would drag on for 10 more minutes and most certainly lead to your defat anyway.
And since there is no real punishment, many players do this, which in most cases dooms the current game for his teammates.
These problems all existed for years. They are all known to the developers.
But they are not addressing them over fears of further segregating its small playerbase possibly leading to mass exodus.
So the game is slowly dying, entertaining few and frustrating many.

Let me start off by saying that Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a game for those that would consider themselves avid fans of the Metal Gear Solid series. It provides a brief but satisfying glimpse at the game play mechanics of the upcoming title Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. Game play is fun and fluid. The stealth mechanics are solid and you can go about completing the mission in a multitude of different ways. After completing the abysmally short campaign, you are given a few more side missions to complete in the same small map, Camp Omega. Gorgeous VN, providing a nice variation from the mainly anime style VNs available. The character designs are beautiful, they are also pleasingly expressive for the amount of detail on each of them. (I'd gladly buy a poster of madame Ghede or the fairy to hang on my wall, if one were available :L) The backgrounds are wonderfully atmospheric, particularly around the fairies' lake, perfect for the fairytale story it's based on. The music also attributes to this atmosphere setting the tone for each scene.
The characters are enjoyable, the opportunity to work with Cinders' step-family was a nice variation to the original story. Cinders also stood out as she was a very likeable protagonist, with a lot of personality.
The major con of this game is it's length, there are relatively few endings, it would have been nice to see more possible love interests/lifestyle paths for Cinders as a lot more of it is based on who is allied with her at the end and whether she is good, or bad. You can finish most, if not all, endings in one sitting, so it, unfortunately, has little replay value story-wise.
Overall, I'd recommend Cinders as a beautiful and atmospheric experience, utilising it's game qualities to enhance the events taking place. My only wish is that there were more events.
TLDR: atmospheric & beautiful art, with interesting characters, but is relatively short/has fewer endings than most other VNs.

This was such a refreshing and interesting visual novel. It took me four hours to get through the story and get my ending but I did it in one sitting. I simply couldn't stop playing!

A well-written, beautifully drawn, and gorgeously scored gem.  The characters are all multifaceted, and you genuinely root for all of them.  (Making the "evil stepsisters" sympathetic was an artful twist.)  This reminded me of why I love the visual novel genre, and what it can do.

Cinders, a twist on the classic Cinderella fairy tale, is all about its characters. It has all the elements of Cinderella: A ball, a prince you can pursue, evil stepsisters and stepmother, and a fairy godmother. However, Cinders herself is a strong, optimistic, and self-reliant woman capable of taking her future into her own hands. Her stepsisters and stepmother are well developed characters that you can get to know and maybe even understand. The fairy godmother isn't perfect and neither is the prince. Add to that the Captain, the town witch, and Cinder's old friend the merchant, and you have a variety of extremely interesting characters with their own stories and complicated relations to you and each other. Throughout the game, your interactions with them and your decisions for Cinders helps her decide which path to freedom to take. Each broad ending has a variety of unique and lovely sub-types.
If this hasn't told you this game is worth playing, then add to that the lovely artwork with small background animations and very realistic and expressive character art, the beautiful music, and the tiny fact that the dialogue speed matches the speed of the character speaking. This last fact really helps you mentally hear how people are speaking. Honestly, it's as close as you can get to voice acting without actually having voice acting in it.
tl;dr Go play Cinders. It's amazing. 10/10

Cinders is a choose your own adventure visual novel. It is a re-telling of the classic Cinderella story. The writing, artwork, music, sound effects and characters are all surprisingly well done. The gameplay is smooth and the dialog is entertaining and not boring, even though we all know the basis of the story. There are many decisions to make throughout, and each decision changes the story and leads to multiple endings. Not only are there multiple endings, but several variations of each ending, depending on the choices made. When re-playing to find alternate endings, you have options to skip dialog that was previously encountered. That was a great idea by the developer because having to click through all the dialog again would have been a drag. Overall this visual novel sets a high bar in the genre and I have no complaints. Recommended.

This isn't your typical anime visual novel......and that is what makes this game fantastic!

Your answers/choices make impact on lots of elements: what kind of person will Cinderella become (trust me, this Cinders can become anything: scary child that lives in her dreams; cold and calculative; seductive lady that wants everything...and everyone...and gets what she wants; a bad girl...in lot of ways), relationship with family (with surprising outcomes), her love life (and we are not talking just about the prince...), even how will she end her life (this game is not all about "living happily ever after", trust me)...
Story and characters itselves are well well written and shaped.
Overall, this is not just great visual novel, this a great game by itself.

Victoria II is another great grand strategy game brought to you by Paradox Interactive. My favorite feature is perhaps the population system that is very in-depth. Basically you have pops which represent a group in a certain province, in a state, in a country. Pops can be soldiers, artisans, carpenters, and on and on. Pops have political leaning and can be influenced, they can be killed, migrate, and assimilate. While Victoria II does have a learning curve, it only took me several hours to get the hang of how the game works. It will be quite easy if you are used to other Paradox titles, however you will notice differences. The population as mentioned above is one. Another is Spheres of Influence which mirrors the tributary system in EU4 in a way. In conclusion, Victoria II is a great game, I recommend you pick it and it's DLC's up whenever they go on sale.

The economy system is incredibly difficult to understand, and isn't fun once you do.  Managing populations is the same, and if you watch a lets play on youtube, you'll be treated to exciting "whack a mole" nonsense staring at a diplomacy bar.
Do yourself a favor and buy Europa Universalis IV, because it's actually fun to play and not needly overcomplicated, while neglecting war.
