Do you like "b" zombie movies with no production values?  Do you like zombie movies with little or no plot?  Do you like buggy zombie games that make no sense?  You can see where I am going with this...  I finished "chapters" 1 and 2 but ran into way too many issues and won't be playing chapter 3.
Game is a mish-mash of high-low card, match 3 and hidden object games and unfortunately none of them are good.
The high-low card game is basically way too easy and it seems that some of the levels were gimicky, especially at the end of each "chapter".  Each chapter had at least one level where you had to use the "zombie blaster" (a bomb) to destroy half of the layout.  If you looked in my library, you would see that I have quite a few of these type of card games, and in general the ones I have purchased have been challenging and the special cards you can buy such as wild cards, bombs, etc add nice strategy elements to the gameplay.  Here, not so much.  There are only four "power up" cards, a one card remove (Zombie Slap Baseball Bat), a two card remove (Zombie Killer Shot Gun), a whole stack remove (Zombie Blaster Bomb) and a Joker (Timed Clown).  In reality only the shotgun and the bomb are useful.  In fact I have never really seen a stack destroy or time wildcard implemented in a game like this before.  The bomb especially makes most of the "harder", later levels trivial.
Now for the match three levels.  These can not have been game tested by the devs.  The game gives you a choice of two difficulties on these levels.  First there is "normal" which has a turn limit, and in theory anyway, allows you to obtain three stars for killing all of the zombies and removing all of the special tiles from the grid.   Then there is "casual" which has no turn limit but only earns one star when the level is completed.  After about three of these levels in chapter one, you eventually figure out that "normal" mode is pretty much a waste of time.  The turn limits are extremely low and the number of zombies, the odd layouts and technical issues make them nearly impossible to win on normal.  So you might as well play "casual" and kiss some of the acheivements based on number of stars goodbye.
The hidden object levels are mainly just to move the "story" along.  They give no stars, no gold and are really just an annoyance.  Even worse in chapter 2 they become down right irritating as they give no indication what you are actually trying to find.
Then we get to the bugs and poor design descisions.  I had several times where legal moves both tn the match 3 and card levels would not register even with wild cards in the solitaire levels.  These would eventually clear up after a few frustrating minutes where the game would eventually "wake up" and accept the move.  Also in the solitaire levels, the Zombie Killer (Shotgun) and Zombie Slap (Baseball Bat) had odd behavior in that when you used them they would also draw the next card from your deck.  This eliminated all strategy in using these cards.  Say if I was trying to play on a 2, and an 8 was covering the 3 I needed, I could shotgun the 8, but then the next card was drawn and my 2 was gone.
Anyway I would not recommend these games.  I bought them on sale and am disappointed I spent money on the two chapter bundle.
Overall Rating: 3.5 / 10.

Zombie Solitaire 2, Chapter 2 is a take on the classic spider solitaire genre in a post apocalyptic scenario. In spider solitaire, you must complete a board by matching cards of any suit, one up or one down from your drawn card. This is a casual card genre that adds strategy and depth by creating complicated game boards with extra mechanics. Mechanics are mostly locked cards – cards that are locked by chains for example and need a machete to be found, OR cards that are protected by birds and need a bird deterrent to be shot. They’re pretty simple, but add a small layer of extra strategy that you need to think about. You’ll want to go for your special items first, to open up as much of the board as possible and chain those c-c-c-c-combos.
The aim is to clear the board – or get as close as you can to zero cards left. You’ll be awarded one, two or three shiny golden stars for your efforts. Who doesn’t love a gold star? Or alternatively you’ll get swarmed by zombies and have to flee and restart. I didn’t find it massively challenging to get two or three stars on most levels without using any boosts, although I’m very experienced with this genre, having played hundreds of hours of Fairway Solitaire on my iPad. If you are struggling, boosts are available in the form of specials that you buy with gold, or wild cards that you can either buy or collect randomly.  Gold rewards are generous and awarded throughout the level (so you don’t need to complete the level to get some rewards) so unless you don’t understand the concept of numbers, you’re not really going to get stuck ever.
Zombie Solitaire 2 has some fun match 3 levels that are actually significantly harder than I expected, especially as boosts aren’t available on these levels. There are also a couple of hidden puzzle backdrops to progress with the story, and a few choose-your-own-adventure style text dialogues that have different results. All these little extras give this game a fun edge that puts it ahead of just a normal solitaire game. I like the small touches and think it’s broken up well into sections that kept me interested. The graphics are cute and the story, whilst predictable, is light-hearted and amusing in places.
There are 100 levels in total, which should easily take 20+ hours to complete so there’s quite a bit of content if this is a genre you enjoy. If you’ve played chapter one, it’s more of the same – but with different boards and levels. There is enough variation there to say if you enjoyed the first one, you should enjoy more of the same but be aware the gameplay appears nearly identical. Competitively priced as a casual game, I’m happy to recommend this to fans of the solitaire / casual card genres.

A loving parody. Evoland is unquestionably that. It conjures memories of the all-time greatest RPGs, like Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, Diablo, and Dragonball Z.
Yes, that is definitely all of them. No other RPGs have ever been significant.
I can't help but gawk at the lack of content. This is supposed to be an homage to the history of RPGs? This feels like I paid for a tour of an art museum, and was shown three rooms before being thrown out onto the street. The laziness shows through at the seams. They didn't even bother arranging the small amount of content they had into a full map, instead clustering every location together and then filling three-quarters of the world with impassable mountains.
The length of the story is also a disappointment. Part of the problem might be that it does the job of reminding you of other games too well, or at the least, too bluntly. Despite the fact that many great RPGs can be completed in a single sitting, this game fails to acknowledge those games at all, choosing instead to constantly reference series that create the expectation that both the storyline and the difficulty curve will be slowly, patiently built up. However, since this game is so short, that doesn't happen. The endgame remains pitifully easy, and the "expected" RPG scenes play out in quick succession without bothering to give you enough context to make anything matter.
It doesn't even work as a parody. It's about on par with the "Movie" movies. References are not the same as jokes. The few actual jokes that could have been funny are skimmed over in favor of getting on to the next thing as quickly as possible. Don't buy this game as a gift for a friend. Buy it as a gift for an enemy. Then apologize.

So where to start with Ground Zeroes? I guess first off, I'm a fan of the MGS series as a whole, and that should certainly be a prerequisite for playing MGS:GZ. This would be a terrible starting (even though it's the first one released on PC) and is certainly not going to convince someone to love MGS if they weren't a fan before. But for those of us that enjoy the previous iterations, it's worth looking at.
The biggest caveat with this game though, is that it's crazy overpriced. You are basically paying $20 for a tech demo. I currently have 3.8 hours playtime, and that was more than enough time to complete the main mission and one of side missions, even though I took them very slowly and experimented with the mechanics rather than going for completion.
Maybe even more of an issue than the price, is how repetitive it is. $20 for a preview game with 6 missions wouldn't be so bad if they weren't pretty much all the same. The missions are all the same map, with just different objectives like rescue prisoners or sneak in and eliminate a target. Completing the missions basically means sneaking into the same base 5 times (plus 1 forced loud mission) to complete tasks that aren't really that different from each other. And if you want to complete everything, you then have to do them all again on Hard difficulty. I realize that repetition isn't completely out of character for MGS (it took at minimum of 12 playthroughs of MGS4 to unlock everything I believe), but this is even more apparent in MGS:GZ because it only consists of one short missions.
So far I've been pretty negative, but I'm also recommending the game, so I should elaborate on that. First off, the FOX engine looks incredible, and the visual presentation in this game is outstanding. I also really enjoyed the gameplay, which takes some of the better facets of MGS4 and builds on them. The enemy AI is also really fun to interact with. Here's a good example the complexity it presents. I shot out a camera at one point rather than going around it. But as soon as I did, a guard was dispatched to check it out. I hid in the area to see what happened, and sure enough, a guard came over to look at the camera. Not wanting him to report it in and set off an alarm, I tranqed him. But as I was sneaking over to his unconscious body to hide it, headquarters called his radio for a status update, and then triggered an alarm when he didn't respond. From my experience, you really have to adapt to the AI and you take a risk when you eliminate someone.
I play a lot of steath games (no kill, no alarm runs of DE:HR and Dishonored for example), and the stealth feels a little off here. Well, to be fair, it feels like MGS, but stealth games have evolved a bit since the last MGS release. Not to say that this is a bad thing, but it's just different. After playing more recent stealth games, I was surprised at the lack of safe hiding places like the vents in DE:HR. This isn't a negative, but it is a different design and keeps you on your feet a bit more.
So all in all, I really liked the presentation and gameplay, but the total package here feels a bit lacking. I'll still recommend it though because most importantly, it got me really excited for MGS5, which is really the point of it's release.
*SPOILER*
I'd be remiss if I didn't call out the bomb scene. The concept of it was fine (bomb hidden inside of a prisoner that's going to be rescued as a trap), but I really didn't like the presentation. It was overly gratuitous and rather unpleasant. The MGS franchise has always had a very skewed view on women and sexuality, but this scene crossed the line for me and I hope it isn't representative of what we'll see in MGS5.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes
What to say about this game?
I was reluctant to buy the game myself, after reading reviews saying how "short" the game was.
I received it as a Christmas present, but I can say now, I would have gladly bought it myself.
The game is as long as you want to make it.
I've played for 30+ hours now, and still keep finding things to do.
It's true, you can beat the main mission, pretty fast, depending on how you play.
If you go with a stealth aproach, the game gets that much harder, and in my opinion, that much more fun.
There are so many different ways to play.
You can go in all guns blazing, but that'll usually end up getting yourself killed.
When the "Ground Zeroes" mission is completed, you'll unlock "Side Ops" missions.
There are two "Extra Ops" missions which must be unlocked, but I'll let you figure out how to unlock those yourself.
It becomes addicting trying to achieve an S rank on all the missions.
With each rank, you'll unlock rewards, for the mission.
Higher ranks, unlock the lower rank rewards.
So, if you get an S rank, you'll get the rewards for S, A, B, C, and so on.
I'm still trying to achieve an S rank on all missions, on normal and hard difficulty.
I've replayed every mission several times through.
Each time I learn a new way to get through the mission faster, and new ways to take out the guards.
You'll get very used to the little patch of land, as every last mission takes place in the same area.
It sounds bad on paper, but it actually works out very well.
Things are changed enough, to keep you on your toes.
As you grow accustomed to the area, it makes getting through the missions that much easier.
If you don't explore, and simply do what the mission guidelines state, you'll be missing out on a lot.
I played one mission 4 times, only to realize the 5th time through when I was goofing around, there was more to the mission.
Make sure to try and interegate as many guards as you can, through-out all the missions.
I could say a whole lot more, but I don't want to spoil anything.

Do you like Super Puzzle Fighter 2 Turbo?
If you don't know what that game is, then go search it up on the internet.
The second question you must ask yourself is:
Wouldn't Super Puzzle Fighter 2 Turbo be even better if you had a Super Meter like in Street Fighter 5?
If you like versus-style reflex-puzzle games and those two questions didn't scare you off, then this game could be for you.

A unique language-learning experience. Although it can’t teach an entire language, it does allow the opportunity to pick up a few words from any of the available languages.
I selected Japanese upon opening the game, as I’m interested in learning the language, and I can say, I had a great time with the game. Don’t expect to learn the language from the game, but instead, a couple hundred words and their pronunciations (given time). And yes, I’m still terrible at pronouncing Japanese words, even with this game as a guide.
Basically, you’re placed into an apartment with various objects scattered around. You can click on anything,
, and the word for said object will be displayed and pronounced for you. It’s a pretty cool experience, being able to click on the obscurest of objects (try “ketchup”).
There’s also a few minigames to aid in the memorization of sets of words. After hearing a word, you have the opportunity to add it to a personal dictionary of sorts, which can then be used to initiate minigames. One of these games being a “time attack”-ish mode, in which you’re tasked with finding and clicking on objects in sets of ten from your personal dictionary.
Overall, Influent is a solid, educational game. It does a great job of teaching some basic words from whatever language is selected and has some pretty nifty minigames.

Cinders is a pretty fantastic visual novel, full of strong female characters and decisions that have consequences. It's a darker, more mature take on the classic Cinderella fairy tale, but with some clever twists. The artwork and music are really gorgeous and add a lot to the story. It's also worth noting that this is one of the rare visual novels that uses an art style other than anime.
The game's a bit short and even going back and playing several endings won't take much longer than a few hours. Unfortunately, there isn't a lot of replay value. While there are a lot of different endings in the game, things become a little tedious after you've played through a couple of times. Other than achievement hunting, there's not much payoff for getting all the endings.
Even though it's brief, the story and characters are engaging and it's an enjoyable experience while it lasts. It's also a visual novel that's a bit heavier on the novel part than straight-up dating sims; several different pairings can occur, but the focus isn't entirely on romance.
I personally think that the $20 price tag is a little steep for such a short game though, so look for sales or bundle deals.
I loved this game! The art was gorgeous and it felt like my decisions mattered. I've ran into too many story games that fall short in both areas. Great job!

In a MOBA, there are typically levels. You level up and your stats increase, and you usually gain a large amount of money. Now imagine that you're playing LoL, DOTA 2, whatever your choice MOBA is. Imagine that when you get a kill, your
gets a huge amount of EXP and money. More than you would get if you had
CS(Creep Score) at that point in the game.
This is what Awesomenauts decided to do with the EXP system. Upon killing an enemy(which will happen before one team even reaches level 1),  the
EXP shoots through the roof, giving ~1.5 levels. For this level up, the team gets a large amount of Solar(the game's currency, used to buy items), and their base stats increase, namely HP and Attack.
Before this EXP system, there was no way to get stronger but by purchasing items. This added a level of depth to the flow of the game, as leaving to buy items was a time-consuming process. You gambled everytime you decided to stay out after killing an enemy, chanced that you would still be strong enough to take on your enemy, who had just bought items. Leaving at the wrong time could cause your turrets or teammates to be decimated by the larger enemy force.
By playing your cards right, you could turn the entire game on it's head during these times, defeating foes as a team that you would usually lose to by yourself, or boldly attacking turrets head-on when no enemies were around. This, however, could make games a little longer. And 40 minutes might seem like a normal game of any other MOBA, but for Awesomenauts, that was
, because typical games were 25 minutes, and that was with plenty of back-and-forth.
The creators of the game, however, wanted to make games shorter. It's an appealing concept, but Awesomenauts was already very, very fast-paced. I never noticed that 25 minutes had passed, because there was just so much to do, and the possibility of coming back after a team-clearing battle was entirely possible. Awesomenauts was a game that made you interested, and you
to be focused, because
Some new characters(namely Rocco) ruined this aspect. You now had Ashe in the form of a bird, and he could hit you through turrets, from his own spawn. He could teleport back and fire an arrow to ward off or even kill enemies that were going after turrets. Coming back wasn't the most viable thing in the world now. But it was still entirely possible.
And then they introduced the EXP system. At first, I was intrigued. Some characters were quite hard to get going at the start of a game, even if you got first blood. So I was hoping this would rectify that, and balance out some of the "late-blooming" characters.
I was wrong. The EXP system changed the game from this mysterious, complex game of back-and-forth into a game where first blood was all that mattered. A game where one slip-up, a little bit of lag leading you to get killed meant that you
. The game was not forgiving anymore, bending to the way of skilled players who may have died once or twice in a game, but was now rigid, placing a wall between the team who didn't get first blood and any shot at victory.
Some people might like this new system, it does turn the first 1-3 minutes of every game into a toss-up, and makes those >3 minutes really tense. But after someone gets a kill, it's just a matter of watching that team win over the next 5-10 minutes.
So, if you like games where one teammate or a single slip-up costs you the entire game, buy it.
But if you want a game where anyone can come back, the underdog can win, and the game is determined by not just skill in a single kill, but skill over an entire game, in strategy and observation?
You missed it. It's gone.
And I'm sorry you missed it, because it was easily the best MOBA I've ever played. The community loved the game, and the game loved the community.
Thanks for the good times, Awesomenauts. But I guess the best things never last.

If you are reading this: Ignore the bad reviews saying the game is impossible, you're gonna die repeatedly, pressing the buttons doesn't work blah blah blah. I have the planets shortest attention span and temper, and I managed to not only play but finish this game. I did get stumped several times, and it's NOT because of faulty controls, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game mechanics, or glitches that the developers "ignored" - it was because this is one hell of a good puzzle game. It's somewhat short - it only took several hours *checks phone* roughly 4-5 hours - but it is well worth giving it some patience and, if you get really stumped, checking a walkthrough to get you just over that little stump.
Put Portal and the like out of your head, this isn't a physics puzzler, more of a classic puzzle game where you have to find a part, or follow a convoluted (but interesting) path, etc.
I will say this: when the game wants you to hammer "E" or "space", using a keyboard sucks♥♥♥♥♥ I played the entire thing with my steam controller, and with a slightly modified mapping (I'll upload the map, check it out) it was flawless. Hammering "B" or "A" on a controller is far easier and less cramp inducing than keys on a keyboard.
When I first started playing, I had it in mind that I was going to come here and leave a ♥♥♥♥♥♥, scathing review - but once I figured out how to play the game I came ot appreciate the details. One hint (not a spoiler): when you gotta hammer "E", DON'T STOP WALKING. That's all I'll say.
The graphics are gorgeous, the audio is fantastically done (the player says and acts like you would expect a college kid to act in such a situation). Overall it's a well made game - and the FIRST ONE this dev made, Their very first game. When I purchased Stronghold HD, Stronghold Crusader HD came bundled with it and since I loved the original (my review of Stronghold HD can be found
), I had high hopes of it. The original was a great and unique combination of a castle/city builder and siege-simulator and this game is no different, basically the same game all over again, except that it's not that great anymore. The game feels like an expansion to the original game and not a sequel, mostly because it uses shamelessly everything from Stronghold HD, which wouldn't necessarily be a problem, but it
.
The milieu is the (not so) vast deserts of the Middle East in the Holy Land mostly during the Third Crusade. The so called historical campaigns are separated from each other and seem rather inconsistent, so there's hardly a plot which makes the single player game unsatisfying. The skirmish missions are even less entertaining, so those don't help the game either. There's also an expansion called Stronghold Crusader Extreme HD, which is super disappointing and all it does that it allows the player to set custom games (which we can do in the main game as well) under extreme conditions and fight multiple opponents at the same time who tend to start with more resources than us... I managed to beat 2 at the same time, but it was a very poor experience, reminding me of old-school 'real-time strategy' games that functioned like meat grinders, where you train more and more troops and just unleash them on your enemies. Some 'strategy'...
The main difference between the original game and this one is mainly the environment: instead of the beautiful English forestry, we get to play in deserts. It makes the game harder because now anything can catch fire and that introduces the only (!) new building (the other new one is basically a tent): the well. Yes, we can only put out the randomly appearing fires using wells (or instead of several small ones just one big well). Of course the wells also require workforce, so it is vital to have a few extra peasants. Naturally wells can't prevent the occurrence of fires, so the building on fire is going to take damage and if it's the armoury full of weapons... well, we're in trouble. The other factor is the oasis, which is the only suitable area we can build food production buildings on and needless to say, their size is quite limited. At least the oasis makes the game harder in a good way (requiring careful planning), as opposed to the random fire occurrences.
In a few missions we can play the Muslim side, but these are commando missions (can't train units, have to make do with the given ones) only, so we can forget about larger sieges, the main strength of Stronghold. Of course there is sense in the Muslims having no buildings: they should look different than the ones the crusaders have... By the way the crusaders do have Middle-Eastern looking buildings which is a bit strange, but at this point it's really just one of the smaller problems.
There are Arabian soldiers, mercenaries we can hire from the previously mentioned tents, for gold (instead of resources). This is an interesting formula as it can speed up the process of training quite a bit, but again, it can turn the game into grindfests at the expense of sieges. The new soldiers are fun (the slingers are fast and cheap but are weak and can attack at short range, the horse archers have great range and are very fast, but expensive and not as accurate as the normal archers), but they are mostly reused versions of the already existing units with readjusted strengths, except slaves (super cheap and weak units who can set buildings on fire) and the assassins (can climb walls and open castle gates). The assassin does have potential and can make a siege more interesting and a bit easier for the attacker. There's also a new fire ballista, a perfect tool for decimating defending archers on towers and it's also a welcome addtion to the attacking side.
Some issues that were in the original are also present here: the transparency of the buildings is still a problem when rotating the map and trying to rebuild certain sections of the castle wall and the lack of hotkeys is fatal in the fast paced matches when trying to vanquish multiple opponents. The voices of the peasants are still provided by the same person, which was fun at frist, in Stronghold HD, but this time it's obviously budget related.
Stronghold Crusader HD is obviously a letdown, not mainly because it feels like an expansion, but because it seems like a rather cheap duplicate of the great original. The new setting with all its accessories is a setback and the developer must have also felt the absence of the evil characters of the first game, because in the last mission we can meet them again (don't ask).
You might think, "what is this guy talking about, this game isn't that bad" and you might be right, but if you played the original (and you really should have) you'll see how bad it is in comparison.
Accordingly I can't recommend Stronghold Crusader HD to anyone: not to newcomers and especially not to fans of the original. If you want to experience a good siege just load up Stronghold HD again.
PROS
+ some useful additions and readjustments to the game
+ last mission is challenging
CONS
- less emphasis on castle sieges
- issues from the original are still present
- campaign is not as enjoyable as the one in the original
- feels like an expansion rather than a sequel
- cheap ways to make the game harder
RATING
3/10

Evoland is a concept full of wit, charm, and nostalgia. Take a trip down memory lane as you relive the mechanics of role-playing games from the 8-bit era, all the way up until modern day hack 'n' slash lootfests. Your young hero, Clink, starts off as monochromatic pixels, but along his journey recieves numerous upgrades that change not only the art style, but the gameplay as well.
The game takes heavy inspiration from the Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy. The gameplay is not revolutionary, but is meant to be more an homage to these older titles. Every chest grants you an upgrade, some change the graphics, others the music or gametype. You go from playing a 2-d Zelda-esque adventure to turn-based JRPG battles, to 3-d dungeon crawling and puzzle solving.
Gameplay is novel at times, but the character design is endearing enough to make the entire experience give you that warm, fuzzy feeling. Evoland is not particularly long, but it is paced well enough for one playthrough; a playthrough that is several hours long if you decide to collect everything.
I did however find myself wanting more. Shiro Games could make a full length and fleshed out RPG and I would want to play it, Evoland was that great!
Great ride of nostalgia from the early NES days through modern era RPG cliche's. Controller recomended for full effect.

It works great as a follow-up to Peace Walker and introduction to Phantom Pain. Seems like a paid demo at first, but there's much more to it. One big map, but with different missions, and most of all, lots of randomness, emergent fun and replayability. I love it.

As with all MGS games, the missions are not very hard to finish, but the easiest ways will give you a much worse rating than the more skill-intensive ones. I cleared the main mission in an hour, and that was even after restarting from checkpoints several times to correct my mistakes, so don't buy this if you want a long campaign to march through.
The most enjoyment you will get from this game can be gotten from side missions and self-imposed challenges such as getting a good score, looking for collectibles and playing through missions without killing anyone or being detected.
Honestly though, if you've bought an MGS game with the intent of rushing through the main story and then shelving the game, you haven't been doing it right. These games are made with replayability in mind, and the more open way the map is set up in Ground Zeroes gives you even more freedom to approach the objective and dispatch of guards the way you want.
For example:
You can steal a tank and annihilate everyone on the base.
You can sneak around and tranquilize the guards without making a noise.
You can choke one guard until he passes out, then throw him at another one to knock him out too.
You can put guards out of play and gain bonus points by carrying them to your helicopter.
You can force a guard to call his buddies over for you to take them out in one fell swoop.
You can play through an entire mission without even touching a guard by just throwing empty magazines around to make noises for them to investigate.
... Or you could just run straight for the goal and kill everyone who triggers Reflex Mode on you, but that's the lame and boring way and does not impress the virtual judges.
Sadly, your arsenal of weapons and gadgets is much smaller and less varied than in previous installments, though I suspect they will remedy this in The Phantom Pain. After all, this is just an appetizer before the main course.
The graphics are great. Controls are tight. Strong recommend.

An excellent introduction to the latest installment of the Metal Gear Solid series. As with it's predecessors, Metal Gear Solid is at the forefront of pushing the boundaries of gaming, constantly re-invnting itself and tackling real world themes such as war, love, hate, genetics and fate.
This prelude, whilst might put some peope off for the length of the story mode will be suprised to find enormous relayability and longavity due to the extra content included, such as side operations and collectables and secrets.
The game is a sort of "hat-tip" to fans of the series and gives player's the chance to feel out the final game the Phantom Pain will become.
As gameplay goes, the controls are intuitive and fluid and extremly smooth for a PC port. The map is open-ended and missions can be accomplished in any manner you wish.
An example:- You are tasked with destroying three targets on the map. You Begin at a pre defined location and how you enter the base is down to the player. You can sneak through, becoming a "phantom" place the explosives and get out without anyone knowing you were even there. Alternatively, you can crack open an armoury and blow through the targets with a rocket launcher. You will alert everyone to your presence and present yourself with greater risk etc.
There are some downsides to the game especially on PC. Without a decent setup, you will encounter a few crashes and framerate issues. This however is constantly being monitered and sorted by the developer who are working round the clock to fix these gripes.
Additionally from a story perspective, whilst the game does include a backstory diary and a "previously on Metal Gear" menu, it does little to introduce players to the overall story so if you are a newcomer, you will play this game not knowing what a Cypher is, exactly who Kazuhira Miller is and generally being a bit lost. A suggestion would be to pick up a copy of the HD collection (or the Legacy collection) and book the week off work and enjoy a fantastic and gripping storyline that would leave Chris Nolan's eyeballs spinning.
Overall. A fantastic game if you are a fan of the Stealth/Action Genre and a must-own for any fan of the series.
as a final note, I've heard it rumoured that your bonuses collected in ground zeroes, unlock something special for the Phantom Pain so this is definitely worth picking up just to secure your juicy goodies.

I believe that the match engine/experience itself hasn't progressed as needed considering all the bells and whistles that have been added in the last 3 or 4 years.
The lack of feedback on what's going on in the match is becoming a serious issue hampering aspiring managers in the game.
I shouldn't need to watch a full match of repetitive scripted animations that has no resemblance to real football whatsoever to try to spot a gap in midfield, A player tackling too hard or a full back moving two steps forward than needed. Especially when you give us an ME that's a crossing fest like last year.
Here is a list of concerns:
- Ratings:
I remember on the good old days if I had all my team on 8's and two players on 6 then they are not performing and probably this is the cause of my worries.
Now it seems that if all your players are on 7's and you are 3-0 down its fine because and I quote one of the deluded mods on SI forums :
"Player ratings are an indicator of how your players are performing up to that point.. not any kind of indicator on the match or the opposition as a whole,
Just because your players have ok ratings, doesn't mean they are doing what they need to be doing to win."
- Player performance/Body language:
Again it has no clear meaning and is detached from the match engine completely. Even SI can't provide an actual explanation on how it works just like team talks. Does anyone actually use it?
For example how can everyone be playing okay when we are 2 or 3 nil down? ....Or a scenario where all the goals come through our right back and it says the left back is having a bad game and ignores the actual cause.... Unless the ME is not consistent with the other features and is very limited in what it shows us.
- As for the ME itself, I'll ignore the 3D animations because I don't think it's that important how it looks as long as it plays right.
I remember playing 2D on FM 2008 and being able to differentiate between a pacey skillful player or a player with vision. Now it's just a player running in a straight line then crossing or a silly scramble where everyone stands like a scarecrow.
The commentary at that time gave us hints about how the game is going. In 2016 the commentary is the same if not worse considering the limitations they had in the past.
By 2017 I'd expect to see one twos, triangles, proper sweeper adaptation and maybe some more physicality. I expect the commentary to talk about a lot lot more.
It's frustrating when you spend 2 hours tuning your tactics and going through all these fancy positions and roles and shapes to end up with 3 identical crossed goals, A bad backpass or a player with a longshot stat of 2 scoring 3 screamers for the first time in their career.
The new features are an absolute joke, Instead of enhancing team talks, press conferences and giving us a stadium creator with a kit designer and sponsor choices, We end up with a face generator and a twitter gimmick that adds nothing to the game and is better implemented in iPad games.
Of course on their official forums, You get some nazi level of modding that prevents anyone from expressing any concern, And a number of users that act like hunting dogs for their masters going around insulting the intelligence of everyone. This game awakens my inner desire to conquer Europe and exploit uncivilised tribes.
+ Population/migration mechanics
+ Economy
+ Industrial revolution
+ Internal politics
+ Short play time so you don't get bored
+ Many possibilities to suit different playstyles e.g. fascist Ireland
+ Depth e.g. raising taxes too high can bankrupt your people and make them believe in communism
+ Diplomacy and spheres of influence give great powers such as the UK considerable power projection
- Desync in multiplayer
- Combat mechanics do not evolve to compensate for changes in technology e.g. WWI
- Migration to the new world is slightly OP
- Capitalists investing in factories that aren't profitable making liberals getting into power an issue for your economy
- Both DLCs absolutely essential
- Learning curve
- Technologies that give extra research points are essential while most naval technologies are irrelevant
Overall I would recommend this game as the best grand strategy game paradox has released so far, with small issues that can be fixed. There are a variety of mods to play if vanilla does not suit your tastes, such as the Historical Project Mod, which makes the game follow a more historical path. I mainly play vanilla, however, as it provides more freedom with how the game will play out.

PC, XBOXONE, and PS4 versions of the DMC HD Collection are coming in early 2018.
As you are currently reading a Steam review, I assume that you would ideally like to purchase and play this game on PC, so I would recommend waiting for the PC release of the DMC HD Collection, as there is a 99% chance that it will offer a far superior PC play experience of DMC3:SE than this version does.
In the years since this version's release, fans have done extensive modding. These mods can be used to improve its performance and add some significant quality-of-life changes from DMC4 (style switching & less restrictive teleport movecounts.)
After such a significant time investment on the modders' part, I have my doubts whether they will bother modding those same QoL improvements into the DMC HD Collection version of this game when it comes to PC, so if you are already an experienced DMC3/4 player that wishes to experience the game with those QoL improvements, then this version is probably worth purchasing.

Endless Legend was one of the first X4 games that I tried and one of the first that really got me hooked. I think my just over 300h played in this game gives that away, hurr hurr. The game itself has to me a solid mixture between fun, strategic challange and a pretty nice learning curve. Easy to learn, hard to master. I've mostly played multiplayer and my experience is that when it works, it works and its fun. When it doesn't, it can be long and dreadful games with lag and people dropping due to the nature of the games network programming.
It does have plenty of room for balance issues among the factions, also it does have room for improving the map generation and placements of various items such as strategic resources, anomolies and of course placement of the actual empires (you and your foe's).
I know that in a perfect world you would seize your opportunity and adapt to the situation, regarding of where you end up in the world. This is also very possible. However, if you end up being the one forced to adapt and your opponent(s) does not you are at a very compromised situation. This is where I think the game needs the most work to get that edge that it could have. Right now everything is random, the generator is built on random. I like random. BUT there should be a limit to the randomness, or you should atleast be able to make the randomness even for all the players. As in if you use the setting "MANY" anomolies, it should be regions that will have many anomolies. Not the world. Then you eliminate the issues with one player having 0 anomolies in his region whilst another one get 7 on his first city, ultimately giving that player a huge advantage.
Apart from that, I am still having a blast while playing this game. I would totally recommend it. Is it perfect? No. Could it be? Definitely.
Best thing I could recommend if you want to eliminate the issues I've spoken of is to find a group of friends and reroll the map a couple of times until everyone is happy with their start.

I have to say it's the best 4x game I ever played ! !
I have to say sorry about my comments to people that are in other opinion about Endless Legend. I'm absolutely sure they never did get it, to understand the game mechanics...
That leads me to
The ingame explanations (tooltips) are not as informative they should be. It's absolutely necessary to get additional informations from gameguides. Me myself played many months Endless Legend, but I'm far away from "pro-gaming".
If you want to play
, the AI is not a kind of challenge in late game. But you can make it much more difficult by changing difficulty level and map settings before starting map. I have to admit, that the AI was improved in many ways after last patches. I'm sure there will be more patches (but not as soon, because the developers are concentrating their ressources on "Endless Space II" at the moment). If you want to have a challenge, play multiplayer (with experienced players...) instead of single player. It's like in very game, humen are the real challenge. I see single player as "training" for multiplayer, to get an idea of the basic game mechanics.
You should visit the official Endless Legend Forum and post every question about game (technical, gameplay, etc.) there. The community is very nice and really helps fast and professional. The admins answer very soon (not the weekend...), what I can't say from most forums...
The game is not a kind of: "I play for two hours and finish it !" It's 4xgame...
If you want to have an idea of the gameplay-dimensions from Endless Legend, you must have a look at the game guide from "Jojo_Fr". He's a "pro-gamer" (crazy guy^^) that wrote a gameguide which is really impressive:
* random maps
* multiplayer (up to 8 players)
* many different factions (in basic game 8) what leads to very specialized and absolutely different gameplay from game to game (one more faction from "Shadows"-DLC and one more faction with next DLC "Shifters"). Look here:
* lovely fantasy setting/-graphics
* really good support and communication from devs and engaged community
* different tech trees from different factions
* different diplomacy options, depending on chosen faction
* really good fighting system (if you know what you are doing...)
* weapon and armor upgrades, pushing items for city-governors
* "missions" you can get from ruins on map
* you can specialize heroes to city-governor and/or to general
* heroes got special skill trees
* you decide, if you want to pacify or fight the minor factions (unless you are allowed to parley/pacify... by tech research and/or chosen faction)
- strategical and other ressources
etc.
* you need time to play Endless Legend (especially in multiplayer)
* your partner/family could leave your life... (did not happen to me^^)
* the ingame tooltips/instructions explain max. about 20% you should know about gameplay... it's necessary to get informations from gameguides and/or official forum
* later in game (playing larger maps with about 6+ players) the game tends to disconnect sometimes (online game). Reload autosaves (often two or three rounds before) does help (and very useful is to have a look at official game forum about technical game optimization)
* fantasy game setting (if you don't like fantasy)
* no linux version (but possible to play on linux, by using additional programs, look official forum for info about)
* if you play multiplayer game, containing "pro-gamers", you realize you know nothing about game, even after months of excessive gaming^^ this can be very frustrating...
I hope the people that wrote bad reviews about game will find back to Endless Legend, by "studying" the links above. It's worthy, but in parts really work...
Hope we will see one day in Endless Legend multiplayer, as long as I have time for...
For people thinking about to buy the game, use google, bing or whatever to find best price for...

So it's not bad, just not quite up to its potential in this area.
The story itself is slightly adapted, and I have to say the developers did a great job. The wicked stepmother and the two evil stepsisters are actual characters with personalities, and through the story you can understand some of the reasons why they behave as they do. Truly a tremendous spin on a stale old tale.
The developers also get into why there is a ball, which is pretty interesting.
The most annoying character is probably Cinders herself. In some ways she behaves like any normal person in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation would. However, other times she's a bit whiny and preachy.
My favorite character was actually the stepmother. She's less of a demon when you get to know her reasoning and motivations. And her drive is impressive.
The side characters beyond the main ones (Cinders and her step-family being the core characters), are less interesting, and it seems like there are some interesting mysteries into their backgrounds that unfortunately don't get fleshed out. Like what the relationship is between Cinder's mother and some of the other side characters. What happened to Cinder's mother?
As with most visual novels, it's mostly reading. However, at key points you get to make decisions. I wish I had read about the game before playing to better appreciate the impact of decisions. It would have let me know how important it is to use all of your (I think) 10 save slots so that you don't have to restart the story from the beginning to find all the endings.
Basically, you can be good, neutral or evil based on your decisions. And your decisions impact your route to the ball, which suitor you end up with, and whether you're even happy at the end. I overwrote a lot of my old saves as I went along, so I was really limited in my endings. However, I think there are a total of about 12 variations.
Pretty incredible, eh? The game itself isn't amazing, but when you realize how the developers freshened up the source material, you can't help but be impressed!
8/10

This is my FAVORITE STEAM GAME EVER!!! The choices are meaningful, it explores the complexity of family abuse, child raising, sibling rivalry, classism, reputation... it's the most REAL exploration of a "fairy tale" I've ever seen! And there aren't any excuses thrown around to justify having only-white characters- there's actually people of color (well, Madame Ghede, who is amazing) and every. single. character. is made real and given life. After a few play-throughs you really get a feel for WHO Cinders is, who her sisters and stepmother are, even who her dead mother and dead father were, PLUS all the romance options, AND the prince, and even side characters who are just townspeople!
I would scream with joy if this company/group made an entire serious of games just like Cinders, but exploring the other fairy tales... Snow White, Rapunzel, the Snow Queen by HCA, AS MANY AS POSSIBLE. Then they could start bundling them and selling them as packs. Just a suggestion... or more of a heartfelt wish.
Normally $20 is too much to pay for a game, but I ASSURE YOU that this game is WORTH IT!!! I played it for hours and hours and hours and I still never got every single ending!
And the game is NOT just a dating sim- who you make Cinders, her values, her beliefs, her choices- these all have long term implications for the nation, the ruling family, HER family, and her life. But the dating is pretty fun, I gotta say!
A real high point in the visual novel genre. Beautiful art and a thoughtful and compelling story.  A great take on the fractured fairy tale. Complex female characters. There's a lot to like here.

With some regret, I have to say that I do not recommend this game.
I really wanted to like this game; the premise was promising and the art style is beautiful (though the scenes are limited; don't expect much variety).
This visual novel has the makings of a great novel--great artwork, interesting characters, a wealth of different options, the ability to skip scenes easily on a second playthrough (viewing only the new content you haven't seen before), and most importantly to me, your choices change the outcome of your story. Every choice matters.
The only real fault I had with this game was the atrocious writing. It was painful--unrealistic language, blatant foreshadowing, laughable and sometimes downright confusing conversations. The makers of this game went so far into making sure that the player was aware of the nuances of each character that they beat you over the head with them, and then beat the horse you rode in on too. I like subtle, complex characterization, and character growth should be something developed over time and with a touch more realism. Rather than creating nuanced dialogue the game screams it at you, and then has the main character repeat it to herself in her alone time just to make sure you didn't misunderstand anything.
I paid $4 for this game via Humble Bundle , and spend roughly 3 hours doing two playthroughs (with numerous bouts of getting up for pizza and tea). If I had paid $20 via steam, I suspect my review would be that much more vitriolic...if you go to the effort of making a well-crafted game, you should spend some time crafting the text with the same dexterity shown elsewhere.

I have played games similar to this one so when I first saw it I was very excited! I have tried it and I have to say that I'm slightly disapointed with the experience. I mean, don't get me wrong, the game itself is quite nice, it has wonderful artwork, the characters and scenario are very well made but, to me, it just lacks a few touches that would make it even more special.
One of the things that really bothered me right from the start was the awful sound you get when the text is being shown. After awhile it almost feels like needles in your brain! Since I couldn't take it I turned it off and to my surprise there wasn't a single alternative other than pure silence. Like I mentioned before, I have played similar games and most of them have someone reading the lines, which makes it less boring and easy on the eyes. I mean, lets face it, having to read several lines from beginning to end can get extremely boring after awhile. Especially since most people will have to do multiple playthroughs and the game doesn't offer a proper way of skipping the lines you already read. Yes, you have the option to re-read the previous line but you can't skip to the next. You can click several times to make the text appear a bit faster but imagine doing that, pretty much, from beginning to end...
I believe the game should have other small touches such as background noises. For example, when we have the outdoor scenes it would be nice to have the sound of birds, wind, etc; when attending the ball at the palace we could have music playing, people talking or when Cinders is at home, in her room the sound of the fire in the fireplace. Those little details, apart from having different people reading the characters lines would make this game better and interesting than it already is. Plus, I believe it would help justify its price. To be completely honest with you, and even though I recommend it, don't buy it unless you can get it cheap.

is a colorful, emotionally-vibrant Visual Novel, starring Cinders, a wide-eyed, fiery-red, female protagonist. Cinders is about to embark on a journey—a journey of choices. The story will most certainly bring to memory another classical tale of romance, intrigue, betrayal & the pursuit of happiness.
Choices are the core gameplay element in
. The choices you make really do matter. The world will unfold around you according to the decisions you make—and you will always be aware of how they affect what occurs next. The gameplay mechanic for this is that a budding branch will emerge from the corner of the screen to denote an event playing out that has been mitigated by previous decisions. This conspires to make a living world, where you’re not an observer but a participant.
While choices are at the core of
, they dance around the diverse characters. The characters are complex, disturbed, scarred, & much more. None of the characters are simply good or bad. They reach out and play with your emotions as if they were flesh & blood.
The artwork in
is colorful & vibrant. You’ll oftentimes find yourself looking at the background scenery, to catch a look at the swaying shrubbery, or the flickering fire. The soundtrack is diverse & emotionally fitting to each scene as it unfolds. It’s easy to get lost in the simple background melodies.
has a full screen option, with the option to choose screen ratio. The game looked great on a 30” screen at a 16:10 ratio playing in full screen mode.
In conclusion,
is loosely based on one of the classics, & most certainly worth a look if you’re interested in the Visual Novel genre. It will make your heart tingle & your nerves race as you take an emotional journey with Cinders.
9/10

Runs more smoothly than original Ark did a couple months ago.  Added graphic option to turn off something that was making the original game seizure envoking on some computers.  I'm comparing this with the original Ark of 3 months ago, I don't know if they made these large improvements to both.
The idea of this solves a lot of problems with pvp enabled survival games.  You can be compeditive based on your skill, rather than how many months you've been playing.  Since it's a fresh match from scratch, you don't risk loosing hours/months of work to being away or a bad battle.  I think a lot of survival games are almost forgotten before pre-release is over, because it's far too easy for new players to be squashed before they have a chance to build up.  To me, this is a massive problem with the longevity of the genre.
Interestingly enough, this has the apperance of an FPS, but with a feel more like an RTS (simulating fog of war, tech tree, rush tactics, multiple team composition strategies).
I'm surprised it works as well as it does.  I'm not totaly sold on it and I'm new to it and not very knowledgeable, but I love the idea, and have had fun in the couple matches I've played so far.  I have original Ark, but have played it only a little as my computer plays it painfully bad, and the already teched up starting areas are a huge turn off to me.  It's worth trying to see what you think, thus the thumbs up.  But be warned, there's a steep learning curve.  I think a small sandbox practice area with no more guidance than a checklist could improve the barrier to entry.  It seems to assume you know the original Ark mechanics/tech tree.  You can learn it here, but be prepared for a LOT of losses before you can even be compeditive for a win.
A big criticizm I'd have of the game though is it's down time.  The lobby wait is too long.  Not for people to join, but once everyone has joined.  This is laregely because of choosing your custom apperance options, name, and team after entering the lobby.  This should all be done before the game launches (if not before even entering the queue).  Then, the action portion of the game is very short in comparison to the running around / stalking / crafting time.  Too many matches of 40 minutes of prep/wait time for under 60 seconds of action before being eliminated drains on you after about 2 matches.  This may just be the nature of the style of play.  I have no idea how to fix that without loosing what the game is at it's core.  Just something to be aware of.

Within the first hour or so of gameplay, you will likely have found out everything there is to do in the game (with the exception of perhaps finding all 420 words). The question I guess is "Is it worth it?"
I bought the Japanese DLC as I wanted another resource/option when it came to learning the language and had
apart from obviously being able to learn something.
It is an interactive way of learning basic words ( Nouns, Verbs, Adjectives ) and perhaps that is what it is meant for - Learning SOME basic words.
At the end of the day however, do I recommend this game for $10 USD (or the price according to region) for what it offers?
...If you asked me that in a nutshell, I would say No because to any beginner trying to learn a language, chances are it might do more harm than good. ( Yes, you learn words but having googled to confirm the definitions I am skeptical as to what I learn is indeed what is translated in-game. )
However if given the chance to elaborate and tell people "Look, this is what you're going to get and a lot of things require confirmation on the internet." then yes. Mainly because, this is another resource that can interest and provocate people to stop procrastinating and start learning a language (although it definitely can be improved in many ways). For me, that is good enough because I know motivation and determination are one of the hardest things to muster.
Maybe people were looking for something better but thinking about it, how one would go about explaining all the parts of the language from sentence structure to specifics on the language (in a game) might make it too complex for a beginner and confuse them even further.

Awesomenauts is a 2D League of Legends/Dota 2. Correct me if I'm wrong, because I played only one match on both games. They were so horrible I couldn't take it. Awesomenauts at least manages to be, you know, fun.
I can only DARE to even TOUCH the bot battle button. I never have the courage to play real multiplayer. Tryhards and competitive players totally ruin this game for me, so I only get enjoyment by playing by myself with bots (sad face). The servers are also almost always extremely laggy. I find the most enjoyment out of playing with friends and screwing around with the settings on a custom match.
Alright, so if you don't play League of Legends or Dota 2
then here's how the game is. 1: You have a base. 2: You must defend it. 3: Buy upgrades with money. 4: Get money (mostly) by killing people. 5: Take down turrets that are defending enemy base, and defend your own turrets. ...That's about it. There's also a tutorial to go along with the game, so I guess that's nice.
An upside compared to League and Dota 2, however, is that it's not pay-to-win. The only thing it is is pay-to-have-your-*ss-handed-to-you. Again, I only have fun with bots, not real players.
Beware, however, this game only has about 5 or 6 maps, all being fairly small (because it's restricted to 2 dimensions). The character selection is okay, there's a lot and they each have their own cute little bio/backstory along with a theme which is pretty cool.
The only thing I think this game lacks besides levels to play on is CHARACTER BALANCE. Much like any other game that has not-enough-characters-appearently, there's always one or two that are always overpowered. There are also the rest that are underpowered. This leaves the game constantly getting balancing in updates, and totally destroying the combat system, as you realize you JUST settled into how it worked last night. That's the only problem I have, is the characters are changing too much to "balance" them, and I just can't get used to it anymore. It's why I don't play it nearly as much as I used to.

Endless Legend is a Civilization 5-like 4X strategy game. However, despite me saying it's Civilization 5-like, it is only similiar to the Civ games at the very base. This game is far more complex, with far more to do and to explore, and so on and on. But, even though it is not very similar to Civ 5, I still highly reccomend it to anyone who enjoyed those games, and hungered for something more demanding, as I had. This game, is prisitne. It is perfect. It is all I could possibly ask for in a game, and even though my profile says I've not put in a lot of hours into the game, I've probably put in several thousand offline hours. This game has a massive replayability factor, with completely randomly generated worlds, and many different ways for each faction to win the game. All the factions are very different from one another, and suit a different playstyle. However, they do not fit into a standard rock-paper-scissors format, as many other games do. Endless Legend excpects the player to work hard for victory, and it will push and shove you at every possible moment. This game is perfect.
Game with DLC review: Me and this games DLC have a love-hate relationship. Basically, some of the DLC are things that should either be in the base game, or free updates, such as the DLC that adds more minor faction missions. However, it does add even more to the game, with which I am always happpy. The Guardians and Shadows DLC are very good, and you should definetly get them. They add new units, quests, mechanics, music e.t.c, and the Shadows DLC even adds a new faction that is actually VERY fun to play as. Overall, if you have some cash to spend, I highly recommend getting all the DLC. In the long run, it makes the game a lot more fun.

Now, this is a fantastic game. What really stood out for me was the stunning art. The visuals are very well-done and they really help set the tone for Cinders. The characters felt alive; they're not shallow like the ones in the fairy tale. A lot of thought had definitely been put into the dialogues as they're engaging and witty at times. They really speak to the characters. The storyline follows the generic one of the Cinderella, with many interesting variations thrown in to make Cinders stand on its own and speak to the players.
There are four endings to the game, with some variations which are shaped by your decisions. In theory, Cinders has very high replayability due to the sheer number of choices and branches that it has. However, I lost interest before discovering all the ending variations. For one, I found the variations to be minor. Two, it was tedious to have to go through the same events and dialogues over and over again, even in fast-forward. After a certain point, it was just not worth the effort to go through the motions to see how else the conclusions could vary, especially since I was quite satisfied with the ones I did get already.
I think a contributing factor to my eventual lost of interest is that I feel the choices I made reflected my values and overall outlook. You could find that some decisions really speak to you and there's just no desire to choose the alternatives; it's likely that you'll like the first ending you got the most. And that's the case for me.

Overall rating: 9.5/10
To anyone who enjoys visual novels/choose your own adventure stories, I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
Story:
In terms of story, they did an excellent job weaving a narrative that places the story of Cinderella in a context that makes sense. Your stepmother and stepsisters are more than just villians, they are characters/people with lives and motivations that you can choose to understand/learn about or not. The other characters you meet in the story also have histories and distinct personalites. Cinders' relationships with other characters are also affected by choices you make. References to the past/history are very fluidly revealed in conversations with people. The game does not just dump a bunch of backstory on you for seemingly no reason. The game is also filled with some excellent dry humor, and amusing banter.
Gameplay:
If there is a game where literally every choice has an impact, big or small, this is it. There are multiple personality types for Cinders (I've discovered three) that are shaped by the choices you make. Cinders' personality type will affect certain dialogues, the availability of certain choices, and the consequences of certain choices. Certain scenes or dialogues with other characters will also change depending on previous choices you have made. There are multiple endings with several variants of each, and it does not come down to one or two "big choices" at the end or anything simple like that. Whether or not you succeed in achieving your desired specific ending is dependent upon the cumulative effects of choices you have made throughout the game. That being said, the replay value is very high, in my opinion. I have enjoyed replaying it to find the different endings/variants and get the achievements.
The only downsides in terms of gameplay are minor, but still exist. There is no good "rewind" function. If you missed a line, or want to return to read an earlier part of the conversation, you are limited. The game is divided into "scenes" probably for program/design sake. However, you cannot scroll further back than the first line of your current "scene." This could be several lines back, or just one. Fast-forward is sub-optimal. It just cycles through dialogue at rapid speed until you come to a scene/line you haven't viewed or a choice. You can't "skip to next scene" or "skip to next choice" which is disappointing on replays.
Presentation:
The artwork is pretty, from the character portraits to the backgrounds and facial expressions change over the course of conversations. The music is good, and fits the scenes quite well. My only gripe was that introducing a character meant briefly interrupting a scene to focus on the character on a leafy-flower design background and a change in music that felt a little out of place.
Pros:
+ Story
+ Characters
+ Artwork
+ Choices & Consequences
+ Replay Value
Cons:
- Limited/sub-optimal fast-forward and rewind functions
- Awkward character "introductions"

This was one of my favorite games back on the early days of the 360, and is a really nice introduction into some Smite or Paragon MOBA-esque mechanics.  Such a shame that a really entertaining game like this had to die out (kind of like Savage Resurrection).  Even though the MNC community is completely dead, there are still 2 dedicated servers that I know of that are still running.  So if you have 3 other friends, and those 3 friends don't mind spending 5 bucks, this is an amazing game to play, even just 2v2.  SMNC is free, but it feels and plays very different to MNC.  MNC player movement is slower and the Time-To-Kill is longer.  Maps are pretty varied, but are stuck to one lane of minions per team, which turns out fine if you're only playing 2v2 (game doesn't make bots to fill in players spots D:).  Howver, there's tons of verticality and variances in lines of sight (except for the 2 gimmicky maps) in this game.  So if you're thinking that one lane per team feels small or limiting, you'd be happily surprised.  Though this is not marketed as a MOBA, this is an economy game.  You get $$$ for taking out towers and minions, and get a lot for taking out boss minions and players.  Character progression is linear, but the $$$ can be used to buy extra lane minions (specific to each class), detonate bombs on the map, and buy a type of minion nuke (that is always placed in the center of the map and is only available at certain times --> causes huge, frantic firefights).  On top of the fun gameplay, the game has a lot of humor to it.  Because it's paroding sports games, there is a commentator who comments on everyone's actions in-game.  There's enough dialogue variations that what he says doesn't get old or annoying.
If the game was still alive and/or you have friends to play with 7/10.

This is a great game and a great concept, but with limited applications.  I'm a few hours into two languages with which I'm pretty familiar, for context.  It's essentially a creative and fun way to practice vocabulary.  If you're a beginner, or want to brush up on your household vocab this is great, but don't expect more than that.  The aesthetic is great, the music is nice, the controls are mostly good.  The "fly-by" mode could be a bit easier to control.  I find myself spending more energy trying to control the plane than remembering the words, but then if you don't want that the regular time-attack mode suffices.  I have found a number of places where the controls give me trouble clicking on smaller objects (ie: answer is "wrench" but I fail time after time because the mouse selects the toolbox instead)
On the language side of things, this game is wonderful.  The fact that it keeps the lists, keeps track of your answers, and has a randomize function is amazing.  Additionally, it does non-roman scripts very well.  Japanese is presented in 3 options (Kanji, Kana, or Romaji) and there are multiple options for Chinese and Russian as well for those starting off on vocabulary, but who haven't mastered the related scripts quite yet.  I'm 50/50 on the issue of articles.  The game DOES have them.  When you select a word and bring up its details the gender is listed underneath the word.  But those pronouns (el/la, der/die/das, etc...) are not in the spoken notes, so you have to remind yourself of them on your own.  (ie: the audio is "Computer", but the text is "Computer - [Masc]").  Those spoken demonstrations of vocabulary have been in my experience mostly good, but ocassionally not of the best quality.
All in all, well done.  I hope this game develops further in the future.  That front door is just begging for me to master x number of words and be allowed through it and out into the big wide world full of fun vocab to practice.

Awesomenauts is a 2D League of Legends/Dota 2. Correct me if I'm wrong, because I played only one match on both games. They were so horrible I couldn't take it. Awesomenauts at least manages to be, you know, fun.
I can only DARE to even TOUCH the bot battle button. I never have the courage to play real multiplayer. Tryhards and competitive players totally ruin this game for me, so I only get enjoyment by playing by myself with bots (sad face). The servers are also almost always extremely laggy. I find the most enjoyment out of playing with friends and screwing around with the settings on a custom match.
Alright, so if you don't play League of Legends or Dota 2
then here's how the game is. 1: You have a base. 2: You must defend it. 3: Buy upgrades with money. 4: Get money (mostly) by killing people. 5: Take down turrets that are defending enemy base, and defend your own turrets. ...That's about it. There's also a tutorial to go along with the game, so I guess that's nice.
An upside compared to League and Dota 2, however, is that it's not pay-to-win. The only thing it is is pay-to-have-your-*ss-handed-to-you. Again, I only have fun with bots, not real players.
Beware, however, this game only has about 5 or 6 maps, all being fairly small (because it's restricted to 2 dimensions). The character selection is okay, there's a lot and they each have their own cute little bio/backstory along with a theme which is pretty cool.
The only thing I think this game lacks besides levels to play on is CHARACTER BALANCE. Much like any other game that has not-enough-characters-appearently, there's always one or two that are always overpowered. There are also the rest that are underpowered. This leaves the game constantly getting balancing in updates, and totally destroying the combat system, as you realize you JUST settled into how it worked last night. That's the only problem I have, is the characters are changing too much to "balance" them, and I just can't get used to it anymore. It's why I don't play it nearly as much as I used to.

This is what I call a game! Fun to play, an awesome graphics, a great atmosphere and simple to control. Your goal is to get a little jelly (or pudding) riding on a rollercoaster car from an entrance to the exit. But watch out! There are plenty of monsters that are trying to scare the little jelly out of his mind! While your car is constantly moving you can manipulate tracks, scare away monsters and place some traps to stop them. The game offers four worlds each containing 12 levels. The difficulty is of great variability from the first easy straight-forward relaxing world to the last one full of complicated and long tracks. All levels are fun and they never get too frustrating but once you finished them there is no replay value (you can collect the vip coupon in every level but you'll probably collect them in the first run). Overall The Great Jitters is entertaining little game with only one bigger drawback being it's short length.
Pros:

Cons:
-A little bit short
-The game would greatly benefit from a widescreen resolution (max resolution is 1024x768, but 1280x720 would be ideal so you can see more of the level)
-Can get slightly repetitive in the last few levels

I like this game a lot. It took playing some strategy games with worse graphics to realize the treat that this one is. It's idiosyncratic, which for me is a plus in a game; it means finding the shortcuts victory among a million different possible paths, and Endless Legends really does offer a lot of paths, so many it's overwhelming at first. This sense of confusion is added to by the fact that much of the description in the world management system (in-city; descriptions of tech being researched . . .) are often not very hopeful, sometimes outright vague. It takes a few play-throughs in other words to know which techs are worth researching, which aren't, and if you're like me you'll forget anyway. Luckily the battle system - though fraught with its own flaws - is beautiful to watch and the token units (there could be more available, say, a supersecret bonus unit in the second to last tech tier; that'd be nice) really are fun to modify and level up. I should say, too, that though the game balance feels off (the beginning is a slow slog and the end can feel like a sprinting race), this does seem to be a deliberate choice by the developers. At any rate, it's a strategy game worth its salt, encouraging multiple play-throughs and fun to look at.

I'm a graduate in both Philosophy and Economics and this is my favourite game of all. It is an absolute gem! The world market system is a masterpiece and the socio-political dynamics manage to reflect reality's complexity.
The true beauty of this game lies in the limits imposed on the player's actions. No leader can decide everything, nor can he bring things into existence through direct action... The world is more complicated than that. This is precisely why I love this game. Also, it does not fall into the trap of midlessly conquering the world as if the culture of ruled people does not matter.
PS: My actual in-game time is higher than the one clocked by steam. I bought a physical copy of it when it was launched. Only much later, did I purchase it on steam.
PPS: The dynamic historical accuracy is not great. Those like me who want to enhance it without affecting too much the original game, should try the "Historical Project Mod".
