Cinders is definitely a departure from what you normally find on Steam. A stunning and interesting adaptation of Cinderella, Cinders is a visual novel and Choose Your Own Adventure story that captures, in a grown-up way, the spirit you had and the magic you felt reading as a child. The only two things creating this world are artwork and music, as the dialogue – the heart of the game – is all text. Surprisingly, I did not come across many grammatical errors, and being the English major I am, I was certainly looking. Editors have done quite the job. The storytelling was thoughtful and well-crafted; the writing was intelligent and contained more adult humour than I expected. In the short period of time it took to get through the first playthrough (roughly five hours), the writing delved into the pasts of a few characters and built them up to be more than just one-dimensional.
Though most of the art is static, the odd flicker of the fireplace, shimmer of water or subtle eye and lip movements somehow bring it entirely to life. Though more colourful and detailed, the artwork does remind me of that which you would find in old hardcover fairytale books. The ambient music is absolutely beautiful and changes with each scene, though because it was the only auditory element it did have me longing for even more variety at times (as the songs are repeated); I wish the soundtrack contained even more.
Though based on a traditional story with a subdued and passive female protagonist, this modern adaptation takes some unexpected and satisfying departures and shines more light on the complex relationships between the characters and Cinders’ struggle for independence and thirst for freedom. There is a focus on family and the conflicts between taking care of others and taking care of oneself. The heart of the story is finding one’s own path in life and understanding that each choice you make has a consequence, either immediately or in the future, for both yourself and those around you. In this way, the replay value of this game is pretty spectacular: it has four possible endings. And in all honesty, I think I am actually going to play through to see all of them.
If you enjoy reading and visual novels, Cinders is absolutely with a playthrough (or four!).

I LOVE this game! The art style is one of the most beautiful I have seen and the different background scenery is really atmospheric. I love how you can shape Cinders' character through some small actions and the story is a brilliant, mature take on Cinderella. I found it really interesting to see the different characters and hints of their backstory, giving the impression that you don't know whats going on and why they act in a certain way - the characters felt very realistic. I really like the reward system and how it displays it; it was a small touch but I loved it! On the rewards page it also shows you different paths and how much you have completed of each which really makes me want to play this game until I unlock every option it has. So far I have played through the story twice and noticed a few subtle changes in dialogue that made it feel like I was making a new character both times.

PROS
- Cinders's personality is up to the player via dialogue choices
--> Consistency is rewarded, while random personality choices don't serve as well
- The art is beautiful, from the backgrounds to the characters
- Morality is ambiguous, unlike what you expect from fairy tales
- 4 different endings, all with many variations
- The dialogue flows well and is interesting to follow
- The stepsisters and stepmother are relatable, vulnerable people with real problems
- Branches in the storyline feel like they matter for the events that happen no matter what
- Two different forces of magic can help Cinders for the ball
--> Both have a connection with Cinders's mother and provide different background info respectively
- All the characters have issues to work out, the relationships Cinders makes from the player choices feel like they develop in a realistic way; nothing feels forced, like in the fairy tale
- 3 different goals for Cinders, not just marrying the prince and living happily ever after
- 3 different love interests
- Can re-watch endings and variations after you unlock them, very high replay value
- Skip function for dialogue you have already read
- No tedious stat building!! :)
CONS
- Cinders's name... It's a bit difficult to take a scene seriously sometimes when characters call her "Cinders"
- The game doesn't tell you what personality you have stacked or what progress your relationships are...so sometimes it's hard to know how to progress and confusing if a certain dialogue option doesn't work
--> Leads to lots of trial and error
- Failing to get the variation you want can be a bit frustrating for completionists
- The music isn't too memorable
- No homosexual romances, all 3 love interests are male
- No customization of how Cinders looks
- No voices
This is a wonderful, extensive visual novel and possibly one of the best I've ever played. I've always criticized Cinderella as a character for being one of the most passive protagonists in the history of fairy tales, but in this game you can make her to be the woman you always wanted her to be. She also doesn't always have to marry the prince and sometimes the ending isn't going to be happy. You could even die and have no one mourn over you. The possibilities are vast, giving it lots of replay value. All the art is gorgeous to look at as well so oftentimes I just stop reading and take in the scene.
The developers were right in advertising this game as a "mature" take on the fairy tale, as all the characters are ambiguous. You can never truly figure each of them out and most of the time, they will surprise you. The game does a wonderful job of consistently claiming that no one is so simple as "good" or "evil" and even the kingdom is going through a metamorphosis if you pay attention to the Prince's plot. Speaking of which, the writing is downright brilliant and atmospheric since it is a western visual novel. There are unfortunately no voices, but little nuances in what the characters say give your imagination plenty to give the characters voices of your own.
If you enjoy visual novels with emphasis on dialogue choices, protagonist identity, relationships, and no stat building, definitely buy this game. I hate tedious stat building myself and much prefer making decisions through dialogue. All relationships are accessible provided you have made the choices to develop them; they don't rely on you being "cute" enough or "intelligent" enough. Despite my glowing recommendation however, Cinders is by no means perfect and I eagerly await anything else the developers have building off of this amazing genre.

Cinders starts off as an interactive version of
, but quickly gains a large amount of depth. The multituide of different choices and how many different results branch off the beginning are astounding. The art style is lovely and the narrative progresses in an intriguing way. The different characters are each interesting in their own right, and watching the way that they develop and help or hinder you throughout the story is fascinating.
For some people this sort of game (text-based adventure) could be a little too slow and possibly boring, but this is a prime example of a good T-B-A. It's not overly long (2.5 hours per playthrough depending on your speed and choices), and gives you hints as to how diverse the story could be on multiple playthroughs. This diversity of narrative is suggested through a collection of trophies that correlate to particular plot points that you unlock through role-playing in different ways. I've played through the game twice and have still only unlocked 3 of the 8 possible tropies, and definitely plan on playing through this game a few more times.
4/5 - Would thoroughly recommend to any fans of this genre of game, but also to anyone contemplating trying it.

Lovely art, above-average writing, some replay value.
One of the most impressive things that sets this apart from other visual novels (from any country) is the incredible attention to detail.  The fonts, text boxes, and interfaces are attractive and professional-looking; dynamic lighting makes the already-gorgeous backgrounds look even better; and characters' eyes actually move back and forth (although this sometimes can cause character models to veer into "uncanny valley" territory).
My only real complaint is that, on one or two occasions, the parts of a conversation that were affected by my choices and the parts that would have been said regardless (i.e. main plot stuff) did not flow together naturally, making it difficult to determine whether the relationship between my protagonist and a particular character was friendly or hostile.
Still definitely in the upper-tier of visual novels.  If you like VNs, this is a quality product and likely worth your time.

I guess by now you have read many reviews that repeat the very same pros and cons again and again so I wont bother to repeat them here.
What I will bother do however is say this:
How the heck do people give to this game a very positive rating when the cons are so seriously and overwhelmingly bad? It is like rewarding the laziest possible attempt while at the same time we do recognize the lazyness involved. That is because you read a review, you see all the abysmally bad things mentioned in the cons... and then you see a thumbs up as well. WTH.
Yeah the graphics are neat... but also yeah... there are like 8 enemies cloned to death on a game where you actually do NOTHING else than seeing their faces, bodies and equipment while you quicktime event killing them again and again and again and again....
Yeah the moves are neat...but also yeah...there is absolutely no freedom, strategy, tactics or skill involved. In fact I would rather have the developers have a button, which if you were to press all the fights would be resolved automatically while you sit back and you enjoy a.... b-movie story with AAA movie production values. The fights after about half an hour or so get so boring that feel like a chore that you get to perform just to see the next awesome graphical setting.
Do not get the game if it is not on a 75% off sale, and even then you might think that your $5 could be much better spent on something else.
It is quite telling that I played this for about an hour and a half, I quit and I found myself playing Mount & Blade: Warband which has ABYSMALLY worse graphics, animation, production values...you name it... and nevertheless it is a vastly superior game.
I am not trying to compare the two as they are completely uncomparable. Different genres, different styles, different everything. What I am trying to say is that graphics is not everything in a game, and in this particular case, although you cannot go much better than that graphics wise, the game feels so hollow that one has to wonder what the heck the developers were thinking.
And to go back to my initial point... what the heck the reviewers - that keep thumping it up - were thinking. Do they want companies to produce more games like this, or do they want to push gaming developers in a better direction?
I would give to this game a 2/10 while being extremely generous.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a short but good entry of the MGS series. The gameplay itself is like that of it's predecessors, not counting Revengeance, but it gives players some twist such as marking enemies, finding alternative routes to an objective (such as hiding in a truck, crawling in a vent, or just sneaking through the door) and looking beautiful even on low settings.
The game does suffer some flaws. For one, it's short. The campaign itself is just a prologue for the upcoming Phantom Pain so it's just one mission, not counting the pseudo-historical missions. Another flaw (though subjective) is the fact that the checkpoint system can be abused to refill tranquilizer ammo for those that want to be the technical pacifist (I say technical since you might just end up knocking out the enemies via CQC.) though it is at least evened by penalizing players in subtracting their ranking score.
Overall, Ground Zeroes is an entry of the series that is worth playing, especially for those on PC who either want to play a Metal Gear Solid Game and/or those who want to play a game that emphasizes the importance of stealth.

I have recently played through the main Metal Gear Solid Games and also played Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance. A great series with great characters, great story, great atmosphere, music, graphics, and gameplay. Metal Gear Solid 5: Ground Zeroes is the latest in the MGS series and serves as a prologue to Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain.

Ground Zeroes is a cheap, smaller game than what the Phantom Pain will offer. This is both a strength and a weakness for the game as it's very short. However, the game offers a large open area to experiment with the new mechanics and weapons. Metal Gear Solid 5 marks the series going open world in level design. Just from Ground Zeroes' big level, it gives me a lot of optimism for the Phantom Pain's open world levels which will be even bigger.
However, here's the problem with the game and why people are flipping out about it. The game is just a few missions in one level. Only one mission is the prologue to the Phantom Pain and can be finished in about an hour or two depending on how you approach the level. The mission is really good and you get to really get a feel for the new mechanics which will be fleshed out even further in the main game. It's a good mission but it ends too fast and you feel  a little cheated and ripped off (I paid 13 bucks during the sale so it's not too bad for that price and there are people who spent 30 bucks). The game has a few missions after the main mission and they are fun for the most part and reach new levels of campiness. If you noticed from my play time, I found ways to extend my playtime and have a blast. I'm only about 40% done with the total progress too so there's a lot more for me to do such as all the Hard modes and getting S ranks on all the missions. There's a lot to do for a small game and if you are a Metal Gear fan, you will have fun with the Deja Vu mission and Raiden mission which are bundled for free in the PC version.
Graphically, Ground Zeroes looks amazing, especially in the main mission and the late afternoon missions. It also is a solid (No pun intended) port that is scaleable on all kinds of hardware. This is all because of the FOX engine which looks and runs incredibly well and looks nearly photorealistic. Some of the settings are tough to run but I played on some Extra High and High settings and got 60fps throughout. It's amazing that Kojima Productions made such a good port despite their long break from PC porting. It's a shame more devs aren't putting this kind of effort into their games on PC (I'm looking at you Ubisoft).
Overall, Ground Zeroes is a great sub-game to give you a taste of what the Phantom Pain will be like. However, that taste is kind of like a tease and makes you hunger for what the Phantom Pain will offer. It's a great game and if you can get lost in Camp Omega, you will get your money's worth.

So here's a game that tries to parody a whole generation (or several) of role playing games, most prominently Zelda, Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, and (somewhat surprisingly) Diablo. It's not a very long game, nor should it be. It is rather, as they say, a love letter to the RPG genre and its fans. If you grew up with RPGs somewhere in the period between the mid 80s up to the second half of the 90s, you'll definitely recognize not only the individual features that made the RPGs of those eras so memorable, but also the evolution of said features throughout time. Take those features, put them all in one game, and you get Evoland. A game that's more about the history of gaming than about the (deliberately) weak main quest.
This is a game that's meant to be played through in one, maybe two sessions. The transition from one visual style to another is lost otherwise. And it is precisely these visual and gameplay-related "unlocks" (that come in the form of treasure chests) that drive you forward, as opposed to the attainment of the very generic main goal of Evoland, which is to destroy the evil lord Zephyros (yeah) with your side-kick, the magic user Kaeris (that's right).
But while the gameplay in itself is fairly weak, and the graphical evolution does not go to very far lengths (it seems to stop at around 2006 in terms of graphics), it is an enjoyable and quirky game filled with self-deprecating humor that gets a few laughs.

With this game going F2P -- and in light of the impending concomitant influx of players -- I thought maybe I'd add some substance to this review. First off, ignore all the people inexplicably spamming negative reviews either in response to the game going F2P and thus "robbing" all the players that paid good money for it, or to the developers removing the offline mode. The latter complaint is simply false for many reasons; offline games are still very much in the game ("Custom Games" mode), though these cannot be played without an internet connection, and even if for some reason you *don't* have an internet connection, the previous patch which allowed for this is still possible to play (the devs remarked on this recently and are planning on implementing a more permanent solution b/c they are great and care immensely about this game). The former complaint is also bullsh*t because 'Nauts has always been dirt cheap (especially considering the endless hours of gaming you get out of it), with countless sales and game keys given out for free as well. Plus, they are giving special rewards to people that have owned the game previously.
Now that I've gotten that out of the way: this game is rad as hell. Play it if you have any interest in platforming fighters or MOBAs. It is easy to pick up (simpler relative to other MOBAs) yet extremely difficult to master (here I am still sucking after 2000 hours of play). It has a sweet soundtrack, great skins, and a diverse and interesting cast of playable characters. It is fairly well-balanced and has an active competitive scene. Above all, it has a fantastic, loving set of devs who have poured tons and tons of work into it despite its indie nature and a relatively small playerbase. Now that it's finally polished with a good-looking GUI and decent progression system, and IS FREE TO PLAY (soon) download this sh*t and start playing! Counter-Strike Nexon is a Counter-Strike game with Zombies. It has literally all the same assets as CS:Source, only as far as I can tell, it has worse chickens. As far as I know, there is only one map, though if there are any more, I bet you that each one, is ripped straight from one of the Counter-Strike entries.
There are many gamemodes, but in my opinion, none of them are worth playing as the game recommends you play Zombie Hero.
How Zombie Hero works is... Call of Duty Infection Mode. Literally. Only instead of people being weapon-locked, they can choose any they like and the Zombie is chosen at random. There are 10 zombie classes (Yes, Normal zombies are just zombies, they don't count because if you include Zombies in your game, you literally need them to exist) and each seem to do something different from one another via special skills. Every zombie class has the same weapons though, effectively.
You can level up your Zombie classes simply by playing. Speed is leveled up by walking around, and I'm sure others are similarily leveled, by simply doing all that is possible. Normal Zombies aren't the exception here.
Sadly... The game, like any "good" Counter-Strike entry, is boring. Games last too long on a single map, and each round only lasts for about 5 minutes. As usual also, every weapon is essentially the same like every military, modern-era FPS, only with specific... buffs and debuffs to certain stats.
The Counter-Strike mechanic of the absurd decrease in accuracy the longer you shoot is here. With Zombies. This could be made to work perfectly well, if the zombies didn't have 5000 health and take more than a clip of an LMG jsut for unupgraded normal zombies without dying.
But don't worry, because everytime you shoot a zombie, they are instantly kept on hold, their momentum utterly removed, no matter where they're hit from. So, so long as you can keep constant bullets on an enemy, most of them cannot move or do anything.
Maps haven't been really altered at all. Maybe the skyboxes have been removed to emulate "night" but honestly, it's probably because they wanted to crank this out and was lazy, even if this has been out for atleast a year and a half now... and skyboxes aren't hard to do. Just look at Starforge and Castle Miner Z.
This means any stupid, high-up places you could get to before, now are the most camped spots for humans.
Essentially maps are the equivalent of taking Assault maps in UT, and simply copy/pasting them into deathmatch. It doesn't work like that.
Going into greater detail, Matches last too long on maps not really designed for continuous play. Said maps would have actually differentiating geometry, but like nearly every map for Counter-Strike games (choose any one of them) they're linear and basic as crap corridoors, usually without roofs.
Alot of gripes with this game, I'll have with every CS title. Repetitive matches, the maps not being designed really too well, mostly all being rectangular rooms with some parts to make the shape barely different. Weapons are all the same essentially, It's visually Counter-Strike and Left For Dead if the maps and zombies looked worse.
Ultimately... it's Conuter-Strike and Left For Dead with all of the fun of Counter-Strike, just with only 80% still remaining. Fun after the first few minutes, until you realize every server is hosting only one map and maybe because the game isn't designed well enough to not hide in places you must crouch-jump to get into in order to win.
It's Free To Play, but has a system that lets you pay to progress faster. If this costed money. It would only be worth 5 dollars.
Altogether the game is fun for the first few minutes, or the first game, or the first 10 rounds, until the CS nature shows with it's repetitiveness, only with actual variations between teams and... well... zombies.
The only real silver lining is that playing as the zombies offers an actually new and fun experience. Unless you've played Left For Dead's versus mode. It's like that, only each class has skills different, and not actual differences, like mechanics differences. You will find yourself ignoring the buy menu and walking up to the zombies, or AFKing until you are turned inevitably.
Honestly the game is a 4/10. I'm already bored of it, I'm likely never to actually play it again. I'm being rather generous as after a match, your pinky finger will start to hurt. Unless you happen to offer yourself to the zombies like I did.

Cinders is seriously one of the best visual novels you will ever play. I got sucked into this game and I've absolutely loved it. I have some critical feedback for it, but that by no means negates the magificance of this interactive story.
Pros
+ The writing is definitely the best I've ever encountered in a Steam visual novel. If you're a story-motivated gamer who appreciates a solid piece of high-quality writing, this game will be a breath of fresh air.
+ Characterization goes above and beyond. No longer do you see the flat, 2-dimensional characters you've come to know from Disney's Cinderella. All the characters, even the "bad" ones, are more than what meets the eye. You also have a hand in tailoring Cinders's personality to your liking, which is fun. Cinders can be passive, manipulative, friendly, sensual, rebellious, responsible, romantic, family-oriented, or murderous... whatever floats your boat.
+ The story gives you a feeling of control, which is imperative for me to enjoy VNs. Your choices *do* make a big difference, even if it seems like they're not really doing anything at first. The choices the story presents you with open up different paths and will give you different endings. Some choices create vastly different outcomes, others give more subtle changes.
+ The artwork is stunning. Not only is it a unique style, but everything from the backgrounds to the characters looks polished and detailed.
+ The characters are animated beautifully. Their expressions change, their postures change, and even their eyes move! I thought this was a nice touch.
+ The soundtrack creates the perfect ambiance and it is simply exquisite to listen to.
Cons
- It's not that long (I think my first playthrough was maybe 5 hours? but I read fast), especially when you do replays to get achievements and epilogues. A lot of time is spent skipping over scenes during replays because, depending on your choices, it's possible that only a few lines of text will change.
- All relationship stats and personality stats are hidden, so you don't see how your stats are changing when you make choices. This makes it harder to see if you're on track with what you're wanting to do.
- I wish there were more routes that could further deviate from the traditional Cinderella tale. For example, I wish there were options to not go to the ball, to choose no "fairy godmother" to help you, to gang up with your step-sisters to overtake Carmosa, to romance some other unexpected people (the Shady Character maybe? hahaha) or... the possibilities are endless! Basically, even though this game is already amazing, it could have been even cooler if there were some other creative pathways you could take.
Overall, I whole-heartedly recommend this game. It's earned a special place in my heart. Though I can definitely find areas for improvement, this game is too much a great experience to pass up.

I don't write too many reviews unless I actually have something to say. In this case, I definitely have something to say, but I'm tired right now so I won't say too much and the fact that I recommended this game probably says enough.

This game is fantastic.
Think Civilization 5, but with a truly workable narrative based on your faction, and perhaps a bit deeper in strategy.
The city management/construction system will be immediately familiar but turns out to be deceptively deep and enjoyable. The tech tree allows a ton of freedom on what paths you decide to go down. You equip your units with what items you choose, which harkens back to the days of Alpha Centauri. You have options for units, but it's not so many that it bogs you down--it strikes a great balance.
The combat system is merely alright. It is by no means is bad, but compared to the other facets of the game that are wonderfully polished and/or pleasantly original, the combat, which would seem perfectly in place in a game that was merely good or great, seems to lag behind the otherwise stellar showing of the other aspects. Again, combat is not bad, to be clear, just a bit different and slightly clunky.
I'll mention the narrative once again and also the flavor texts because I like that kind of thing if done lightly. You never get blasted by walls of text, and you can ignore any and all of it if you wish, but taking a few seconds to read the extra sentences of fluff, I've found, really ties the world together. In my first couple of games I actually almost felt as if I was playing a scripted campaign, not a compeltely random map. The music even has me humming along occaisonally, and further adds to the atmosphere and respectable production quality.
I bought the game on sale, then a couple of days later bought most of the DLCs just because I felt like I owed them more money. The base game is worth full price, and I'm a bit ashamed, as a fan of the 4X genre, that I hadn't gotten this when it was brand new.
I don't know what else is left to say other than that at 20+ hours in, I am sure I'll be spending quadruple that in the next few months in Endless Legend. I am looking forward to starting up the next game as a new faction to see how the game plays through with them, as the two of them I've tried thus far are distinctly unique in their playstyle. Playing a multiplayer map with some friends is bound to be a good time as well.
Truly solid experience.

Statement: The RPG that made Bioware famous to non-PC gamers may have one of the most spoiled game stories ever. Spoilers are why I didn't finish for 9 years, and much like ESB, the impact is less if you know ahead of time. But KOTOR isn't just one of the first great Western console RPGs.
Explanation: In 2003, two Star Wars prequels & The Matrix Reloaded left many dejected. This was the blockbuster people WANTED. There had been Star Wars games before, but here was a setting wholly untouched by George Lucas. Though much is evocative of the original films, many of the NPCs are rough drafts for Mass Effect's.
Observation: The setting hides many of Bioware's now-maligned shortcomings; here the binary morality makes sense. The "Bioware romance" can't really come into full effect either. But sci-fi trappings aside it's literally D&D for all the clunkiness that entails. I grew up on Baldur's Gate, so I can deal.
Conclusion: The assassin droid HK-47 is the greatest. Play for him, meatbags!

As a long time Metal Gear Solid fan, I have to recommend this game. This is some awesome Metal Gear Solid action. I do have some gripes about it, though.
First the good: Metal Gear Solid has never looked better. This may be a port, but it's a damn good one. The controls feel fluid, the graphics look amazing, and the gameplay is engaging. After the very short main mission, there are all these "Side Ops" (other missions in the same setting) to play which is nice. Not to mention, Metal Gear Solid fits pretty well in a large area. I wouldn't call it "sandbox", but there's plenty of room for roaming around and trying new tactics.
Now the bad: As a long time Metal Gear Solid, I now officially hate Kiefer Sutherland. It may be a small detail in the larger picture, but removing David Hayter as the voice of Snake is blatantly offensive to the ears. It's jarring. Snake feels like a stranger now. Before, he was this time old icon, the embodiment of apathy towards violence due to decades of constant fighting. David Hayter had that down. He *was* Snake. Kiefer Sutherland... he's a stranger. It may seem petty, but it's a big deal to me.
But now that Metal Gear has come to PC, it's now capable of being modded. Maybe, in a dream world, David Hayter will agree to work on a fan-based voice acting replacement mod. Then... this game (and Phantom Pain to come) will truly be great.

Do you feel lucky?

I mean, do you like Metal Gear Solid?
Did  u enjoy previous Kojima productions, shed a tear at snake eater ending, and spend days reading about the story online? If the answers to previous questions were yes, im glad youre feeling lucky and u should get this game. The main mission on first try is about 2-3 hours of top notch stealth action quality gaming, with amazing cutscenes, bloody and dark themes  (seriously, this might not be a game for everyone), great voice acting and everything MGS has always been. With all the lighting effects, sharp textures and fluid animations sometimes it's hard to belive its not rendered CGI . With addtional side ops, easter eggs, ranking system, the replayability is quite high, no to mention story itself was designed in such a way that in order to fully grasp it u have to  do multiple playthroughs and search for cassetes. Add to that a high difficulty curve, with enemies on hard having better sight then most humans, amazing PC port (no crashes, fluid  60 fps on high/very high, only problem I had is display turning off randomly for few secs during gameplay) Not to mention getting highest ranks and learning the game mechanisms, the whole"getting gud" part, were  one of the most satisfaying experiences i had in gaming in years. If youre looking for a reason no to buy it - perhaps 20 euro for a engine demo is a bit steep, also the learning process is quite painful, with countless retries and "that wasn't my fault... okt maybe it was" moments. Other then that, if u love MGS and can't wait for TPP, GZ will drill a hole in your skull that will give u certain distate for every other game that isn't The Phantom Pain, and make every day without TPP seem boring and wasted.

On another note, I really miss David Hayter as the voice of Snake.

Considering that it is a milestone and it comes really cheap, especially on sale, it might be worth giving a try; however, history never turns back, and you will never appreciate it as much as you would have back when it was brand new.

Absolutely one of the best Real Time Strategy games bar none, having been playing Stronghold Crusader for what is probably a couple years short of a decade I am a very large authority on determining the replay value of this game. Having made it most of the way through the original Crusader Trail, and currently working on (near halfway or a little past  halfway of) the Warchest trail, I can definitely attest that this game is definitely not a casual pick-me-up in terms of the campaign. It begins pretty easily in terms of either campaign, personally boasting a completion time in some cases of two minutes or less in some of the beginning missions. However, it works the player up to the difficulty in the two campaigns slightly and then really tosses you into some challenging and interesting scenarios designed to make you think and put you out of your comfort zone. Experiment with different tactics and tower placement, send a detachment of horse archers here or there, and you can really work the battlefield in your favor. This is really a game for the RTS lover as well as those new to the genre, as one can play the less difficult Historical Campaigns to become better at the game, or cruise around in the Custom Games sector and you can formulate your own battles and challenges to overcome. With many different computer oppenents with mostly each opponent being unique, there is a very large portion of depth and ability to really challenge and engage the player. Each opponent has a different personality for the most part, and they each ask and send goods as well as manage armies and their economies in entirely respective and different manners. Having in some cases very beneficial troop movement strategies and in others there may be a lot to be desired. This however adds to the difference in difficulty with each of the different opponents, allowing for--again lots of different customization in scenarios as well as replay value just in the Custom Games sector alone. Not to mention, all of this is about the offline play. Definitely a good purchase at any price, you should really add this gem to your collection.

Endless Legend brings a whole new view on turn-based strategies. Nations with tens of characteristics, a changing world, unique atmosphere and balanced gameplay – all these things make the game a significant milestone for the genre. However, It takes a while to get going, it doesn't present complex information to the player in a concise and understandable way, which means it can sometimes be a frustrating experience for new players. Took me a couple tries before I got the hang of it. Once I did, it's been a fun game indeed. Endless Legend combines fantastic fiction with compelling strategy. Underpinning it all is a strong design philosophy that connects the tenets of the 4X genre together seamlessly, while providing a plethora of options. It takes a classic strategy formula, but makes it feel fresh, offering a fun, addictive and almost unique experience.

I've played most of the main paradox games eg EU4, CK2, HOI3, HOI4 but this one for me really stands out, it so eloquently re-creates the victorian era full of nationalism, great powers, technological achievemnt etc etc. For me its very addictive as its not merely a war game as other games tend to be in this genre but a whole living world, you can build factories do social reforms, and perhaps one of the most fun things is the politics as you can hold on to the old order against the rising liberals and communists/socialists or you can embrace new paths. Each politcal option (eg fascism or liberalsim) offer a unique way to play the game. Even the technological discovery is a real beuty i think, instead of arbitarily discovering tech you merely discover sections eg Medicine and inside those there are inventions such as vaccination in medicine (literacy rates affect this a lot, which I love, making Sweden a technological giant thanks to the high literacy is great) this system is one of the best i've seen in these kind of games. The population system is the best things though, it truely makes countries seem real, seeing battles knowing that actual people in your country will die or embracing immigrants from Europe as the US makes this game really stand out.
I can go on about this game but the simple fact is if you like grand strategy games or even just history, get this game, its very cheap for what you get and in my opinion a true masterpice that is unrivaled by any other game in representing the victorian era.
ps: make sure to get the beta 3.04 patch in the properties and all the dlc which tbh are kinda mandetory (same as HOI3) and certain mods like historical project mod (found on moddb) elevate the game to the next level.

TL:DR;
Attempts to simulate politics, industrialisation era and so forth; fails miserably at pretty much everything.
Game is dated in a very bad way. Disregard graphics, it was never a strong point of Paradox games.
However Victoria 2 just fails at anything that matters:
- AI is a joke
- Politcs is severly limited for no reason what so ever
- industrialisation does magic with supply/demand, goods vanish into thin air for no reason
- everything is so limiting, like province development - you can build fort or railroad but not both at the same time
- Military is a joke as well. There is an issue with unit production cap, which is highly decentralized
- Wars are insulting. If you shieldwall your borders AI will walk all the way around it and through the country it asked for military access to just pour units into your territory and have them anihillated
- Combat is a joke as well, you can win almost any battle provided you rotate units in combat to have them regain organisation and manpower
I could go on and on, but this is possibly the worst Paradox game I have played so far due to totally nonsensical limitations put on the player for no reason and broken simulation mechanics.
Save yourself money and time. You will not miss anything by not playing this game.

Now this is the kind of visual novels I love! You get to choose your own personality and make your own choices as you play the game and the characters adjust their attitudes towards you based on your previous choices. It's a very mature and complex version of the Cinderella story. The writer turned the ugly stepsisters and evil stepmother into surprisingly realistic characters. They all have reasons for being the way they are and actually some fairly decent redeeming qualities. You don't end up hating them by the end. The game leaves you really feeling for them and trying to understand what they're going through. My only regret is that the game was not longer and that there aren't more games like this out there. This is the perfect example of my favorite type of games. It has epic artwork and music; good, quality characters and is just wonderful in every aspect. If you like visual novels then I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

I do not play a lot of visual novels, but I tried Cinders.
And I loved it, why? Well..
First of all, it looks great. You do not just look at pictures, but the backgrounds are moving slightly giving the game a great look. And the characters look good as well.
Next, the characters. They are very well written and react to the choices you made during the game. They can be friends or hate you, your choices matter. And all of them have an agenda of their own.
The plot. You do know the story, but what if.... Cinderella was trying to run away. Well you can try in the game, it has several endings and your choices come back to you in the endings. Makes you wonder what would happen if you made some other choices. And that is the real strength of the game, you want to play it again to see what would happen if... It is that well written.
Last positive, the fast foreward button. After a playthrough you get access to this. All the dialoge you read before will be skipped, but the game stops if it is new. So after 2 play's you can skip bits of the story to get to the new and interesting part. A great feature.
I do reccomend this game, very much so. If you like stories and choices, pick it up and give it a try.

I wanted to like this game. A visual novel retelling of Cinderella, with beautiful graphics, the opportunity to come to see the characters in a new light, and a rather rewarding UI innovation that tells you whenever the dialogue snippet you're seeing could have gone differently had you chosen differently at some earlier juncture, making the game feel much more interactive.
Alas, I couldn't, for the game had too many things that broke my immersion. The protagonist, like the classic Cinderella, is supposed to be living in a small medieval village and have been working basically as a servant for her family for the last several years, yet when she speaks to her stepsisters, she sounds as if she had been reading several books worth of modern pop psychology. At one point she even tells one of her stepsisters, "you are the unknown variable in this equation". Just how did she and her stepsister (who seems to understand the expression just fine) have the chance to learn algebra?
Furthermore, although the process of Cinders winning over her stepsisters and allowing us to see them as people who had their reasons for treating Cinders badly could have been an enjoyable subversion of the original story, things seem to happen much too easily. At least with one of the stepsisters, the process starts with a conversation where Cinders basically asks whether the stepsister has considered that it would be nicer for everyone if they could be friends, and the stepsister goes "oh, you're right". (It's been a little while between me playing the game and writing the review, so I might misremember the details slightly, but even if they're a little off, this is still a good characterization of how sensible the conversion came off as.)
I finally stopped playing in a dialogue when a conversation with one of the stepsisters seemed to be going well, but suddenly she started lashing out at me for no reason. That could have been intentional, but it looked more like a bug. Ordinarily that wouldn't have been a game-killer and I could have just gone back to an earlier save to see if I could get around it somehow, but with this game, it was the final straw.

I recieved Cinders as a gift, and it has become one of my favorite visual novels of the year. The story follows that of Cinderella in a more mature light. It's a good vocabulary learning tool, but it won't teach you a new language. Vocabulary is clay, but possessing clay does not make you a sculptor. If you want to learn a language, this is a great first step. I bought the French pack, and I've "mastered" in game terms 50% of the content in two sessions of playing. But the game only aims to teach you 420 words, which is a very basic vocabulary. The average adult has a vocabulary of 12,000-17,000 words. Furthermore, the game teaches you no grammar. You might know what Yogurt or door mat is after beating a language set, but you won't be able to build a coherent sentence.
That's okay. Influent offers a very limited scope, but what it does offer it does rather well. If you are interested in taking the first few steps to learning a language, buy this game. It's worth the $10.

First of all if you're just looking for a linear story experience then buy something else, this is not the cutscene heavy go from point a to point b typical metal gear game.
If you can get over that and actually adapt to the new gameplay style you will vastly enjoy this game and get more than your money's worth. This is a game about exploration and experimentation. There is one main mission and six side missions, two of which are unlockable. If you just go through the missions just to beat them you'll probably get 4-5 hours of content, possibly more depending on how long it takes you to tackle those missions.
The real meat of the game is experimenting with the new fox engine and how to tackle those missions. For example there is a side mission where you have to assassinate two targets, now you can just go and kill them, you can go and grab a sniper rifle and take them out from a distance to more easily escape, you can extract both of the targets by chopper to get more information, it's up to you.
There's also prisoners and hidden secrets in every mission and context sensitive events that can be uncovered and triggered. All of these hidden secrets are the main story of this game. If you want to understand why certain characters act a certain way during the main game or what happened before you got there you have to uncover the tapes, they also potentially reveal information about The Phantom Pain. There's also XOF patches to find to unlock the two extra missions as well as unlockable weapons that can be placed at the starting point of each mission.
The gameplay is amazing in this game, with the addition of open world gameplay you have no radar so you have to mark and pay attention to enemies, there are such small details added that affect gameplay like the difference in knockout time between choking a guard, tranquilizing a guard and punching out a guard, how long a guard will stay asleep in a dark area versus a sunny area and other features. Reflex mode is an optional bullet time that triggers when you're spotted and it balances out the guard AI which can spot you from anywhere and from far distances especially on hard difficulty,
As a PC port of a console game this is one of the best PC ports I've ever played, there are so many customization options and it has been optimized perfectly and the controls are excellent with the exception of no mouse control in menus.
There is also a lot of mod support for this game and I have no doubt the modding community for this game will expand and produce more content in the future, this game is amazing and definitely worth the money if you can accept it as a new type of experience.

If this weren't simply a prequel I'd have given it my personal Game of the Year for 2014, but I expect Phantom Pain to deliver that for me in 2015. In case you're wondering, GOTY 2014 for me was Wolfenstein: The New Order.
In my mind this is a complete return to what made MGS 1-3 so fantastic. 4, while great in it's own way, was largely a playable movie with a bit of gameplay thrown in. Ground Zeroes has almost as much gameplay as 4 if you do all of the side missions and challenges so don't believe the rumors that there isn't much to this. Replayability is huge, take the time to train for Phantom Pain with some of the new features, because I found about a dozen ways to beat each mission and had an absolute blast doing it.
The ambience, gun control, stealth mechanics and general visual appeal of Ground Zeroes was near flawless for me. I love stealth games in general with MGS being my all time favorite franchise so I can be very picky about how it's done.
I'd love to see a little bit more consideration given to challenge timers for those of us who feel the need to kill enemies now and then. I love to do complete stealth runs of all types and I thoroughly enjoy the pacifist approach, but a challenge timer for simply getting in and out without being detected would be fantastic. I like to roleplay this series so while I do go completely pacifist at least once I find it logical to kill people now and then.
Overall, worth every penny, can't wait for Phantom Pain.

If you're picking up this game for the nostalgia factor, I'll give you a word of advice: Don't.
I don't care if it looks cool or something that may interest you, this is just a bad game.
I will admit, the graphics are pretty good and the concept's enjoyable, it's just heavily flawed and priced at $10 which feels like $5 more than I would care to give it.
You see, Evoland is a game ABOUT the nostalgia factor, it embraces the tropes of its forefathers and parodies it in a delightful (if not openly obvious) manner, the gameplay takes time to be varied to show the evolution of the Adventure RPG, and it even comes with a cute little card game which is genuinely interesting. But it's ABOUT the nostalgia factor, so rather than be a game that can stand on its own, it makes itself feel like every game it "showcases," just not as fun. Its most unique feature is a point in the game where you can shift between the "past" and the "future" to make it through an area, which was enjoyable! But that's literally the only unique feature it has. The rest is a lackluster adventure that is blatantly inferior to every game it pays homage to.
If there's one good thing Evoland does, it serves as an example when games choose to be retro, thinking that it would be simple, and put no thought into just what made it simple and fun. While it may be funny, that isn't enough to justify a four hour slog.

Do you want to conquer half the world and focus on war?  Play EU4 or HOI4.  Engage in court politics and backstab your rivals?  CKII is right up your alley.  Conquer the world without worrying about DLC?  Nope, that's not Victoria II either, that's EU3.  Instead, Victoria II is a game of rival imperial powers, a game where image - prestige - and economic development are ultimately more important than pure military might, and as a result it plays quite differently.
Part of the fun is the variety of different styles you can play through.  In one of my recent games, I decided to try to keep Russia as an absolute Tsardom throughout the whole game, while having a wealthy and highly educated society - and sure enough, by the early 1900s, the were serious revolts almost every other year.  I started avoiding wars intentionally, knowing that the equivalent of the Great War in real life would topple the monarchy and lead to civil war.
In my most recent game, I took on the reins of Spain, focusing on industrial development, liberal democracy, and establishing a new Spanish empire in Africa, while being pacifist in Europe.  Although things worked out in the end, they very nearly imploded in 1858 - 1860, as my economy cratered due to more-industrialized France, Germany, and Britain taking the bottom out of the wine and liquor market which large parts of my artisans depended on.  This resulted in tax revenues falling by more than 50% and a painful lesson in what happens when you are on the wrong side of industrialization.  Tax relief for the middle class, their acquisition of more diverse trades, and investment in basic farm and mine production over the next decade would stabilize the economy, but it was something I didn't expect to happen in-game, yet which made sense once I loaded up previous saves and realized what had happened.
Victoria II is a game where the learning curve is steep.  My first few games, I didn't know what I was doing or how to really influence my nation.  In most governments, your direct control is pretty limited, and change almost always happens slowly.  It was only with lots of experience and lots of reading the Victoria II Wiki that I really came to understand it well enough to enjoy it, particularly as a liberal nation with lassez-faire economic policy.
But once you get the gist of it, it's in some ways the most sublime of the Paradox games.  Your population is varied, and its desires evolve - and while you have some influence in that, a good chunk of that is due to the changing of the times.  You often can't simply build more buildings to improve your economy, or recruit more soldiers - you have to create conditions to incentivize building creation, or encourage your citizens to join the army - all while not neglecting other priorities too much, or raising taxes so high that your populace can't afford goods and starts revolting.  Unless you want them to revolt.  Sometimes your political establishment needs that angry voter base to take the action you desire.
The expansions really do add to it.  Heart of Darkness is particularly notable, with crises in particular spicing up the game.  While crisis can occur over colonization, often they happen over national liberation movements in the mid-late game.  A nation (say, Serbia) will seek to revolt against its imperial oppressor (say, Austria-Hungary), and if tensions get high enough, Great Powers (say, Britain, France, Italy, and Russia) may support the revolter nation, whereas other Great Powers (say, Germany and the Ottoman Empire) may support the ruler of the oppressed nation.  Sometimes, these are solved diplomatically; sometimes, they are settled on the field of war.  Regardless, it keeps the diplomatic situation uncertain, and thus interesting.  Do you always side with your allies?  What if they wind up on different sides?  What if it looks like the other alliance is stronger - do you side against your allies in the hopes they concede withour war as a result?  What if you miscalculate and a war starts when you really didn't want one?  You never know for sure if one side will concede.
On the whole, I'd definitely recommend this game, but I also wouldn't recommend it being your first Paradox game.  It requires patience to learn, and is relatively rare among strategy games in that military aspects are, if not a minor part, at least a secondary part.  Pick up EU4 or CKII first, and if after a game or two of those you find yourself looking for more economic detail, or politics that involves more parties and fewer dukes trying to poison your wine, this is where to turn.

I was expecting a tender and intimate story of a man who values superficial ideas like sex and partying highly and learns to grow past them. That's what I assumed from the way Only If presented itself.
What I DIDN'T know is that this game would be a pretentious piece of sh**.
See, Only If revolves around isolating and confusing the player; and it's nonsensical story certainly attests to that. Seriously, who is Vinnie? Who is Sam? What the hell is going on?
I get that that is the point of this game, and it does succeed- but it leaves so many holes and questions behind in its story, that I personally felt unfulfilled playing it. And the undertone message is either about... us being products of our environment and having a lack of choice in anything we do? Or is it learning to step away from video games and appreciate nature? Or is it a way to delve into the mind of a misogenystic man, who has to confront what a terrible person he is? It feels like its cramming so many random artistic messages into one game, that it turns into a big mess.
It is pretty to look at, though. That's the only saving grace for the poor labyrinthine design and even worse platforming and quick-time events. Seriously. There is platforming and quick-time events in a walking simulator. And both are annoying in their own respect.
I like some elements on this game. But for the rest of the game, it feels like a college student trying to do something postmodern in a lousy attempt to create art, without having something significant to say. And I'm gonna give it a 5/10

I like that each complete playthrough adds to the title screen (oh, and achievements obviously but who collects them these days?) which gives me a sense of fulfillment after each playthrough.
And thank the Gods for the skip function or those 3hrs would have been much longer and really all I wanted was Perrault (Still didn't get the ending I wanted but I know where I went wrong and oh gods why did I only save once?)
But yes, multiple endings, each with a little 'and so the story ends' because if there's one thing I appreciate (other than skip functions and swordsmen with way too many belts) it's finding out what happens to the story AFTER I've clicked my way through it amidst giggles.
My one annoyance is the ball scene. The next line is kind of a spoiler, I guess?
Regardless of the choices you make, it doesn't change because Cinders will still dance with His Lordship, who'll flirt and she'll smirk and coo 'tell me more darling' while I sit here wondering if she's forgotten her dear Captain's poetry already.
Maybe if I make more drastic choices it'll change, but I doubt it.
That said, that's honestly an incredibly minor detail (because skip function. I may mention this a lot but have you ever played an interactive novel without one? Don't.) and as above, the writing and endings definitly calls for replays.
Plus I kinda wanna see if I can get the girls on good terms because ho boy would that be an awesome ending (please be an awesome ending)
This is definitly a game I'd recommend to those that enjoy a good story, witty text and a pretty art style.
It's Cinderella, but with more spunk, a good dose of sass and less frolicking vermin.
I should have started with that.
Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go laugh about a well-respected guardsman making odd animal noises in the bushes.

This is a great visual novel game with multiple endings and a variety of different paths to choose from as you play.
The artwork is gorgeous, both the character designs and particularly the background scenery are very impressive.
The soundtrack is great too with a wide range of pieces that draw out a variety of emotions suited to each scene, from tense moments to quiet peaceful mornings.
The dialog is pretty solid and well written, I've definitely seen a lot worse in these kinds of games. The plot of the story is great, holds a lot of mystery and introduces a variety of interesting and distinct characters. With the varied endings, multiple playthroughs can be drastically different depending on the choices you make.
I've only finished the game once and am on my second playthrough at the time of writing this review, but there are at least 3 possible "romantic interests" for Cinders to end up with that I can see, perhaps more that I have not realized yet.
The dialog choices are interesting because it really feels like you get to shape the kind of personality that Cinders has, whether you choose to make her defiant and rebellious or more meek and complacent, or something in between. There is a lot of variety here and it helps create greater depth and adds to the replayability.
Even if you haven't ever really played visual novel games before, Cinders would be a great choice to break into the genre. It has a lot to offer and does a lot of things well.

MoaCube* has broken an arm, leg, thigh--heck, let's throw in hands too while we're at it. Praise to the writers in this project. Because of them, my expectations for visual novels have been a little more quenched.  The writing is ridiculously good compared to all visual novels.  Great quotes. A lot of time has been put in each choice point. Most of the time, the "better choice" is not clear or possible-there may be more than one. It's pretty fast pace.  The story quality is on par with Jisei/Kansei/Yousei in that aspect. A bit slow towards the end though. FYI This is NOT a game stressed as a dating sim. Your choices will give you an ending that doesn't really stress on the "person" you are with but rather, your final situation. First of all, if you aren't into visual novels this isn't for you. But on the otherhand, if you are then i garuntee you will love it if you play it all the way through.
PROS:
This game has four different main endings each with a couple different epilogues you can get through the choices you make. I've seen some reviews on here that say the choices don't matter, which i have to disagree with. Every visual novel game will have choices that seem meaingless and pointless and may not exactly contribute to the main story, but they are there to give you a sense of control. Other choices will be vitally important like the first choice you make. It can change the whole story depending on what you choose. Some people are bothered by no voices or terrible music or any other thing that falls under that category, these people will be so pleased with the musical choice the creators went with. It is beautiful and one of my favorite soundtracks of any game i have ever played. It makes the game 10x better in my opinion. Like i said before, there are four main endings each with their own epilogues; if you are one of those gamers that like to get all they can in a game but hesitates because it takes too long, you will be pleased to find that you can skip through all the dialogue so it makes the replay value go up. Another thing to add would be the artwork for this game. It is amazingly beautiful. Most visual novels have static(stay still) artwork that changes when you move forward in the conversation, but this game has dynamic artwork that moves. Granted it is not much but fires flicker, and dust particles in the sunlight are visible.
CONS:
Saying all this, there are some faults. Not many, but they are there. Some characters seem useless and very unnatural along with some situations. Sometimes the words lag behind if you are running something in the background. There, that's all the cons in my opinion. Time for the assessment.
ASSESSMENT:
Story: 8
Replay Value: 10
Music: 10
Characters: 8
Artwork: 10
OVERALL: 9.1
If you like visual novels, you will thoroughly enjoy this game.

Goggles – World of Vaporia was a game that really fascinated me when I was performing research on indie games for Steamified to cover. There was clearly a lot that I found appealing about the game. Thus, when I finally got my hands on the game I was filled with excitement and hope. Unfortunately, it turned into one of the more disappointing titles that I have reviewed. But there is much potential about the game if the major weakness that I find in the game is improved significantly.
I dearly love the way in which the game is introduced. The comic is absolutely a smart way of creating an introductory cut scene. The atmosphere of the game is immediately set and there’s quite a lot of hope that you will become immersed deeply into the game once it is finished and you’re finally beginning the game. The soundtrack is a highlight that contributes to the positive atmosphere of the game. I’m glad that the soundtrack is available for sale on Steam but I’d like to have seen a bundle (game plus soundtrack) deal instead of just selling the soundtrack individually. The atmosphere is there throughout the game and this is quite frankly the biggest advantage that the title currently has going for it.
My biggest criticism of the game is in its control and camera set ups. The game supports controller as well as keyboard and mouse play. The problem is that neither of them felt comfortable. I didn’t find the controller was nearly accurate or fluid enough. I found myself having enormous difficulty using the weapons accurately with the controller. It’s simple enough to fire your weapon pressing the right and left bumpers but it felt clumsy and very inaccurate. Aiming the camera in the right direction was very difficult and I didn’t know when I was actually in the direction that I wanted to shoot. Driving was also an issue with the controller with the keyboard driving much more accurately. When using keyboard and mouse I found that it altered the camera too much. With no option to turn down mouse sensitivity this made play highly frustrating yet not impossible.
Another negative towards the game – which would be remedied by an increased player base (before I played the peak number of players for the day was zilch, zero, nada and had been that way for at least two weeks according to SteamSpy. Unfortunately, the number of owners (343 to 1061) doesn’t scream that that is likely to change very much in the immediate future. For a game that bills itself as a cross-platform multiplayer arena game it is another disappointing sign. Unfortunately, I believe that Bit2Good Ug priced themselves out of the market with the Steam release.
When you’re attempting to combine the mechanics of a racing game and a shooter, two genres that demand accuracy, and it is your greatest weakness it makes it difficult to recommend. Sadly, the game hasn’t had an update since October 29th. Although it has potential to be a very good indie game I fear that it wont get there. Unfortunately, it isn’t worth the current price of US$19.99. There are much better games available on Steam that don’t have close to the same asking price. This is the same asking price for  Resident Evil 0, Rocket League and Rust to name just three which offer players much more value at that price. Given that the developers have taken advantage of Steamworks the next logical marketing steps for the game would be to lower the price, introduce a 4-pack (4 for the price of 3 at the new price), add it to the Steam weekly sales with a 25 or 50% discount (when the 4-pack is introduced and have that discounted as well). I’d then revisit the game a month after these changes take place before considering the bundle sites and if nothing has changed then insert it into a bundle (Bundle Stars preferably).
To leave this review on a positive note, which I’ll always endeavor to do, the atmosphere, sound track and the comic features of the game are highlights and kudos must absolutely be given for them. World of Vaporia is the debut Steam title of Bit2Good Ug and shows that the developer has potential. I’ll eagerly await future titles with the hopes that the studio’s potential is fulfilled.

First impression: Goggles - World of Vaporia is a fun light harted game with lots of charm and unique ideas. The story brings you to the steampunk planet Vaporia where evertything's run by machines. After an incident all machines become possessed and start attacking everything. The levels, while a bit difficult to navigate at times, are a joy to look at and the art style overall fits the setting nicely. Nothing in this game looks generic.
The four characters seem to be specialized for specific tasks in the game which makes me think that the focus of the game is more on multiplayer co-op. That said, single player is still fun, just a bit harder when playing Tesla or Vules Jerne. The weapons you can use reach from rocket launcher and steam hammer to cannons and a zapper gun just to mention some of them.
The dialogues between the characters, which are all voiced btw, are funny and continue telling the story during gameplay and in comic cutscenes between the levels. The cutscenes themselves are all hand drawn and really add to the overall atmosphere of the game. Speaking of atmosphere: the colors and light effects change the more dangerous the level gets, which looks pretty cool.
Also, the soundtrack deserves a mention: It sounds great and I've had it stuck in my head for days now. Especially since I found out the Wise Guys are featured in the title track!!

Interesting game, feels a bit like Banjo Kazooie: Nuts and Bolts, minus the crafting/quests.
All 4 characters are available from the start, each have alternate vehicles, weapons and overdrive powers. Combining these together means multiplayer should work well, though unfortunately I was unable to find players. Initially one arena is available with more available through game progression. Restricted by a global timer and locked gates, each level has 3 areas filled with enemies. Clearing out 'voids' raises a percentage and hitting certain targets rewards further access to the map. Once all 3 were cleared a boss spawns that requires killing to complete the level.
Graphically it looks quite beautiful but I do feel the gameplay becomes a bit rinse repeat. While a few different 'mini games' were available that decreased the global timer, still ultimately killing enemy XYZ or collecting random items. Story was all voiced, most characters sounded okay while some were a little rough. Game runs on unity, supports screen resolutions of 4k+ along with full controller remapping in-game. Few framedrops on a single 970 though it was nothing gamebreaking.
Overall a fun game in short bursts, just feel like it could have offered much more. Maybe some more meaningful quests, clearing voids and reducing global timers through group and mini-boss fights does get a little stale. If it were $15 or less, would be a solid recommend. With all the above mentioned and nobody yet playing multiplayer, it might be worth wishlisting instead if funds are a tight. Copy was provided by developer, doesn't change my thoughts. Cheers.

Truth be told, "Goggles - World of Vaporia" is not your new "100 Metascore" - game. It has its Flaws.
For instance:
Sometimes I keep getting lost in the different districts, especially in the inventors district (... well, to be fair: even if you're new to that game your only possibility to get lost is the inventors district. For example when Mr. King (I believe his name was) punches the floor, causing something like an earthquake in progress, which damages your character. I took me some time to realize that (but to be fair, it just could have been me who wasn't paying attention).
....
To be honest here, these are the major things that could "annoy" me. There are more things I like about this game than I "hate". I like the way it looks and how the different characters play differently (It's the same with the boss battles, btw). E.g. Quentin and Tesla do not play the same way. With Quentin I can kill my opponents from a distance (which is a wise thing to do by the way) while I have to rush at my enemies with Tesla. Frank is a more tanky character which can be usefull when you're playing with friends. Haven't touched Vules yet, though...
In addition I have to admit that I love the dialogues between the characters (ingame as well as in cutscenes). They really do make me smirk. If this weren't simply a prequel I'd have given it my personal Game of the Year for 2014, but I expect Phantom Pain to deliver that for me in 2015. In case you're wondering, GOTY 2014 for me was Wolfenstein: The New Order.
In my mind this is a complete return to what made MGS 1-3 so fantastic. 4, while great in it's own way, was largely a playable movie with a bit of gameplay thrown in. Ground Zeroes has almost as much gameplay as 4 if you do all of the side missions and challenges so don't believe the rumors that there isn't much to this. Replayability is huge, take the time to train for Phantom Pain with some of the new features, because I found about a dozen ways to beat each mission and had an absolute blast doing it.
The ambience, gun control, stealth mechanics and general visual appeal of Ground Zeroes was near flawless for me. I love stealth games in general with MGS being my all time favorite franchise so I can be very picky about how it's done.
I'd love to see a little bit more consideration given to challenge timers for those of us who feel the need to kill enemies now and then. I love to do complete stealth runs of all types and I thoroughly enjoy the pacifist approach, but a challenge timer for simply getting in and out without being detected would be fantastic. I like to roleplay this series so while I do go completely pacifist at least once I find it logical to kill people now and then.
Overall, worth every penny, can't wait for Phantom Pain.

Evoland is a game with a good concept but terrible execution. In Evoland you go through the different ages of video games; from 2D to 3D, and even through different styles of games like Diablo, Zelda and Final Fantasy. It sounds pretty cool right? However I was very disappointed with the game.
My biggest problem with Evoland is that everything is so simple. The games Evoland are referencing are fairly complex (like Zelda and Diablo) but since Evoland lacks depth these sections quickly lost their charm and became a massive grind. Relying on the occasional funny reference to keep you playing.
The worst offender was the Final Fantasy section. This area has timed battles, but the the main character can only attack and heal which made these sections so frustrating to play. There's no summons, leveling up or any of the depth that FF has (you can't even heal OUTSIDE of battle). Depth is what makes Final Fantasy fun. Like think of the difference between a level 1 and level 50 character, now you're forced to play as the level 1 character for the entire game... yay?
Next the story... it sucks. Early on it's fine since stories weren't a big focus back then... but it never improves. You only ever get 2 party members and by the FF section the story is still "the bad guy is doing bad things, kill him". I wish the story went completely wacky and over the top (as FF's are known to do) but it never puts in the effort to improve it. The game is also filled with unmemorable and bland characters which doesn't help.
The rest of the game handles fine. The music's nice with some good tunes, the controls are smooth and the artstyle changes with the different eras of gaming (from 2D to full 3D models). For anyone wondering these changes happen after you find them in a chest.
Evoland relies on nostalgia and witty remarks over good gameplay and story. You might find a funny reference, but at the end of the day the game is so shallow that it just feels like a waste of money. I finished it in two and a half hours and I would not recommened Evoland.

A lot of sequels strike out in new directions, and end up falling flat for their trouble. Sometimes they get too far away from what made the original great, and other times they find a way to ruin that original appeal. The other side of the coin is that just giving players more of the original risks making the series stale. This is the approach that Stronghold Crusader took in the wake of Stronghold's success, but the sheer volume of content more than makes up for the lack of innovation.
Just as you did in Stronghold, Crusader challenges you to erect and manage castles throughout a variety of scenarios and skirmishes. Once your keep and granary are placed, it's up to you to site farms, mills, workshops, and homes to keep your people safe and happy. So long as you remain a popular ruler more people will come serve at your castle, but more people means a greater drain on your resources. In the midst of balancing these two factors you'll need to raise walls and armies to fend off invaders seeking your crown.
The familiar moors of England have given way to the marauding Moors of the holy land for this outing. There are a few big changes to be aware of, most notably the desert maps. Gone are the rolling fields of the first game, instead leaving you with small oases to supply your essential farms and woodcutters. A mercenary post allows you to recruit new Arabian units, everything from armored swordsmen to wall-scaling assassins. There's even a rudimentary diplomacy system, allowing you to form alliances and request resources.
Stronghold Crusader features four historical campaigns, focusing on different parts of the Crusades. Each campaign is five scenarios long and features a gentle learning curve that provides a fair challenge by the end. There's little story to be found here in contrast with Stronghold's tale of political maneuvering, just some blurbs about historical relevance. The real meat of the game is the Crusader mode, a campaign of up to 50 battles against AI opponents. Right from the get-go you can access all the buildings and options the game has to offer in pursuit of conquest, building your perfect citadel and laying siege to nearby enemies. The strategy of castle-to-castle warfare takes a little getting used to after the easy pace of the campaigns, but it's thrilling to launch pitched battles and deploy siege engines to topple your foes.
There's not a lot of innovation to be found here over the original Stronghold, but there really doesn't need to be. Crusader instead gives you plenty more to see and do, especially on the military side. The graphics are a bit improved, with sharper structures and cleaner animations, and the sounds of both peace and battle are just as immersive as before. Honestly, I consider this the superior game just due to the depth of content and the little additions to the proven formula. If you're looking for endless conquest and sieges, this is the Stronghold title you want.

Awesomenauts - A Game I Can't Leave
Nauts is a game that I have had for over a year now and have probably played at least 1 round per week since I have gotten it. It is a game that I keep coming back to and never lose interest in it. In fact I have more time on this game than any other game in my steam library. I always love inviting friends and playing with them to see if we can pull off fun combos with characters or abilities and whenever we do the whole group is excited. Whenever the game is updated (which as of recent is really often) I like the update for the most part. I haven't had a day where I think "Oh Ronimo has really ran out of ideas.." or something of that sort. They typically take feedback from their playerbase and add what they believe will help the game whenever they can. They even run a livestream every week to talk directly to the fans and tell them news and hint at future updates. Yesterday they revealed a brand new character so now is a perfect time to start getting into awesomenauts. For easy reference, I will now list Pros and Cons of awesomenauts.
_PROS_
-Keeps you coming back for more rounds

-Every character has personality and backstory to them
-Has a system set to show your loyality to the game using Prestige badges that is nice. It has flaws though and I will get into that below.
-Has Steam achievements you actually want to get (I hope they add even more!)

_CONS_

This doesn't sound like a con but when you factor in that the way you get it is by basically resetting your level (which is used for upgrades on characters in later parts of their kit) it becomes obvious how big a handicap that can be.
