As someone who has been playing this game ever since it was released on PS3/XBOX 360 back in May 2012, I REALLY want to recommend people to play this game. There is a lot of fun in this game due to the 2D side-scrolling gameplay, which I find very interesting for a MOBA game back in 2012, and the fun characters including new ones (most of which is free) that roll out overtime. The maps can be challenging as cetain characters can take advantage of it. For example, when Ayla's Rage can damage driods under the area of top turrents (which I find BS sometimes) at Ribbit IV. Sentry's Black Hole Sun applies too as this ability can drag and hold players when placed under them despite some form of ground inbetween the players and the hole. Another thing I like is that matches are pretty fast compared to popular MOBAs like League of Legends, DOTA 2, etc. You don't have to spend almost an hour on ONE match. In Awesomenauts, the average match is about 15-20 minutes with the longest I've experienced is about 40 minutes (this is before the XP system).
But as I outweigh the pros and cons of this game, I find that the cons are
higher than the pros, especially with the new XP system. As some people mention it before, the purpose of the XP is to make matches go faster by creating a snowball effect. Any kills, whether it is creeps, driods, or other players, will raise their team level. On paper, the idea is great since in the past, there were some matches that drag out too long. As for execution, this is debatable. People who win a lot with this system will likely say there's little to no problems with it. People who lose a lot with this system will likely say the XP system is broken and unplayable. Personably, as someone who used to win a lot of games before, I can agree to the fact that this can be a problem. The XP system requires to have little to no mistakes when playing because every kill is exp points for the other team. Pair this up with the
matchmaking, those claims that this is unplayable may have some truth in it. The old system makes you work hard to gain a victory. The new system is on drugs as anybody, no matter what rank/league you are in, can simply win if one team is screwing up. It's subjective to how everyone feels about the XP system, but everyone can agree that this can be frustrating when you are paired up with team members who are either new to the game, new to the character they are playing as, or has no sense of teamwork or coordination. And honestly, I suffered way too much with that.
Other things to note is that there are no ranked matches, there is no surrender option, and there are matchmaking issues. For ranked matches, I don't understand why this does not exist since we have leagues/tiers, ranked points, and such. I want to play with experienced people without the need to go over to community and organize games. Not all of us has the time to go over to the fourms and ask if people wany to play. For me, I play it like a lot of multiplayer games: hit the matchmaking button and hope the team you are in is actually good. For surrenders, why isn't this a thing? If a game is going very bad to the point where you and your teammates cannot do anything but feed the enemy team, why can't we be given the option to surrender instead waiting for the enemy team to destroy almost every turrent and finally destroy the base. This happens way too often even though I tried to carry my team. I think we can prevent a good amount of people ragequiting and going AFK instead of waiting for the match to be over. If time is the issue (like people wanting to surrender less than five minutes in the game), then set the limit to activate surrunder at the 8-10 minute mark. For these two issues, it has been almost
years and Ronimo still haven't resolved this, or rather walked around it. Lastly on the
matchmaking, we can all agree that we had experienced being with bad teammates against very good players or being placed into a match where the team you are in has only one turrent left a handful of times. I understand that Ronimo is trying their best, especially since they are just indie developers, but why not just give us the option to choose a game instead of the matchmaking be random. Why not give us the option to prevent us from joining mid to late games randomly? This is infuriating because I have experienced this crap for so long.
It is also note that you lose more rank points if you leave a game versus losing a game (for those of you who care about your rank). While this encourages people to stay in their match and finish it (or wait till you lose), any disconnect is considered a leave. To be clear, leaving a game means losing half the experience points towards your league and unlockable skills (especially if you prestige) when you win a match. It may seem like an annoyance, but this is a warning for people who is tempted to leave a match just to find a game you can win in.
I know this is a very long review, but this is a game I have put so much time in since its original release, and only to feel like being stepped on due to these problems. And the thing is, I want this game to succeed. This game has a lot of potential to be a unique MOBA game that is diferent than the typical and popular MOBA games out there. If anything, I want to say that Awesomenauts is my favorite MOBA, but I can't. The game had undergone a lot of changes, for better or worse, over the years, and while it is not as bad as most people who didn't recommend this game says it is, this game still need a lot of tuning, epecially ever since the new XP system. I know the Overdrive expansion is coming soon with it promising better matchmaking. But as it stands right now, be very, very wary when considering to buy this game along with the Starstorm expansion. Wait for a sale if anything.
: The game is mixed IMO due to frustrating issues, both common and personal, that has not been resolved or has been walked around. Wait for a sale.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game — although it would perhaps more accurately be described as a 'choose your own adventure' novel, of the kind I loved when I was a child. You are given enough choice to influence the game and feel as though you have control over your own fate, but not so many choices as to make each individual choice feel meaningless or to ruin the narrative structure.
After finishing it the first time, I loaded a little while back and tried to try out some other choices, and was initially very disappointed — it felt that no matter what I chose, there were very few endings open to me, and they were virtually identical. It wasn't until I started again from the beginning that I realised this wasn't because my choices were meaningless, but because all my previous choices and developed the world in such a way that those outcomes were the only realistic consequences of the character I constructed in the situation I placed her in.
On the whole, if you don't like Virtual Novels, you won't like this one. If you're looking for something a bit more 'gamey', like Long Live the Queen, this will probably be too simplistic for you. But if you like reading, even if you were never into 'choose your own adventure' stories, this is probably worth picking up.
Game-play aside, the game is ~gorgeous~ and the music lovely. Several of the backgrounds are in my desktop wallpaper rotation they're that pretty.

Some people help themselves learn a language by labeling everything in their house in the target language. This is exactly the virtual version of that, no more, no less. I certainly enjoy getting the benefits of that without the real-world eyesore or effort, but it is a very limited tool in learning a language. I would only recommend it as a fun practice tool for those already learning a language in other ways.
What it does, it does well. But it doesn't try to do much.
Tip: The Spanish language version teaches in a Spanish accent, as opposed to central/southern American which may be more desirable to learn for those in the US.
Annoyances: I find the controls a little awkward and I'd like to customize them (say, remap keys), but this isn't an option. No controller support. The UI leaves a bit to be desired. You can only get to some things from the third-person view, for example, and it is really unintuitive to set up language lists. Two days playing it and I can't figure out if there's a way to get a hint when looking for an object. Words are coded with icons and labels whose meaning is not immediately evident. And I wish it would remember my VSync  settings. I'm sure a little more polish can solve these problems, and I hope the developer keeps at it!

A different take on the Cinderella story, Cinders is a beautiful visual novel with interesting choices and character development. The game is about 5 hours long and it was fun trying to get the other endings after finishing it for the first time.

If you are looking for a fun way to gain "word recognition" (mostly of nouns) then this is a fun way to learn household objects in whatever language you choose.
You will not learn "travel" related words, and even the model airplane in the game is label and translated as "toy" rather than "toy airplane." For the great, low price of about $10 you can start a really fun way of learning a language. If you decide you want to try to learn these same words in other languages, then the DLC option is an inexpensive and incredibly affordable way of learning.
The retail price point on this software (currently $10 for a base language and $5 or less for another language) is very fair for what it is and does. I hope the developer expands the four room "house" to include some outdoor items one day, but that is a large venture when they plan to support so many languages.
CONS: The words have only one speed of pronunciation, and sometimes the recorded audio has some volume problems that is not baseline with the rest of the audio files. Also, there are a lot of other "common life" items that could/should have been included; for example, instead of a just a "photo", the creator could have had a photo, and next to that a "family photo" with a "man"/"father", "woman"/"mother"...etc.
Overall, I'd really recommend the software if you are looking to dive in and gain some rot memorization skills in a language. Don't expect to read, write, or speak a sentence with this, and you will be happy with the gameplay and results of you learning some new words in another language.

Bought the French pack. Seems pretty cool so far, though I've only spent about a half hour in this. You interact with things in your environment and learn their names in your chosen language, and when you've picked up enough words, you can review them in minigames.
I'm not sure I'd recommend this to a total beginner to French. This might be something that comes up later in the game, but I was confused to see that the game omits the proper gender articles for a given word. For instance, the word for "book" is "livre", which the game tells you is "masculine". That's correct, but then the game doesn't tell you what that means.
The minigames could use a little bit of work. Time Attack was my favorite one, where you're given a word and you have to run around and find the object the word corresponds to. So if you're given "mur", you have to go and double click on a "wall". It's easy enough, but things get stressful when you have to click very precisely on a really small or skinny object and you're trying to do it as fast as possible to get a good score. I wish the hitboxes had been bigger on these objects, because even if I turn up mouse sensitivity, a stylo is SO MUCH SMALLER than the bureau, and it can be a pain getting my cursors to line up with a tiny object. The sluggish walk controls don't help much either.
The other minigame I tried out let you take control of a model plane and zoom around the room shooting objects that match up to a given word. Thing is, you have to shoot several times at an object (presumably to tell the game you REALLY, REALLY, REALLY do know the meaning of that word, even though the repetition isn't a feature of the other minigame) and your plane is constantly moving towards whatever point in space you're focusing on. This means that you have to sometimes turn around to get more breathing room to fire on the object until the game finally tells you you're correct, and THIS is an issue because the plane controls rather sluggishly, and also explodes upon touching just about anything.
Still, it was a good refresher for some vocabulary I'd forgotten. I could see this being useful as a side tool for a more in-depth language course.

The game is simple but fun. You walk around a room and double click objects to see what they are called in the language you are learning. Add these words to a list and when you have 10, you can test yourself on them. From there you build more lists and earn stars for mastering words that are used to unlock more complicated words such as adjectives and verbs.
The Chinese that is being taught is the mainland Beijing accent with simplified characters. Both Chinese and Japanese have the ability to switch to their English phonetic variants respectively (pinyin/romaji). However, if you already know some Chinese characters, kanji, hiragana and katakana the game is helpful in reinforcing those areas as well as teaching new characters. As far as I can tell there is nothing in the game that reinforces your ability to write the characters, but the game will definitely help you learn how to read and recognize hanzi (汉字) and kanji (漢字).

Cannot recommend. Overall 3/10, 6 hours of game play, steam says 8, before finished at medium difficulty. Does not seem to have much replay value.
Good stuff: Beautiful visually, and I really like the characters, well the villains characters and the voice acting in the cut scenes are fantastic, the way the enunciate and gesture feels real, like a life-action movie.
Pet peeve: You cannot pause or skip any of the, sometimes several minutes long, cut scenes, extremely annoying I think, but might not matter much to others. As far as I can figure out you cannot even re-watch cut scenes anywhere (besides likely finding them on youtube or other) so only option is sitting and keeping up with the “riveting” plot. It is one of the several small annoyances that just adds up to the game looking high priced (graphics), but feeling like something that did not even have the money for a test-run.
Lack of diversity in combat/enemies: Compared to a much older combat with quick time events game like God of War, Ryse Son of Rome have a fraction of the enemies. Basically there is: Archer, un-shielded warrior, shielded warrior, heavy attack warriors (3 versions, shield wearing, duel-wielding and big two-handed wielder) and then some bosses that are variance of same. Sure some are dressed as Romans, some as “Britons” and some as cow skull headed scots, but really, they all have the same mechanics and executions/quick times done to them.
The repetitiveness of the combat system and the warriors makes you question your characters sanity, as he is fighting 4, not only functionally identically, but even visually identical enemies, right down to their nipple tinsels (no joke, the fat male warriors wear them). The boss fights are even worse I think, nearing the end I think I literally died of boredom in some fights after having to go “parry-parry-dodge stab once” over and freaking over to get to the damned end.
Compared to other combat games God of War have dozens of functionally different enemies, unique quick time events or even stages to take them out as well. Again though, RSR have better character voice I think, they seem much more real.
Setting: I am no historian, but what with the occasional magic/gods in the game, setting in weird timeline where Rome/Britons have huge medieval castles in a somewhat united Britain, seems weird. I think the setting would’ve been better off being Warhammer, Lord of the Rings or even Song of Ice and Fire. Something where the game did not have to try one hand to be all “oh we’re so historical” while with the other hand waving gods, magic and “Totally not chaos worshipping beastmen” at you (pretty sure there was at least one star of the chaos gods at some point).
I really liked the formation combat part, but again, very repetitive after awhile, would have been nice if more was added to it. Plus there was very little introduction to it, compared to the beginning of the game which apparently have to explain to you that “Left mouse button = sword attack” and other really simple stuff. Which reminds, if you mess up and die, there will occasionally pop up a message reminding you of which buttons you should use (remember to dodge/make perfect parry or what have you) but the help pops up AFTER you have entered combat, are likely already mashing buttons to survive, so you are likely, as I did many times, to remove the help before you even have a chance to se it. Changing it to a “Esc to remove” rather than any-button might be smart. Unlike the damned cut scenes, I mean really, just a “Are you sure you want to skip?” and allow us to watch it later, cannot be that difficult.
Short game, still repetitive, weird setting, good voice/character acting, lots of small fault/annoyances: 3/10 game, would NOT recommend for more than 3-5 euros top.

I first tried the co-op modes (there are 3 variations of two-player modes to choose from: Arena, Survival, and Round-to-Round) with a friend. Spent an hour and a half there, and had a good time. My biggest complaint after that experience was that it would've been a lot more enjoyable if the various game modes had a little more variation to them. They all felt pretty similar to me, and generally lasted the same amount of time. I'd go back to play those modes if a friend asked me to; I enjoyed the co-op executions, and the more free-feeling combat.
Then I went to the game's campaign mode (single-player only). The story had no real buildup or anything to draw me in in the first couple of hours (the game took me about 6.5 hours to complete). But the first couple of hours were more enjoyable to me than the rest, I'd later find out. As I reached the game's mid-point, the theme started reminding me a lot of the TV series Spartacus, which I loved watching. So that's alright, even though I feel like a lot of those story ideas have been run into the ground. The game lacks its own unique personality to back that plot up, though. Everything was extremely predictable, the characters were forgettable, and I was not satisfied with the game's ending sequence, to say the least.
The reason I say the first half was more enjoyable for me than the second half is mostly due to the heavier inclusion of "boss battles" later on. What separates boss battles from normal combat is one very simple thing: scripting. When entering a boss battle, you simply lose the ability to take advantage of the game's combat systems and the creativity involved in the variation. Rather than coming up with your own way of tackling a boss, you're guided to enter a back and forth strategy of dodging attack 1, 2, and 3, then getting one slice in with your own gladius. Repeat 10 times, enter a cutscene, and then for some battles, return to a boss with a once again full health bar to do the exact same thing. This method of combat became extremely tedious. I tried a handful of times to alter my strategy outside of what the game was instructing me to do during boss encounters (by way of different colored QTE highlight prompts), but every time I tried, my attacks were all blocked regardless of whether or not I managed to get my opponent's back towards me, or if I had bashed them first with my shield, or if I had blocked one of their attacks. It made no difference.
And then the ending of the game. Oh, the ending. I streamed the game, and a friend who was watching summed it up pretty nicely with the comment "At least the gods are having fun."
If the game is on sale and you can snag it for less than $10, the 2-player game modes can be fun with a friend for a while. Outside of that, I do not recommend the game.

A Zelda and Final Fantasy fan love letter.
This title is pretty short and full of RPG in-jokes, and that's part of its charm of course, but the real accomplishment here is the standout blend of nearly every genre defining aspect of retro (and in some ways even modern) RPGs.
Evoland starts in a very gameboy-like monochrome pixelated setting, and you start by unlocking the arrow keys for movement, and then the scrolling screens so you can move to different areas, and then enemies, and then a weapon to fight said enemies. Get a little further still and you'll unlock a color display! Wow color!
The unlockable everything aspect sort of reminded me of Half Minute Hero, though thankfully Evoland doesn't have that title's frantic "time is running out constantly hurry hurry hurry!" methodology killing its fun factor.
It's neat to look back on the progression and see how things evolve as you play, and it's a fairly good reminder really to the way games of old have matured over the decades.
I'd say the two plain-as-day obvious biggest influences on Evoland are the early Zelda titles, and in particular, Final Fantasy 7. However there are a number of other small references here and there to others as well: Secret of Mana, Final Fantasy 4 and 6, Final Fantasy 8 just to name a few that I was easily able to recognize.
The story, well there hardly is one, and again, see Zelda/FF7 for the majority of parallels, sometimes downright ripoffs honestly. Still the concept remains interesting throughout the relatively short campaign (it took me about 8 hours for 100% completion).
The fact that you don't have to sink 100+ hours into it is actually welcome. It gets the point across and manages to be enjoyable without requiring a month's worth of your spare time.
If you are a fan of older RPGs and indie titles you'll definitely find something to like here. Just having multiple battle systems and graphical presentations in a single game and having it work well together is reason enough to give it a try. Not to mention the trip down memory lane.

I would give this game 1/5 stars.
This game was supposed to be a fun 'concept' game, making nostaligic references to the classic RPGs which we all know and love. The problem with Evoland is that it tries to be a game in itself; A very lengthy, monotonous, repetitive game where the 'evolutions' happen infrequently, inconsistently, incompatibly, and generally do not enhance the gameplay experience. The problem is that all of the evolutions and references to RPG classics are highly watered down. If anything, I would describe Evoland as the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized version of otherwise good games. Don't get me wrong; the trailor for the game looks exciting and is the reason why I purchased this game, but the excitement stops there. Within minutes of playing, I already feel the dread of doing the same thing over and over and over again. The turn-based battles are inconsequential in that all the of money and experience you earn amounts to nothing important, and does not give you an edge in the game. The majority of the game is a primative take on Zelda 1/3ish, containing substantially fewer features than the original. If this game were significantly shortened in length, or if the puzzles weren't boring, repetitive chores, or if the gameplay experience was actually enhanced rather than watered down in relation to the referenced RPG classics, then I would recommend this game. But no; I'm afraid that this game was a complete waste of time. Out of obligation, I completed the game in five hours and unlocked the majority of the achievements (the rest would have been easy to attain if I felt like doing more repetitive gameplay), but honestly, knowing what I know now, I wouldn't have bothered playing the game if it were given to me for free. I wouldn't play the game if I were paid $25 to play it; those five hours of my life are much more precious than this waste of time.

Getting this game to run on a modern PC and with a newer controller can be quite the hassle but the extra hardship setting up is definitely worth it. I can see that Devil May Cry 3 is the series’ fan favorite for a good reason. The combat has been fleshed out significantly more than the game’s predecessors and manages to feel oh so satisfying. Personally I feel that this game is when the “character action” genre finally came to fruition as a well polished experience. Everything with movement and fight feels great and manages to stay true to the games stylish roots. The number of weapons and combos are greatly expanded from the previous games as well and of course there are lots of challenging bosses to test them out on.
A lot of the charm of this game comes from how over-the-top and cheesy the cutscenes can be. It’s almost as if parts of it are straight out of a B list action movie with how ridiculous it can get. However this doesn’t detract from the experience and gives the games it’s own unique personality. Of course the story still manages to have serious moments and lots of sequences building excitement for what's to come. The amount of replayability is outstanding as well. The combat feels so good that immediately after beating it I went straight into doing a few missions on the new difficulty and then lost track of time playing the Bloody Palace mode. Overall if you’re looking for a stylish and challenging game and are willing to do a little extra to get it working on your PC, I would definitely recommend picking up this game.

This game has a VERY HIGH learning curve, but once you master it, the game is an absolute blast to play!
I really recommend that you put 50-100 hrs into the main ARK game before you attempt to play this game. This game is EXTREMELY accelerated version of the original ARK game with several elements that test quick thinking, game skill/strategy, and most important of all FORCED CONFLICT. If you do not take your time to master the elements of the original ARK game (harvesting, taming, tech trees, crafting, building, weather survival, fighting, etc) I could easily see how you would be completely lost in this version of the game. The game is so fast paced that you have no time to experiment, you must act very quickly to survive.
The game offers arena style play. Basically identical to The Hunger Games in every way. Every new match begins in what my friends and I call "heaven". It is a floating land above the arena where you see everyone that is about to play. You can talk to eachother, text chat, join tribes, create/load tribe flags, and begin your strategy. After 5 minutes of heaven, you will descend gracefully to the center platform via a beam of light. This is the middle of the map and it marks the beginning and ending of the game (the game will eventually force you back to the center at the end of the round).
As soon as your feet hit the ground you can run. You basically begin with two options, do  you run to the middle of the platform where random drops have been placed which offer supplies like food, armor, and weapons, or do you begin heading outward trying to get a headstart and distancing yourself from other players.
Hint: Its almost always better to run out and avoid the center. You won't encounter the backstabbing CLUSTER F#%@ that ensues in the middle. It also reduces the risk of the chasing that happens right after the drops are collected as people try to get away and into the woods.
Once you find saftey you want to start collecting basic supplies. This includes armor, weapons and tools. Obviously build a pickaxe first, then an axe, then a spear. The spear with two shot any player this early on. Next I suggest building a cloth hat. This only gives you 10hp but it does mean that people can no longer one shot you with a bow. Then finish out your armor. While you build these tools you will level up. I suggest putting all level up points into speed and hp. Too many players go for melee damage, but remember that as soon as you graduate from the spear to the bow which is about 5 minutes into the game, you will no longer use any weapon that can take advantage of melee damage, unless by chance you decide to use a pike late game, but that would be a bad choice anyway. Remember that bows, guns, and crossbow don't benefit from melee damage. A few points toward stamina is also handy so you can run longer. But focus most your points towards health and movement speed.
Now you can start taming dinos or building like you would in the main ARK game. You will find that leveling up and harvesting is all accelerated, as is taming. Taming a dilo takes like 2 pieces of meat and 1 minute of time. A trike is the best early tame to get. They can pack weight for you and harvest berries (narcotics). They are also tanky which is nice if you run into a carno or raptor early and want to tame it. A trike takes about 2-3 minutes to tame. So the whole process is very fast compared to vanilla ark.
Things to remember about taming is that once you have finished a tame, your dino will automatically have a saddle. You do not need to build saddles in this game, they are attached to dinos and any ridable dino will come with a saddle as soon as it tames.
Building is a good way to level up, but don't waste too much time with a fancy base. I usually build a 2x2 base and i often use thatch since you may likely need to abandon a base quickly. I often will not worry about a roof. Your primary focus is to get metal asap. Build refining forges and start harvesting a little metal. You need 10 metal to get started and then stop harvesting. The 10 metal will turn into 5 ingots. You will use 4 ingots to make a smithy and 1 ingot to make a metal pickaxe. Once you have the pickaxe your mining will yield 5 times as much metal from a metal node, making it more efficient to harvest metal. With the pickaxe you want to go get 300-400 metal so you can yield about 150-200 ingots. This is really all you can afford to work with in this period of time. It will be sufficient for you to build several guns which is your primary focus for surviving late game against players.
You may find the walls of the world closing in on you. At about the 30 minute mark of the game, the boundaries start to close in, pushing you towards the center. The farther out from the center you are, the sooner you will have to move and abandon your base. The farther out you are however, and the more metal you will find to harvest. It is best to act quickly and start harvesting metal as much of the metal gets cut off at 30 minutes in. You can only survive 30 seconds outside the boundaries, but your dinos can last forever.
You will need to learn whistle commands for your dinos to get the most out of them. By default "J" will tell all dinos around you to follow you. This allows you to call them all and run. It is best to keep an eye on the wall and be ready to travel before the wall gets to you. This way if a dino gets stuck you can get him unstuck before the walls close in.
Eventually as the timer goes down, you will move closer to the center. You will become more likely to encounter other players as it progresses as the area of play shrinks. The final minute will be only the center platform of the map. This is where the final players duke it out with dinos and weapons in a fight to the death.
When you die... its over. There is no respawn. All your dinos will be unclaimed and anyone can come claim them.
I found the game exhilerating. I remember when I was going into the final arena solo against a two player tribe and my heart nearly pounded out of my chest. It was a legitemate rush I rarely feel in video games anymore.
I enjoy the accelerated timeframe of the game. I usually play 2 player tribes which is a 1 hour game. This allows you to have the ark experience in a nice 1 hour chuck of time. It focuses much more on ark gameplay than it does on the grind that most people complain about in the vanilla version of this game. Speed is critical in this game and strategy is everything. You get the PVP experience of Vanilla Ark, but it feels much more fun and balanced. Part of it is because when you do die, you don't feel like you lost as much. You didn't spend 1,000 hours building a base, just for it to get wrecked by an alpha tribe when you were offline. In this game, everyone literally starts in the exact same place. Everyone has the same opportunities and chances of winning.
Sure, there is some luck to the game. There have been games where we happened to get swarmed by Sabertooths before we even had cloth armor. But these are forgivable and understandable. Sometimes you will struggle to find anywhere to build or harvest or struggle to find anything to tame. Once again, this game forces you to adapt and that is what I enjoy about it. If you planned on getting a powerful dino tame but ended up not finding one, then you may have to adjust startegy partway through and either start building weapons and out power the other players or maybe just go hunting for other tribes in hopes of killing them and stealing their tames and resources. This is part of the game and I enjoy the unpredictable nature of the game.

This is one of the greatest games ever made, and probably Paradox Development Studio's masterpiece.  If you love history and economics, this game is the holy grail and will become the best game you've ever played.
The mechanics dealing with the worldwide economy in this game are so extraordinarily good that you will wonder how they did it. It’s magic, and it’s probably the pinnacle of interactive simulation.  Seeing how your people, factories, and resources fit into a worldwide economy as you try to position your nation among the others is a treat.
The crisis system in this game is, as far as I can tell, unequaled.  No longer are you warring against a set of aimless nations, but instead, against a series of alliances that are hobbled together to suite each AI’s needs.  The AI, in response to most crisis, typically knows the stakes, which side they want to win, and where they fit in the puzzle.  You simply can’t say that about any other AI in any other grand strategy game.
I mentioned it before, but in this game, you have a nation of people, and not a nation of provinces like every single other strategy game on the market. The choices you make regarding the people in your country are pretty binary, and I’ll admit that there’s only one real strategy: educate and liberalize.  Yet, seeing your populations expand and change during the industrial revolution is striking to behold.  With every factory built, you feel more connected to your country.  It gives you the same feelings that you get when you build tall in a civ game.
The warring action in this game is pretty sub-par.  There’s not much to it.  If someone somehow combined the best parts of HOI3 (not HOI4… please, god no) and Vicky2, they would create the greatest game of all time.

There is no doubt that if you love the idea of managing a team with all the myriad problems and challenges it brings then FM is without peer. A serious alternative might well be the driver for revolutionary change - but, as we have seen in other areas, this may not necessarily be a good thing. The game's jewel in the crown for me - and what makes this game such an  enticing challenge - is still the unfathomable dark heart of FM's match engine. --THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE GERMAN VERSION OF THE SOFTWARE--
RECOMMENDED...but with some notable caveats.
VOCAB GENDER: I was hesitant to purchase this program at first because I wasn't sure if it would identify the gender of the vocabulary words. Gender is VERY important to speak proper German as it modifies many other words in a sentence (mein, meine, meinen...etc.) While the game DOES give the gender via text when selecting the word, it does not speak the gender in the audio or when doing the games. I would much prefer if it included that, since the games are meant to bolster your vocabulary it should include gender in spoken audio.
ONLY TEACHES VOCAB: If you want a program focused on creating sentences and communicating with others, try Rosetta Stone. This is first and foremost vocab software. Go elsewhere to learn how to employ verbs correctly.
GOOD VOCAB, BUT MISSING ELEMENTS: The list of vocabulary words consists of "around the house" items. While useful, it does not cover things like ordering in a restaurant, traveling, etc.
A GOOD COMPONENT TO LANGUAGE LEARNING, BUT NOT A COMPLETE PROGRAM: This software is excellent and fun for learning basic vocabulary, but limited in many ways. My dream language program is similar to this in 3D/FPS style, but including many places like restaurants, train stations, work, and with NPCs whom you can interact with and "discuss" topics, such as your boss, a waitperson, a buddy at the bar ("Kneiper"), a date, a hotel staffer...sort of a Rosetta Stone meets Second Life. Literally a 3D immersion in the other culture. This is not it.
The final word,
KNOW WHAT YOU'RE GETTING INTO: This is a vocab program. Basic, but good, and fun to boot. But at the moment it can only be a component to a more comprehensive language program, not the foundation.
(For those that know/care, I would gauge this as a level A1 program under the Common European Framework.)

Even though this software will not teach you any kind of grammar, it will help you increase the amount of word your have in your vocabulary. I wish there was more software like this especially for grammar.

My opinion: Evoland was a good game, but I was expecting way too much from it.
I was sorely disappointed when the game ended. But that doesn't mean it was bad. On the contrary, it was, for the most part, pretty enjoyable. Evoland shows the history of game design (limited exclusively to adventure games) from it's very beginnings, but disappointingly stops short of modern day. This made the game surprisingly short, but they weren't kidding when they said 'A Short Story'. My major gripe with it, is that it's not the evolution of adventure games as much as it is 'The Evolution of The Legend of Zelda and Final Fantasy Games'. There's obviously more to adventure than that, and even though those two are both superb series in themselves, the spotlight could have been cast to others. And the fact that those two games are featured so predominately kind of makes the slight reference to Skyrim and League of Legends seem out of place.
But aside from the limited scope, that limited scope is done fantastically. Since this is a game about gameplay evolution, new mechanics and features are introduced constantly. But their introduced so seamlessly that it feels natural. You never have to take a pause to read instructions or do a tutorial, you just get it. That's where the game shines. It sets out to show gameplay evolution, and that's what it does. If you're an veteran of video games, you'll enjoy being able to relive some past experiences that you just don't get in AAA titles today. But, if you're a veteran gamer, then you'll be annoyed at some just as you smile at others.

I admit I'm new to the visual novel scene, but as a starting point, I found Cinders to be very satisfying. The art is gorgeous (especially backgrounds!) and chock full of effects. It also makes me happy that the relationships between the female characters are the crux of the story - the stepmother and Cinder's sisters are complex characters, neither good nor evil; Cinder's behavior towards them brings out other sides to them, and lead to different futures. It also pleased me that the endings aren't entirely depended on whom Cinders falls in love with - they're about her choices for her future and who she wants to be in life. A hot guy can come along if he wants, sure. But Cinders is more than just a vehicle for player romance, she's a young woman looking for her path in life, for better or for worse. It was a pleasurable experience with lovely visuals, and I'm really looking forward to the team's next game, which looks like it will be even better.

Cinders takes a classic fairytale and returns it with a much darker, more entertaining twist. You /could/ be sweet and marry the prince, or your choices could take you down an entirely different path. The endings all have variables, so who helps you get to the ball, who you decide to pursue as a love interest, or various other factors on Cinders all affect the ending you see. As a personal note one think I love about the game is that the romance isn't necessarily the focus. Instead the focus is how Cinders decides to take control of her life and change it. You could do that via romance, or you could do something else.
None of the characters are just stock characters. They're all developed and have real personalities and reasons for acting the way they do. Even Cinders has a base personality that you affect and develop through your choices, but she never feels like a blank slate. If ever there was a visual novel where the choices matter, it's this one, a fitting trait given the focus of the game.
Other factors about the game feel obvious. The art's gorgeous, even more so than the screenshots suggest. There are subtle movements in the background to enjoy that give Cinders that magical feel fairytales ought to have. Cinders is well written and well developed. Any fan of visual novels should pick this one up, and if you're interested in the genre this is definitely the game to start with.

Unique take on a classic story, beautiful graphics, and several different endings depending on choices made throughout gameplay. Some arguments between characters can carry on a bit too long, but that's a minor flaw compared to all the positives. Overall this is a fantastic game, and definitely worth the price.
Wonderfully drawn, mature and brilliant visual novel reimagining Cinderella's story. It’s highly replayable, well-written and absolutely winning on the field of gender representation.

Ok, real review time.
I love eSports. Like, a lot.
I play CS:GO (700 hours), former Dota 2 player (about 200 hours), League (level 14, not bad though), and I've touched some other eSports like Hearthstone.
I also watched Free to Play (which, if you haven't seen, go check it out. It's free to watch on steam, and it's all about Dota 2. Even if you are a league player or just hate Dota, I'd go watch it.)
This is a documentary about the Intel Extreme Masters season 9, primarily focusing on the San Jose tournament.
Some people have said that there is CS:GO in Dota in the trailer and that it's misleading, so I will just clear it up here, this is almost entirely about League of Legends, and the little bit that isn't is about Starcraft 2.
Now, even if you don't like League of Legends, and prefer Dota or any other eSport, I think it's worth watching just for the eSports background. This is about among the largest (if not the largest, I haven't checked the stats recently) gaming tournaments on the planet, and it is very well made.
The documentary is very well done, I really enjoyed it. Nothing seemed unprofessional about it (from a filmmakers perspective), and it was very clean.
I found it very entertaining, hardest part was to keep watching because I wanted to go play League so badly after watching only the first 30 minutes.
So, TL:DR
You a league fanboy and love eSports? Get it right now.
You love eSports and the history and all that? Get it right now.
Other then that, wait until it goes on sale (if that will happen, it's a video so I don't know).
I found it worth the $10, but if you are skeptical still, you can always wait until it goes on sale.

I've played all Paradox grand strategy games since Hearts of Iron 2 - 4, Europa Universalis 3 & 4, Crusader Kings 2, and Stellaris - and none of them keep me as enthralled as Victoria 2.
Your relationship to your nation and its people changes depending on the decisions you make. So instead of the same old, "Get this resource and war this guy," you have a living breathing population changing their lives and their philosophies in reaction to your choices. On my last playthrough I got Brazil to 1930 with:
No social programs at all (no unemployment, healthcare, hour limit on workday, nothing).
And we still had slavery.
I was bringing in hordes of luxury goods, kept my taxes rock bottom, and my people lived fat and happy. So why did they revolt every year or so?
People wanted the vote.
They didn't care about unemployment or hours or any of that mess because they were all rich as hell. No one was standing in bread lines. Everyone had a huge savings account and money to spare. But I wouldn't let certain people vote and that just got all up their butts. So they revolted over and over and over, even though I had hunter-killer groups set to take down rebels right when they popped up.
Then I tried to go to war through the jungle and lost my armies. The rebels won, and what did they do?
Did they give unemployment? No.
Did they reduce working hours? No.
Did they FREE THE SLAVES? Hell no.
They just gave a few more people the right to vote.
Then they went straight back to their fat cat factory jobs and ate gold-encrusted croissants and stopped giving a holy hell about anything else. Decadent freaks.

Yet, this game has a certain charm to it that I think can't be found anywhere else. It's set in the Arabic desert, where you must fight for survival by mastering as many factors as you can, including some staple RTS features, like economics, resources, troops, and workers. This game also features two main ways to determine whether you succeed or not. This comes in the form of managing how much gold you have to buy troops, and how much food you have collected. Running out of food will cause your castle to start losing happiness, and people will begin to leave if it gets below halfway.
Since the food plays a major role in your economy, lacking it presents a severe problem of unbalanced gameplay; people won't be able to keep your economy going if they leave, which means that, if you don't have enough gold to buy food, you're basically doomed. You can't buy troops since you don't have gold, and if, by some chance, you happen to be out of other supplies, it's best to give up if you don't have any allies. Even then, the allies aren't guaranteed to help you, especially if they're A.I players.
This is where the unbalanced issue comes into place, because not everyone is good at managing their economy, and pitting people with little to no sense of economics against people who do know means that the latter are going to win. Every single time.
This is still a great game, though.  If you are willing to learn how to manage economics, I recommend this game.

They have refined this game into a jewel. As a long time MOBA player (I have played Smite and LoL extensively, and sampled DOTA, Newearth, and a few others), this MOBA holds a special place in my heart. The fact that you can modify the base skills to do different things is really a joy - it makes it so that you can tailor your favorite character to counter whatever team you are playing against. Although the same can be accomplished with items in other MOBAs, the way they approach items in Awesomenauts makes the choices easy and good for a casual, enjoyable experience. The community seems very welcoming, and the UI is clean and modern. I love the way the profiles are set up, and am always interested in checking up on my own stats. The side scrolling aspect will at first pose a challenge for other long time MOBA players, but the new perspective is easily mastered and adds another dimension to gameplay.
The variety of maps and the different "traps" and features of each is really awesome. The fact that your spawn timer mostly consists of flying to earth in a rocket ship while picking up solar is badass, and makes staying engaged in the game easy and fun. I'd definitely suggest this game to anyone looking to pick up a simple, fun MOBA - there's something for both new players looking to learn the ropes of MOBAS, and experienced players looking to just have a bit of relaxing fun.
I look forward to playing this game for a long time to come, and purchasing the expansions when I get the chance.

The enemy AI in this game is absolutely why I continue to play, and replay this game at least once a week.
When I play stealth games, I'm not interested in learning patrol patterns and sneaking around them with no problem. What I'm really interested in is an AI system that has context and situational awareness. This game has both. The main mission takes place during a hurricane, naturally this gives the AI reduced sight/hearing and what have you. I'll give a very brief example of the AI's contextual awareness.
After getting spotted and going into the, as I understand it, new slow motion 'second chance' system where you can take out the enemy that spotted you and go unnoticed, I shot the unlucky guard in the face with a suppressed weapon. Minutes later I intercept a radio transmission from the control tower the the guard I just took out. From what I can tell each guard is assigned a number 'Delta 1, Delta 2' and so on. Since the guard they were radioing was out of commision, they sent another guard to check on him. Soon they found the body.
In most stealth games you'd expect them to see the body and then either that guard doesn't tell anybody and searches for you, or other guards that have no idea what happened all know you're there. This game was different.
He assessed the situation and radioed back to the tower that he died of a gunshot wound and since nobody reported hearing one, concluded that the intruder responsible must be using a suppressed weapon. After hearing this information, the entire base went on alert with sirens going off all over the place and backup arriving just a minute later.
Most stealth games these days have me feeling pretty confident that I can hide around a corner and I won't get spotted. This is not the case for Ground Zeroes. If you want to get 20 feet inside this base without getting seen or heard, you need to find a vantage point and survey the area for a good 5 minutes, tagging enemies, trucks, watch towers ect.
This is as true to life as any stealth game I've played has come for me in the past 20 years. If you like MGS, this is worth checking out to get a taste of the Phantom Pain. If you like stealth games, there's enough here to keep you busy without knowing the setting or story.
This is just an example of how advanced this AI is for this type of open world setting. I'm a new fan of the MGS games and other than the Metal Gear Acid 'board games' for the PSP is my first time playing any MGS game. I can already say that without a doubt, I'm buying Phantom Pain when it releases and for stealth lovers, this is a lovely distraction from the wait until Phantom Pain comes out.

Ryse: Son of Rome is an excellent game, in both graphics and story. Throughout it, you find yourself captivated with the intriguing plot as well as the photo-realistic graphics.

If you're a big fan of Roman times, then you should automatically pick this up even if it does have some flaws.
The two noticable flaws in this game are it's story and repetitive combat system. Stripping down to the story as a basic "I want revenge" type of deal. The story doesn't go into any depth at all about the interesting characters that you meet and see along your journey but instead you have to roam around and find scrolls that unlock interesting tidbits here and there.
The combat system while it will amaze and be astonishing at first, once you've seen the same quick timed moves, the flavor of it can quickly diminish. I have to give credit when credit is due, even though 80% of the time you'll find yourself in a QTE, the executions are very well done. It can feel a bit "button mashy" at times but it keeps you on your toes and forces you to try different things against various enemies.
Soundtrack wise, one of the great ones out there. Very atmospheric and every scene you head into has that perfect music in the background to set the tone for you.
Another strong point to this game is its excellent voice acting. All the voices suit each of the characters perfectly. The graphics are top notch although I did run into a few bugs during cut scenes and a slight framerate drop here and there but nothing drastically noticable during the experience.
Multiplayer is good but unless you're playing with a friend or even another random person, it can get very boring very quick.
While I don't think this game is worth the full $30, it's worth the price when it goes on sale. There's just not enough content to warrent a full $30 purchase.

Ok, so this game seemed great at first glance. The whole concept of studying language while playing a videogame probably seems fantastic for every gamer like me, who also likes to broaden his knowledge everyday. However, Influent isn't what I expected it to be. I didn't do much research before buying, just a short review by someone who generally praised the game but mentioned lack of insight on japanese "kanji", which immediately put japanese pack off my to-buy list. Therefore for starters, I picked up french pack.
After a bit more than 1 hour of playtime, I can pretty much say that for me the game is a large disappointment. The whole game is situated in a small condo which contains about 400 different objects that you can interract with, and consequently learn more about them in order to improve your vocabulary. Those consist mostly out of basic household items.
In French, gender is of crucial importance, and although the game tells you which gender a certain object is, when you actually learn them, gender pronouns or indefinite articles are excluded from the actual word. For example instead of "une lampe" or "la lampe" you'll study "lampe", which means you'll still need to study gender separatly. Furthermore, the game doesn't cover one bit of grammar.
The game itself isn't particularly fun either, since one is as already mentioned, trapped inside a small condo. If the game would include also some other everyday areas like playground, trainstation, gym, school etc. it would vastly improve the vocabulary covered, but I'm afraid this will either never be available or will be purchasable as a "dlc", for which I honestly wouldn't waste a cent anymore since I don't consider the 400 foreign words to be worth of 10€, while you can learn them for free in (in a sense of content) much better covered "game" called Duolingo, or Anki.
Summary: I love the basic idea, but it lacks a lot of content. Although it is obviously considered as a supplement to your language studies, I still believe that it could've included a lot more than just bare 400 words.

As far as visual novels go, I have to say that CINDERS is my favorite, thus far.  The game takes the player down a very mature path within a classic children's fairytale.  The player has complete control over the decision making process of the main character.  Thus, with each choice the player makes for Cinders, her personality changes as the game progresses.  There is a large number of outcomes for this character based on those decisions she is presented with throughout the game.  For instance, with the decisions the player chooses for Cinders, she could become very evil or good, very sexual or timid, and/or anywhere in between.  I honestly couldn't believe the number of outcomes this game presents the player with!  The replayability is enormous.  The artwork is absolutely gorgeous.  The music is beautiful.  I applaud how the devs implemented the 'fast forward scene' ability within the game as even though this is a VN, thus a lot of reading, it allows the player to choose whether to read through a scene over and over if they wish OR fast forward through a scene that they have previously experienced.  Please remember, there are NUMEROUS outcomes to this game and over 300 different possible decisions to be made (at minimum)!  The player can also choose the rate of speed that the dialogue is presented, which gives the player a chance to choose either the slower paced dialogue which visually allows 'emphasis' placed on certain words or phrases 'spoken' by each character OR to speed it up and read at the players pace.  I literally just finished the very last outcome for this game before writing this review.  I sat back and just said "WOW!"  (yes, it's that good!)  I highly recommend this game to any VN lover --- and would really like to see others at least give it a shot.  It truly is a very well thought out game!!!

I'm new to visual novels, and the concept and writing drew me in. Choices are presented frequently and sensibly enough, with a flower appearing in the top-right corner to note when your choice impacted your playthrough outcome. The nonlinearity of the choices provides multiple interesting paths to four basic outcomes with multiple permutations based on your relationships with other characters, as well as your protagonist's personality. Subsequent playthroughs are easy, as dialogue can be skipped (super fast-forward), automatically stopping at new dialogue or choices.
The writing is generally solid and engaging, with very few spots that are slightly clunky but easily forgivable. Character development is deep for the four women, and amusingly and probably intentionally, the supporting cast of men are somewhat one-dimensional. The concept of a reimagined Cinderella itself is quite fun and more contemporary with an emphasis on female protagonist agency, with some very helpful friends to retain the fanciful nature of the original story.
If you're new to visual novels but like things like Joe Dever's Lone Wolf saga, RPGs with deep character development, and Telltale's Walking Dead series, and consider the possibility that games can be art, you would probably enjoy this.

Easily one of the best (if not THE best) character action games of all time. Unlike the rest of the games in the series excluding the first, every puzzle piece fits to form a coherent whole: No excessive or mundane platforming, enough content to fill the entire 8-10(ish?) hour experience without any major backtracking, a fair and consistent difficulty curve and a narrative that manages to compel the player without interjecting with excessive cutscenes. Accessible but deep, challenging but fair: DMC3SE hits all of the right notes.
BUT
The PC port is garbage. Limited resolution, botched controller support (Xinput didn't work without excessive tinkering and the use of third-party mods, and the legacy controller I had was simply unrecognized), downgraded graphics from the PS2 version (missing effects, seemingly lower resolution textures in some areas?), very inconsistent performance, and missing music are the highlights of this seemingly rushed release. Many have found success with the Style Switcher mod, which not only fixes most of the issues listed but also adds the gameplay element of switching styles that was previously not present. Unfortunately, as with all mediocre ports, these solutions can often be inconsistent. After multiple reinstalls I was seemingly unable to get my controllers working until I downloaded a cracked version of the exe that fixed the issue.
A cracked version of the game's executable from a shady website solved problems that the patch could not: this is the type of port you're dealing with. You can fix a lot of issues with the game, but as I've shown, those fixes may not always be conventional.
If you can deal with this, I can wholeheartedly recommend this title (the game itself) to anyone who loves character action games as the peak of its genre, If you are inevitably turned off this due to the shoddy port, there are alternatives: the game can be emulated fairly well on higher end hardware, or can be purchased with the excellent HD collection for the 360/PS3.
As it stands, don't pick up the game at full price. If Capcom re-released the HD collections version on PC for this listed price I would almost certainly recommend it, but as is, the stock game is a glitchy mess. It's worth noting that certain third party websites have versions of the game available with Style-Switcher pre-installed: I'd recommend one of those if you know where to look, as the game isn't worth the dough in the state that it comes in.
This thumbs up is for the game itself, and not the mediocre port it is attached to.

After the series' inception by Hideki Kamiya, Director of Bayonetta, Viewtiful Joe, The Wonderful 101, and other outstanding action titles, the Devil May Cry franchise gained three sequels. The first of these sequels, Devil May Cry 2, was not received well, but Capcom fixed all of its mistakes with the next entry, Devil May Cry 3 Dante's wakening.
The game is a prequel, and explores the relationship between the eponymous hero, Dante, and his twin brother, Vergil. This is handled very well, and the player will quickly find themselves enthralled in the two brothers' actions.
The gameplay consists of the player fighting hordes of enemies while traversing a large stone tower, Temen-ni-gru. The first Devil May Cry was originally going to be Resident Evil 4, and some Resi design choices still remain here- you find the shotgun in a typical Resident Evil manner, there's plenty of backtracking with new items, and the game even uses fixed camera angles at time. While surprising, this helps Devil May Cry to set itself apart even more from your typical action games. The combat, too, is very well handled, with guns mapped to one button and Devil Arms (or melee weapons) mapped to another. On top of this, your 'style' action is mapped to another button, though this changes based on what the player decides to play using from the Trickster, Swordsmaster, Gunslinger, and Royalguard styles, or if they have them unlocked, the Quicksilver and Doppelganger styles. Combat is difficult, due to large numbers of enemies being on screen at once, and none of them waiting their turn, but this keeps it exciting and ensures the player knows how to dodge effectively.
Bosses are the highlight, and while some lesser bosses, such as the gigapede, miss the mark, all the main bosses are incredibly well designed, with the three escalating fights against Vergil being the standout, using attacks that are similar to Dante's and being a true test of the player's skill.

As someone that has spent over 800 hours into Monday night Combat (for short MNC), I think I can you give a somewhat good view on what to expect in this game. One big problem though before I start. The game is literally dead. Only one fan server left. If you are planning to play the multiplayer part of this game, get yourself a friend or join in "hotshots forever". Otherwise you won't be able to play this game with people besides occasionally 1vs1.

But what is MNC even about? Basically, it is a Third-Person, Class-based, Tower Defense, MOBA -Shooter (for more details read "Game Modes"). In this game you have 2 major game modes. Crossfire which is your multiplayer PvP mode and Blitz which is your coop mode where you can also play solo.

In Crossfire, everything turns about destroying your opponent's glowing floating ball (Moneyball) on the other side of the map. You destroy them by escorting your bots from your base to the enemy moneyball. You lead them through enemy turrets that you either destroy or let your bots take it down. When your minions have reached the Moneyball, they jump on it and break its shield. that's your chance to attack it. Destroy the ball and win. Blitz is basically the same as Crossfire. Just you versus endless waves of bots. Defend your Moneyball by destroying bots and building Defense turrets. That's basically the game and what you do. You can also upgrade the skills of each class while playing like in any MOBA (LoL, Dota) and pick one of six classes which remind you from their weapons a lot on Valve's TF2. For example, Supportplays like Medic and Engineer at once.


However, the balance of the classes is really off. Most of the classes do work well and are okay balanced. But 2 classes, one in particular are really a pain to deal with. For clarifying reasons, here is an example: If you are experienced enough. a Sniper can easily take on a 2vs1 and win. That is because of his instant kill headshots. that's especially a problem for the other classes. A Sniper can always get better in aiming. a Gunner player on the other side will soon reach the point where he can't deal more damage (or one shot kills) with better aim. The only way of beating an aim god is by playing smarter and using all your tools. But there kicks the problem in. If your enemy aims really good, you already have to play smart. BUT what if he aims good AND plays smart. That just means GG. if you want to have fun, make sure no one picks him. Hard to really enjoy a game with a sniper in. Besides this issue, everything works really good in terms of balancing.

Graphic and sound design wise. It is alright, don't expect a master piece there though. It is alright for a 2010 console port.

This game is accessible and enjoyable for beginners but has an incredibly high skill ceiling.  It takes a while to learn each player what your teammates need and when, but it feels fantastic when you figure it out and really play as a team.  I do wish that some in the community were more understanding and nicer to newer players.  Be friendly, don't take criticism too hard, or simply turn off the in-game chat.  That said, there are plenty of very nice people out there and you will find friends you like to play with in a hurry.
There have been some negative reviews lately because of the new XP system the devs added.  It's important to know that Ronimo is a small Indie team and that updates rarely come out perfectly.  The XP system was a little unbalanced at launch, causing snowballing, but now I think it has been balanced properly and adds interest to the matches.  It does allow for greater build diversity than was previously possible and helps break ties when games go too long.
In the year that I've played Awesomenauts, the devs have never dissapointed.  They are constantly listening to the community and the tweaks they make seem to be directly in response to player feedback.  The game is getting better all the time.  Go for it, you won't regret it.

Nostalgia goggles still firmly in place, I can't help but rave about this game. There are so many terrific homages to the games I grew up with and loved. Nods to The Legend of Zelda and Secret of Mana gave me the most warm and fuzzy feelings. Plenty of Final Fantasy VII references made me say, "Ah, yes." But more than references to games, Evoland references the very culture of gaming that I was raised in. The evolution of graphics and other technological advancements is presented in such a compelling way, I'd recommend this game for classes on pop culture or video game history.
Taking the nostalgia goggles off, I find this game tight, well paced and well designed. Nothing seems to be filler and evolutions happen at a rapid pace so as to keep things interesting. The tongue-in-cheek storyline unfolds neatly and with no annoying spelling or grammar mistakes. New play styles are compelling, as well.
While I appreciate the brevity of the game, some may not. It's not a terribly long story though I found there to be some replay value after completion. Players expecting a full RPG that will keep them going for a whole season will not find what they are looking for here. As for me, it took an evening and a morning to clear the story and I commend the designers for not fattening the game. It feels like the right length to make the most of the gimmick without making it feel annoying.
I highly recommend this game.

Nice little game that pays tribute to RPG classics (Zelda, Final Fantasy, Diablo...) while making fun of genre conventions. Dimension shifting mechanics with shift from 3D to 2D etc. was a great idea. However the game is guilty of two letdowns.
First, as the subtitle says, it's a SHORT story of video games evolution and that's not what nostalgic fans of 50hrs+ old school games might expect. There's not much replay value, except for 100% completion which is neither that hard to achieve nor that satisfying.
Second, it makes you realize that some game mechanics are not so great on their own and should stay buried in the history books of the game industry (Random encounters, I'm looking at you !). Almost makes you wonder how they got the ATB system in FF7 just right :D
Nevertheless, the game can be a lot of fun. Various gameplay elements which you unlock through the course of the game will make you chuckle with their fitting descriptions. For the short time the game lasted I had good time. Just keep your expectations in check before playing

Evoland is a 3 hour or so game that has a great concept but pretty much only lives by that concept. A game of evolving Adventure/RPG elements through the times would be a great idea if executed nicely, yet this one fails to deliver on a challenging game with actual evolving of mechanics, both in gameplay and actually evolving. It seems to only ever try to be Zelda or Final Fantasy, with only one instance of it being Diablo (which played exactly like the Zelda sections only with more enemies and money drops). It only switches between the first two, and the plot is pretty much an abridged Final Fantasy VII after the initial area. Even the second character you can play as is named Kaeris. You can guess what happens to her before the end of the game.
There is a fine difference between a homage and a game with references everywhere, and I'm afraid this is more of the latter. Kind of disappointed.
Pick it up on a sale if you want something to do for three hours, but it isn't something you need to get to remember the old days. You aren't missing anything by passing it up, and there is no replay value after you have completed it unless you want to go achievement hunting. It drives on your nostalgia and nothing more.

If you're a fan of RPGs - especially oldschool ones at that - then this game is definitly for you. Evoland makes you feel like you're playing a game that's evolving (hence the name) from oldschool pixelated black & white RPGs to 8- & 16-bit games & onwrds, and you will find elements that feel inspired by some of your favorite RPG and adventure games. You really can't go wrongby picking this title up.

Ryse: Son of Rome is a Hack and Slash set in a fictional universe in where a giant horde of barbarians have fought their ways into Rome itself. You play as Marius Titus who is a centurion defending Rome and guides his emperor into a safe place then Marius decides to tell him his life's story for some reason. We are transported back in time when Marius has just become a Roman solider and is visiting his father in his villa. After a quick sparring match with your father, things quickly go wrong and events unfold that kick off the barbarian uprising. You will be searching for vengeance from then on and will spend most of this game fighting hordes of enemies. Which is where the game falls flat on it's face and is made unenjoyable due to a bad combat system. You have a button for shield bashing through their guard and one to attack with a sword. Switching between the two makes it harder for them to dodge, allowing you to get bigger combos. Combos are broken when you are hit, though enemies start moving in slow-mo when they are about to attack so it is insanely easy to press the block button on time. You can also roll but it is made useless due to you being able to block even heavy attacks if timed right.
Damaging an enemy enough will allow you to preform a QTE execution in where they glow in the color of the button you are supposed to press and are violently killed in slow-mo. While awesome the first few times, it quickly gets old since there are few animations and it interrupts fights due to being invulnerable all throughout while the other enemies just stand by and watch their friend meet a violent death. You will be able to switch from one of four perks that grant you different benefits like dealing more damage or healing yourself after each execution. Even if you press the wrong button during the execution, it will continue the animation regardless and the only downside will be that you get a bit less points. It is like an incredibly boring game of 'Simon Says' where you can't lose. While you don't have to do executions that would result in having to hit the damage spongey enemies some more, instead of quickly killing them off. Sounds like a minor complaint but after so much non-stop “action” I just wanted the fights to end as quickly as possible due to the boredom they bring. I never felt even slightly threatened in a game with a ton of savage barbarians wiping the floor with your once great Empire. That is mostly caused by how over powered  you are, enough that it makes you think why does Rome even have an army when they can send Marius to murder all their enemies while not even breaking a sweat.
That may as well be the case since all your fellow Roman allies are useless in battle. They will not help you in any way, shape or form and will more likely than not get dominated by a tribesman with neither armor or training. At times you will be able to “command” them to form a defensive formation and make your way through a volley of arrows. Sounds a lot cooler than it actually is, you will pretty much be slowly walking in a straight line and blocking when arrows approach. Another form of “commanding” your units pops up sometimes where you can pick one of two options like telling your archers to shoot an approaching siege tower or to shoot the catapults that are pelting you with stone instead. The only way I can see someone losing this game is by not defending their legion well enough and their health bar depletes. For ranged attacks you can carry a few pilums that will kill most enemies in a single hit. You can take your time and aim it or you can quickly throw it mid-fight which is far more likely to miss your target. The game randomly takes away your pilums after story sections and it frequently results in you having to collect more just in case you ever want to use them. No real need to since Marius is so overpowered but it is the only other weapon in the game so you may as well break up the monotony of your normal sword & shield. Turret sections are also present in this game and they come in the form of a ballista that automatically reloads itself somehow.
Getting combos and performing executions will net you points which can be used to buy more execution animations, carry more pilums or to increase your health. Strangely enough you will be able to afford every single one of them by the second level and the very last upgrades well take you the rest of the game to unlock simply due to not being level 7 or you can easily afford those to. I'm guessing it has something to do with the included dlc that comes bundled with the PC version. Bosses are pretty much the same as regular enemies but with a new skin and much more health. You deal with them by blocking their attacks at the right moment to break their guard and slowly chipping off their health. They are no fun to fight though the set pieces in where you fight them are impressive to say the least. One boss in particular took way to long to finish off. Every time you deplete his health bar he would get back up in a “haha not dead yet!” manner, time and time again.
Story is forgettable and uninteresting for the most part. There is a few cool parts when they show things from the barbarian's point of view but never amounts to anything. The story feels a bit jumbled since you are playing through what is a tale of Marius's life and are traveled from one location to another instantly. It's not a bad story and it does it's job but don't go into this game expecting a engrossing tale.  Or a decent ending for that matter, I can't state the reasons why it is awful but it comes off as totally unnecessary and dumb. It is really best to turn off your brain and treat it like an action film all throughout. Characters themselves are memorable and excellently voice acted. Where Ryse really shines is in the graphics. Everything looks stunning, from the slums of Rome to the carefully animated jiggle of a fat barbarian's man boob. I mainly purchased this game as a benchmark test of sorts and in that regard it did not disappoint. Every level is filled with cool set-pieces to awe at and you can't help but just stare at everything for a while even if someone currently wants to rip your face off. Enemy variety is really low and since each character is so detailed and different from one another it is very noticeable you are fighting the same batch of enemies over and over again. Unfortunately the levels are all extremely linear and inconsistent. At times Marius can leap very high into the air and at others he can't vault over a waist high fence. That leads to feeling a bit of confusion as to where the game wants you to go next though they do put a giant cursor to point the way if you take long enough.
In addition to the campaign there is a gladiator mode where you and another player can fight side by side against enemies. What is rather cool is that you start off with simple loin cloth and a helmet but as you win matches and money you can purchase more and more items to customize your gladiator. Before the start of each match you can pick which of four gods is your patron for different benefits like extra damage or better aim. During matches the crowd will either grow bored or hyped depending on how well you do and it is in your best interest to keep them entertained as you get a nice cash bonus for your troubles. Sadly this mode felt boring as soon as I tried it since it is still the same combat mechanics from the base game with executions animations and all. After 6 hours of a campaign where you spent the huge majority of the time fighting I've had enough of this game's terrible combat by that point. When all is said an done Ryse: Son of Rome feels like a heartless game with amazing graphics, animations and music but fails to have either an interesting story or fun gameplay. Unless you want a tech demo this is a game you can safely pass on.
