Only If is, in my opinion, one of the best free-to-play games that Steam has to offer.
PROS
-nice atmosphere: every level if unique
-soundtrack: goes with atmosphere. But I found the soundtrack to be pretty soothing
-graphics: I didn't expect much from a game that was free-to-play, but I was astounded at the beautiful graphics, especially in the Park level.
-antagonist: The man in the radio (Vinny) is an oddly likeable character. At first he was frustrating but as I kept playing I grew to really like him. Vinny is snide, cynical, and mean, but he does seem to have moments of kindness or mercy.
-protagonist: Anthony is surprisingly likeable. Most FTP "horror" games have dull, boring protags who offer little (I'm looking at you, The Forgotten Ones). However, Anthony's personality and reactions to what happen to him are relatable and make sense for a teenage boy.
-puzzles: the puzzles in Only If are difficult and actually make you think, though I will admit some are very hard.
CONS
-volume/voice acting: while I adored the soundtrack, it was too loud and wouldn't turn down when the characters were talking. While Anthony could be heard easily, Vinny was difficult to hear at points; hearing him is critical to the story making sense to the player. As far as I know there is not an option for subtitles either.
-puzzles: while some were great, others were arduous (mostly the Blind and Immensity levels). It took me a while to figure out what was actually going on.

A very solid side scroller which reminds me greatly of Contra and the original DukeNukem. The graphical options are cute and gameplay is fairly typical of traidtional side scrollers--with mouse aiming. Play is fun, though there is a limitation in the raw number of levels-but then it is still an early access release.
My greatest "complaint" is the jump mechanic. I find the game is vertically unforgiving, with some areas being missed if one drops too low too quickly.
The collectable mechanic is typical of many side-scrollers, though I have found some "wall clipping" issues (the sewer level for one turtle for example) which have forced a restart of the level--though the collectable was still counted.
Mid-level save flags, reminicient of Mario, are helpful, however, all stockpiled weapons are typically deleted--which can make for some difficulties if the level is new to the player.
Weapon options are still thin, with 4 primary weapons available (Unlimited ammo base machine gun, flamer, rocket launcher, grenade launcher). Ammunition is very limited for the flamer and rocket launcher (the weapons I've also found have the least utility unless opening a wall etc.) The nade launcher was useful for blowing open some floors and vs. a particular boss but otherwise I've found the best utility from the starter machine gun. Some additional development to make the lesser used weapons more viable is hopefully on the horizon.
Levels are generally well designed and fun--if you enjoy the side scrolling format. The "hide in the shadows" element can be useful and the bull charge is fun.
Boss mechanics are generally well done, with identifiable patterns if one is paying attention.
Overall, this is an enjoyable "time-waster" with a limited backstory and a fair bit of humour with references to other games and shows/movies.

In my first few playthroughs, I found the game difficulty ridiculously easy and it would take about 5 stabs with my bayonet to kill one zulu. Here is what I found and changed:
New Update
Devs have fixed 8 bugs since releasee and they keep in regular communication with the community. They also explain what's coming up in future updates before they arrive which I appreciate. They listen to EA ideas and respond with enthusiasm. I certainly trust the devs with sticking with this excellent game.
The Review
I'm going to give this game a tentative thumbs up for now.
I've been anticipating the release of Zulu Response for a few months now and now that its released, I have mixed feelings towards the game.
First impressions are not great. The visuals are very outdated with player models looking more like tin soldiers than life like characters. The foliage is quite convincing but again the texture detail is very basic. The animations of the characters fair a little better, with Zulu warriors breaking into tribal dancing and British soldiers stretching their weary legs, unfortunately the animations aren't convincing in the heat of battle. British soldiers don't yet seem to know how to aim down their Martini-Henry rifles yet and the Zulu's who primarily use melee attack with their asagai's don't quite know how to throw them.
Please note, if you have a good PC or laptop and you have Nvidia, then you can up the graphic capabilities in Nvidia control panel and the game in EA can look like this:
However, there is something about Zulu Response which gives me optimisim for its future and that's it's completely broken command system. I'm not quite sure why the Developers decided to place the complex command orders for your squad through a hotkey (K) rather than a command wheel as seen in Insurgency, which would feel more intuitive to use and drastically reduce the confusion that players may have, however having said that the commands you can order are historically accurate and quite fleshed out. I think this is where Zulu Dawn's strength lies. If the devs can simplify the command orders using a command wheel, instruct the AI to actually go to the correct position and fire on command then I think this game can go far.
To be sure, the visuals need a complete overhaul to compliment the "realistic gameplay" and the animations need a lot of attention but those are relatively easy to accomplish than if the command system was lacking in historical detail. The small dev team have said the game will be in EA for about 8 months. In those 8 months, I believe they could make the Zulu's Response even louder if they focused on enhancing the realism of the game, fixing the somewhat broken AI and changing their command order system.
One area of the game that does stand out is the audio. Whilst the fighting sounds are rather simple, the music which accompanies the action, with the Men of Harleck and the Zulu's singing is rousing to the soul and does intensify what is rather a bland combat experience as of now.
Oh and please, please devs remove for now the frightened/ suppression system it feels as though I am on the high seas and it could make some people violently ill. A simple grey out would suffice.
For now I'd rate Zulu Response with a decent 7.5/10. Given time, I'm optimistic that Zulu Response will be a "must have" for anyone remotely interested in the Anglo-Zulu war.
Update: I was having issues with performance on my laptop, however I noticed it was running on the integrated graphics card. For those who have Nvidia control panel, Zulu response is under UDK (Unreal Development Kit).
Having almost reached the 2 hour mark now, I can say that I was slightly too harsh on the audio and combat mechanics. I was just in Rorkes Drift defending the farmstead with 30 men and the inevitable Zulu charge really made me see the huge potential in this game. The Zulu amassed on the South wall, but I had placed my men on the North wall. I had to order my men double time to cover the South entrance and as I was doing so three of my men fell to spears. The Zulu war chants and the speed in which the Zulu arrived unnerved me, and I ended up taking out my sword and swinging it wildly at the mass of oncoming Zulu. I was wounded and decided to order my men to form ranks and fire on command. Zulus fell before my eyes as smoke filled the air. The hospital during this assualt was set ablaze, which was a sad sight to behold. As more Zulu's arrived, I ordered an orderly withdrawal to the Kraal Biscuit boxes and it was there we made our last stand. The bugle player sounded his last command, as the Zulus overran our lines.

A delightful little trip down memory lane, my only complaint is that it falls short in the fact that it emulates retro gaming a little TOO well!
If anything, this game made me remember why the stop-and-go pacing of JRPGs like Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest just didn't gel for me.  It always seemed like the combat was just getting in the way of the story!  Unfortunately, this game has very little story that is can actually be called compelling, so it's like all of the tedium with none of the payoff.
However, those setbacks did not stop the game from pleasantly surprising me.  All those complaints I made in the preceding paragraph?  The game knows all about them, but rather than trying to adapt those elements for a new generation, it celebrates them, shortcomings and all!  This game isn't about reinventing the wheel or even treading new ground, it's about reminiscing the past and paying respect to some of the greatest moments in gaming; the moments that defined gaming in the past, and without which we wouldn't have gaming as it today.  In that respect, this game succeeds.
It's a cheerful and lovingly-crafted tale of bygone days, and while the retro-style throwbacks in gameplay may confuse and fail to amuse the younger crowd, for us retro gamers it may spark some wonderful feelings of nostalgia.

'Cinders' is a take on the classic Cinderella story. You decide what direction the story is going by choosing between different options Cinders have in different situations. The game has tons of different endings, I've replayed it five times now and have still not discovered them all. Original characters, beautiful artwork, replayability value - this game is definitely worth your time.
I will say, though, that it is not worth it's price. I'd pick it up on a sale. It's definitely not a fast paced action game, but it is interesting.
A new and more realistic take on a timeless tale, Cinders is an experiance I thoughly enjoyed and one I whole-heartedly recomend.

A visual novel based on the story Cinderella.
This game really presents itself well; it's probably the most polished visual novel I've played, with the only real issue being a typo I found. Simple things like the effect of text appearing on the screen look really great.
The art style is colorful, beautiful, and detailed. There's some animation effects on the backgrounds which adds a lot more to the feel of the game than you'd expect. Just small things like water of a lake shimmering, fire moving, sunrays, and things like that. The only character animations are really facial expressions, and sometimes they'll shift poses, but that's more of a rare thing... though the characters will change outfits or poses for different scenes.
The music is really well done and there's a good variety here, but nothing I really focused on much.
There are 4 endings, but multiple variations of those endings based on how you treated certain characters and things like that. So there's some replayability here, but the story still plays out mostly the same, with just some extra scenes and dialogue peppered in based on some choices you make. A lot of times I felt like the banter back and forth may not add a whole lot to the story, and doesn't create that much extra character depth... ultimately leading to longish periods of time between choice branches. This could also limit replayability, but there is a button to fast-forward through the dialogue that will still pause when there's a choice to be made, or when you reach a new scene you haven't seen before. A really awesome feature. Even though you can skip through quickly using this method, it still takes a LONG time to fast-forward through everything. The story is kind of that long... I think when I started a new story to get a different ending, it still took me an hour to play through even though I fast-forwarded through the majority of the story.
The choices in this game can affect a lot, I think. Even though the majority of scenes STILL happen no matter what, the differences in the story with how the characters treat you (and even how your character treats them) provides a more personal feel... rather than picking options that feel out-of-place of your character, your character changes with your options. It's pretty nice in this way.
Another really awesome detail this game provides is when you unlock achievements (which relate to the story and in-game decisions.) With each one you unlock, a change happens to the main menu screen... most of the time an item gets added to the scene. It's really a nice detail and just goes to show how much attention was put into this game. There's also a "reward" menu where you can see all the unique things you've unlocked, which is nice.
Overall, the game is plenty long... I think my first play-through took around 3 hours... which is fairly typical. The long-windedness of some of the dialogue is the only thing that started to fatigue me. There are a lot of choices to be made to keep the interaction up and keep you engaged... the pacing is pretty good overall. When I first started playing the story seemed to throw in your face the fact that the story is Cinderella, which I found a bit annoying and obnoxious, but after that was over with I really enjoyed it. It's Cinderella, so don't expect anything crazy with the main story... you're able to personalize it a bit with your own choices, but all the major plot-points are always hit.
I'm definitely keeping an eye out on what this developer puts out next. I hope it's a new, unique story with the same love and care put into it that this game had.

Recently, you will see many "not recommended" reviews criticising Paradox's DLC policy. These reviews are not at all relevant to Victoria II, as the final product has been unaltered for years, and in my mind should not be allowed as reviews for this product. I would ask that you look at the number of hours that people "not recommending" the game have played, could they really play a game for that amount of hours and not enjoy it?
Victoria II is an older but still amazing grand strategy game, with many active mods ongoing to improve the base game even further. It has a very unique mechanic for populations, which many aspects of the global economy and politics are reliant on. As a fan of other grand strategy games, I often go away from Victoria with a desire to have the population mechanics in those other games, and I believe that is because it is an incredibly interesting and robust system. One word of warning is that the game is quite difficult to learn and could do with better tutorials and tooltips. While I have less game time in Victoria than some other grand strategies, I enjoy it and would certainly recommend it at current or sale price.

Victoria II is a fantastic game. It's also a game with a clunky user interface, and have mechanics that border on the obtuse. But it'a worth the steep learning curve. It have some of the best music in a Paradox game, and I keep getting drawn in by the in-depth simulation of your population and the politics of your country. There are so many choices that influence each other, and sometimes things can cascade in unpredictable ways. You can try to steer your country through the industrial age into the modern age, but you can also end up trying to manage an rebellious population with other ideas about how the country should be run.
Compared to other Paradox games, a game of Victoria II lasts much shorter. You only lead your country through 100 years of history, but it's a short and sweet ride that leaves you wanting to come back for more.

The game is not a game of revolution, but one of refinement. Transfers are smarter and more involved than previous FM games, and the faster player development and streamlining of information are welcome. The perennial strengths of Football Manager are stronger than ever, yet it’s the furtive improvements to the match engine that really set FM2017 apart from its immediate predecessor. Sure, I still have gripes with the tactical interface, and there isn’t anything new there worth writing about. While the tactial interface is rigid and in need of an overhaul, the match engine is enjoyable again. New features are lacking, and those that exists are trivial, but match days are more involved and pertinent information is easily accessible and well presented. But if your rear end has ever been entrenched in the virtual dugout or you're just a fresh-faced hopeful looking to begin your journey, Football Manager 2017 is easy to recommend to the budding manager.

If you were to ask me my opinion of Awesomenauts before patch 2.13, I would have told you it is a fun game and I would give it a positive review. Now that patch 2.13 is here, Awesomenauts has a negative review.
The main reason patch 2.13 is so awful is because it changes the game in a way that is not for the better. Before patch 2.13 games were won with teamwork, communication, strategy, and strategy. It was a completely legitimate strategy to farm creeps and not focus on kills if the other team is passive. Just out push the lane. Patch 2.13 changed all of that with the XP system. Because the XP system is about leveling up the whole team, the early game is no longer about pushing and out farming the opposition, it is now about early game team composition and trying to get kills before the other team kills you. Most of the games I have lost in this patch have been games where my team did not get the first kill.
Early kills are more important now than ever before. They boost maximum health and maximum damage. Before patch 2.13, the other team could get kills but not all was lost, because you still had the same amount of health as they did, and you still did the same damage per skill based on their upgrades and your upgrades. Patch 2.13 tore away with those ideas because now the team has 1) more solar and 2) more health/base damage. This all leads to a snowball effect. The other team has even a less chance of winning against that team than before. If a player has a teammate that is not as strong of a player, the team is pretty much doomed.
The snowball effect doesn't give players a reason to stay in the game either. There is still no penalty for leaving a game and players really don't have a reason to stay once the other team is a couple levels + above them. I've seen people feed and ragequit more than I have ever before.
Please rethink the XP system. Don't just make this game free to play because of a decreased flow of players.

The premise follows that Cinders acts as a retelling of the classic Cinderella legend, except that, in an attempt to actively subvert what is known as the "Disneyfied" 1950's animated film that can in many ways can be considered nothing more than glitz with a bit of a moral, this game allows not only for very distinct and non-black-and-white player choice options but fleshes out each character in new and unexpected directions.
And I *love* it.
Gone are the cookie-cutter Step-Mother drones Anastasia and Drizella and enter their respective counterparts Sophia and Gloria, and while Gloria does questionably attempt to enact her mother's will on the other two sisters, Sophia constantly snarks, talks back, and even actively rebels against both Gloria and Lady Carmosa, this game's (not-so) Evil Step Mother. This visual novel is all about giving us reasons to understand why these characters act the way they do, and obviously I don't want to spoil anything, but contrary to the popular notion that the antagonists (or anti-heroes in this story) are in cahoots, *nobody* likes each other. And despite her cruelty, even said step-mother has her issues, where most of her actions are explained, understandable, and sympathetic. (In my playthrough, I never got a good answer for why she treats Cinders like an old rag, though.)
Of course, what to do with this information is for you to decide. If you feel like disregarding any understanding of these characters' own personal plights and personally attacking them whenever they get in your way, you are allowed this option. Maybe you want to pick a side in this sisterly conflict and get close to Sophia or Gloria; this is something you may do as well. In fact, participating in the subversion of this fairy tale is entirely up to you. You may wish to ask the fairies for help, marry the prince at the expense of your sisters' and step-mother's chances, and live Happily Ever After The End, assuming you can even reach that point. You can also be like me and revell in the story's subversive qualities, actively trying to understand and unite the sisters against their overbearing mother. It's all up to you, and no matter which path you take, the game's story never ever falters, because it's the story *you* want to make. It helps that the game's writing and story are (mostly) beautiful in each path and never fails to at least be interesting.
Also, if you couldn't tell by the video and screenshots, the visuals and audio are top-notch. While the somewhat sparse and somewhat static character models can be a bit stiff in their animations (Cinders herself seems to be placed in a perpetual slouch, which, when you think about it, is kind of the point), the backgrounds are always stunningly gorgeous, with details that come alive despite through their hand-drawn aesthetic. The BGM makes up for its limited selection by being amazingly well-produced, even while synthetic (nobody would have expected a full orchestra from an indie studio anyway). The design here is elegent in its subtlety, with slightly differing text sounds for different characters' speech and dim auras surrounding the current speaker.
I only take small issue in some of the design choices. For instance, I wish that the game wouldn't notify me whenever a consequence of a certain past decision is being played out. Every time I make a choice, its resulting difference is noted by a small plant symbol that appears in the upper-right corner of the screen. Often these are made up of small speech alterations that have little effect on the main story except for alterations in the character's dispositions and their own personal decisions, and sometimes I couldn't tell how a certain sentence would have differed had I made a different choice, or what choice with which that particular piece of text was even associated. Regardless, I'd much rather the mystery of how my decisions change the story be left to my own intuition.
Also on the subject of choices, I wish the game wouldn't limit the ability to rewind through decisions made to see all of their immediate effects, especially if the feature's primary marketability involves important and lasting changes that won't necessarily take affect until much later in the story (and at that point, who wants to rewind that far back?). If the game wants me to shape the story the way I see fit, then there's really no need to limit this feature. I understand that certain decisions are meant to be important, lasting, and heavy, and perhaps a rewind feature would take away from this heaviness (there was a moment late in the game where I was confronted with a decision that would essentially determine the ending I'd get and I had to think very hard about my decision), but there are just as many conversational choices that have exactly the opposite effect of their perceived intention. I found myself in a conversation with Gloria on Day 4 during which I said some things I wish I hadn't, and, given the option to take them back, I probably would have. Perhaps this is meant to reflect the weight of real-life decision-making, but this game isn't about that. It's about player choice, and if I'm given a choice that, when chosen, results in the opposite of its intended effect (e.g. Cinders says something rude and condescending when I meant the comment to be compassionate and understanding), then I'd like the option to take it back.
Finally, and least importantly, some of the writing in the game is a bit off. Cinders often goes about psychoanalyzing literally everybody she meets, and while this isn't chiefly wrong, since it supports the game's concept of fairy-tale subversion by revealing very real character traits in the people she encounters, it is a bit heavy-handed and perhaps a bit too obvious. Sometimes I wish I could figure these things out for myself without necessarily having Cinders tell me (and the character) directly, and there are other ways for Cinders to handle the conversations and actions she engages. There are a couple of blatant (but necessary) exposition dumps, but this isn't too horrible. There is also some questionable grammar, like the use of -t instead of -ed (e.g. "spoilt" instead of "spoiled") but this may be era-specific, or the use of a "than" in place of a "then" or a "where" in place of a "were."
These are minor complaints compared to the quality of the game. If you want to play through it four times to unlock all four endings, it's definitely worth $20. Each playthrough will last you about 5 hours, depending on your reading speed. If you only want to play through it once, it's in the current Humble Bundle (as of writing this), or you can wait for the next big sale.

Cinders is a lovely and charming game. I'm a sucker for fairy tale retellings, and this one really does do it for me. The variety of endings you can get based on your choices makes this extremely replayable, and none of the endings or paths are directly linear. Of course this does mean you'll have to revisit a lot of conversations again, but luckily there is a Skip function that will glaze over scenes you've already seen.
Needless to say, the art is beautiful. So much love and care went into the details of the environment, as well as making sure the characters properly emote. Writing is pretty good, with my only complaint being that the dialogue for Cinders felt a little out of place from the setting. (Possibly an attempt to be more relatable to the player?) It's a small nitpick in a sea of praise though. I loved this game, and would be all over another fairytale retelling from the developers.

Out of all the VNs I've played on Steam, this one takes the cake. It has a lot more content, variation, and depth compared to most other titles and it's an interesting take on Cinderella. The choices are not limited to A or B and the multiple variations per ending add a nice twist for those who enjoy somewhat specific/customized paths. The art is also very beautiful. I just finished this story for the first time. It was beautiful and extremely well written. I enjoyed it immensely and found the story very moving. I was often crying because of its wonderful twists and turns. Already I am wondering how things might be different, what if I romance a character, choose a different goal, or a different method.
There are so many obvious ways to change the plot, and yet the beatiful branches that appear suggest that there are many subtle ways to influence it also.
I'm a person who will reread a book over and over if I find it good enough. This is no different, I would love to read this again even if it would be exactly the same, knowing that I can make it different each time only heightens my desire to read this again.
As you can probably see, I'm reviwing this mostly as a story. This is because that is what it is. I am glad they didn't try to put a thin veneer of game onto this story because I think they focussed on what was important, and that is a part of what makes this so good.

The unfortunate flaw of this game is that even if someone goes for every achievement and story outcome, the average amount of time to accomplish this is around 15-20 hours, depending on whether you get help from walkthroughs or not. I think most people can agree that more gameplay time is preferable. However, I'd like to say that this is the ONLY flaw of this game (obviously, that's just my opinion though).
If you like visual novels, I highly recommend this one. Every single choice affects the ending of the story. There are also about a dozen different story ending combinations to be made. As the description of the game states, it is an adult version of the Cinderella story. However, Cinders (her name in this version) doesn't have to be the traditional character she's known to be. She can be villainous, independent, strong-willed, ambitious, etc. She can have whatever type of personality you want her to have. The best part is that she doesn't have to go after the prince. She can plot revenge against her stepmother and stepsisters, unlike the traditional character. She can be absolutely defiant and rebellious, also unlike the traditional character. But let's say you want her to be a nice, good person, but still establish her independence (from the Prince and her stepfamily), you can do that combination as well! Point being, this doesn't have to be the typical Cinderella story unless you want it to be. The story and the character are what you make it and for a visual novel, that's the best a gamer can ask for.
Other good things about the game:
- The artwork is beautiful (and sort of gothic).
- The music is well-done and fitting to the atmosphere of the game.
- There are other suitors Cinders can go for other than the Prince.
- The gamer can see the point of view/character development of the stepsisters/stepmother if they wish to (making them more human than the original story).
- The game truly causes the gamer to put thought into the choices they make.
I'll say it again: if you like visual novels, I HIGHLY recommend this game.

tl;dr: this game is not worth the asking price. Even though it's free.
Games like this hinge entirely on their story, and the story here is a hot mess.
It hints at a lot of semi-meaningful ideas, but instead of engaging with any of them or actually forming into a coherent narrative, the game just stops at some point, revealing that the main character was just on drugs the whole time.
The creator even has an explanation posted, walking you through the game step by step and explaining it. It's riddled with spelling errors, doesn't correct or enhance anything in the game, and reveals, basically, that any effort trying to find some sort of over-arching message for this game is a waste of time.
The puzzles rarely involve the player actually finding a solution. "Run forward counting to six, then turn right" is not a puzzle. Most of the game is the player being guided from one point to another by notes, trinkets, or voices. The other kind of puzzle in the game is look around the room until you find the thing you can interact with. I would say there were 3 moments in the game that required actual problem-solving, and in each case I had figured out what to do immediately, then the game took me aside and told me (in a slightly veiled metaphor) exactly what to do.
The only difficulty comes from first person platforming, which is probably the worst thing in the history of gaming. If "The Stanley Parable" were a video on youtube, "Only If" would be the dregs of its comment section.
Edit: I should mention that I played through the "White Pawn" ending. I notice a lot of the negative reviews are from people who took the other path, which is apparently much worse in terms of both story and gameplay.

The game is good for what it is, but realize what it is: a linear, hack and slash title.  It's also not that long, but that's not necessarily a negative, given the nature of the game.  My overall rating for the game is 7/10.  It was definitely worth the $10 I paid for it, and I think it wouldn't be a terrible buy for even $20, but I wouldn't pay any more than that.
On paper it seems like I'd hate the game since it's a pretty repetitive hack and slasher, but somehow it ends up being more than the sum of its parts.  I thought the combat did a good job of capturing the brutal and visceral nature of close combat.  It was fun enough to play, even if it was pretty repetitive.  The story was also solid, and I think that helped the game a lot.  It held your attention and kept you motivated to fight through each part.  Had the story been bad, I'm not sure how enjoyable the overall game would have been.
The graphics were also pretty good, and felt like they captured the feeling of ancient Rome, although at some points the architecture was pretty clearly exaggerated compared to reality.  The environments are definitely not 100% historically accurate, but I could accept the areas where creative license was taken.  The Arena section, in particular, was pretty cool.  The levels were all totally linear, but that seemed to work alright for this game.
The upgrade system to me seemed like it served very little purpose.  In my opinion, you might as well have automatically leveled up.  I bought upgrades throughout the game, and they probably helped, but nothing I purchased had an obvious impact on the game play.  I didn't even spend all my exp toward the end of the game, as I simply forgot to do so, and it really didn't seem to make much difference (granted at that point I was already pretty upgraded).  It just seemed odd to me that they went to such effort to add an XP system, but then didn't really do much with it.
Lengthwise the game was pretty short.  I estimate that it only took me about 6 - 6.5 hours to play through.  Steam says 7 hours, but I know there was some AFK time in there.  That being said, I think the length was actually a positive, because the game play could not have held my interest for more than another hour or two.  If the game was 8 hours instead of 6, I doubt I'd have gone away with such a positive impression.
Overall, my biggest complaint is I feel the game could have been so much more than what it was.  I think they had a solid core idea with the combat, and the story/setting, but they should have expanded on it somehow.  I'm not sure exactly what direction I think they should have taken things, just that they missed the boat somehow -- the story and setting had a lot more potential than what the game ultimately delivered.

Why Awesomenauts? Well to be frankly it is Awesome.
Awesomenauts is a deep multiplayer battler with the approachability of a Saturday-morning cartoon. With its new innovative gamestyle Awesomenauts brings some fresh and needed tweeks to the MOBA-escque type of games. The elements of a platformer and the 2D style mixed with the cartoonish feel cant help but bring me back to the old-school Megaman I used to enjoy on NES, and the flavours of a late 80s action cartoon like Thundercats close to mind. Sounds impossible? No, it sounds like Awesomenauts to me.
But what exactly makes this game so fun besides its visual cosmetics, its catchy tunes and the trip down memory lane you may ask.
The game starts out with you having to unlock characters by playing games and leveling up, the starting characters provide valuable insight into how the rest of the characters work and are a bit easier then some of the later unlockables. Some of the first characters you will see in the game is rapping frog, a robot cowboy, a french cameleon and even a super intelligent space-race monkey with a jetpack stating a few. The game currently has 23 playable with more on the way, some are made in cohesion with the community like Vinnie & Spike the pufferfish that is voiced by youtuber Total Biscuit.
Some may say the game is unfair to new players cause its takes tons of hours to unlock all characters, but myself thinks thats part of the fun. I've never enjoyed games that doesn't give you something to work for and the starting characters are just as good as anyone of the others. However not having all skills in the begining makes it a bit tougher, but its not only beginners who doesn't have all skills. Anyone who wants to prestige loses them and starts over and as you can prestige 10 times its likely you are not the only one without them. I should point out that characters and maps stays unlocked of course.
The game is pitting teams of three against one another with standard moba elements like jungle, lanes and so on. But besides the 2D what really makes awesomenauts stand out is the simplicity, the platfomring elements and the diversity among the characters. Its way of playing like i mentioned brings you back to that old school Megaman. And that mixed with the competive play of a MOBA gives you a game that is easy to learn but hard to master, very addicting, and above all... Really fun to play. With over 300 hours spent in this game, I can say with my hand on my heart this is one of the best games I've played.
But of course it has it's flaws just like everything in this world.
* Ronimo is currently reworking the matchmaking system to make it more rewarding for the veteran players, and be less daunting for new recruits.
* Switching servers to their own for more stability as some may have problem with lags, myself havent had much problem with that though.
* Adding more characters with a new expansion in a couple of months and constantly tweeking them to make sure the games is as balanced as possible. New community-made character incoming too.
* Working on a visual update as some of the character is starting to feel a bit outdated.
My only wish for this game is that the community grows cause this game deserves it.

I liked Cinders from the very begining. I was drawn to it just from the image Steam gives you to click on. The trailer was really cool and I was BLOWN. AWAY. less than I minute into the game. I'm only in the middle of my first playthrough but the art is absolutely MIND BLOWING, there are a TON of interesting, unique little details, the story drew me in (and will more than likely do the same to you) and the characters are WONDERFFUL. It's done visual novel style, but even if you absolutely HATE visual novels this is still something you should check out!

Although it is a retelling of the classic fairytale Cinderella, the new approach makes it seem like another story altogether.
Genre: Fantasy/Adventure
Duration: 2 to 3 hours for one ending; 10 to 15 hours for all endings.
Developed by: MoaCube, 2012
By playing as the namesake protagonist, you are introduced to a fantasy world in which you must deal with your stepmother and stepsisters at first, later meeting nobility, fairies, salesmen and townsfolk. You do so through choices and map movement intermissions in the narrative. So as not to leave you confused, the game flashes a wooden branch icon on the upper right corner of the screen everytime a previous choice is showing its consequence.
Cinders is structured so as to give your choices an aspect of freedom: there are not correct choices and you will always reach a satisfying ending that reflects your behaviour throughout the story. This means one single playthrough will last for about two hours, but one ending is just a glimpse of the stories Cinders has to offer.
The greatest strength this visual novel has is probably its characters: no character is completely redeemed nor degraded. They are complex, round characters with motivations and goals that you can relate yourself to, enhancing the moral aspect of the choices: each and every character has a lot to be explored, making for a consistent world with strong characters - and many strong female characters - and a sense that you are free to make your own judgement.
This groundedness, however, doesn't stop the game from sporting a most pleasant fairytale atmosphere. The art and the music, through coherent design and stylistic choices, gives Cinders a fine identity and a unique feel down to minute details, such as small animations on the background and on the sprites. As such, it's easy to get used to the art style even if it's not commonly used in visual novels. Such attention to identity helps in the establshment of an emotional link between you and Cinders' world.
If only fow how bold it is, Cinders is a must for anyone who appreciates story-driven experiences with complex characters and a lot of room for the player to decide what happens next.

Negative:

*Though the game shows when a choice is reflected on the progress of the story, some choices are still lost in perspective

Endless Legend is one of those games that captivated me instantly. From gameplay to lore, from artwork to music, this game is one of the few that I can say I adore.
I won't go too much into its gameplay, as many reviews point out both the great mechanics of the game, as well as its flaws. In short, I believe that Endless Legend is a very polished, and still growing, 4x game that is complex, fun, relatively easy to access, hard but enjoyable to master, with unique factors to consider (like winter), while also being unique in its diversity of factions with substantially different playstyles.
Rather, I wanted to delve more into what makes Endless Legend a unique 4x experience to me that has not been seen since Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. I am, of course, talking about immersion, narrative, and lore. Though Endless Legend does not have a story campaign, I found myself instantly engrossed and invested in Auriga, a dying planet, with its myriad of children scrambling to secure their survival.
Its roster of factions is unique and highly creative, with ideas and concepts that are seldom seen or approached in such a way in fantasy. From honorable vampiric knights torn between expedience and honor to Insane robot cult bent on destroying the legacy of their creators, Endless Legend provides a breath of fresh air to the fantasy genre (by in large part, infusing healthy dosages of Sci-Fi into it without compromising the Fantasy aspect).  Each faction's lore and story is explored through faction quests, a unique aspect in 4x, providing for those who wish it, a narrative experience and objective that goes beyond the traditional victory conditions present in 4x games. Each new game on Auriga is a new story from a different and engrossing perspective.
This immersion into the narrative of Auriga and its children is supplemented by minor quests which add much to the lore of the minor factions of the planet, in addition to an exceptional and beautiful artstyle that is, to me, incomparable. This is all topped off with an incredible and amazing score by FlyByNo, who perfectly captures the ambience of Endless Legend and its lore with every track.
Gameplay wise, Endless Legend can proudly claim a high seat among the best of 4x games, with an active development team that constantly listens to feedback and improves the game. But if one is interested in complementing a fun gameplay experience with immersion and fascinating lore, then Endless Legend stands unrivalled with its head held high.

I used to play this game just over a decade ago when they updated it as "A War Apart" so when I saw it rereleased on STEAM as an updated version I HAD to get it! So why the thumbs down? Well after playing it for a few weeks I realized that there has only been minimal changes, some are good, others not so much..
The Pros:
-Awesome music, especially when entering black holes, the fast paced music really immerses you into the combat. Even when travelling between star systems, the music kept me entertained and in the space exploring mood throughout my playthrough.
-A lot of new ships and Weapons to choose from and experiment with.
-The new Pirate Organization with a ranking system and space stations that work just like the Coalitions Military Stations.
-A living breathing galaxy, the world actually moves around you, which gives a huge feeling of immersion. I liked how I could sit around and watch other NPCS move up military ranks and live their lives without any player interaction.
-Fun combat elements, turn style combat which allows you to pause and strategize which was a nice feature since it allowed some micro-managing.
-Open world Freedom, I like how there are no specifics one what skills you HAVE to get up first. If you want to trade, become a trader, if you want to be a jerk and rob people (Which I personally prefered) become a Pirate! The easiest and safest route I found to be was sticking with Ranger military.
Now, THE CONS:
-Planetary battles, the AI is incredible lack-luster in terms of reliability. The idea of putting an RTS element to an RPG game isn't necessarily a terrible idea. What IS, however, is doing it without developing a proper AI for that specific feature. For example: When telling my troops to move forward, instead my troops may walk a bit left, do a loopy-loopy to the left and down, maybe to the right a bit, walk into the walls for a few seconds, then start heading up. A process that may have taken 6-9 seconds to fully perform, when they should have taken the initial 2 seconds to just WALK FORWARD.
The same goes with attacking, they pick the weirdest targets, Instead of shooting at a target that is attacking them, not even two unit lengths away, they are aiming at another target miles away in behind my own troops. I didn't mind the battles TOO much, as of writing this review I have 24/40 planetary battles completed, so I'm not saying they are impossible but what is frustrating is most of the difficulty which comes from the battles is trying to get the terrible AI to work properly for you.
-Liberating Star Systems, Most of the time I find myself buying military operations which seem to have next to no effect. They will gather maybe 5 ships of extreme garbage quality, that fly into the next system and get shot down immediately. There is no intelligence behind it. Even when looking at the Galaxy map, I'll see a system currently being liberated, so I warp in to find allies fighting the dominators. But once I show up and start fighting, ALL OF MY ALLIES start warping away from the solar system. Then when I try to liberate them myself (Late game) allies will only warp in once theres only  a few dominators left.
-Relationships with other Captains, I find the relationship meter with most other captains broken. I will be flying through a star system only to be interupted by another ranger demanding money from me, I tell him no so he starts shooting. If I return fire, I am now hated by other rangers in the area. This is kind of weird, seeing as I'm the guy whos getting robbed, its like walking into a walmart, only for the greeter to say, "Your wallet or your life!" And if you refuse, the rest of the walmart employees will start throwing items at you while you try to leave the store.
-Pirate Organization ships, They use too many missle launchers. When flying into a star system, its strange to scan over 15 different ships to see each and every one of them using 5 missle launchers. In fact the game starts lagging, which stops the immersion quite quickly when the game is now taking 3-5 seconds to load in between each turn because of exploding stray missles.
-With new ships comes imbalance, The sizing of a lot of ships makes the game stagnant. By mid-end game I found most ships had around 1500+ hull. Not only transports and Liners, but most rangers and military are also flying around with 1500 even up to 2000 hull size witch shield generators and droids too, which makes a lot of the fighting extremely long and repetetive.  By the very end, most fights became more of a chore than anything else.
TLDR;
It's mostly just poor AI which brings this game down for me. It's not like its a BAD game, its just not amazing is all, I'd say Space Rangers 2 is "Alright". I think where I'm most disappointed is that it has been over a decade, and they released such minimal things on this game when instead I wish they had fixed the AI issues that they had known people were having since the original release.

Ok... awsomenauts is a 2D moba about people fighting in space. Your question is "Is it a good game?"
My answer is. Kind of.
The only reason I am saying this is because this game does alot of good things. But of course with good things comes the flaws. There are good characters, and their moves sets usually come with their pros, and their weaknesses.
But with these characters with the weaknesses and pros, there are characters who have pros, but no weaknesses. Such as Yuri, He can fly and he has mines. He has the pros of having high powered mines. But what is his weakness? He can fly, So he can just avoid the other characters that are on the ground. There is a character named Leon. He has the power to go invisible and he can stay like that until he wants to attack. Stealth is his pro. Again, what is his weakness? He can just stay invisible, He is kind of like Loki from the game "Smite." But again, What is his weakness? If he attacks, he can just stall you until the 9 second cooldown ends. Thats another bad thing since the cooldowns are so short If im right the longest cooldown in the game is 11 seconds and thats for the strongest move in the game(Derpl's Rocket Launcher.)
Either way, I should get back to the weaknesses and pros thing. Now if this game had things like temporary boosts like jump boost, or and all seeing eye so you can see the invisible I would be fine with the fact that they dont have weaknesses. But the fact that they dont, makes this game harder to play. But this is really my only complaint.
The gameplay is pretty smooth and its only really slow if you have bad internet connection, or your playing with someone with a bad connection.
The community is pretty bad, They would probably end up making fun of you and calling you garbage if you arent doing better than them. You would usually end up finding this from leauge 8-6 they usually end up being super annoying but you can switch to the EU servers if they bother you that much (Or vice versa.)
Last but not least. There is no story so this part dosnt count.
So lets add this up Ups (Gameplay, Characters 1/2.) So thats about 7 points sunce gameplay is a main factor to a game in my opinion
Downs (The whole Pros and Weaknesses thing, The Community) so thats minus 1 point. You might ask"You went so far into the pros and weaknesses thing and it only lost 1 point?" Well thats not for all of the characters there are more than 20 characters. The characters with no weaknesses are just played alot. Also, the community dosnt mean much you can just switch the region.
So my final rating is 6.5/10 So I DO recommend this game,

Definitely one of my favourite games to lose endless hours to.
The game combines many different genres into one seamless package. You have a great mix of strategy (turn based and real time), role-playing, trading, text adventure and open world exploration. The story is simple but well presented. You can dive into it with ease, or just ignore it and go explore the galaxy, coming back at your leisure.
As you play you'll earn XP to level up your pilot, allowing you to improve various skills. These affect your combat abilities, trade prices and other such things.
The main gameplay element is a turn based, top down, strategy mode, where you're flying your ship across the stars, visiting various systems, planets and space stations. It's very well balanced, with a huge assortment of equipment that you can deck your ship out in. Each ship has a varied number of slots for different equipment, along with a max amount of cargo and gear your can carry. Picking the best ship your play style, be it heroic Ranger, trader or pirate, is important. As is knowing what targets to go after and when it's best to just run away.
There are also wormholes you can dive into, which will take you to random places in the galaxy. However inside a wormhole you have to face various enemies in an action heavy top down shooter style of play, where all your weapons have their own firing styles.
But just flying around in space (as awesome as it is) isn't all the game has to offer. Going to various planets will let you take missions for the different factions. You can have simple trade missions (or just focus on trading freelance to make money), you can escort others or be asked to take someone out, you can also be sent to take on the Dominators, an evil robotic foe made up of three unique factions. There's also ground missions where you will play out real-time strategy missions, constructing your own robotic armies to repel the Dominators.
And there's my personal favourite, the text adventures. Many missions presented will give you missions that play out in a classical text adventure style. You're presented with various scenarios and have lots of options on how to proceed. These missions vary vastly, from hover bike races, to testing experimental weapons, to capturing rare creatures to pizza making competitions (I'm not kidding). They are wonderfully written and present a very fun way of handling special events. This style is also used for the prison mini-game, which basically happens any time you're arrested by one of the factions. You can be a model inmate and follow the rules, try and survive being a snitch, or try to be the Don of the prison. Along the way you'll be focusing on keeping your mind and body sharp, taking part in talent contests, cockroach races, dealing with contraband, and all sorts of varied and surprising prison activities.
Graphically the game is wonderful. The graphics are detailed and crisp, and just flying around space is an amazing visual experience. The text adventure sections have hand drawn pictures to go with them. The only part of the game that's a little more simplistic is the RTS battles.
As for sound, there's some great musical scores to the game and quite well done sound effects. There's no speech, so you don't need to worry about hearing it over whatever else is going on in the game.
As for replay value... the universe is randomly generated each time you play a new game. There will always be certain home systems and home worlds that appear, but where they are and what's around them, along with what space stations are available (which you can fund to help construct more of) will differ each time you play. Missions, ships and equipment will vary each game as well, so the course you take through the game can vary greatly. Definitely a game you can come back to again and again.

Ryse: Son of Rome is about going to beautiful places and repeatedly stabbing everyone you meet there.
Ryse’s story is delivered out of chronological order. Rome is crumbling under a barbarian assault, and Marius, a proud and decorated Centurion, is escorting Emperor Nero through his palace. One moment later, Marius is a fresh-faced greenhorn of the Roman army. As I progressed, I enjoyed learning more about how the circumstances became so dire. And despite the abnormal structure, the story was never difficult to follow even when it took a few unanticipated turns.
Ryse’s biggest issue is that not even halfway through its modest six-hour campaign, you’ll have seen and experienced a vast majority of your offensive options. Combat consists of basic hits, bashes, blocks, and heavy attacks.
Enemy variety does a bit of work to liven things up. Some foes are unblockable, some charge you, and some assault you with a flurry of dual-sword attacks. Dealing with them requires you to care about your blocks, attacks, and movements, which is fun until you figure out their repetitive patterns.
With my GeForce 980-equipped PC I played Ryse without a hiccup.

English review / Análise em português.
Beware that i may edit this review to be better for everyone plus i will work to write the portuguese from brazil version of it. Any suggestion is greatly welcomed.
Now, let's start.
Altough i rated this game as recommended,  beware that not everyone will be happy about this game and with valid reasons which i'll explain in the end of this review.
First, i'll start about the graphics, animations and sound effects. They are nothing short of amazing, just like you could expect from any metal gear game. What impressed me more was the animations, which felt really realistic for a game. Plus you'll see great water effects on clothes, walls and even on floor, reflecting light pretty well and on floor it even reflects nearby enviroment, which is something i havent see it yet on any game (i may have noticed in some but this is really the first time i saw it). And the sound effects and voice acting are pretty good too. Don't listen to those bashing Kiefer Sutherland, who acted as snake. He did a pretty good job voicing. You may prefer David hayter as a original voice actor, of course. But you can't deny the good job by kiefer sutherland as well. So, you see, the technical part of this game is pretty solid. REally, this is may be the best port i have ever seen on pc. I can run it on ultra with 1620 p resolution with a steady 60 fps. And on 3820 x 2000 p with a steady 35. (Using a gtx 980). Nothing short of amazing, didnt have a single noticeable fps drop while playing this game. Only bad thing is the depth of field. There's no separated option to turn it off. If you disable it, in the screen processing settings, you'll disable AA and water reflection. I'm really waiting for a patch or mod that allows me to remove the annoying dof.
Second, the gameplay, i really enjoyed it and Kojima once again made a pretty immersive stealth game. If you are a newcomer, the game is mainly about you do your missions avoiding being seeing. You'll get better ratings and awards if you don't kill anyone and don't get caught. But you are still free to engage combat and in this game you have more ways than before to spread chaos, since you can even drive armored vehicle and use them to shoot enemies, but beware that you'll never make S ranking that way and you cant take much damage or you'll die. This is a great thing imo. It offers for both stealth and combat players and this game delivers nice quality for each of them without decaying in quality. Really liked how sometimes the AI act more varied than before, like sometimes changing patterns of patrolling. What i liked it most was when i was doing a mission where i had to deal with two targets. Each one were in different areas already pinpointed in your map. if you take some time to reach them, they may start moving to other areas of the map, thus making you having to either search them (in my case, one just showed up near me, while i was far from his area, which scared the hell out of me because almost trigered an alert.). Another good stuff is how you can threat your enemies when you hold them and they can give crucial informations about your objectives or point areas with weapons or useful stuff for you. It feeks awesome to get these.  Still, i miss how you could knock walls to atract enemies . I guess it may be removed to be more realistic, like you couldn possibly make knocks sounds and the enemy go to investigate and then claim it was his imagination.  But nevertheless, the controls may get some time to get used to but once they do, you'll start playing pretty smoothly (i used 360 controller, cant say about K + M). To end this, you have more than just one mission to this game, which gives replayability value, since you can beat them in different ways. Just like peace walker, but more open world and free. I really enjoyed this and i think this is something that every MGS fan will as well. But an annoying thing is that kaz doesnt't stop talking and repeating basics and stuff. I wish i there was a way to at least make him talk less
3, the story. Well, you cant expect much about the story. Is just one mission just after the events of peace walker. If you havent play it, don't worry, the game will provided the previous story for people to understand it. But the the small bit it was showed in the game about the story is pretty good and immersive. If you are a newcomer to the series, beware that this game is known to have pretty long cutscenes. So expect one in the beggining of the mission and other in the end. A thing worth noticing about the story is that kojima is trying to make this game kinda polemic. What i mean is: expect some pretty cruel torture torture here. Just like war, which is what kojima is trying to show how bad and cruel it is. And in a bit of the game, he succeed very well in doing it. Just warning it to some players who may not like very gruesome stuff. It is not a con imo. But i understand why some people may be unconfortable, specially when that's the objective of kojima.
Finally, i really liked this game, bought it while it was on sale and at least i felt it was worth. I really liked this game and i played more than my play time sugests ( iwas having problems with internet). Does that mean i can recommend this game to everyone? Unfortunately, no. here comes the thing that annoyed most people: the game indeed doesnt offer much content. You only get one map to do all your missions. A somewhat big map, sure. But just one. And the enemies will be in similar positions in every missions. If you played peace walker, you'll understand this. You'll have side missions in the same area of story missions. And this is the case, all you do will be in the same map. If you are not ok with this, i can completly understand and i can say that this game isn't for you, unless you get it on a sale or with price drop. Just notice that is not as bad as some people say like "wow, a demo". This game offers more than a demo but still doesnt offer enough for some people for it's price. So do THINK ABOUT THIS IF YOU PLAN ON PURCHASING THIS GAME! But i can say that i already cant wait for the full game.

Should be called Endless Frustration.
I really love strategy. And I love fantasy. I love 4X. I like RPGs.  I have played CIV 5 over 1000 hours, EU4 500 and AOW3 200, and list goes on and on. So this game should have been like a match made in heaven. Oh how wrong I was.
I dont like to make conclusions with so little playtime and without even finishing a single game but my god, does this game make finishing a single match painful.
First of all,  a 10 minute tutorial? What?  This doesn't prepare you at all. It is normal that in 4X matches take hours. There is no advisors like in CIV 5, tha guide you or comprehensive ingame manual like in AOW3. Its so stupid to go wiki every ten minutes of the first playthrough. This game doesnt tell you anything. You will be extremely frustrated, and will fail, just because game doesnt tell you what EVERYTHING MEANS. (Just like EU4 but thats a different story)
Second. The combat. It's so sad. So bad. Easily the worst combat system of all the 4X games I have played. You have very narrow control of your troops, and this leads luck and AI being a HUGE factor. And without proper war, or combat... Well the  Exterminate part is really lacking in this 4X. Oh, and there is no naval combat.  Really the combat mechanics is what killed this game for me personally. Endless legend is a 3X game if you ask me.
You can and probably will use autocombat option, but thats not really a justification to combat being absolutely abysmal. Manual combat is also really slow, which just kills the little enjoyment you actually could get.
Third. Lack of options.  No animation speed  settings. No help options. TWO UI settings, which both I found terrible. Missing/Lack of available key bindings/shortcuts. ( no split, no merge, no embark etc.) Very little graphic options, only few presets. (no ability set shadows etc)
Fourth. Game is littered with dlc. Well thats nothing new to a veteran EU 4 player, but still. Why do you make me play the TUTORIAL with a faction that doesnt exist in the BASEGAME if I dont buy the DLC. That's just a slap in the face.
Fifth. This game really doesnt innovate does it? All of the features (except maybe the winter) I have seen in other games and have been done better. Combat blows. There is no naval stuff. (Every game ever does it better) There is no spells. (AOW3 does it better) Quests are fetch stuff, kill stuff or build stuff. (meh)  Wonders are just boring stat boosts or effects. (CIV 5 does it better) The unit designing was cumbersome and retrofitting was even more stupid. (Fallen Enchantress does it better) Tech/research was... Well, honestly I didnt get it. Why was it a great idea? (Lets just say it wasnt anything revolutionary. )
Sixth. Game is reeeeeaally pretty and music kicks butt. Factions seemed really diverse, although I have to wonder if they are really balanced.
TLDR: Beauty and  music cant save this hot piece of carbage. Just get AOW3, AOW2, CIV 5 EU4 or FE. You will have better time.

Stronghold Crusader was and still is my all time favorite stragegy title ever (followed closely by A Bridge Too Far and the older Command and Conquer titles).
Having tried the whole Stronghold series I've found the rest of the titles to be a failed attempt at getting the recipe correct.
Stronghold Crusader 2 Hasn't worked it's wonders on me either.
Anywho! Crusader is a 3D effect 2D title with basic graphics (good for it's day) and superb gameplay.
The title has been remastered slightly to allow for more modern display resolutions (hence the "HD" in the title) as before you were limited to 1024x786 on your shiny 1080p screen!
Now you can see a full 1080p so play on huge TV is even possible!
The aim of this game is simple, start mission with barely any resources but usually enough to build the basics and start your first line of defence, your castle!
Once in full swing you'll have peasant turning into bakers, diary farmers, pub landlords, woodcutters, stonemasons and many more to build your stockpile and granary. You'll need to balance these carefully as the more peasants you have living in your castle the more food they need.
Once your resources are taken care of you need to build an army.
Building an army is done of in one of 3 ways, either supplying the armour and weapons (making these from iron, leather etc) and combining these with jobless peasants to create a mega army, making an army from mercenary posts (not as strong as a self made army but a quick way of buidling numbers) or relying on a outpost (disabled in some missions).
Your objective from this point is clear... destroy your enemies.
Why is Crusader special? It's got a certain charisma and charm, it just feels right. It's very easy to pickup so great for beginners and advanced gamers and will keep anyone interested for many hours!
Did I mention the castle builder and map creator modes?
Castle builder is for those who just want to create a castle and be left alone for hours on end until it's self sustaining.
Map creator is for those who want to (let's be honest now) create a map with an unfair advantage to the other players.
System requirements are so low you could run it on anything from a super low spec Intel Atom to an 16core Xeon.
Overall I'd say a solid 10/10 and a must have for anyones steam account.
I hope there is a Crusader 3, but I strongly hope they base it on this title rather than the other Stronghold series.
Also, if reworked slightly for Linux compatabilty, perhaps getting it to run on a Raspberry Pi 2!

Cinders is a realistic retelling of the classic Cinderella story. It's like a visual novel with a whole lot of reading (obviously), but it also gives you a choice from time to time. Choices that affect the story. As a result there are several endings to be unlocked, and a single playthrough can take anywhere between 3-5 hours I think. The art is done remarkably well, even if the faces lack of bit of character and the whole thing feels very polished. Except for a few typos, that is.
I would recommend it to everyone who knows the story or just likes reading. But please note that it's not so much a game, but more of an interactive book. There's very little input required. And let's not forget about the price which is absurdly high. So for now I suggest waiting for a sale.
[Rating: 73/100]

Basic Premise: Shape Cinderella’s character, attitude, and reactions to her upbringing and choose how she escapes. The many character trait and action choices that actually impact the story’s end make this visual novel stand out. I’ve played through it several times and still have not found all the paths.
Music: Most visual novels’ and sims’ soundtracks have me hunting for the mute button, but this one is gorgeous.
Visuals: Gracjana Zielinska’s art has a detailed, ethereal quality without becoming prissy or cutesy.  It’s beautiful.  I’m so pleased she’s returning for Solstice.
Programming: I appreciate the ability to quickly skip through already viewed scenes with one button press.  All visual novels should implement this.
Writing: *thunk**thunk* *thunk*  That noise, dear friend, is the characters’ dialog and the insights into their behavior being delivered with all the subtlety of a frying pan to the back of the skull. The reader is never left to infer anything. Cinders’ inner monologue or other characters will spell it out. During the first long conversation between Cinders and Sophia, they tell their back-story and motivations to one another without the reservation and self-protection that the back-story would naturally have bred.  It drove me crazy until I remembered Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov. Yes, the two works don’t seem to have much in common but bear with me. Like Karazmov, Cinders uses characters to represent a consistent type of person rather than how you and I would interact on a day-to-day basis. Once you go with it, they both deliver a good story and observations on human nature.  Boom. A 2012 visual novel saved by Dostoevsky.
Writing: The banter between characters usually makes me smirk (Sophia and Gloria should have their own spin-off). The only exception is the romantic dialog. Excuse me for a moment, game, while I fetch some nachos to go with all this cheese. Fortunately, the game has many endings with no romance whatsoever.
Writing: The grammar, spelling, and word choice are nearly perfect. Kudos to the editor.
Female Characters: The writers clearly spent more of their effort developing the women. Cinders, Carmosa, Gloria, Sophia, and Madame Ghede all have distinct personalities and goals. Sophia’s snark is always welcome: “The only things missing from this picture is holding hands and singing. And dancing. Possibly in circles. In the middle of a flowery meadow. I think I might throw up.” I want an ending in which she and Cinders escape together.
Male Characters: The men aren’t bad, but they lack the depth and care the women received. I won’t dwell on them (particularly since the developer has already addressed this), but here’s a brief run-down.  Tobias is a childhood friend who tends to deliver motivation speaker advice with the aforementioned frying pan; I want to like you, Toby, but you have to stop thwacking me over the head.  Perrault is a guard captain caught between duty and ethics; he is my favorite of the three.  Prince Basile is he least developed of the three, though the conversations between him and Perrault are good. He and Cinders discuss Levia Malich’s work in a scene ripped straight from Ever After, but other than that I enjoy their interactions.
Bottom Line: I recommend this to anyone (not just women) who wants a strong, competent protagonist and enjoys tinkering to discover different endings. If you happen to have a snarky sense of humor, even better.

What initially drew me to Cinders was the combination of the female protagonist, visual novel category, and the lovely artwork. From the looks of it, Cinders seemed like it would be a wonderful game, and it definitely delivered! I just started my second playthrough, and I have been loving every minute of gameplay.
First, I absolutely must rave about the gorgeous art by Gracjana Zielinska! The character designs were unique and stunning, and the backgrounds were lavish and interesting. I loved how little details would appear or move in the background - that gave the graphics a "little something" extra to catch the eye! I could not get enough of the beautiful visuals and tried to research if she had done work on other games. I found out about Solstice, a mystery thriller visual novel coming soon, and Phantasmat, a hidden objects game. I am much more into visual novels, but the artwork alone is compelling me to give Phantasmat a chance also!
Second, the gameplay placed player choice front and center, and especially in a visual novel, I appreciated this greatly. Choices were frequent and truly affected the story; the "Rewards" section from the game's menu lets you see how many of the variants you've explored to the ending, and in my ending, I've only explored 25% so far, so there is still a lot for me to experience! I did do some saving/loading to see what would happen with certain choices and was very pleased with the level of difference I discovered. In addition, certain choices add adornments to the menu page - this made game progress even more exciting because I wanted to see what else would be added where. :) ... and it brought out the completionist in me! I am excited to unlock all the endings and as many variants as I can.
Third, the characters were unpredictably rich. Coming into a fairytale-inspired game, I expected the same character tropes, but while the characters were similarly-situated, they were far deeper than the superficial Cindarella cast I was used to! Cinders, for example, can be played to be quite pragmatic, or pig-headed, or honest, or devious, or a mix of the aforementioned, and based on my ending, I think the choice of these traits truly affects the outcome of the game. Madame Ghede was a favorite character of mine - I wanted to know so much more about her! She was enigmatic and wise, revealing a hint of the effects of what seemed to me a very detailed life. The stepmother (Carmosa) and step-sisters (Sophia and Gloria) were also multi-faceted, and there was more than meets the eye to Captain Perrault, as well.
The game's soundtrack suited it perfectly -- it was not overbearing, but rather complementary. Chimes indicated decisions, and subtle pieces (like at the Lake) would round out an enchanting experience. I wish the soundtrack had been included in a bundle because it would be a wonderful way to relax. :)
If you like visual novels, female protagonists, gorgeous artwork, fairytales, lots of choice that affects the ending, and a hint of romance, I highly recommend this game. If you adore Gracjana Zielinska's artwork (like I now do), you should also check out the upcoming visual novel from the same developer (Moacube) Solstice and the hidden objects game from Big Fish, Phantasmat. Enjoy!

-Stronghold perfected

-Multitudes of new units, including arabic units that need only gold, and monks that can be trained at the cathedral

This is it.  This is the best stronghold game.  Everything after, while sometimes good, failed to measure up.  And Stronghold 1, while perfectly fine, didn't have the added depth this game has.  While this game lacks a proper story mode, it focuses on what there really is to love about this game - the gameplay.  There's a main campaign which consists of 50 skirmish matches against progressively harder scenarios, and another 20 in the "expansion" that comes included with the HD version.
There are a multitude of different computer opponents to fight as well, and they can range from comically inept to frighteningly capable.  Maps have a wide range of setups, from the vanilla "everyone starts with the same basic setup and resources" to the maps which have no farmable land, to the maps that give one player every resource and all the others very few at all.  The game is fun, and there are so many different ways to play that it will continue to challenge and entertain you.
One of the only real downsides is that there are still times when you watch and wait as your economy chugs along and your opponent builds his army, and there's just nothing for you to do but wait.  Firefly did a good job of reducing that so it isn't as stark and noticeable as it was in Stronghold 1, but it still happens.  A fast forward option would have been nice.  Even more so if you like using swordsmen in sieges - you will legit wait five to ten minutes for them to get from your stronghold to the other guy's stronghold.  Still, this is a very minor complaint in an otherwise flawless game.
There's a strong online community creating more maps and scenarios that can be downloaded and played.  The addition of the arabic units with all their unique traits gives Crusader even more depth than before, and really just rounds out an already fantastic game.  This is one of those games I've kept coming back to over the years, and probably will continue to do so for another decade.
