Again, its obvious you will not see Wayne Rooneys taste for the elder ladies come into fruition, Cristiano Ronaldo is not gonna write off his ferarri on his way to training. Big Sam will not be caught with his pants down over circumventing the third party ownership laws and of course there won't be a massive scandal over the head of Fifa taking bungs left right and centre because THATS NOT WHAT THE GAMES ABOUT! you just won't see that in any game!
The crowning glory for me in terms of the new additions is the Brexit. The fact that you can start any new game you want and it will be completely different from the next because of this. YOU WILL NOT GET THIS IN ANY OTHER GAME!
Yes, there are alot of the same old same olds, but, its a football management game. I'm pretty sure there's only a finite number of things you can do when you break it down. I don't get what people want out of the game when they say this.
The only things i've noticed that have swayed from the realism is team names and the German national team situation.  It seems like that is the only thing that has gotten worse from previous years. There are no Brazillian team names any more, or spanish. You can work it out, but they are named differently for some reason. That is a negative.
As far as managing the team, playing through the matches, moving up the leagues, winning games, losing games, buying/selling/dealing with/training players, even the realism of transfer fees and the finances going on in the game and the influence of the Chinese leagues are concerned.. this is second to no other football management simulation game. Fact.
So stop moaning about not being able to win games, that one glitch that cost you a goal, that you hammer teams statistically but can't score for toffee, or even that the came crashed one time and you were on a good run (USE THE GODDAMN SAVE BUTTON AND AUTO SAVE OPTIONS!), about the bug fixes that come out (which FYI, auto download through steam and other than the january transfer updates move seamlessly into your save games),  about the gameplay (because that has actually improved alot over the years) and realise that this game is still the number 1 in football management simulators. All of them things can boil down to the work arounds i've already provided above or one simple thing.... BE A BETTER MANAGER!
if i could give this game a star rating i'd say 4 out of 5. MGS Ground Zeros is like a prequel short mission that will introduce players to the Fox Engine and the gameplay of the upcoming Phantom Pain which is due to release in summer 2015.
The game plays and looks fantastic on the PC and if you are a hardcore MGS fan you probably bought this day one like I did. The Deja Vu and Jamais Vu missions are both included in the PC release but need to be unlocked by collecting all hidden Fox patches.

The dictionary defines the word glorious as: delightful; wonderful; completely enjoyable; brilliantly beautiful or magnificent.
As far as games in general go, to me this word describes Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes.  This is one slick, content filled package with not only beautiful graphics but more importantly beautiful gameplay as well.  I've been a fan (not die-hard) of the Metal Gear Solid games since Metal Gear Solid for the Playstation which also made its way to pc way back when.  Metal Gear Solid 2 Sons of Liberty blew me away and probably my favorite entry thus far was Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater.(though I finished that game with great difficulty due to the hideous camera system, the setting's been one of my favorites)  I never quite finished MGS4 but I enjoyed my time with it.   MGSV however is priming itself to be my favorite in the series if it keeps going this way.
I'll start off by saying I first bought and played Ground Zeroes on the Playstation 4.  My sentiments are the same for that version.  I went ahead and bought the pc version as a litmus test to see if it ran like everyone says it does.  True what has been said, this is an amazing port of a console game.  I have the game maxed at every setting save for SSAO which I left on high with 1920x1080 resolution with vertical sync enabled and she runs like a dream.  I probably have at least seven to eight hours in the PS4 version.  I just bought the pc version today and have clocked an hour and 34 screenshots.
There is a lot of content here alongside the main mission.  Kojima filled this prologue chock full of side missions and other elements.  Just soaking up the lore through listening to recordings on your casette player is great.  The gameplay is classic, pure third person stealth.  The control scheme is very comfortable and easy to get used to.  I personally think because it was designed well, that a controller is the most ergonomic way to play this.  That coupled with buttery fluid animations and an open map that you can approach at any angle make for superb gameplay.
I won't make the assumption that if you are a MGS fan that you'll like this but because I am I think you will.  Its still that beautiful production value and presentation that we know and are accustomed to.  Down to the little sound effects and camera work this game oozes detail and atmoshpere.  I also believe that if you are an old school Splinter Cell fan (Splinter Cell, Pandora Tomorrow and Chaos Theory) that you too would love this game even if you've never played a MGS game before.  In fact this would probably be the place for you to start as anything prior to MGS4 would probably frustrate you.  Believe me there are things about the series that have frustrated me over the years.  Mainly because of the control schemes and the fact that the game is known for Boss fights and I'm the type of gamer that loathes Boss fights.  But for the Metal Gear Solid franchise I put up with them because I enjoy the series very much.  I love the deep, confusing themes, conspiracies, mysteries, presentation, production value and almost operatic drama of these games.
I've been gaming for twenty-five years and this is a wonderful game.  I can not wait for the Pantom Pain to be released.  If its anything like its prologue which I'm certain it will be, just bigger and even better, we have a real gem of a game to look forward to.

Although this isn't a spectacular game, it's not a terrible one either.  I would recommend if you can find it on sale and you're a fan of the whole pointy-clicky mystery/adventure genre.  I wouldn't pay the full $11.99 for it by any means, but with a good sale it's a reasonable time-killer.  This is one of those games where an option between "yes" and "no" would be helpful.  The "maybe" button would be appropriate.
This is a typical first-person point-and-click mystery that suffers from a somewhat lackluster plot and occasionally tedious locations, but is redeemed in my opinion by the beautiful scenes themselves and an interesting sub-plot that interested me more than the main one (one being a current mystery and the other being a fascinating pseudo-historical background story).
The locations are photographic (rather than animated/graphical) and lovely.  However, the locations are also sometimes far more sprawling than they need to be.  With 360 degrees of view (four static views per room), if you're someone like me that is used to games that are packed with useable or inspectable objects in every corner, you'll find yourself getting annoyed with the sheer expanses of emptiness.  I probably could have finished the game an hour faster if I didn't feel compelled to check every nook and cranny for something, anything, that I could use.
And then, there are times when you finally find something you can interact with, and it turns out it's just there for the hell of it.  You can poke it and prod it, but then you have to put it down and move along, all the while wondering why it was even there.
There is full voice acting for this game but they sound absolutely bored out of their minds.  Very, very "blah" dialogue.
What to do next isn't always that obvious, but there is a handy in-game guidance system in the form of your player character's notebook (although it would have been nice to see incremental hints; there was one part that I just wanted a quick shove in the right direction and instead it gave me the entire solution to a puzzle in gory detail).
So if you can find it on sale and like this type of game, it's worth a go, especially if you've exhausted your supply of comparable games.

I learned about Carol Reed games when I was adding profiles for Neoseeker. Given the fact that I frequented a lot adventure games sites, I naturally was drawn by the Carol Reed series (which was at the 5th game I think). I've immediately liked the quality of the photos and the concept of being a foreigner in Sweden.
Unfortunately, back then, I couldn't order MDNA games. And with my life evolving, I"ve kinda forgotten about them. I knew about Bosh's Damnation after adding the profile on Neoseeker last year but still, I didn't order anything. I don't remember if I saw it going through Greenlight. But when I saw the title in the upcoming list, it was wishlisted. And when I saw the release, I didn't hesitate to spent money for it.
So in other words, what's a Carol Reed game? It's a game about a young woman, loving Sweden and solving cases around like a private investigator. This time, a cleaner called her about the disappearance of his employers. Carol began to investigate until the family is giving a sign of life. Carol forgot about it... but in the summer, is brought back into the family's business as the daughter's boyfriend is found dead at a barn and the murder isn't from yesterday. Guess who will snoop around?
It's a point and click game, you find objects, you use them, you solve puzzles thanks to clues and you speak with people. The game is done with real life pictures and real people. There is no video inside but you can see differences in the pictures: people are making differents expressions, if you open a door, you'll see it open.
It could be a walking simulator as you're walking from scene to scene without having to search something and each close-up doesn't bring everytime a clue or an object, just a nice view... and the fact that in real life, you would have looked at that. In other words, Bosh's Damnation, which is the 10th game in the series, is trying to stick to reality.
The soundtrack is quite good, the mystery is well done too and the voice actors are also good. But the quality of the pictures and the beauty of some are also the strongest points for the game.
I really enjoyed it. Even the hint system is quite interesting.
I recommend it, mainly for those who love solving mysteries.

Endless Legend is a 4X turn-based fantasy strategy game which offer a very unique experience for me and I love it, but still feel incompleted. I recommend this game right now, though, why?
Because it has some thing that good-old-Civ doesn't: the element, the stories in each major and minor Factions, the writing. Yes, stories are something that I feel fresh everytime I play another factions, it feels like you could understand more about what you are controlling, and the lore behind it. Even more, each major Factions has a different playstyle, keep you busy and change of pace to suit you best. You can even name your unit, I just, wow. Other than that, the game has the same victory conditions like other 4X games.
The game has unique music and setting. In Endless Legend, your mother planet is dying. It even shows in you game, each turn passed, seasons change from summer to winter, and vice-versa, but as time passed, you will notice the winter dragged more than summer, and finally, an eternal winter. How can your people get out of this? This, this is your to manage.
Everything of this game is so much fun to play, but something, something at the end is very anti-climatic. Yes, I will told you beforehand. That is... the end game.
Just a screen.
Yes, just a screen. You will... what? I stick to my people, love them, doing quest with them, feel their lifestyle but when I finally reach the end, only a screen appear tell me what kind of victory I have. The end. Very dissapointed, I wish something, a video, some more lines to clarify everything. any of the sort, to tell me  what could be the end, or my people's fate. Please Developer, you going through so much to create storylines, then you have to end it. Not a screen that tell me I win, No, I feel lost, really.
I really love this game, I feel alive whenever I play it, but because of above statement, I can't bring myself to end a game session. If you can spare that, play this game, you will love it.

It's like civ 5 without forward settling ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, cooler tech web that forces decision making, armies that have intriguing battles, barbarians that matter more than grinding your units to certain levels and other cool mechanics that differentiate it from other 4X games and improve on the formula. Would recommend.

This has been a long time coming. SC is one game I have loved from day one. For the first time I played a game that was so complicated it took me a few days to master the economy. I had dreamed of a game like this since I played Warcraft as a small child. A game so realistic you actually had to gather raw materials it was a dream come true. Games have come and gone but SC always remained it was the only game that continued to hold my interest through the years. Even my friends got hooked and my wife who is by no means a gamer. The graphics were subpar even for the time but the gameplay was so entertaining it didn't matter. The attention to detail was beyond compare the concept of citizens you could not control was genius. Every building was bustling with people doing work and sounds of every trade rang out in a crowded village square. I developed many working strategies over the years it was as if there really were no rules. You were limited only by what crazy attack you could think up and how well you executed it. But it wasn't just the gameplay that was exceptional the programming was amazing. The 2D drawing of 3D objects made the game tiny and playable on the oldest computers. I used to carry a copy in my mp3 player so I could play anywhere. It worked on any network without any errors ever seriously in 12 years! I swear this game would run over two tin cans on a string. At some LAN parties we didn't even bother setting up a network we just plugged all the computers into a hub and SC would work even when windows didn't show any other network locations. I still play my original copy and have only encountered a few glitches. I wish they would just remake this game with top of the line graphics. I'll be playing this game till the day I die -SEF

Maybe it's because I've been playing DoW the past several years, but it kind of bothers me that the range for all of the weapons is so short. For example, the missile launcher shoots 4 squares? Lastly, it seems the AI is beefed up (i.e., cheats) by having more accurate and damaging weapons than my own troops. I understand it's easier to do that than develop a good AI, but people have been doing AI in games for decades, this kind of trick is just disappointing.
I've only played the campaign and challenges so far, so maybe multiplayer is a lot more fun (wouldn't be hard!). However, don't know if I'm willing to put in further time to find out, I'm sure that brings its own set of problems.

2 Planets Fire and Ice Review:
This is a match 3 game just like Popcap's famous Bejeweled. You have to match 3 or more of the same colored jewels and they disappear. The more gems you group the better specials and combo's you get.
2 Planets Fire and Ice itself is a lot of fun, every level has a different objective. Remove all of the same colored gems, remove all fields with only special items, balance the amount of 2 colored gems that you destroy. It gets more addictive once you understand the objective you need to get. Some levels are easy, some ridiculously difficult and will force you to try multiply times. There are a ton of power ups like time freezes, fire bombs, line destroyers, free moves and many others.
2 Planets Fire and Ice game is good casual fun especially if you like match 3 games.

The best grand strategy game for the victorian era, hands down.  It still runs well on modern operating systems, in fact, Paradox has done a great job modernizing the code to work with higher resolutions.  There was actually a time when this game crashed on most Windows boxes trying to run a freshly installed steam copy.  Not anymore!  Runs fine.
So, what is this game, how's it like?  If you have played Europa Universalis, this game is similar to that, but Victoria 2 has population and an economy.  You actually have resources in your provinces, and build factories that require X amount of resources to produce goods, that get sold, and you get money and happy peasants.  Moving on, you run a nation, any nation.  Literally, you load a new game, and pick any country in the world during the Victorian era, any year in the game range too, and nations do change with time...  Anyways, you are supreme ruler of your nation, you manage the economy and build your army / navy.  Then fabricate claims against your neighbors and have at it.  The AI is well done and challenging.  New comers will likely struggle for a time, unless they pick super powers like Prussia, England, or France, and follow guides.
The only negative with these Paradox games is the learning curve.  However, if you are familiar with Paradox games, even the Clauswitz engine, then this game isn't too tough to learn.  If you are a total grand strategy newb, or new to Paradox titles, then be prepared to read and research, you will be rewarded, however.
Overall, I have yet to play a game that encompasses all phases of war, economy, nationdom, and diplomacy, as well as Victoria 2.  I prefer Vicky2 over Hearts of Iron 4 and EU4.  Vicky is hands down my favorite game, simply because the population factor.  Which may be removed if Paradox makes a Victoria 3, because genocide, and politically correct BS.

Relic Hunter Zero is very competent top-down shooter with rogue-lite elements. The game is about one thing – shooting evil space ducks and turtles. I played almost two hours and this I my first impressions of the game. Oh, I almost forgot – the game is absolutely free!
Options are pretty decent. Fullscreen or window, resolution (it's actually windows size, but it's the same thing), max dynamic objects, particle effects, dynamic shadows,  persistant objects and reflections. There is only local co-op, but one person have to use mouse and keyboard and the other controller. Finally, the keys can be rebindable.
Graphics are pretty good, nicely drawn pixel art. Characters you play and the enemies have more details put on them than the levels. I wish for more visual variation of the levels, because they are kinda bland. They differentiate moslty by color – orange, red, blue etc. What I really like here is the minor details. When you kill an enemy he doesn't disappear, he stay dead on the ground or when you dig you throw dirt everywhere and so on. Those little details contribute for making the levels looking like a real battlefield and a little bit less bland.
The gameplay is pretty simple. It's a top-down shooter without any complicated mechanics. You can jump into action right away. There is a tutorial if you feel like going through one. In the beginning you can choose between two characters – Jimmy and Pinkyy. They have different stats. I choose Pinky and her primary weapon is … giant fists. She hit slowly, but do tons of damage. It feel so good to one-hit enemies. Pinkyy is like a tank with giant fists. Shortly after the beginning you will find your first weapon – a shotgun. It's highly inaccurate at long range, but at close is a beast. You can carry only two weapons. As much as the fists are good, soon you have to ditch them, because in later levels is required a certain distance from enemies. Also with the RMB you aim with laser sight. This also shows you the range of effectiveness of the weapon. You move slower, but the guns are more accurate. As you progress through the levels you will get a lot of different weapons – SMG, machine gun, pistol, sniper rifle and so on. You get them from dead enemies or they are just put on a box somewhere in the level. You have three types of ammo – light, medium and heavy, which you collect throughout the levels. The best weapons, like the sniper rifle which is my favourite, are using heavy ammo.
Except health, you also have a shield, which regenerate, and a stamina bar. You can dash or run.
Inside a level beside weapons and ammo, you can also find big and small med packs, overshield and bomb, which is super shield.
Since you are relic hunter you will dig for them. Each consists of three parts. Before moving to the next level sometimes a horse will tell you that he detected part of one somewhere in the area, so you go and search for it. And you better do it. The benefit of finding all parts of a relic is that they give you buffs, like more health. Also you can buy them. After every third level there is a shop with three items. They can be part of relic, a weapon, ammo, health etc. The cash for them you get from collecting pink stars after enemy is dead. They are your bounty.
The rogue-lite part is when you die you get back to your space ship and start all over again. There also you can equip the things you unlock – weapons, relics, ammo etc or change your character, choose a stage and play endless mode. You can even buy the stage you want to start.
Speaking of levels, they are okay and have some destructible envoirment and don't overstay their welcome. There blue boxes and pipe-looking bushes, that can be used as a cover, but the can be blasted to pieces. Spread around the levels are ammo, bombs, health and shields. When you defeat all enemies you'd better search the level for all those thing I mentioned, because it's vital for your survival.
Sound design is great. The music is really good. Some are fast and like the heart-pumping action, other have more jazzy feel. Yeah, chip tune jazz. I like it. As a whole it's awesome. Sound effects are great too. The shotgun have this meaty and powerful sound, pistols sound weaker as a pistol should be, sniper rifle feels like it's going to rip off you arm and so on. Great work.
The game is fantastic! There is no doubt about that. It have great gameplay, soundtrack, a lot of stuff to unlock and the only negative I have is the campaing is too short (only 12 levels), but I can counter that. There is an endless mode. One more thing. The game is open source, so you can create mods easily. Go now and get it. I highly recommend it.

This is a quick, yet fun romp through the brutal and bloody world of a master melee combatant in the form of a roman legionary.  Very impressive on the graphical front despite its age, the gameplay is also solid and - dare I say the cliche - deceptively simple.
While the game does have quite a bit of allowance (I completed it on the normal difficulty setting in 5 hours), it really shines when you're playing it well.  It has the seemingly now common fighting mechanic that you see across the Batman games and Sleeping Dogs, where timing matters quite a bit and things play out like a very hectic and bloody Simon Says.
The name of the game is executions.  Being able to switch out execution bonuses on the fly and reading your opponents is what makes this eye candy shine.
Five hours might make you think "What is this crap!?!" - but you'd be wrong.  CoD4: MW was over in the same amount of time, and in both these games the time is just enough to get the message done.  The fighting is intense, rarely lets up, and gives you enough freedom that a second playthrough for myself is already on the horizon.
I have yet to play multiplayer, but if it's any good as the single player at the visceral level, then I can't wait!
About the only negative I can give is that the ending... oh... I can figure why it was done the way it was done, but why?  I hope this is not common thing that goes on.

There’s been just one game that I finished in a single sitting, and that’s Metal Gear Solid IV: Guns of the Patriots on PS3. This fact is more a testament to the design of MGS IV than my unwavering commitment to the franchise. Let’s be clear: I’m not a Metal Gear Solid or Hideo Kojima fan boy. The reason it kept me hooked was the ebb and flow of the missions as well as even distribution of gameplay sections and long cut scenes (some long enough for you to consume entire meals while watching them like a TV show). But primarily it was the accessibility. MGS IV was a walk in the park compared to Ground Zeroes.
You’re probably aware of the biggest complaint people seem to have with Ground Zeroes. The game can be ‘beaten’ in around 20 minutes. If you’re looking to simply finish Ground Zeroes, it can be done with minimal to no effort at all, but bear in mind that you shouldn’t be playing it in the first place if that was your intention.
Ground Zeroes is a showcase. It is Kojima Productions experiment to craft an open-world with a difference—not one merely filled with side quests and characters to interact with, but one of an enormous scale in which you are free to explore everything without having to suspend disbelief. And by God, have they succeeded. It’s just a shame they’re asking you to pay $19.99/`1,200 for the recently released PC version. And while this is the definitive version of the game thanks to native 4K support and inclusion of bonus content from both Xbox and PlayStation versions, one can’t help but wonder if Kojima-san wanted to give away this game for free, and was promptly overruled by the evil corporate overlords at Konami who sniffed a revenue opportunity.
After a trademark intro cut scene, you find yourself in the shoes of Big Boss with the task of extracting certain prisoners of war from an island prison. Do this successfully and you’ll open up extra missions and situations, as well as bonus objectives. For the completionist, Ground Zeroes is a wet dream, with different ways not just to beat missions but traverse the excellently designed sandbox of Camp Omega and discover something new every time you do it.
There’s a tonne of stuff here for fans (who have probably bought this anyway), but for those on the fence, there are several reasons to pick up Ground Zeroes. First, it’s the most complete stealth action game available today. None of the mechanics are watered down, it is intuitive but not accessible, and it’s mostly unforgiving to careless play. Guards may follow certain patrol routes, but they will surprise you with their intelligence and unpredictability on occasion. Get caught, and you’ll have once chance to headshot your potential captor—miss your chance and you’ll be in a spot of bother to say the least. MGS has been guilty of limiting gameplay scope, preferring to go down the cool-but-linear party tricks route, ‘meta’ gameplay and easter eggs. Ground Zeroes is the exact opposite, with a strong gameplay basis and true open-world mechanics.
However, you’re likely to get the most out of this only if you’re a hard-core MGS fan or find Splinter Cell too easy. For the rest, there are games out there with ten times the content Ground Zeroes offers, and with more variety (Far Cry 4, for instance). Without a doubt, I enjoyed Ground Zeroes, as I’m sure anybody who plays it will. But the game also makes you wonder at the type of company that charges ₹1306 for a demo.

When people ask what kind of game Space Rangers is and I answer RPG, they typically respond with a slightly bewildered look.
No, it's not an action game. It's not a top-down space strategy game. Gun slots = weapon slots. Shielding = chest armor. Ship hull = (hybrid) defense stats and inventory space. Destroyed ships drop loot or the galactic equivalent of gold coins. You get quests from NPCs. You sell stuff you've found for stuff you want.
It's a classic RPG hidden beneath a facade of galactic space-faring. And it's better off for it.

Being a 4X strategy, Civilization is the first thing that pops in your mind when looking at Endless Legend. I've postponed this game for long, ignoring my friends' good opinions. In retrospective, I couldn't be more wrong with this one.
As the third (if I get it right) installment in the Endless universe, Endless Legend is lacking in more that one place. Tech tree in the late game is dull: it's essentially nothing more that bigger numbers. Numerous places lack polish - for example, you can merge "anonymous" privateer armies and armies openly carrying your banners without any restrictions. Balance is out there somewhere, but its existance is questioned, and rightfully so. Diplomacy, while good, still leaves more to wish for (a mod for freely trading cities, an illogical worsening of relations when you greatly outnumber your competitors in military - just to name a few). Uncompleteable quests (like asking to bring a settler from Cultists). No sea combat means that any water is a "safe zone" where you can easily hide from an outnumbering foe (or vice versa). It is a flawed game, and the devs have a long way to go.
Yet at the same time it's a great game, nevermind the obvious (or less obvious) flaws. The lore is what made me cry from joy like a teenage girl. Where else can you find valorous knights with vampiric powers? The whole nation of hikikomori basement dwellers? A transgender hero?
Quests are strong with this one. Aside from typical fetch and kill, there are more unique ones, like "conquer that region", which becomes a real challenge (especially if that region belongs to your old ally). You need resources? There is more than one solution. Search the ruins. Conquer resource-rich regions. Make more money and buy on a market with floating prices. Trade with your neighbours. Complete quests offering resource rewards.
Every nation is unique and has a unique questline, making gameplay completely different. Cultists have only one city and, as such, only one region, but every converted village brings them a piece of region's resources. Vaulters can drop reinforcements across half of the continent into the besieged city. Broken Lords easily buy out settlers, population and buildings, expanding at lightspeed.
There are many more things to mention. Battle tactics, the relief that does have significance. I've standed severely outnumbered in a narrow mountain pass, 300 vaulter crossbowmen versus cavalry armada - and won. I've stormed cities with privateer armies and plundered rare resources, not being able to buy them. You are no god, and not all of your commands can be executed as the situation on the battlefield is fluid, but that's only realistic.
I like to describe Endless Legend as "Civilization meets Disciples", but in truth, roleplaying system is akin to many strategy/RPG crossbreeds out there, while still being unique. You can make a combat hero, or a city governor hero. Or a little of both. You can get your troops reequipped, making archers more mobile or changing cavalry focus from ranged slayers to infantry slayers. Every hero class has its features, and heroes from different nations also differ.
And then there's Winter. Winter is coming, and it can be either your greatest foe... or the most valuable ally.
Endless Legend is that long-welcome taste of something new. And while it is not perfect, it honestly strives to be good, and it's quite successful at that.

Endless Legend is not just another 4x game or Civilization (V) rip off. In fact it is a beautiful piece of art that, as oppose to other Games, does not only offer a more challenging gameplay, but thanks to the soundtrack and story, an outstanding atmosphere.
While playing Endless Legend you do not only feel the 'need' to win, but to survive. Auriga is dying and you can feel it the more you play it, the more time you spend on the planet and the more winters you outlive. The whole game is being underlined by an excellent soundtrack that perfectly fits into the world where you have to solve quests which might award you with huge advantages towards the other races and change a combats outcome. Speaking of which, it is a bit different to fight your enemies. It is somewhere in between the battles of the Civilization series and Age of Wonders as you have a hero with an army that you can move through the map, but while you are in combat these units are taking their positions on it instead of dragging you into a completely different map. It makes the battles more tactical than in Civilization, but not as overdrawn as in Age of Wonders.
The units' design fits perfectly into each faction and they can be modified with new weapons while you explore new technologies, but it does not change their appearance and the units are usually limited to 4 different kinds per race. Every faction offers a unique gameplay. They have various motives (which are usually comprehensible), storylines and therefore individual quests. The heroes of each race have, instead of the ordinary units, different artworks and some of them might only be obtained by finishing quests.
The game itself is getting a bit more difficult the more winters you survive as they keep on lasting longer, dropping your production and limiting your units' movement. It is especially outlined by different and beautiful terrains that also offer variant gains. The games' design may remind some players of Endless Space and might confuse you at the first look, but as you spend more time playing it, you learn more things about the resources, units, and advantages as well as disadvantages that come along with every tactical choise you make.
Overall this game adds a surprisingly refreshing gameplay which stands out from other 4x games with its charm, beauty, tempo and atmosphere, but cannot completely satisfy with its battles and poor number of units and their slight customization. I would definitely recommend this game to every 4x or strategy games fan.

For my 300th review, I have decided to write about two of my favorite topics on Steam. The Warhammer franchise and successful PC overhauls of indie mobile games. Warhammer 40,000: Space Wolf represents a successful mix of both, since it’s as much of a competent simulation of the (simplified) W40K tabletop mechanics, as it is an excellent PC port of a popular game that has been downloaded and played by a large playerbase. I may not play mobile games, yet I keep an eye out for any ports that make their way onto Steam.
Any free-to-play game that has been around mobile platforms for many years already (2014 for iOS and 2015 for Android), makes you both wonder what they improved on PCs and creates expectations which really need to be met and perhaps exceeded. Fortunately for us, developer HeroCraft has both 15 years of experience and three dozen releases so far. A small selection of their projects, have been ported on Steam and I already reviewed Strategy & Tactics: Wargame Collection and Tempest: Pirate Action RPG, so I knew what to expect from this dev team.
It was about time for the Space Wolves chapter of the Space Marines, to stand proud in the spotlight. Why should only the Blood Ravens (Dawn of War), Ultramarines (W40K: Space Marine) and Dark Angels (Space Hulk) get portrayed in video game series focusing solely on their chapters? The Wolves of Fenris, the 6th Legion deserve a title with their own exploits. Warhammer 40,000: Space Wolf is naturally, going to focus on the eponymous Space Marines and their ongoing struggle against Chaos Marines and their ragged followers. As always, this involves some sort of an uphill battle in terms of both difficulty and complexity. Outnumbered, but never outgunned. The Space Marine way.
The Space Wolf Strike Cruiser carrying many of the chapter’s finest warriors gets ambushed over Kanak’s orbit and forced to crash land. The planet is a deadly mix of dense jungles and volcanoes so it’s no surprise that you’d find Chaos fanatics in such an inhospitable environment. What the Space Wolves didn’t expect however, is the presence of the elite Word Bearers Chaos legion. A traitorous Space Marine chapter which betrayed the Emperor of Mankind during the Horus Heresy. And if it’s one thing the Adeptus Astartes hate more than Xenos, then that must surely be heresy itself. The lore is out there, online. Easy to find and quite enjoyable for any Sci-Fi fan. I won’t spoil or detail anymore on the plotline. Have fun discovering it by yourselves.
Same as its mobile counterparts, the Steam version of Warhammer 40,000: Space Wolf is powered by the Unity Engine. The similarities fortunately end there, since I doubt that any smartphone could run the game at 4K resolution and stable 60fps. Not in 2017, anyway. It looked decent on the Android terminals, from what I could gather by watching YouTube gameplay vids of it. But it certainly can’t hold a candle to the Steam version, ran maxed out. If your PC can handle it, by all means the graphical details won’t disappoint in the slightest. Everything from the flames, object diversity, particle effects and even textures, all confirmed to me that Steam gamers won’t get a weak sauce port but an actual overhaul.
The soundtrack and sound effects were adequate, but I felt the absence of voice acting even if there isn’t a lot of interaction between NPCs or the Space Wolf squad mates. There weren’t any typos in the speech subtitles, so at least the story is conveyed in a proper manner. A few lines of spoken dialogue can have a huge impact on the players’ impression though.
Been a while since I last played a turn based stategy title (Total War doesn’t count, since the battles are in real time) and Warhammer 40,000: Space Wolf manages to combine TBS with card elements which ring closer to the tabletop originals, but without the dice rolls of course. What doesn’t get lost in “translation”, is the chess-like feeling and that strategic satisfaction of beating your opponent against all odds. There won’t be a single campaign mission during which Valgard Twice-Slain and his loyal Space Wolves aren’t being outnumbered and swarmed by Forces of Chaos from multiple sides.
The SP rewards after each completed mission, are not going to change based on the difficulty setting. That is an inspired choice and I can assure you that you’ll get quite a challenge even if you play on Easy. You’ll find it pretty hard, ironically. Perhaps that simulates even better, the true odds of success and survival which accompany a Space Marine throughout his life. Local Kanak barbarians may be little more than target practice, but that can’t also be said of the Word Bearers which can take a beating and possess a vast arsenal of their own.
Speaking of the weaponry and tactics, that’s where the decks of cards show their importance. Survival on Warhammer 40,000: Space Wolf’s battlefields shall count on the player’s wise choice and use of these cards which are tied to certain armor sets that can be picked before starting a mission or multiplayer match. To simplify matters, I’ll refer to them as “Light Armor” and Sniper profile, “Medium Armor” and a well balanced profile and “Heavy Armor” being the Close Combat specialist. What’s a Warhammer game without giving players the option to bash some Xenos or Heretic skulls into oblivion?
Unlocking more powerful cards for your custom decks, involves completing secondary objectives which in turn unlock booster packs and crate forging. If it sounds like a microtransaction hell, do not worry. The Steam version is being sold instead of opting for the F2P route for a good reason. What you see is what you play and paying extra does not enter this equation at all. The boosters & crates are gained by spending renewable in-game points which never beg you for your credit card details. It’s fairly easy to unlock some better cards just by being a skilled player and also by participating in the PvP matches which pit three-man squads against each other, in a balanced fight that emphasizes on deck strength and tactics.
Could the game have been better? It’s still in Early Access so chances are, that it will improve far more by the time it leaves this stage. As it presents itself right now, it is fully enjoyable provided you learned the ropes. By failing, perhaps. There are many lessons to be learned even from personal failures, never forget that. The story is worth it in equal measure to the gameplay. More in-game sounds would provide extra convincing, but their absence isn’t much of a tragedy. The grinding is, and by increasing the valuable card drop rate, this minor nuisance can become a thing of the past. Time will tell, but you can jump right in Warhammer 40,000: Space Wolf and not regret it.

An obscure classic from russian developers that never got that much traction outside due to almost non-existing advertisement.
The game is centered around living as the Ranger, one of the more or less independent vagabonds loosely employed by union of races in order to combat a threat of extreme magnitude. Most of the game is spent in a 2D top-down world that utilizes turn-based system that is usually working as a real-time, until you need to change your commands to something else. The world is extremely lively and probably one of the best simulations out there on the market. NPC are diverse in their goals, participate in combat and trading. In general, the world is living and breathing without much care for the actions of the player.
With that said, the game is anything but simplistic. Player is provided with variety of activities and while some of them are pretty basic (like trading), the sheer diversity is more than enough to compensate. It features one of the best text-based quests I've seen in games in a form of mini-game, somewhat fun real time arcade style combat inside wormholes, a full fledged RTS ground battles mini-game (sadly, with rather exploitive enemy AI). It is perfectly possible to gather a lot of money and experience without participating in the combat. For the most part.
After all, the threat of Dominators, enemies in this particular game, is ever present. With the addition of Pirates as the third faction. The map is regularly changing, with star systems getting preyed upon or liberated constantly. The tug of war is very well simulated, to the point where its perfectly possible for the Dominators to actually achieve full victory over opposing races on higher difficulties, if the player is either too passive or too unlucky. Similarly, the Pirates and Military don't wait for the players explicit desire to fight a battle. They mount regular assaults, in which you can participate, but they certainly aren't going to wait for your arrival. The uphill battle is very well demonstrated at the beginning, with Dominators possessing extremely potent weapons and ships, with even smallest ones suparssing most of the ships available to the player and Military. Only down the road the research pushes boundaries of current weapons and ships, ultimately giving you a pretty substantial chance of engaging even a small enemy fleets on your own. That is if you're not lucky to pick up a miraculously intact Dominator weapon from one of the ships that was brought down by combined effort.
All in all, this game should be quite enjoyable for those seeking complexity and longevity in a seemingly simplistic package. The game has plenty of downsides, but so does something like Mount & Blade. At such a low price point, it is definitely something worth trying out, if you like what you see in the videos.

This is still to this day the king of the character action/spectacle brawler genre. The trifecta would go as dmc3, bayonetta and Ninja Gaiden Black. To this day no other action game has the complexity and freedom that this game provides in its more or less 20 missions. This is no "dial-a-combo" action game, you're free to create your own combos as you wish, just remember that with that freedom comes the weight of complexity as it is no easy game. The skill ceiling goes through the roof, just look at any MAD combo on YouTube. The good thing is that this game is constantly challenging and if you're willing to put the work it will grow with you abilities. There's a lot of difficulty modes which you unlock by beating the game in the difficulty that comes before it and with each new difficulty comes new challenges, a more aggressive AI and even a mode where you cannot get hit. Seriously...this amount of depth has not yet been rivaled by any game in the genre.
TL;DR : if you like action games, tough bosses, depth in your combat mechanics, freedom to play as you want, a difficulty that has a pretty high ceiling but eases you up into it this is the game for you. Be aware that you have to be willing to pull off the mods to make it work correctly and also be aware that this game asks a lot from you as s gamer. If you're up to the challenge and you're willing to put in the time this is s sure recommendation. Just like crossfit or a pretty long book, this isn't for everybody but if you're up for the challenge I assure you you'll love it.

Whole concept kinda reminds of hitman games: you got big locations, you got NPCs with certain algorithms, you task is learn these algorithms and make your way through them to your target. There are events that will happen without of intervention of players, but certain small things are requing you to do something - for example, certain NPC's won't appear until you will reach certain point of area. Maybe it was designed like that for some reason, maybe it's an engine limitations.
Now, AI. It's fine. Sometimes soldiers can be dumb, sometimes they can do something clever. Unlike Peace Walker ones, these guys can detect you much more easily, which is good. Alert system is same derp as it was in PW - combat mode enables not when soldier calls to HQ, but when he screams "CONTACT!!1". They can only call reinforcements through HQ, alert by itself is almost instant. At least this system effectively punishes player for being spotted, unlike old games where skilled player can take down guard before he will be able call to HQ.
Another innovation is a helicopter that you can call through your iDroid or by throwing flare grenade. There are few landing spots, two of them located outside of military base and the other two are inside of it. Two zones inside are good for quick evacuation, but of course landing there will trigger an alert(it's kinda cool how it's triggered towards chopper, you still can be undetected lol), soldiers will try to take down chopper with RPGs and Anti-Air Emplacements(which you can destroy before calling the helicopter). If you are entered alert mode, helicopter will be detected even from "safe" landing spots. You can extract prisoners\soldiers and yourslef through helicopter(another option is leaving a base through "end of the mission zones). Basically this helicopter replaces Fulton Recovery system from Peace Walker and recalls a truck from Portable Ops. Too bad that Fulton will return in Phantom Pain.
CQC got better compared to Peace Walker - CQC chain isn't that OP as before and there is no OP roll from previous titles(it had long range and knocked down enemies, you could even stun them like that lol). Also now you can just mash R2 button and watch how Snake wrecks poor soldier. You still can grab from both back and front, which is bad, it makes grabs too easy.
The most weird addition to gameplay is sprint - you can dash by pressing L3, which also makes more noise. BUT. Dash is endless. There is no stamina bar, you can run like that till end of times. Also you can dash when carrying someone and dash animation goes through carryed person. They must fix it by making dash limited and remove dash ability when carrying someone.
Health regen is another bad addition to the game - it would be much more fun to search for rations and medical supplies than just hiding in the corner and waiting until ketchup will dissapear from your screen. At least it doesn't makes you invisible as it was in demonstration of the game long time ago. Also you can be critically injured, it makes screen blurry and colors it in red tint and you can hear sound from previous MG games that indicates that you are low on health. In this state you can be oneshoted by anything and it won't go off until you will heal yourself through using spray, which healing animation takes a while. This crititcal state balances health regen a bit.
Now lets talk about our equipment. We got iDroid device that allows to listen to the cassete tapes which contains dialogues, important information, or just some music. Also you can watch map and set marks in it. Second we have binoculars, that are allowing to zoom picture and look around. It also allows to listen to the guard's dialogues or another sounds from certain place. Our starting gear is rifle with flashlight silencer and OP tranq pistol with silencer, I hate that thing since MGS3, at least it had bad accuracy because of laser sight in MGS2 and was rare as hell in Portable Ops. There are few weapons that you can pick up from soldiers or from certain places, such as rocket launcher and sniper rifle(thanks god that this one not equipped with silencer and tranq rounds). You also have empty magazine to
distract enemies, few types of greandes, knife(which is usable only in grab) and NV goggles.
Graphics are fine. Facial animation is very good. PC version optimization is godlike.
Worth buying.

MGS V: GZ is great action-stealth game with a lot of replayability despite the short length of the main story mission.
The gameplay is a mix of stealth and action in a single, wide-open area. All of the missions take place in that same, single area. You can approach the main mission as well as the 7 side/extra missions with either a stealth or guns-blazing mentality. The ranking that you receive at the end of completing the missions favors complete stealth with no killing, so you'll find the game the most rewarding if sneaking games are your thing. Certain missions really deter a purely action-forward style by introducing infinite guards when you are discovered. I found that a mix of 80% stealth/20% action was the most exciting: sneak on the way into the base and then let some bullets fly on your escape for a cinematic finish. Rocket launch a wooden guard tower on the flight out, sending the guard inside 30 ft. into the air for extra Rambo points.
FAQ:
Is the game really only 90 minutes?
Yes and no. The main story mission will probably take you around 90 minutes on Normal difficulty on your first time through. However, if you like stealth games like Hitman and enjoy completing the challenges/achievements in them, you'll find a great value in Ground Zeroes. I spent around 30 hours getting a 100% completion rate, which mean that I got S-rank on all 8 missions, both Normal and Hard, and collected all the cassette tapes and XOF patches hidden around the base. I'd say the only lame achievements were the XOF patch and cassette collecting. You pretty much need to have your nightvision goggles on 24/7 and eagle eyes in order to spot them all. You can interrogate guards to find locations of them too but it's just a dumb, archaic gaming trope to have to "collect" items. It was okay in 1996 with Mario 64 but it's been nearly 20 years since then.
Is it a good MGS game?
Yes. It's the most fun I've had with MGS since MGS3. MGS4 was a complete dumpster fire of a game. It's refreshing to see this initial chapter of MGS5 prove that Kojima still knows how to create a real game instead of the awful anime-movie-game that was MGS4. To be fair, the one noticeable thing that Ground Zeroes is missing is a proper boss battle, but that's kind of a good sign in a way too: that Kojima doesn't feel completely chained to the experience of the previous games in the series and really wants to make MGS5 the best game possible.
Recommended to those who enjoy action/stealth games and replay them religiously until they know every enemy's position in the level by heart.

Great game for history lovers! Victoria II allows players to tweak history in their own way, without going overboard like it can in games like Empire: Total War.
When playing the game, it catches two aspects that you need to notice. There is the political side of the game, and the military side of the game. Honestly, the combat in Victoria II is actually harder than the politics, as the AI is actually quite realistic for the general and nation, and will try and use strategies like blockading your ports so your troops can evacuate, all the way to trying to get other nations to let them through their land to ambush you.
The game follows the entire Victorian era, as in its name, to the years of Adolf Hitler's rise of power in Germany. It begins in 1836 (I believe), and will end in 1935. The player can choose if they'd like to speed up or slow down time, as it simulates everday as well. The game could take a few hours, depending on how you want to play it. The first game I played on Victoria II took me about two or three hours, as the United Kingdom, only because I was rushing through everything.
For a beginning player, I'd suggest playing as either a country that isn't threatened by outsiders that much, for example, Tripoli will be facing an Ottoman invasion as soon as you start the game, and generally, Tripoli barely has an army. Then, there is the United Kingdom. It starts out as the number one greatest power, and has colonies all over the world, such as Canada, Australia, South Africa, India, and so on. Although it isn't that easy for a beginner to successfully manage all of those dominions, it is really hard, if not impossible, to lose as the United Kingdom, even if you try. As the UK, even if you decide to release all your colonies as dominions and satellites, you'll probably still be number one by 1935, if not 2nd.
Overall, the game is so fun and addicting! I don't necessarily think it is worth twenty dollars. With games such as Europa Universalis IV and Hearts of Iron IV, Victoria II isn't as realistic and clean as them. I'd say it is a 15 dollar game at most, and you should only get it when it is being discounted. I mean, I got this game when it was on sale for 5 bucks. So, I hope this review helped you out! Thanks!

I do recommend this game, but I have reservations as well. Something I've noticed in my 900+ hours is how weak tactics are translated back to us. For example - when I first started playing, I was seeing the most absurd behaviour from my players; daft goalkeeping errors including "hilarious" own goals, ridiculous backpasses, stupid defensive howlers, players running head-first into opposition defenders to sloppily concede possession, incredible open-net misses, endlessly hitting the woodwork.. the list goes on. It actually feels very unfair; I would much prefer weak tactics to be blatantly obvious so that the uninitiated might clearly understand what needs fixed (or at least why it is going wrong). Sadly all you get as feedback is a load of old nonsense, the kinda things that real-world footballers just would NOT do, certainly not with such startling regularity.
But rcently, since starting to use strong [proven] tactics, I've been seeing a very different game. Beautiful and organic "pass and move" football, regular screamers, up-and-coming youngsters terrorising defences with eery precociousness while I scream in delight (and pat myself in the back for having the balls to name that 17yr old against Chelsea like I never doubted his ability). I've won a few Bundesliga titles, Premier League, FIFA World Cup, UEFA European Championship, UEFA Champions League, Serie A TIM... the list goes on. I am absolutely loving it.
So when you get your tactics right, be prepared to be enthralled with FM17. Get them wrong however, and you will be banging your head against your desk in brain-melting frustration.
DO NOT MAKE PROMISES. If a contract negotiation lists any promises, simply use the "remove and exclude from negotiations" option for each one. The player nor the agent will care and will still accept the contract. If you add the promises (especially "strengthen the coaching team/defence/midfield/attack") you will fail no matter what. Players never notice even when you massively strengthen the area you promised them, and will come back to you complaining that you broke your promise. This can affect the entire squad and WILL ruin your game.
AI Managers are idiots. They never make long-term plans for any club, and will just sign players almost arbitrarily, use up all available budget, put the club into debt if they can, and get the sack when it starts to go wrong. Also - I've never seen Jurgen Klopp or Pep Guardiola last more than a season with Liverpool or City respectively, in more than 20 saves.
One little quirk about FM that I've also noticed - players ALWAYS seem to score against their old clubs, whether that is against your club, or one of your players when you play his old club. I take advantage of this by intentionally playing players against their old clubs and it never fails to deliver; (as an example) I've had Danny Ings score 4 in a single match against Burnley and then not another goal all season until we play them again and he gets a hatrick.
Players also seem to score their first goal for their club/of the season/ever against you. All goal droughts are ended when a human-controlled team comes to town. It happens too often to be coincidence. FM loves drama.
PROS:
Stupidly addictive. Sometimes I forget to feed my kids.
A massive game with a mind-bending amount of players, staff, and teams to manage.
Extremely rewarding when you get tactics right.
It's the only football management game worth playing at the minute.
CONS:
Stupidly addictive. My kids are hungry.
Players promises don't work and will ruin your game. You have been warned!
Assistant manager in-match advice is akin to a parrot on your shoulder.
Game feels very harsh and unfairly balanced if your tactics are weak.
Far too much repetitive media.
AI managers are stupid.

The saving grace is the quality most notably the dazzling graphics from the new FOX engine. The graphics look better than some of today's CGI 3D animated feature films.
The "objective" of this "game" to me is that in 2008 MGS4 was released and now in 2014 MGS5:GZ is released so that Kojima has something to show for what he has been doing for 6 years. It is a trailer video game to showcase the new FOX engine. Some would say this game is a glorified demo.
Should people have to pay for it? No. The proper thing to do with this "game" is to give it out as a reward for fan loyalty. Charging people for this game leads people to wonder if this is just a cash grab. Sure seems like it.

Quick development from stage to stage of gaming.
Very good sense of humor throughout.

A few good challenges throughout. No spoilers, but a couple of the achievements take a decent amount of time the first playthrough, especially without using guides.
Cons:
Not that much replay value if you do a full achievement playthrough the first time, unless you're just speedrunning it for personal fun.
One of the bosses

For English speakers, it may take some time to get used to the accent marks. A world where Middle Eastern, Mesoamerican, and Indian cultures combine is very literal.
However, the first third plays like any of the other numerous Choice of Games. You work your way through childhood studying your preferred stat, and make the rest of the choices based on the stat. Some interesting path diversions occur with the Gods. The first choice, which God do you worship, has the most effect on your plot. Choose wisely, because it has the most effect on how you play (well). Because of the differences in the way each God is handled, roleplayers will be able to do multiple runs. Single-run players are advised to consider their preferences. Gods are simple creatures, and about as broad-minded as Balkoth.
The middle third plays like Choice of the Broadsides or Sabres of the Infinity. There's a war. You can't get out of it. The best route to take is to play to your chosen strength (read stat) and God. You can lose. On a positive note, the game provides some options for recovery. Not every loss or death need be permanent.
The last third is Indiana Jones. You go splunking with your cohorts, meet a few demons, and steal artifacts. It is a dramatic change from the first two sections. There is more character-building. Many of the characters in the first two sections are non-descript, and if you saved/helped them, you aren't sure why you helped them. The last third helps explain.
The game is nice, if short. If you're bored, hankering for a choose your adventure, and you need a jungle adventure/diplomacy checker/big plain battle, it works. It has some good descriptions about costumery, customs, and jewelery that fill out the world. The various Gods provide good replay.
But, it isn't a very good introduction to this play-style. If you've never played a choose your own adventure, this isn't the first one you should pick up. Accent marks can be wearying. Stat specialists are encouraged. The entry into the world, ie. the first question, is very dependent on knowing the world. You can pick up some, read some, restart some, but maybe not enough.
My advice for beginners or intermediary CYOA players is to wait. Play one of the medieval, napoleonic, or oriental adventures. If you like the other game and need more, this game is good.

Victoria II is a grand strategy game by Paradox, a development studio with a fetish for grand strategy based in historical settings. After clocking in 109 hours, I feel confident in calling it one of my favorite games.
The historical period, the gameplay mechanics of running an economy and managing politics and waging war is very well done, the design, the music, it's all superb!
However, there are complaints to be had.
Firstly, the Infamy syatem. It's actually a good system, working similary to World Tension in HoI4 or Coalitions in EU4. Infamy is gained by several actions, such as having war goals discovered by the international community, removing nations from your sphere, certain event options, etc. The issue with the system is that once your Infamy reaches 25.00, a coalition WILL come after you. I feel that the limit for that should be 50 or 40, perhaps 35. This would allow for a much more active experience in the game.
Secondly, DLC. Vic2 is one of those games where the DLC is a MUST. So, you'd have to purchase not only Vic2, but A House Divided and Heart of Darkness for the full experience. I got the full Vic2 bundle while it was on sale, but I cannot deny that the DLCs' necessity and price is an issue (a prevalent issue with most, if not all, Paradox titles).
Aside from those two grievences, the game is highly entertaining and intellectually stimulating. If you like grand strategy...
Why are you reading this? Go get it already. Stop reading and buy Victoria II. NOW, I SAY!

Nauts was a fantastic game. The community has good and bad seeds and good and bad players. I, for one, can say I've made a ton of friends that I regularly talk to in Steam even if not playing a game together.

I HATE rage quitters, but what is the incentive to even stay in matches if you're guaranteed to lose?
Worse, why didn't Ronimo listen to the community? Who infleunced this misguided ship?
If you want a mass exodus, by all means -- keep the game the same; If you want to create competition and engagement -- change it. If you're trying to stop turtling, perhaps nauts who refuse to leave their turret for 60 seconds start taking a 'Death DoT'. If, XP is your bread and butter, then remove all damage dealing skills and make everything about building characters to different utility functions.
Better yet, bring 2.12 back and create an XP system in Nauts 2 that you have time to test and understand without public outcry. We did not want this. I have sadly, uninstalled the game. Best of luck Ronimo.

While the game does have the Roman setting going for it as well as stunning visuals it's brought down by several factors.
Ryse is as linear as linear can be, and it'll only take you about 6 hours to complete in Recruit difficulty (which is the easiest). This is a shame because, while I would not have gone for a true open-world game, I would've appreciated more (any, really) leeway to explore in similar fashion to the Assassin's Creed games.
Combat is very limited. You have but a handful of different attacks at your disposal that you must use against the same enemies (little variety here as well) over and over again (horde mode, basically) before you're prompted to enter QTE finisher-mode, which is also fairly repetitive. Indications in combat that are easy to interpret while holding a controller can be a bit confusing while playing with M+K and I found that the default key bindings weren't the most suitable. Consequently, you'll probably find yourself getting hit a lot. Your only long-range weapon, the pilum, is not particularly easy nor convenient to use since it takes a while to aim and fire (and your character gets riddled with arrows in the meantime) so I forewent its use as much as I could. I did have a fun time using the Testudo formation to charge the enemy from time to time. There are also the required turret sections with your character firing the scorpio at the enemy lines.
There is very little in the way of customization, certainly nothing in the way of cosmetic customization so you won't be changing Marius' armour or weapons any time soon. What you do have is the ability to upgrade your health, gain XP a bit faster, or increase the points you get from combos, among others. It's serviceable enough but it also speaks to wasted potential as it could have been tied to unlocking different moves throughout the game, in a similar way to Remember Me.
The story is very reminiscent of Gladiator with the theme of revenge throughout but throws some mythology into the mix and I quite enjoyed it. Unfortunately, the protagonist does squander several opportunities to enrich the narrative simply by showing curiosity. Nonetheless, I thought voice acting was top notch throughout and across characters and, like I mentioned before, the visuals, both in gameplay and cutscenes, are stunning, joining forces with the soundtrack to strengthen this familiar, yet enjoyable, odyssey of vengeance.
In short, Ryse: Son of Rome feels exactly like what it was meant to be, a prototype to showcase the visual power of the next generation of consoles. However, I am confident a Ryse sequel could be so much more provided the developers focus on strengthening other areas of the game, mainly combat, exploration, and customization. As it stands, Ryse is a good way to pass the time and a sure recommendation so long as it's on sale. At its full price it's a more difficult recommendation to make but hopefully I've given you enough elements to decide whether or not it's worth both your money and time.
PS: Since Steam won't let me publish this review without recommending it either way I'll go ahead and select the, 'Yes' option but, please, do ignore that thumbs up/thumbs down thingy.

I bought this for about 10€ and then finished the campaign in one day. I'd say that was a positive experience.
Gameplay-wise I'd say it's playing in the same league as God of War and Batman Arkham [something]. There are some interesting extras like marching in formation and ordering your men around, but for the most part you time your attacks and get progressively more angry when you want to roll but Marius just stumbles around in slow motion.
I had more fun with Batman's combat system.
The battles against Boudica feel solid though and deciding what your victories should do (health, focus, XP or damage) while fighting makes for a surprisingly good tactical element.
The constant quick-time events however feel kinda lame. Pressing the correct button quickly requires a lot of focus, but zero skill. Seems like someone wanted to give the combat system some extra flair in order to distinguish it from other titles, but it just doesn't feel right.
Also why do combat games focus so much on "executions" these days? It always makes me feel like the game thinks I'm some kind of pervert. And while we're at it, don't get me started about the portrayal of women in this game (which will only make sense to 15 year old boys) or the lame attempts at showing some humanity lost in a parade of execution porn scenes.
So basically it's playable but very mediocre.
"Mediocre" isn't a term I'd use for the graphics though. "Spectacular" is more like it. If you have a fast GPU, looking at the amazing pictures this game generates will be at least half the fun, if not all of it.
To someone who has been playing videogames since the early 90s, this is simply mind-blowing. I was going to write something like "ten years ago, this would have been seriously impressive even as a pre-rendered movie", but to be honest... I don't even know what's left to point out as some "real-time artifact" that would have been better if it had been done in a raytracer. Maybe some of the self-shadows on certain objects under certain conditions... but other than that, it's flawless.
I remember how every console generation meant a paradigm shift in terms of graphics. That kind of shifting has become less and less, but leave it to Crytek to blow your mind once in a while. I think the paradigm shift of the current generation is the disappearance of visual artifacts. Not photorealism (though we're getting there), but it's like aliasing is disappearing completely, you can forget that things are made out of polygons, textures aren't blurry and repetitive anymore, global illumination is actually a thing now, and fancy techniques like ambient occlusion and motion blur don't leave ugly artifacts (like those weird halos in Crysis) but do their part to make the scene pop.
If you are into high-end real-time computer graphics, you'll want to see this game. That's the part I'm actually recommending. The gameplay and the story seem a bit like neglected step-children, but neither is overly pretentious or promising things it cannot deliver. If you like the first few minutes and don't mind doing the same thing for 9-10 more hours with changing (but gorgeous) scenery, you'll like it.

(Firstly there may be one or two errors, I have copied and pasted my FM16 review, with a quick skim through of edits. (Yes, I have taken a Sports Interactive approach to reviewing)
This review is based on being a FM/CM player for over 20 years and someone who only ever plays the full mode, not classic or touch.
Firstly the big thumbs down is based on two reasons.
One: A huge part of managment is the time between games, the training part of real managment is huge. Who is doing well, who isnt putting the effort in, who is fighting for a first team place. What bonds are being formed between the players ect. FM 17: Nothing.
Two: Boardrooms. I only manage big clubs and big clubs in FM17 doesnt even slightly resemble the big clubs I read about in the papers or see on television.. There is no living world above the manager in FM17, just a bland, highly basic, simplistic UI that makes you feel like you are a manger of a non league club with pretty much total control.
This year we have a simulated Brexit. Really?! Its like someone thought this up while they were sat on sofa infront of the news last year. All the things FM lacks and they put in a brexit. Honestly the direction this game has gone in the last few years is just baffaling.
On the Sports Interactive FM forums there is a huge wishlist thread with over 6000 replies. Pick any random page and there are countless wishes for in-depth training, media pressure, player interaction, ME improvments, Board improvements. With the exception of the ME there has been no noticeable improvement in any of these over the last three years.
The game is all to easy to create all conquering teams that win trophies year after year. In real life how many managers stay at the same club and keep constantly winning trophies? Obviously Sir Alex Ferguson and a few others, but it should be hard, really hard to do.
Its just to easy in FM. How many young players who are deemed wonderkids in real life go on to actually become superstars? Not that many, a handful from each generation. Not so in FM, buy a wonderkid, play wonderkid, watch wonderkid fulfill potential. On the other hand, want to pluck a kid from the french second division who no one really rates and watch him suprise everyone (ala Marhez of Leicester), no chance. The constrictive CA/PA system wont allow that until a FM researcher updates it for you. The problem with this system is that Marhez is now a world beater because of one good season, in FM18 he will probably be mearly good, but in a save game which runs muliple years we have a situation where Marhez was awful in FM15/16, amazing in 17, yet neither is a true refelection of the dynamic evolution of a player which has peaks and troughs. Its a system that is showing its age and each player is a snapshot of a FM researchers opinion at a moment in time, but a snapshot that will be set in stone throughout a save game. They may have served the series well, but many of the systems FM17 incorporates are basic and easy to control because they havent moved forward in the last few years.
Football Manager really hasnt moved forward with the times. 15 to 20 years ago a lot of managers did run the club from top to bottom but these days top, top clubs arent run like that. FM does a really poor job of reflecting this, sure there is the token Director of football, the token head of development, but again very simplistic, basic systems that just doesnt reflect top level football in 2017. Managing a top club in FM17 feels more like a quaint throwback to the 90s than an actual reflection of what fooball has become in the last 15 years. Adding a pretty basic social media UI isnt going to modernise anything in a meaningful way.
3 years ago I thought FM was about where it should be. Now its coming across stale and out of ideas. Going by the wishlist thread in their own forums theres 100s of great ideas, but for whatever reason SI has entered the change UI, tag on some light weight features and sell for full price approach. Its sad to see. I will still play it, but every year its getting harder to justify paying £35 for a game that isnt moving forward and is no longer reflecting the sport I watch and read about. I will still rack up the hours, but more because there is no other game to buy than what SI have developed.
The FM series needs a huge shake up. Whoever is choosing the directon of the game, what new features are going in ect needs to be moved on. Every year real life football grows, the juggernaught keeps getting bigger and expanding. Every year that goes by where we have new features like create a club and fantasy draft is another year where FM loses ground on the sport its trying to represent. Its sad that the people in control of the games direction have completely lost sight of what gave the game its cult following. It got the basics of the football world right and let the players imagination fill in the gaps and build from there. The basics of the FM world dont feel right anymore. Without that basic foundation the imagination has no support, FM needs imagination to work or it is just a game and FM was never just a game.

This game was the first video game I really got into on the PC. I played countless hours, and if I had to make a guess, I'd say well over 2000+. Since September 2004, this game has stayed within my top 5 because it is simply just that good.

Now I don't play this game as much, but I still find myself going back to it, whenever a friend wants to play.
.
. Stronghold Crusader includes many different medieval units that you'd probably expect: Swordsman, Archers, Crossbowman, Knights on Horseback, Spearman, etc. But it includes many more like engineers, pikeman, macemen, horse archers, slaves, fire throwers... There are two types of troops: Arabic, or Crusader troops. Both similiar, yet both with their strengths and weaknesses. Some AI lords will use only Crusader troops, or only Arabic troops, while some will use a mixture of them both,
Like I said before the AI can be pretty challenging. Of course, there are very, very stupid AI as well that you could beat no problem if you knew the very basics. But the Wolf, and Saladin are very challenging opponents that can take you hours to beat depending on the style of game you play. The campaign(s) are very challenging to beat and they offer you as little as possible to win...but you do get 3 chickens (passes) and once you beat a level you have already passed on, you get a chicken back.
This game can be played with up to 8 players/AI lords. It can be free for all, 1v1, 4v4, 2v2v2v2, 5v3 or any combination of teams you want. Online or offline. Play with friends and players around the world easily on a program called GameRanger. It works well for me and my sister.
The gameplay is a lot of fun, and not too complicated to understand. You have peasants that stay idle and are useless unless you provide jobs for them. Once you create say a woodcutters hut using the resources from your stockpile a peasant will walk his way to the hut and become a woodcutter. He will chop down the closest trees and deliver wood to your stockpile. You also need other resources like stone, iron, weapons, and most importantly, food. Without food, your peasants and workers will not want to stay at your castle, so they will leave. Make sure to keep the happiness/popularity above 50. Food, negative taxes, Ale/Inn, and large troop count will all be bonuses to popularity. If your king dies you lose. If all enemy kings are dead, you win :)
To train troops, you need to use your resources to build buildings to produce troops. You can go 3 routes: Crusader troops, Arabic troops, or both. Barracks will be required to produce crusader troops. But crusader troops require weapons to be made so you need to make weapon workshops. Arabic troops need a mercenary post and hence the name cost more gold, but they do not require the time, money and resources for workshops to create weapons. Engineers, a more advanced unit, needs an Engineers guild to produce them. They can be helpful by taking castle walls down using catapults.
There is also a free build mode, map editor, and custom scenario mode which offer even more fun with tha already addicting campaign, sandbox, and multiplayer modes.
I highly recommend this game, and definitely if it is on sale. If you're debating over any other Stronghold game go for this one!
