You start out in an 8-bit, 2D, black-and-white, side-scroller world where you can only move to the right, but as you open chests you unlock more and more aspects to the game until it becomes a full-fledged original Zelda clone and even beyond into the realms of Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy. There's a lot of references in the game to other games, including monsters from Super Mario and a smal section dedicated to Diablo. The game has some pretty great humor surrounding all of these references too (be sure to read the description of the Diablo items when you play). All-in-all, I had a blast playing it and it wasn't very long overall, but it was totally worth my $10. Highly recommended!

It's a really great concept. It's awesome to start the game in black and white and slowly unlock all the upgrades that came and went in RPGs. For the most part, it also has a great sense of humor. You'll LOL as you see it implement loading screens when it goes 3D and enjoy the many references to classics like Final Fantasy, Zelda and Dragon Quest. The Zelda segments, however, drag on WAY to long, if you ask me. With very few puzzles or deep mechanics, this game feels a good hour or two too long. Most dungeons are simply a walk and press attack romp and the turn based battles require no strategy at all. I'd wait till this puppy was on sale if I were you, but if you enjoyed the 8-bit and 16-bit RPG era as much as I did, you'll be glad you played this.
PROS:
Awesome Concept
Nostalgia Overload
Cons:
Too Much Filler
Zero Replay Value

Ryse: Son of Rome is a 3rd person action game filled with all types of roman mythology and brutal/bloody combat. I am a sucker for anything based in roman mythology and Ryse: Son of Rome is filled to the brim with it. Along with the great lore/backstory of the game the main story that you follow throughout the game is also great. The gameplay is very fun and seems to be perfectly balanced between combat, QT events, and story filled cutscenes. The multi-player co-op seems to be done well and is tons of fun. The game is an obvious port from the xbone, but it is done well. I didn’t have any major performance issue with my pc set-up. (This can be found on my profile) The keyboard controls work great, but I would suggest using a controller to get the recommended experience. (It was made originally just for xbone) The combat does get a bit repetitive about halfway through the games story, but the story kept me involved. The only other thing to keep in mind is that there is microtransactions, but these are not very intrusive.







Ryse: Son of Rome is an interesting 3rd person action game with brutal combat and amazing cinematic scenes. If you are purely into amazingly polish and complicated fighting games you may want to look in another place. That being said I loved every second of this game from the incredible cinematic scenes to the fun online co-op.

Like Passing Pineview Forest, which I played the other day, The Secret of Pineview Forest is a short(ish) preview of a game to come, in this case the second game in the Pineview series, which is raising money right now.  I haven't played the main attraction, Pineview Drive, yet - bad LinustheBold! /smack - but these two atmospheric dark spooky woods tastes make me want to spend time exploring it sooner rather than later.
This gamelet is more impressive and, I think, less successful than the earlier one.  It starts with a backstory excuse to run with - car crash, road blocked off on either side by dangerous downed electric wires and that elusive species of game-tree that can't be climbed over, with a dark guardrail behind that also doesn't allow jumping or climbing.  Which is here nor there.  Ahead is the menacing forest, which is where you must go.  In the dark.  With, of course, monsters.
And that forest is, as they say these days, Yuge.  I spent quite a while searching for the first relevant area - I followed a leaping buck into the dark, walked along the hilly zone walls, and generally wandered about until I finally found the eventual house.  And then promptly got lost once I was out again; I'm like that in dark computery fields.  Eventually I made my way to the lonely light quietly illuminating a chained fence, and entered the second area.  And then the third, which is *really* big, or seemed that way.
I wish this game had a save; games that force a player to sit through single-session play irritate me.  I understand that it's not that long, but it is an hour's trip, substantially more if you don't immediately find your path (there is no path) or if you miss a bit of inventory or need to backtrack for whatever reason.  It's a late-night game, and what if I get tired?  I have to start over.   In my case I didn't understand immediately that the Use key (E) was different from the mouse click, and yes that's obvious in its own way and I figured it out eventually, but if there was a tooltip about that I missed it and I was wandering back and forth for like an hour looking for something that didn't exist to open something so I could move on, and man, NO SAVE.
Anyway, eventually I worked it out, and shortly after that the game was over.
I like games that give me an interesting, atmospheric landscape to investigate.  I never met the monster here, or in the earlier game either - I'm a hushy sort of explorer, given to moving quietly and stopping when there are strange sounds nearby.  The sounds were effective and I enjoyed the music, which was constant but not narrative or intrusive.  Most of the locations I found - I probably missed a couple of landmarks - were purely atmospheric, which is fine.  I was surprised that none of the mill doors opened, but this is a taste and not a full game.  I enjoyed the walking in the woods, though the plot didn't engage very often and the ending was puzzling and abrupt.
In short: the selling point here is the creepy walk-in-the-dark part, and there's a lot of that.  The story is a little thin.  I played with the gamma at its natural dark setting, because I'm not sure why anyone would play a game about walking in the dark with their screen adjusted so it looks like they're walking on a cloudy day.  The game challenges us to Solve the Mystery of Pineview Forest, and I'm pretty certain I didn't do that - though I did manage to get from my starting crashed car into an interior location where I saw a brief bit of something before the credits ran.  The end was a little jarring; but that night in the woods was pretty cool.  I had fun.
Also, don't be a nerf like me.  There's an object to pick up right where you start.  Pick it up, precisely the way I didn't on my first start.

Back in the day I stumbled across Space Rangers 2, played it, and totally loved it. Only after that I played Space Rangers 1, both of which I have on steam. And yeah, the older Space Ranger parts were once on steam, but for some reason they've been taken down from sales. That is if you already bought them you can still install and play them from steam.
Strictly speaking Space Rangers HD is a remake of Space Rangers 2. It started out rather similar, but with time I feel that HD has really become a new game. There is a HUGE lot of more content than in Space Rangers 2.
Pros:
-Intricate and tactical space combat
-Massively varied hulls and equipment
-The general difficulty, primarily space combat, ranges from easy (the galaxy will eventually mostly fix itself) to nightmare (the galaxy is totally doomed unless you are constantly there to protect it)
-The difficulty can also be adjusted very precisely
-The galaxy is truly alive, and nothing centers around you, unless you get the power to make it so, but even then life will always go on, whether you're there to witness it or not
-Great and emotionally immersing music (this is obviously subjective, I've also seen reviews that claim the music is subpar, something I'd never agree on)
-The addition of planetary battles, black hole arcade battles and text quests makes the Space Rangers universe feel much more complete and immersive, and you're mostly not forced into either of them
-The devs are still active some 2 years after the game has been released and it is very polished, I guess I don't have to mention that this can't be taken for granted nowadays
-Interesting story and you're not forced to approach it in one single way, do whatever you feel you have to do
Cons:
-Planetary battle difficulties range from almost impossible to lose to almost impossible to win, some of the maps are so hard I don't see any casual gamer ever winning them (not without like 24 hours of practice and/or guides at least), and here you have no say in the difficulty of the maps you get, except for taking more resistant bots or more reinforcements on hard maps, which reduces your rewards
-The AI behaves mostly intelligent and acceptable, but there are some exceptions, military ships will sometimes pick their targets so badly they can't even kill one enemy before dying, and your robots in ground battles are in constant danger of committing suicide if you're not there to prevent it
-The devs thought that having ships simply shoot and destroy wares in space is a good way of keeping sectors clean, so you see something really valuable in the system, you're on your way and you see a civilian ship flying by? You can almost certainly expect it to shoot down your loot, the same counts for military ships when you fight dominators, always keep a save handy in case some of the military ships decide it's important to shoot down your most valuable drops (ships will start shooting wares after there are 7 objects in the system... which happens very fast because even the passing asteroids will easily litter 7 mineral pieces into the system)
I might've descibed the negative points in details, but don't let that fool you, the pros vastly outnumber the cons. Is it worth getting this game? If you like turn based space RPGs the answer is: Hell YES!

This is a really fantastic game. It's bit on the grindy side since you'll have to replay stages to get better items, but it's never bad to the point of intruding on fun. There's a surprising amount of item variety in even the early stages and surviving the later stages will demand that you know all of the mechanics inside and out.
The presentation is OK. I'm not a fan of the lineless, unpolished style but there's some semblance of an art direction here. The music has a cool atmospheric feel, going after chaotic mish-mashes of waveforms rather than catchy melodies. The framing of the story works and has a nice blend of nostalgia and original ideas to it. It's all very silly and does a good job with setting the tone for the game.
If there's one big complaint to be had, the controls feel really unpolished. The way you move and collide with objects feels more like a Game Maker prototype than a finished product. And that's a shame, because having tight "game feel" is  really important in top-down shooters like these.
Overall, I'd give the game an 8/10. Relic Hunters Zero is a thoroughly difficult and satisfying experience that's free to boot. Try it out!

Endless Legend is perhaps one of the strongest 4X games released in recent years with solid mechanics that owe something to, shall we say, crosspollination with other greats of the genre. It succeeds at something that Civilization: Beyond Earth tried with only mixed success; it features factions that are both mechanically and narratively different. In fact a large plurality of the  factions have radiaclly different mechanics behind them and feel distinct to play. Even those that adhere to their standard FIDS gameplay have a gimmick beyond simple stat boosts that make them feel more than a reskin of another faction.
The caveat though is that the game has a long-standing bug that prevents you from playing in anything less than 1280x720 resolution. They do point it out in the game requirements but just a heads up if you manage to miss it. The bug literally cuts off chunks of the screen which can make the game difficult to play. If you use a television or a monitor that does not do high resolutions that well, be advised that this can affect your enjoyment of the game.

I really want to like this game.  I've tried multiple times to feel engaged in my cities, armies, or anything in the game at all, and I can never do it.  This game lacks soul.  My first major issue is the non-immersive combat system.  They gain literally nothing by not letting you directly control units like most strategy games.  I feel like I'm watching combat more than I'm playing.
Another issue is the fact the quest system is a thing.  Just... no.  There is no need to have a quest system in a 4x game.  There is even less reason to have it if it's unimmersive as hell.  I just find it annoying and tedious.
Lastly, as I've mentioned, the game has no soul.  The units and races are REALLY COOL, but they don't engage you nearly as much as other fantasy 4x games.  The heroes can't really do much that's special, there aren't enough unique racial units, and they all play roughly the same.
TL:DR:  Awesome concept, lacks depth and soul.  Feels like I'm playing a spectator game.

Sure, it's not a perfect game, but it's exactly what I've been waiting for. I played ARK for hours and hours and ended up feeling like the whole thing was pretty pointless. All the servers were filled with RPers, and even the PvP servers were mostly passive. In this mode, though, it's an all-out brawl.
Pros:
Fast-paced. No more waiting around for nine hours to tame one stupid Trike. And you get tons of resources from harvesting.
Skill matters. I'm constantly outplayed by people who know their way around the game, exactly how to aim, where to go to avoid being pursued, that sort of thing.
Quick matches. I only lasted to the end of a match once, and it was still only like 40 minutes. Most of the time I'm terrible enough to lose in the first 20.
Cons:
Buggy. Nothing that would make me not want to play, but I usually have to restart the client after a match, or it won't let me join a lobby. I've crashed to desktop during a match once.
Laggy. Again, nothing serious, but it happens from time to time. It helps to filter by server region, something that's not enabled by default.
Intensive. I have a nice PC with a very good GPU, and I have to put everything on Medium to maintain a stable 60fps. It's nothing like other people are saying, though. Just knock down your settings and you'll be fine.
Wait times. I don't know why there's no "Start" button when a lobby is full. I've seen the timer tick down from 5 minutes only to have half the lobby leave when it reaches a minute because they're impatient.
Overall, very nice for an Early Access title. And, because it's free, there's really no reason not to play. It's a lot of fun.

Note that I have never played any of the other Space Ranger games before I played this on Steam.
A truly remarkable game with many options and choices, deep and interesting mechanics and simulation with a very unique gear system. Every other coalition/pirate ship out there follows similar rules as you. Think they are being overpowered? You can do that, too! Their hull, their equipment... it is all highly varied and customizable.
In short, you start out a nobody in a galaxy with tier 1-2 gear available. You run some measly errands or try to make a profit with goods until your equipment is up to par with the latest tier currently available (increases over time up to 8, one of the wonderful things of this game) after which you can start picking fights. Note that on higher difficulties progression is VERY hard, with the coalition losing ground rapidly (because all Rangers lack the experience/gear to fight Dominators effectively until around tier 5+). The few negative complaints I have seen mostly revolve around either the lack of information when starting out (read the tips at the bottom bar!) or because they cannot win alone against 5+ ships following similar rules as yourself (doh!). But the fun part is, that there is almost always more to discover, some mechanic you did not know about, some option you did not try... Just remember the game auto-saves every time you leave a planet/station, and you can load this (bottom save) when you screw up and get your ship blown up. You know, for all those times you think you can take on that wretched pirate that tries to rob you ;)
Despite some minor issues with English, I'd still give this game the full 10/10.
Especially since it's relatively cheap, but then you don't exactly get the latest in graphics either.

Ah, so I see the Pineview Drive people have been hard at work again.
"Who?" you ask. Well, back in 2014 they released a game called - you guessed it - Pineview Drive, and not long after, a standalone mini-game called Passing Pineview Forest. Just like the mini-game you are currently holding in your grubby little virtual hands, perusing the box and wondering whether or not it's worth the download, the "teaser" in question was free, and pretty impressive for that fact. The considerably longer and substantially more pricey full-length game it was designed to promote was also quite impressive, though it did suffer from a distinct lack of narrative focus and a world so "open" that you frankly didn't know where the ♥♥♥♥ you were meant to GO half the time.
Fast-forward to 2016, and here we are with another "where-the-♥♥♥♥-am-I-now" simulator, providing the first taste of a new Pineview Drive product about to be released. I admittedly enjoyed this one more than the last appetiser, not least of all because it was considerably easier and I managed to get all the way through the ♥♥♥♥er (Passing Pineview was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-and-a-half, believe me). So how does this stack up as a "game" in its own right, and what does this all suggest about the Rising Storm we are being promised sometime in the near future?
Well, as glorified "tech demos" go, this is certainly a good'un. Technically, in particular, it's impressive as all buggery: vivid visuals, evocative sound...very atmospheric stuff indeed. Sure, there was one odd landing/stairs situation where you had to jump from the top step to the landing barely a foot above for no apparent reason, but other than that it was pretty flawless and certainly had nothing resembling a game-breaking bug. For anyone who regularly plays indie horror games released on Steam, you'll know that this in its own right is borderline ♥♥♥♥ing miraculous. So far, so promising.
So what about "story" then, I hear you ask? Erm...um...I-I don't think there was one, in all honesty. The game tells you that you're supposed to uncover the "secret" of Pineview Drive, and at the end all I got was...well, a suggestion that there is more to come, perhaps. I'll be kind and leave it at that. It's by-and-largely a "walking simulator" without much sense of direction or purpose, but it's certainly quite an immersive and suspenseful wander, even if said suspense never quite pays off (there's mention on the Store page of an "IT" accosting you if you don't watch yourself, yet I somehow managed to never incur the wrath of said "IT" on even a single occasion that I was aware of).
All in all, it's pretty darned good value for zero buckeroonies, but probably only worth your time if you're someone who - like me - enjoys an immersively spooky atmosphere without much to actually "do". As for the upcoming Pineview Drive sequel, I'm definitely keen, but may not be in a rush to spend twenty bucks on it like I did the first game. So if the devs happen to be reading, my review for the first game fared pretty well and I'm now writing for a dedicated horror gaming site as well as for Steam, so...that's two guaranteed reviews for the price of a single freebie should you be feeling so generous, hint hint.
And before all you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥go thumbing me down for that last remark, have a look at how many reviews I've written, and know that I paid for the vast majority of those games. I have no shame. I'm happy to take the occasional hand-out, just like everyone else. Maybe I need to get me one of those YouTube channels, those ♥♥♥♥ers seem to get free stuff left, right, and centre, with nary a complaint in sight. I'M A ♥♥♥♥ING PAUPER, DAMN YOU ALL!!! Is the occasional free game in exchange for a review (and not a guaranteed positive one, at that) too much to ask?

I don't get the hate towards all these simulator games, they are actually pretty fun, but I suppose it is one's like this that turn people off towards all simulators. I love these crazy sim games, and I love forklifts. This game is decent and it is fun... for the most part. It is not 2014 video game era material. It is unpolished, unoptimized, and slightly buggy.
Pros:
1. A good forklift sim. Plenty of different forklifts and I want to say they are realistic but I've never actually driven a forklift. The controls are good on the forklifts themselves.
2. Good selection of levels. Five different levels gives you a decent selection and for the most part they are well designed. However, the one's I played there were a few bugs in them that were quite annoying, like the map was way wrong.
That pretty much does it for pros.
Cons:
1. Horrible grammar. I know this was made by I believe Germans but still, some text is unreadable.
2. No tutorial. Seriously, all sims need a tutorial.
3. Controls. You cannot remap your controls and honestly that is my biggest con of the whole game. It would be fine if the controls were mapped to a different spot but where they are at now is completely counter-productive. My mouse is perfect for forklift controls but I can't map them. Also there isn't even a control layout on the settings page, I had to press every key on my keyboard to find out the controls until I pressed F1 and it brought up all the controls.
4. Poor graphics. Overall they are not terrible but these little things make it bad. No driver for your forklifts, no collisions with the people walking around, and even though I have an old laptop it run's pretty bad, even worse for some levels and points of view.
Overall 5/10. I like games like this and honestly I had been waiting for this exact game. I have Forklift Sim 2009 and I'm not sure it is by the same people but this one is a lot better. Still there is work to be done and I think a lot of the issues could be easily fixed. But, as I've read in the community hub, this developer doesn't actually finish their games, which is very sad because these games have so much potential. When you look at Euro Truck Sim 2, it could easily be a shoddy, unfinished game but instead it has modding, seamless controls, amazing graphics, and a great fanbase. This one could be like that but the developers don't want to and it is very sad to see.

Sometimes with free games you get what you pay for.  "Only If" is an ugly mess.  Stay well away.
Not all indie puzzle games are created equal.  "Only If" aims at the cleverness of The Stanley Parable or the better games of the escape-the-room genre, but it comes nowhere near its mark.  The audio is actively unpleasant - particularly the unseen puppetmaster, trying out his hackiest De Niro impression - and the script shows a 14-year-old's delight in profanity with no particular emotional resonance to justify it.
Puzzles are random and arbitrary; you solve them not by building skill in playing the game and understanding its philosophy but rather by using a ouija board to divine the undercooked whims of the developer.  Failure rarely yields feedback on what you did wrong.  Success merely brings relief from the puzzle, with no sense of accomplishment.  It goes without saying that none of this is well-paced, attractively framed, or set within a story worth caring about.

TL;DR below.
I'm writing this review before having finished the game because I find the negative reviews disproportionate considering this is free to play. Firstly, do not play this if you're unwilling to deal with a little confusion, frustration and uncertainty in order to progress an insantly immersive and brilliantly acted narrative. The mechanics are far from perfect but conceptually there's some really interesting stuff going on here, and it's free! This game is a good example of how mechanics should be working towards having significance to a game's story, i.e. typing when your protagonist loses his voice. There is no hand-holding here, which personally I appreciate; on the other hand arguably it fails to be intuitive enough to compensate and it's possible to find yourself at dead ends, having to restart a level because you're not telepathic.
That being said, this is a mostly well executed experiment and well worth your time because, once again, it's free!
TL;DR
+ Visually impressive
+ Instantly immersive
+ Variety of environments
+ Mechanics have legitimate role in narrative
+ (I cannot stress this enough) For a low-budget indie title - excellent voice acting
+ 2 gameplay paths & sufficiently lengthy for a free title (so + replay value)
+ Little hand holding (hints are present but can be missed)
+ ATMOSPHERE: game manages to be both existentially musing and a little gratuitious (of its time) without being pretentious
- Minor bugs
- Mechanics and therefore objective not always intuitive
Pretty fun if you can find someone else to play with.

Awesomenauts is a MOBA, but fun.
The fact that this game is 2D could be seen as limiting, compared to other MOBAs - but LoL or DotA are not 3D either, since you can't jump in those games. The 2D universe makes for a very action paced game, it feels very active compared to a normal top-viewing moba.
The way the upgrade system works in Awesomenauts is different, and in my opinion, superior to other Mobas. Take DotA, for example, where you can level up skills (simply making them better), and buy items with gold that add little effects.
The skill upgrades in Awesomenauts actually change the way you play a lot. You can instantly feel the power of a single upgrade, be it slowing power or attack speed. In DotA, this all felt very underwhelming to me, but in Awesomenauts the upgrades are very apparent.
Now, like every other game, Awesomenauts is not perfect.
The way lag is handled in this game has always been a controversial subject. Many people claim that lagging is actually an advantage for the player, since in Awesomenauts there is no central server, and every player is responsible for caluclating its own position. When a player is lagging, you will often see the player skipping frames, making its movement very hard to predict. This is a very big deal in a 2D game like this.
But, I don't expect Awesomenauts to have servers like Valve does, and I too recognize that Awesomenauts is not as big or competitive as other games are. I find the community to be very pleasant, the general chat was a very good implementation.
In conclusion, for the price I picked it up (1 euro in the sale(!)), and the scale of Ronimo, this is a very good and fun game. It's a good game to just boot up when you want to have some fun, and not experience the pressure to perform other mobas have. I would give this game a 9/10.

This game is a prologue to what is clearly going to be the next of Hideo Kojima's masterpieces. It is the new Pièce de résistance of the Metal Gear series.
You'll see complaints about the length of this game. To clarify, the main mission in this game averages around an hour and forty minutes long. There are also numerous side missions to complete, which bump the playtime up to an average of six hours long.
To complete the game 100%, that is collecting all cassette tapes, getting all accolades in-game, rescuing everybody you're supposed to, and getting the best rank you can in the game, unlocking absolutely everything there is to unlock, you're looking at an average of at least 16 and a half hours of game-play out of this game.
To reiterate, if you play it just for the main mission and put it down after that, you're going to be disappointed. The intent with the release of this product was for fans of the series to try out the new game, get performance statistics over a wide series of systems, and see how the community responded to major changes in how the game operated.
Choose your own destiny. Are you going to play this as a four minute speed-run of just one mission, or are you going to actually completely play the game and enjoy every last bit of what you paid for?
Performance is excellent. You can tell that the Fox engine has been given tons of love with a multiplatform focus being the centric point behind it. Running a GeForce 660, I'm able to achieve 60FPS constantly in all situations with all settings maxxed (with the exception of SSAO being on high as opposed to very high.)
The controls are excellent, keyboard and mouse users will not be disappointed - you can rebind any key to where you want. Yes, I know it sounds ridiculous for me to even have to say that, but you'd be surprised with the massive number of shoddy console ports that have left this most basic function out. There are also a number of default controller layouts available for users whom are using standardized gamepads.
Likewise, one of the most common complaints people have about the controls is the usage of arrow keys while in the menus - however they are not necessary. Somehow, everybody has overlooked the big prompts that say "1" and "3" in the menus, which should typically be enough to tell people that instead of relying on arrow keys to move the menus left and right, you can just use the "1" and "3" keys to scroll left and right respectively.
Story - 10/10. Yes, it's short, but this is intended as a prologue for the main game. The cassette tapes which can be found in all the missions provide more tastes of the story, making you desire for more.

Also, despite it's short length, it's got a lot of emotional deepness, hidden in the tapes (which you can find during your missions, though you already own some), with Hideo being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and playing with your feelings "like a damn fiddle". You first grow to detest Paz, but then you *might(was the case for me)* pity her fate, and even have sympathy for her. And then you got Skull Face. Okay, how can we put it? Take Volgin, keep the sadomasochist part, amplify it, remove his easy-to-annoy personality, add intelligence, cleverness, and make of him a cold-hearded ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You'll end up getting a character that is 100 times nastier and worse than Volgin.
To put it short, buy this damn game. Loads of replayability (28 hours at the time I made this review, trying to get 100%). It's deep. It's very fun as well ( many Easter Eggs and missions extras that helps to get the sad and serious ambient a bit loose). Also helps explain why Snake goes apparently evil in The Phantom Pain. Finally, it's only 20 USD. Combine a random Steam discount and it's left at $15 or $10 (I got it at $13,30 on the day of it's release). Another fantastic game from Hideo Kojima.

Ground Zeroes has been accused of being a paid demo, a single mission shipped to simply hype MGS5's eventual release. However, I found it to much more than that; My most recent MGS game being 4 at it's release in 2008, I felt quite rusty going into this. Ground Zeroes is a good warm-up for MGS5, consisting of six missions that take place in the same ficticious Cuban military base, Camp Omega. The "Ground Zeroes" mission is the meat of the story, involving the rescue of two minors on opposite sides of the base that were apparently major characters from Peace Walker. Interspersed cutscenes and collectible cassette tapes flesh out the character's back stories and their experiences on the base. The extra missions provide vastly different approaches and playstyles to infiltrating (or assaulting) the base, ranging from a helicopter ride providing covering fire to an assassination mission that fails easily if you are even spotted. After you finish each mission there's still plenty of unlocks and time trials for purists, along with the last two missions for waxing nostalgia.
Ground Zeroes helps to connect the events of Peace Walker with MGS5 and acts as a catalyst for the time jump been the two games. Overall, this probably won't win over any new fans but is a thoroughly fleshed out "VR Mission"-style side game that provides a solid intro to The Phantom Pain.

It's inevitable that when a game somehow catches your attention, you tend to read reviews about it. So when the big websites such as IGN and Gamespot rate this game between poor (4) and OK (6,8), you kinda get septic about spending money on it, regardless of the fact that you are into this sort of gender, you actually love epic/historic stuff, and it can't get more epic than the Roman empire. So you find yourself thinking "they can't all be wrong, can they?". Well.. they can!
Let me address some of those websites claims, starting with the good and redundant stuff:
There is no denying that Ryse: Son Of Rome is one of the best looking games to date. The art and animation elevated the standards not only during the gameplay but also during the simply amazing cutscenes and real time events (probably Tomb Raider or even good old Skyrim are the only ones that can get close to it, since I'm not counting the recently released Arkham Knight).
Although the story is somehow predictable as you begin to get closer to the ending chapters, the storytelling delivers in a way some major movie blockbusters don't.
Oh, and while I'm still at it, the voice acting and it's animation is simply flawless!
The gameplay is acceptable, and levels such as the one at the one in the Colosseum provides us tons of fun and enjoyable replay value without added things to go along.
So I'll move on to what most claim to be the flaws of this game.
Some say the repetitive combat rhythms are usually brainless, the lack of freedom is exasperating, the boss battles are repetitive and the violence is so commonplace it becomes boring. Guess what? I beg to differ!
Being a gamer since the Spectrum days, my gaming style keeps changing as years go by. Depending on the time and mood, I can be a "casual gamer", a "100% achievement guy", or even a "just the main campaign guy". Recently, I beat the 1st 3 chapters of the Arkham franchise, so I was kinda fed up with too much freedom, too much thinking, and games that take me 15+ hours to beat. Ryse, provided me just the daily fix I was needing: A game that shows me the way to go, that doesn't let me think to much, with a simple and fun combat system, with bosses you might not beat the 1st time, but you wont need more than 3 times to do so (Centurion/hard level).
Is this game a masterpiece? No, it can't compete with the likes of a Mass Effect and sure as hell wasn't built to do so! But in all honesty this game takes me back to good old "Streets Of Rage" days, where you could beat a game on the same day, and that keeps me coming for more, even after all these years! The last time I felt this was with The Bourne Conspiracy for Xbox 360.
Maybe, this is why gamers rate the game between OK (6,9) and good (7,1).
Conclusion: it is a good game, that I will beat again, this time around in 4K and legendary difficulty, just because!

The argument for gaming on a PC rather than a console is a pretty convincing one.
If you’ve got a modern gaming PC it will almost certainly bring more horsepower to the table than its console cousins, of course the down side to this is that a decent gaming PC is also likely to cost a lot more than a “Box of X” or a “Station of Play.”
This price of entry (amongst countless other things) contributes to the current dominance of the consoles.
When Little Johnny wants to start “gaming” with his friends, they’ll almost certainly have consoles, so naturally that’s what he’ll want too, which will likely set him on the path of console gamery for the rest of his playing days.
Of course the reason that all his friends have consoles in the first place could be due to the reluctance of “The bank of mom and dad” to fund the cost of a gaming PC when they can pick up a console for half the price.
As PC gamers, we know this is a short sighted view; you can’t upgrade the guts of your “Wee Station Play Box One”, its technology is static, everyday it becomes a little more obsolete until finally the lifecycle of the console comes to an end and “SoMicronysoft” want you to invest in their new box of tricks.
All the while the PC gamer can continue to stuff new hardware inside his box whenever he feels the need; every day is like a new console release day to a PC owner.
If you’re willing to take the plunge into PC gaming, you’re entering a world of higher frame rates, sharper graphics, continual upgradeability without the need to “throw it out and start again” and a modding community the consoles can only dream of.
If that isn’t enough, look up any recent multiplatform release and I’ll bet the PC version is cheaper than its console counterparts.
These are just some of the reasons why I’m a PC gamer and a proud member of the glorious PC gaming Master Race.
...but I do have a confession to make...
Despite everything I’ve written above, my PC gaming loyalty has been tested and I’m sorry to say I haven’t always been faithful.
I’ve flirted with the Playstation, I’ve spent long weekends with the Xbox, I even had a brief fling with Nintendo (we all make mistakes) but even when those console temptresses were leading me astray with their joy pads I always knew that the PC was the one I was meant to be with, you know, deep down...
Why am I making this confession to you now?
Well, my last act of PC gaming infidelity was the purchase of an Xbox One, It was just so tempting, all those Xbox exclusives whispering “play me now”
...I was weak.
One of those seductive titles happened to be “Ryse Son of Rome.”
Ryse was an Xbox One exclusive launch title and ironically, although being one of the main reasons I bought the console in the first place, was never a game I actually got around to playing.
That is an oversight I’m happy to correct now that the game has finally made its way across to the PC.
Console ports always make me nervous; we’ve all played rushed conversions which haven’t been optimised properly for the PC.
It can be heartbreaking to see a game running as smooth as butter on your friends console only to have it stutter and lag on your top end computer.
Thankfully Crytek have done a fine job of bringing Rise Son of Rome across to the PC along with some extra content, FPS improvements and enhanced resolution options that most PC gamers expect these days.
Despite the time that has passed following the release of Ryse on the Xbox, the game is still beautiful to behold, especially on the PC.
Sunlight glints off armour, blood sprays through the air and moody facial expressions are abound.
The locations are equally spectacular, from cliff top outposts to the glory of Rome itself, everything is achingly beautiful to look at.
All of which makes Ryse a great game to watch, but is it fun to play?
The combat in Ryse will remind you of the Batman titles, it’s mostly a block and counter affair.
It can be a lot of fun turning a sword aside with your shield and countering with a slicing strike that fells your enemy in a spray of blood.
This block and attack combat mechanic works well and is beautifully animated, which is just as well as you’re going to be seeing an awful lot of it through the 6-8 hours of play time on offer.
By the time you’re a few hours into the game the combat is going to start feeling a little repetitive, nothing new is really injected into the combat as you progress either which is a real shame, something a little different to break up constant doge, attack, dodge button mashing would have been very welcome.
The story itself is quite interesting , in a clichéd but beautifully presented kind of way.
Set during the time of Emperor Nero, you’ll find yourself on a quest for revenge.
A quest which mostly involves charging at the bad guys and killing them.
When the gory blood fest comes to an end you’ll be rewarded with a cut scene to move the story forward a little.
The cut-scenes themselves are well voiced and again superbly animated; there’s even a little interference by some Roman "Spirits"  to add a little supernatural spice to the tale which is always welcome.
The game is heavily influenced by movies like Gladiator, I half expected Russell Crowe to pop up in a cut scene and give his "Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife" vengeance speech.
My biggest concern with Ryse Son of Rome is that I'm not sure if you'll be motivated enough to finish playing it.
The game play quickly becomes repetitive and the story might not be strong enough to keep you hooked even though the game itself is fairly short.
If you stick with it you’ll be able to finish the 8 chapter single player campaign in a weekend.
There is a multiplayer mode to give it a little extra shelf life if that's your thing.
Whilst you can play Ryse with a mouse and keyboard I would recommend using a controller.
Clicking away with the mouse works perfectly well but this game was designed with the Xbox in mind and a joy pad feels like a much more natural way to control things.
Besides the blocking and attacking controls you can also shove enemies away which will make them temporarily drop their guard, you can also pull off "execution" moves by way of a simple colour coded quick time event during battle. This is a neat touch and leads to some pretty gruesome finishing moves.
Unfortunately, even these "special" moves begin to feel samey and repetitive as you progress through the game, the fact that most of the barbarians you'll face are cookie cutter enemies and you'll find yourself killing the same character model with the same button presses over and over again really doesn't help.
There's a constant deja vu feeling that the rinse and repeat combat mechanics create which only worsens the longer you play.
Having said all that, Ryse isn’t a bad game; my expectations were pretty high before playing which probably tainted my experience a little.
Despite its repetitive game play and it’s by the numbers plot there’s still plenty of entertainment to be found here.
The game does a good job of making you feel like a competent fighter as you slash and hack your way through an almost endless amount of Russell Crowe wannabies .
Visually the game is stunning, I know..... [snip]

[10 unique and valuable pro tips for beating crusader extreme below]
As someone who was addicted to strategy games around the time the original crusader game came out, I would heavily recommend this to people who either like age of empires, who would like to relive those days and to those people who like challenges. The game includes Crusader Extreme HD, with missions 'so difficult' (the first 14 missions took me 1-3 hours each, excluding some start-over missions because i failed) that you need to resort to a very defensive guerilla/ninja playing style to succeed. there's missions where u have to defeat more than 7 opponents on a single map, all by yourself. And everyone starts with the same resources.
After some restarted missions and succeeding (im about halfway now i guess, at mission 14) i found out a strategy that works out for 90% of the missions. If you want to figure this out yourself do not read on, i will not mention anything new. but for those who quit out of frustration heres how you can do it:
1. some missions involve defeating multiple opponents of which some are very closeby, even withing arrow range of your castle (you dont want that). use up all you money to build knights and send them in to kill the enemies close to you. in some missions, its possible to kill enemy lords before they have even built their castle.
2. NEVER forget to build a market in the beginning. not all maps offer all resource types within range or within castle building range, which means e.g. if theres only quarry near the keep, you will have to put as any quarry miines there as possible and sell some of it to buy stone/wood.
3. always start off building 3 more stockpile spaces (free), a market, 2-4 hovels depending on how much starting resources u have, and a combination of 5, 10 or 15 'good things' and a church (or 2, if u can),  and either a mercenary post or barracks + armory. buying weapons to recruit non-mercenary troops is usually cheaper. mercenary post recommended when u have a lot of starting money.
4. build a wall ASAP around your keep with enough space to put in all your buildings needed to recruit ttroops and keep the economy going. set mercenary slaves or regular troops like spearman and archers at work to dig a moat on the inner side of the wall, then build another wall that will actually function as your wall. the first wall is just to protect them from harm while digging. if youre skilled at timing things and monitoring progress, you won't need to but if you have plenty of starting cash in some missions then this is a safe method.
5. do not forget to build stairs at your walls. because it is not possible to build when enemies are close and then your guys wont be able to man the walls/towers you built.
6. if you build a keep, always build a bridge at it right away.
7. save up the rock volley to slowly kill off enemytroop spawn posts during missions. do not use it up for anything else unless you really really need it because you would lose your lord otherwise or enemy is about to breach walls.
8. enemy knights are the biggest problem when they attack early in the game. therefore, just buy leather armour and crossbows and build crossbow archers or when low on cash u will need sligshot mercs who have strengths in great numbers.
9. last but very important tip: if u wanna destroy an enemy castle, bring plenty of archers. like 50+ . and put them in a place where they can hit the enemies campfire where the peasants gather. set attack location instead of directly clicking a peasant cuz they will stop attacking when all peasants are down and hit other targets instead. this prevents them from building new troops while u are attacking, which was often the reason i lost all my troops cuz the enemy started building knights superfast and in the end i didnt have enough troops to get on top of the keep and kill the leader.
10. Try to build a perimiter wall ALL AROUND buildings that involve a production chain. if it's not possible, put a big waterpot near valuable locations and station some archers that can easily kill off slaves who want to lit up your mines for example.
i could give more tips, but these things i found out and used helped me through the first 14 missions fairly easy. you should figure the rest out for yourself through trial and error

The main reason I am not reccomending is for two reasons. The first is that pirates and the weapons Lirecron and Esogapher are completely OVERPOWERED. After spending 60 hours in game with the best ship possible I am still UNABLE to defeat them.
As things stand the only way to combat the pirate threat since you can't engage them yourself is to fund the construction of warships. In other words you need to take it upon yourself to construct the military fleets of the ENTIRE UNIVERSE since the creators of this game had the brilliant idea of creating weapons that can shut down all of your systems.
You've created the best defensive ship in the game? A few hits from the lirecron will shut down your shields and negate your cladding.
You've got the most offensively capable ship in the game? A few hits from the lirecron will shut down your weapons radar and scanner. You are now unable to shoot weapons.
Maybe you've got the fastest hull in the game. A few hits from the lirecron will shut down your engines leaving you dead in the water for pirates to prey upon.
In my current game pirates have taken over the vast majority of coalition systems and I am powerless to stop them despite having the best ship in the game
Who's IDIOT idea was it to give the pirates a weapon that negates every possible in game advantage. This is not even mentioning the Esophager which has similar negative effects.
Furthermore the additional content is fairly horrible. It consists of a few more text adventures and a few more hulls. The new text adventures are needlessly opaque. I was trying to take the direction that would allow me to get rid of the pirates but ended up becoming their leader and helping them win against the coalition.
Pirates are the most OP faction in existence for reasons mentioned earlier. In Space Rangers 2 reboot eventually you would be able to take out entire military fleets by yourself but the advent of the Lirecron makes that impossible.
The second reason I am not reccomending this game is that the creators have nerfed all end game content. Space Rangers 2 reboot had 3 beautiful unique ships obtainable in the end game. If you enable these ships in Space Rangers HD you are unable to get achievements.
Furthermore they have nerfed all end game content. Shield generators now have a maximum of around 50-55 percent whereas in Space Rangers Reboot you could have 87 percent. The default version of the game does not include the unique ships from reboot which are infinitely better than any of the new hulls.
The third reason I am not reccomending this game is that all of the problems that existed in Space Rangers Reboot exist in Space Rangers HD.
Repair costs are still way too high and nothing is done to negate this. With end game gear expect repairs to cost 300000 credits which is a small fortune. The only means of earning enough money in the end game to offset these costs are planetary battles which is a trial in and of itself. Every time I a planetary battle mission instead of seeing it as an opportunity to earn 10+ million credits I see it as an extreme annoyance especially since so many of the maps are poorly thought out.
Good micromodules like Universe and Shell are still impossible to get leaving intact the previous crappy system of getting micromodules. Furthermore the good micromodules like Panzer and Broing have been nerfed and instead of giving 16 cladding the Space Rangers HD equivalent of the panzer now gives only 8 cladding.
Good points:
There are some good points to Space Rangers HD. I like the idea of weapon modifications. Also some of the new gear is decent like nanobrolite engines or upgraded shield generators.
I like the new bertor dominators since dominators were ridiculously easy in space rangers reboot. Now they have adequate difficulty because of the new bertors.
However in spite of some steps forward the fact that Pirates are totally game breaking is a major leap back. There are three versions of this game. Space Rangers 2, Space Rangers 2 Reboot, and Space Rangers HD. The one I would recommend is Space Rangers Reboot.
Fixing this game so that it would be the best of the three is easy. Just get rid of the Lirecron and Esophager or give the player some means of defense against these weapons. As things stand pirates are way too OP. They can shut down all of your systems relatively easily and the coalition can't stand against them without regular investments in new military vessels. These issues NEED to be fixed.

A blast from the past of my own childhood. I loved the entire Space Ranger series as a whole and used to play it non-stop. I loved the game so much and I still love it to this very day.
The soundtrack is simply masterful, especially the Human theme which just rings of glory and sadness at the same time. I used to spend hours just docked on any Human colony world just listening to that theme song, refusing to take off even to defend the system from Klissans, Dominators and Pirates.
Now, the game itself is based around a group of non-military volunteers called ''Rangers'' who are tasked with defending the Interstellar Coalition of Five Races (Humans, Gaal, Faeyans, Maloq and the Pelengs) from any threat that may threaten their security. The Rangers are each their own general, their own corporation or bank and can hire other Rangers to work under their command. In this game, there are tons of ways to improve your combat capabilities, and also tons of ways to just play the game. You can be a Warrior, a Mercenary, a Merchant, a Corsair or a Pirate and just play for as long as you want in a single playthrough. They're literally unlimited.
In the end, this game would probably get a 10 out of 10, but the overall lack of variation between planets and the top-down gameplay is severely lowering the score, HOWEVER, it doesn't impact on the overall game as it's still a perfect space sim of its time and for those who want to await a better one similar in style to this one, but without the top-down limitation.

This is a very unique experience and totally changes the dynamics of counter strike. The PvE was somewhat dry in my opinion, and resembled Sven: Co-Op in that you essentially plow your way alongside other players through a linear map fighting back wave after wave after wave of enemy and completing certain tasks (usually blowing up a barrier that has 30,000 health) to get to the next area. There are buy zones interspersed for you to load up on ammo or switch out guns and it usually culminates in a big boss fight. It's kind of droll and there's not much of a challenge.
WHERE THIS REAAAALLLY ****REAAAAAAAAAAAALLLY**** shines however is the PvP mode where some people are zombies and some CTs each round (randomly selected).
Each zombie type has special powers, like an iron maiden it can slam down to stun enemies and hide behind, or a hoard of bats that grabs the human you aim it at and drags him toward you. The humans (CTs) have a slew of all the classic CS guns and some extras, with a much higher ammo capacity.
This mode can be SUPER intense as you spawn throughout familiar classic CS maps and try to get to high ground with other humans, since one hit from a zombie and you become one and join the hunt. Zombies have thousands of health points, but are slowed down by being hit so a group of humans can often protect themselves or give another a chance to excape, but once the guy next to you takes a scratch he'll kill you.
Playing with just a couple people is really cool too depending on the map... it becomes more like hide and seek and can be VERY intense. I played with 2 others on the classic estate map and I kept jumping as I was attacked out of nowhere, since the maps are darkened to create a tense ambience.
This mode makes it SO worth the download and since it is  free game, you've GOT to try it out... I was hooked after a couple rounds.
Happy hunting! :)

After years and years, Snake is back on PC. After even Raiden making its debut on PC gaming this year, finally the main series is back. But this time is Big Boss himself, arriving for the first time on PC. But is Ground Zeroes worth? It’s almost certainly that you saw people on internet calling it a “demo” for The Phantom Pain, the main “V” game arriving next year (which will be available for PC too). I had played GZ for 30 hours on PS3 and 100% complete(and you can see I’m a big of the series by looking at my steam profile too) it so I prepared this review! Ground Zeroes is the Prologue for TPP, presenting the new features on the series, like the open-world stealth, usable vehicles and new HUD. GZ have beautiful graphics using the new Fox Engine from KJP, it’s really amazing, and for sure the illumination is one of the most impressive ever seen. The gameplay is smoother than the other MGS games, adding vehicles (In GZ you can use jeeps, trucks, APCs and can call for Heli support). You have now your IDroid which you can use to see the in-game map and to use other features like mission info, walkman, etc. The soundtrack is epic, and the cutscenes like in other MGS games are amazing, the ending is a good link for The Phantom Pain, the PC port is amazing, probably one of the best ports of the year, if not the best; and in Camp Omega you have all-new features like binoculars to mark enemies, destructible scenario in some structures and some collectibles. The only bad thing about the game is the short story. Depending in how you play it will take 1-2 hours to complete the main mission, so if you only play main missions on games don’t buy GZ. But if you like to explore there are good 6-8 hours to complete all missions and 20 hours to 100% the game (which is a good time). The game have almost no bugs and now on PC there is support for beatiful 4K and modding! Kiefer Surtherland voice acting is actually good too. I think that he is better to play Big Boss as the game is darker, so, after all, it’s a good voice acting(of course probably David Hayter maybe would be better).As this is a “prologue” there is some features from the previous games that are not included, besides this adds more things. There is no Cardboard Box, knocking on walls, funny items, knife, etc. But all of those we’ll be included in TPP. Camp Omega feels alive too! Soldiers are always doing something, like talking to each others about recent facts and eventually even tips for the objective. It's a cool system. And there are pretty animations. New animations and mechanics includes cool CQC moves, refined interrogation, and new and realistic crawling animations, where snake actually moves to where you are pointing the gun. The AI is one of the most impressive in gaming, the guards working and investigating, mostly on hard difficulty to have a real stealth experience (this series being one of the pioneer in good AI) And if you wanna catch up with the story for the other games, there is a section on menu for that! There is also a few collectibles to search in Camp Omega, including nine XOF patchs, that will unlock two extra ops (besides the four side ops). These Extra Ops are all for fun. It's a good tribute to MGS1 in Dejà-Vú mission, with a lot of challenges to complete, like finding and cleaning all MGS logos, and a lot of easter eggs, like playing with Solid Snake model from MGS1 and even Gray Fox model! And the other is Jamais-Vu, which adds pretty action to the game as you contro the cyborg Raiden, which some little changes to the mechanics, like running, and Raiden is a Cyborg. The four Side Ops are really cool too. They ar eunique, besides the fact that all of them pays on Camp Omega. There is an aciton-packed mission to destroy Anti-Air Emplacements, two cool stealth based missions where yoiu have some targets and a unique mission that you fire from the chopper while defending and then rescuing an agent of yours. The cool thing is that the agent is actually....
. All of those missions have highly replayability and there is a lot of things to find, easter eggs and ways to complete them. There is too another collectibles, like cassete tapes, and special weapons by getting some ranks in each mission. There are cool songs from previous games that can be unlocked and played in a mission, or even custom songs from your computer! There is now doubt that the game quality itself is unquestionable, but what about the price-benefit? Ground Zeroes price is actually good for those who are gonna explore the game and play all the missions, but if you are just gonna beat the main mission, it’s not recommended. But after all, Ground Zeroes is an amazing game, with new mechanics that prepares us for the amazing The Phantom Pain next year. Besides story being too short, is a good taste for MGS on PC.

Before I say anything about the gameplay, let me first address the controversial topic of the game's length.
If you speedrun the game, you can complete every mission in about 2-3 hours. HOWEVER, if you are a completionist or enjoy the replay value that the map and missions have to offer, you can easily get about a dollar-per-hour of value out of the game. I didn't even S-rank everything and I got 17 hours out of the game for only ~42% completion. Be creative and don't expect to be spoon-fed your fun.
Now, for the gameplay. This is an exciting taste of what's to come for The Phantom Pain. There's a lot of loving detail included in the little things. The movement animations for Snake are amazing - 99% of his animations are believable save for a few cases where you can intentionally make him look stupid. The AI is decent, but predictable - however, it's hard to make AI that doesn't at some point become predictable. Having played on both a PS3 controller and a mouse + keyboard, I prefer the controller but the PC controls are ALMOST as comfortable save for a few hitches (which can be helped with some key rebindings.) Above all, the stealth action is challenging but satisfying, rewarding careful planning, quick execution, and ability to improvise.
The graphics are amazing and the game is optimized well. The story is admittedly edgy and kind of grimdark for a MGS game, but the series' brand of quirky humor still shines through in some missions.
Overall, I highly recommend if you like stealth games and like to go for extras/collectibles/high scores. If you don't, it's still worth it in my opinion, but you may want to wait for it to go on sale.

I bought this game on sale because I love everything ancient Rome and actually ended up loving it.
The combat is very fun and visceral. The two player co-op mode is TONS of fun. It's basically like being a gladiator. Survival mode is awesome, basically just endless slaughter. It works best if you have a friend to play with, but this is a game that is also quite playable with randoms, unlike many multiplayer games out there. The only drawback is that it can be hard to find someone to play with occasionally.
The main campaign is very short I will admit. Of my 20+ hours played only about 9 have come from the single player story, the real meat of the game to me is in multiplayer.
Would I recommend paying full price for this game? Hard to say. Like I said, I got it on sale for $13, but in retrospect it would have been worth the retail price to me.
The average person would likely not get enough playtime out of this game to justify the $40 price tag, but if it you see it on sale for $20 I would not pass up a chance to fight FOR THE GLORY OF ROME!

It was like the scene in rataouile when the food critic tries the peasant dish and it transfered him back on his childhood. so i gave it a long shot. so more about the game: It is a space open-universe rpg. you create a char from various classes and races, and you start. there are two basic plots in this edition, but you can follow your own path as well. you can get a party as you progress and theres a cool way of communication between pilots or other npc that makes it easy to control them. Mini game modes for planetary battles reminded me of Z but with customized mechs, text based quests such as prison escapes or even races (WIN-WIN MUD LOVERS) and an arcade style shooter in black holes. combat system is semi-turnbased, lots of little stuff to buy for your ship, lot's of ships, and many times many quests planets npc. Oh also you get to die in this game sometimes as well, it's THAT oldschool. Friends of true rpg or strategy games, space simers or simply rave-dancing drug abusers unite!!!

Space Rangers HD puts a hand in too many cookie jars and doesn't really excel in any of them. It tries to be a Myst-like adventure series with little short, interactive, branching stories, then tries its hand at being a space sim where you fly around a little and barter, and finally it tries its hand at arcade shooting and RTS style gameplay. It has variety, being a jack of all trades, but it doesn't master any of them. On the other hand, it doesn't fail horrible, save for the reading portions where you can be screwed by RNG, especially when you're on the clock. Don't buy this game unless you're sure you want any of those, or you're a fan of the series. If you are a fan, it does exactly what you want and it runs without issue. So I won't give it any hate for that. It's possible that I'm just not too big a fan of the series, and the game isn't at fault, so I give it that benefit of the doubt.

This game never gets old. It's super adictive and a lot of fun! Sure, once you play non stop, it may get boring, so you step away from it for a while. A few days, weeks, perhaps even a month or more. This is normal to many if not all games.
However, once you decide to turn on this game again, you get sucked into cozy open-world Universe and can't stop playing for hours if not days, weeks, months.
Clever A.I., great writing, interesting gameplay, and the best part is, you play the game you want. There's nothing holding your hand and pushing you to finish it. You really do feel like a small person in a huge world. However, you also have the ability to make all the difference if you try. You may fail countless times, but every vicotry will tast very sweet!
Personally from me, I found a wingman for my self by accident. It all started when I just wanted to test something out and realizing that it didn't worked out, I thought about going solo again. The best part is, it's been nearly 20 in game years and we still fly together. Not because it's easier for me or because I get an advantage in anything from my wingman. In fact, sometimes it's even harder to fight battles because I don't want to lose her. But the feeling of sharing victories together is what makes us fly together!
This game may not be for everyone, but if you have some extra cash, give this game a chance. Who knows, maybe you'll find your wingman that you'll never want to split with.

When I was young, there was a mouse-driven space game called Escape Velocity. That game and its sequels was awesome and I poured hours into it.
Space Rangers is like a modern, even more awesome (if possible) take on EV. It is hands down the coolest top-down space game Ive ever played. There is something for all sci-fi lovers. Trading, fights, arcade sequences, RTS, combat, story, dynamic worlds and planetary movement (youd be surprised how many top down space games have stationary planets). Everything. I haven't played the originals, so I cant compare the two. The only thing I dont like is that the Pirate faction seems kind of OP, but you can turn their aggression down iin the fully-customizable difficulty and game-play menu. That is an awesome feature, being able to control nearly every aspect of the gameworld -  alien behavior, planets (types, how many) enemy faction behavior, trading behavior and so forth.
I love in-cockpit space games too, but theres just something fun about the top driven ones. And this game is the king of the top-down space games!

I've played quite a few 4x games including way too much Civ 2,3,4,5 and Galactic Civ.  This is a real winner for a number of reasons.  The art is beautiful, music is good - that's a fine start.  For us strategy vets - especially for us builders/peace lovers it is brutal at the higher difficulties which is actually a good thing (too easy and you lose interest).  The most interesting thing about this game is how every turn in the early 1-40 turn range is hugely important and the learning curve to figure out how to do things is significant (again, a good thing).  This is a war game but it has enough "building" to satisfy us less bloodthirsty types.
This is a fabulous and flexible game, and as a player who has tons of experience at strategy games I appreciate all the nice touches and innovative features.  Perhaps you have to have this vast experience to understand how much perfection this game has - as a few others have said I can't recommend this enough.  IMHO ignore any bad recommendations as folks who need a better documentation and who have limited 4x gaming probably do not understand this gem.
The best way I can put this is that the developers of this game obviously learned a great deal from previous strategy games and actually devised solutions to deal with peoples frustrations.  They also devised a game that has a flexibility in playstyles that should make everyone happy.

Chapter 2 kept to the high standard that chapter 1 set, if not raising the standard altogether.
Higurashi when they cry is a sound novel series. The games use sound effects, images, and appropriate music to generate an atmosphere for the story. This is done much better than the last game (Yse, I know it seems almost impossible) as they have added more music that really helps to get you immersed (Cheesy though this may sound). The key characters have sprites to help you get a better idea of their appearance, and their current mood. Images tend to be scenes so you can get the idea of where the character(s) is(are).
Like the last chapter this game has a brilliant story, however does not directly follow up from the last chapter, it is set over the same few days where a different chain of events occur instead.
The story could be described as an emotional joyride for what kind of emotions your character feels (And that what it wants you too feel too) The character you play expresses himself in a manner of ways of goes through happiness, sorrow, hope, despair, regret, fear, feeling sympathetic towards the culprit, and what is almost love. (Though not in that order)
Your character is still new to hinamizawa, however you have the knowledge of events from past chapters to take a different standpoint on events. After breaking a taboo of the village, people start to go missing, all of which had some connection to the chain of events leading up to your breaing of said taboo. Your character wants to find out what is happening, and, if possible, put a stop to it before anyone else you care about gets hurt.
As said once before the idea of this game is to put you in the character's shoes, throughout the main story you shall see what he sees, hear what he hears, know what he thinks, and (dependant on your immersion) feel what he feels.
The optional tips give you (The player) to learn more about the situation than your character.
For the experiance, I'd say this game is definately worth the cost (Much like the last game.) The playtime at the time I posted this was around 16.7 hours. So in my books, chapter 2 is worth the cost as much as chapter 1 was.
After you have completed the game, you unlock the "After Party". This is also titled as the "All cast review session". In it, the characters break down the 4th wall and share their opinions on the game, and their theories behind the inccidents, also discussing what the beta players thought. (A surprisingly nice way to end the game, as it somewhat doubles up as a brief recap.) It also makes some hints at preperations for the third chapter (For which I also have high expectations for.)
This game, as said above, was great. I just fell into the world they were trying to portray, even after seeing the anime, some elements of the game surprised me. (There are differences between the anime and games.)

Space Rangers 2 is a unique and improbable blend of space trading/fighting, robot-war based RTS and choose-your-own text adventures somewhat erratically translated from Russian. You play a Space Ranger trying to save the universe from the plague of a trio of evil AIs and the growing threat of pirates.
Or not.
You can ignore the story of the game and choose your own goal - and let the universe crumble around you. Sometimes you will be trading or running fedex missions between worlds. Sometimes releasing probes on unihabited worlds. Sometimes you will be jumping into a system infested with AI space vessels and trying to do your bit for the cause. Sometimes you will tracking down some rogue pilot for the money you need to buy your next ship. Sometimes you will be running a ski resort. Sometimes trying to get elected as president - or winning a Fonzer race - or just surviving prison as you wait for your release.
If you can't imagine what that might be like, then you ought to try this game. It is a one-off.
The pacing is all over the place. The turn-based space battles make mass combat a puzzle, rather than an adrenaline hit. Not a bad thing if you like that kind of thing. The planetary robot battles are long drawn out affairs of attrition rather than inspiration and the text adventures are... mixed... and involve a hell of a lot of reading and even more head scratching. But both are optional and feel almost like entire games all of their own. It can be hard to find your feet - the manual has vital information that the tutorial doesn't cover. It really is a bit of a stitched together monster.
However to find all three genres in one game - and a game of so many options. Advancing tech tree - dynamic economy - an enemy expanding into your turf whether you like it or not - named competitors and rivals to fight, or hire. To have a story arc of a galactic battle against three baddies that you can choose whether to engage with - and how. And then to find you are a small cog in a vast machine of traders, pirates, military vessels and rangers who get on with their own lives with or without you. It's a glorious anarchic riot that has (either by luck or judgement) found a beautiful patchwork mix of the bizarre.
For all of its faults - craziness - frustrations - iffy translations. It is, quite possibly, my favourite game.

As far as 2D space sims go, I would vote Space Rangers to be the best of all time, even better than Star Control 2.
Space Rangers offer a great variety of gameplay: combat, trading, piracy, exploration, salvaging, upgrading ship and skills, text adventures, planetary battles, arcade minigame. There is always something to do, and all playstyles blend nicely together for a complete and satisfying game experience.
This game has a living and breathing world, where every NPC has a purpose. Traders carry goods from one planet to another, pirates try to convince them to offload those goods to them, diplomats and transports fly between planets doing diplomat-y and transport-y stuff (gameplay-wise, they are either used by pirates to extort money, or fight the said pirates). There are also rangers, like yourself, who can be pirates, or traders, or warriors, and who behave accordingly. Each of these NPCs is persistent, which means they don't just disappear forever when you leave their star system. In fact, you can use the in-game search functionality to track any NPC across the galaxy, by simply typing its name (you could even play it as a stalking simulator).
I want to mention that Space Rangers have a very flexible game difficulty setting. On the lower difficulties, your enemies don't control many star systems, so you can freely fly across the galaxy, trading and completing government missions. On the highest difficulty, the enemies control most star systems, and you are left with half a dozen (or less) systems that you can visit without getting annihilated by a swarm of enemies within a minute. This adds a kind of "fighting a losing war" desperation feeling, when you must fight for the very survival of your species, which I personally find enjoyable.
If you are not averse to the idea of turn-based space battles occuring on a 2D plane, you should definitely give Space Rangers a try. And even if you are averse to 2D space battles, Space Rangers HD offer the option to play text adventures, planetary battles and arcade fights separately from the main game, so you can buy it just for that. Speaking of additional content, this game also includes a MP3 soundtrack (no DLC necessary) with 33 awesome space-themed tracks - you can find them in the "Soundtrack" folder in the game's installation directory.
P.S. "Space Rangers HD" is actually an updated version of "Space Rangers 2". If you, like me, prefer to play games and watch movies starting from the first part, there is also "Space Rangers 1", which you can probably find somewhere on the Internet (it's not on Steam, sadly). It's a bit rougher around the edges than the second part, but it still possesses the same qualities that make it a great game.

This game is... something else entirely. It's not even so much of a game but rather a story and an interactive experience.
This is by far the most beautiful and fantastically imaginative game I have played in a LONG TIME; the world map, the units, the buildings, and the attention to detail have been beautifully crafted and methodically thought out to create a world of imagination, fantasy, and legend. There is a gaming aspect to it, but the world sucks you in and leaves you curious and wanting more every single time you press, "Next Turn".
The UI is sleek, the graphics without challengers, and the balance wonderful. There is so much to do in this game, but at the same time, it really guides you through and makes your quest for empire amazing. I have not been captivated by a game like this in my endless years of gaming, and that is truly astonishing to say.
It's no Civ V: it's certainly better as a 4X strategy game. Civ V is historical, but this game trumps every card it has and it's not even based on history: it's based in a beautiful and creative world that feels alive and awe-inspiring, and you as a player are right in it.
Read the storylines, enjoy the quests, enjoy the canon, and you will fall in love with this game as I have.
Get this game.
P.S. The music is probably some of the most beautiful, hypnotic, and tear-jerking work I have ever heard in not only a video game but also in general. It is a mix of classical, melancholy, and soothing but passionate tones of what sound like cellos, basoons, French horns, light strings, and non-diagetic sounds that really engulf your ears in beauty and, sometimes, what feels like sorrow, pain, loss, and heartache. Considering the fantasy aspect of the game, the music is just unrivaled in immersing you in the fantasy world.
