It took me a total of 7 hours to complete the main campaign and had a run on the multiplayer.
Campaign
The story is acceptable to say the least, but OK story development. The combat is reptitative - block, slash, slash. Wait for counter, slash slash. It's the same from the start of the game to the end. The upgrade system of health/focus/gain is pretty lame and there's no unlocks of special abilities. You get to use 4-5 weapons through the game but mostly ever use your default sword and shield. The QTE can be satisfying at times - similar to what Shadow of Mordor gives you. Mostly, it felt more like Warhammer Spacemarines just back in the time of the Romans. Voice acting is alright, but there isn't much to look forward to. Scenes are predictable, which isn't a bad thing if it's executed well. The game is better played on a controller. I used a M&K which took a lot of getting used to as the keys are not mapped natively. You'll find yourself feeling rather awkward throughtout the game.
HOWEVER. The beauty of the game is just in it's stunning visuals. But the linear sequencing of each level without the ability to free roam again takes away from what could have been a very pleasing experience.
Multiplayer
It's pretty much handling waves of the same enemies. There are options to upgrade armor through the purchasing of booster packs, but after having played the campaign, it leaves you with very little interest of more of the same combat.
Should you buy it? If it's on sale.
Should you get a friend to buy it? Yes. if it's on sale.
5.5/10

Really enjoyed this game,
It's refreshing to find a game that actually challenges you to make decisions.  First, I have to start with the obvious, the visuals.  I'm running this on a Core 2 Quad 3.4, 8GB RAM (DDR2) and a 970GTX (Fantastic Card and great value).  The beginning loads up into a cut scene to begin the story, so I'm sat there watching, drinking my coffee and then realised that I was being slowly hacked to bits by Barbarians, I thought it was still a frickin cutscene!  The graphics are absolutely gorgeous, the attention to detail is immense without a single element of lag, fantastic work by the developers.
Combat can be slightly frustrating, particularly against some of the later boss characters where you have to combine dodge, with perfect and I mean pin-point precision blocking moves followed up with a quick attack.  Initially, the combat is great and the execution moves are a nice touch but just when it starts to get repetitive, the developers throw a few elements into the mix, like the scorpion artillery piece which really is a rapid fire machine gun (not entirely historically accurate) or commanding troops ducking behind shield wall formations at the click of a button whilst being fired on by archers.  Their are some features of the game which blatantly copies other games such as focus (Think Max Payne and several other games of note) and some features which are don't really have much of an affect like the ability to build up your damage meter.  Character progression is great being able to upgrade your execution moves and so on.  My only gribe about this game is replayability, I finished the game in 2 days and now am looking for the next best thing.  I have yet to try multi-player and will update this review when I do.  Overal though, if you want a decent John Cena turned Roman Soldier meets Gears of War with the ability to chop off a barbarians arm with the swing of a sword, then this is game for you but don't expect to replay the story line because once done, the surprise elements are gone. 8/10

The bad news first: the AI in Endless Legend sucks. "Hard" and higher difficulty levels only make the AI 'cheat' a lot, meaning it gets boosts towards production, science etc. However, the AI still does little with its advantage. It declares war on the player, but instead of sending a massive invasion force, the AI only sends small armies, one after another that get butchered. The same picture when defending. It is way too easy to make the AI spread out its troops. Instead of setting up a line of defense and holding it, armies can be easily lured away. The stupid AI's behavior extends to diplomacy, too. The AI declares war for no reason (e.g. the empires have no common border and the attacking AI is surrounded by other enemy empires), breaks alliances and peace treaties seemingly randomly. I never did multiplayer, but if that is what you seek, then buy this game. I can image it is a lot of fun when the stupid AI is replaced by human players.
But there is a lot of good stuff in the game. I really like the "one city per region" concept (4X game creators out there: this is definitely a feature to copy!). The available factions are all
different, with some nice special abilities. There is enough variation in the game in terms of heroes, units, resources, technology and quests (though some quests are bugged and cannot be completed unless you know how to avoid the bugs. This is pretty bad for a game that has seen alot of patches). Both graphics and music are decent for the genre and the GUI is ok, too.
All in all the game could have been awesome. Unfortunately, its faults make it only pretty solid 4X.

Ok, so honestly, this game ROCKS. I'm a fan of games like this generally, played some 500 hours or more on the civ series, and played games like AOW3 too. I've never seen a game quite like this though. It's like they took their last game, Endless Space (which I have not played), and said: "hmm, lets see what a fantasy version of this would look like." That game is Endless Legend.
The art style first and foremost, is phenomenal. Everything looks and sounds GORGEOUS. I enjoyed just zooming in and out to survey my growing city. The music is moving and beautiful, and a welcome break from the typical epic soundtrack sound that permeates fantasy games. Also, THE FACTIONS!!! From the suitably dead but noble Broken Lords, to the vibrant Roving Clans, this game has diversity, an important thing in our PC culture. But seriously, all the factions are hugely different, and I've barely scraped the surface.
The gameplay is difficult, maybe too difficult, as I found myself getting stomped on newbie difficulty. However, there's a lot to learn, and I can admit that. There's intrigue (much better than Civ 5's version), amazing diplomacy, and a lot of fun quests that really flesh out the game. The only thing I found annoying was the combat, which I autoresolved most of the time.
Overall, this game is fantastic. I'll definitely be addicted to this game for quite some time.

There's a reason I'm nominating this game for the "Just 5 more minutes" award. This is one of my most played games on steam because it does pretty much everything I want from a grand strategy. It goes into all those details most games skim over. Details like the individual political leanings of population groups, broken down into culture, religion, job and location each. Details like a full economy where money appear and disappear but persists, causing price variations as demand and supply change, and accidently setting taxes or tariffs too high or too low can cause your entire economy to crash. Details like a seperate upper and lower house with different powers and political parties that act differently depending on circumstances.
I'd recommend that after a few tries of vanilla you get the POP Demand Mod, it adds so much new content and improves many of the base mechanics, including a huge overhaul to many late-game features, the area which the vanilla game sadly is left wanting.
Oh, by the way, the difficultly curve is more like a difficulty wall. Just a heads up.

I first bought these shows on GOG, and now I'm buying them again to support the makers. Witty, well-performed, and with good use of special effects for an indie budget. An excellent series for the price.

Here is the review I've written for this series on GOG:
What is JourneyQuest? To me, it's a really funny fantasy series with great characters and also some real emotional moments (although the latter mostly happen in the second season). This first season is about a group of adventurers: Perf, the most incompetent wizard you will ever meet, Glorion, a (in his own opinion) truely brave warrior who - in his braveness - kills every evil creature in sight, Carrow, a cynical cleric who (during the course of the story) undergoes a transformation that he isn't O.K. with at all, and Nara, a mysterious elven ranger. So far their attempt at adventuring hasn't been very succesful, until (through sheer dumb luck) they stumble upon an immensely powerful relic - which brings them into all sorts of trouble. A b-plot focusses around a bard who (in hiding) chronicles the adventures of the party.
Why do I love this show? The characters (as I've already said) are great. Glorion's attempts at solving every problem through stabbing it with a sword are laugh-out-funny. Perf is so incompetent and yet tries so hard to be brave - which is really endearing. It's really cool to see the trope of the bard treated in a serious and (by fantasy standards) realistic manner. The script is very aware of the standard fantasy tropes and deliberately plays with them (for example, there is a male orc who says that he always wanted to be a female). This is a true indie production with a low budget - but with a surprisingly high production value given the circumstances. Especially the make-up artists did a great job.
The second season really increases the scope of the story, but the first one is also great on it's own. Evoland is an original game, with a great idea, but to be honest, it doesn't really work as a game, no matter how small or big it is.
It starts off brilliant, in black and white old school 2D. Opening treasure chests grants you access to other features, features frequently seen in other RPGs, like 3D mode, loot and NPCs. That all sounds amazing, right ? It is, but the game lets you unlock all the features way too soon. Halfway through (the game lasts about 3 hours, 5 hours max if you want to collect everything) you've seen everything there is and the game starts focusing on the story (if you can call it a story). I was a bit disappointed by that, because the things that made the game so original became unoriginal and uninspired near the end. The random battles were especially starting to annoy me, since it triggers every few seconds and it's not always clear where to go. Like I said, it's something you see a lot in other RPGs, but in Evoland it backfires. A 3 hour game shouldn't become boring that soon.
Get it when it's on sale. Because even though it isn't the best game out there, the idea behind it is good and should be witnessed by others.

A fun action RPG with lovely characters and a cute lesbian romance story.
You play as Arnice, an agent for the Curia, an organization working to stop the advent of the Night and keep the Nightlord sealed. For this, a Saint is choosen and sacrificed to keep the strenght of the seal.
But this time the choosen one is Lilysse, Arnice only and dearest friend. And she's the one tasked with protecting her until the moment of the ritual.
Playing as Arnice you keep doing missions, sometimes destroying foes, finding an item in some map or just finding things that Lilysse lost. You can also plan daytime activities which can raise stats later used to buy new skills.
The combat part is fast paced and fun. You can have four servants, which can give your buffs, heal or deal damage. You can customize them with items allowing for some variation.
The best part anyways are the characters and the story. Arnice and Lilysse interactions and blossoming romance are lovely.
And the secondary cast is pretty fun to watch. And everyone ships Arnice and Lilysse. Good for them!
Long story short, a nice and fun Action RPG with a lovely yuri romance. The cons are the limited maps and can become repetitive in the long run.

I can see how someone might have issues with this game, but I really enjoyed it.  I bought it in the sale pack along with Atelier Sophie and figured I'd hate this game and love Sophie, but the reverse has turned out to be true.
The breast mechanics are especially silly, and the "Platonic" love story is absurd.  But ARPG-wise, you get some pretty solid battle mechanics here with variability like combos, Servans (summoned monsters that follow you around that you can control via issued commands and a "Burst" command - which executes their special move), weapons that you can change during combat, etc.  Graphics and music both help keep you engaged.  And Lloyd has got to be the most hysterical video game character of all time.
No GOTY candidate or anything, but a much better experience than I might have expected.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is the entry title into Metal Gear Solid V. Released as a standalone story, the game is offered to allow players early access to some of the features of the FOX Engine, as well as the new gameplay mechanics being released in The Phantom Pain.
The game offers a short story after the events of Peace Walker, as well as a few side missions. While the content is limited, there is a lot of content in the gameplay. There are side missions the user can play, as well as smaller objectives in each mission. While it probably plays closer to the older MGS1: VR Training game (Which was just mini-games and released at full price, mind you), the game offers a much more enriching experience than previous titles.
A lot of the systems in Ground Zeroes are scripted, but there are a lot of subtle variations, sometimes leading to some big changes. Example: I witnessed a guard kill another guard with their jeep, check, and then drive away. This led to an easier time for me to get through that area.
Other than that, the game IS short, but there are a lot of things to do. I, for one, enjoy getting this experience rather than being completely without. :)

Here's a great game with a great storyline. The Romans pitted against the Britons in an ultimate clash of war with a story of personal loss, and the graphics that Crytek outputs as well as gameplay is phenomenal. Unbelievable. Unreal.
HOWEVER.
It is within my ultimate 'History Geek' right to step forward and say that the elements of the environment and contributions to the culture make it seem too much like a fantasy of Rome. Here's why:
-The Arena in gladiator mode is WAY too f*cking mechanical for ancient era technology
-The armor, gladius', scutum, and other accessories seem a bit too 'designer' and don't fit actual historical appearance
-In ancient times, the legions of Rome were camped outside the city and never set foot inside. Therefore barbarians wouldn't invade THAT easily with those armies camped outside due to sacred tradition. (Edit: parts of the legions did occupy the cities as police, but they would muster on the "Field of Mars" in the event of an invasion)
-The Colosseum should NOT exist, it was built AFTER the time of Nero.
-Damocles was a Greek, not Roman legend
-Marius Titus is a backwards name. Marius is a clan name, and Titus is a first name. Jones Peter, or Peter Jones?
Overall I like this game for the action, and the acceptance that this game IS initially about Rome and contains at least the main elements that make it Roman based so my thumb is pointing up for this one. But, because of the major inaccuracies of the historical, cultural, and environmental themes; it gets marked off some points.
7.5/10.0
Edit: There is mention in the game of the "eighteenth legion" which is another inaccuracy. In 9 A.D at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, the 17th, 18th, and 19th Legions were wiped out in the massacre; afterward were never used again in the Roman army's legionary lineup for the disgrace of losing so terribly on that day/days (the battle lasted three days). Since this is well after the reign of Augustus Caesar into Nero's time, this again presents itself as another element of the game's story being backward with history.

Monday Night Combat is the fastest paced shooter I have played. If you like a shooter with some surprisingly interesting map strategies and a true test of your reflexes then this one is worth a try. The atmosphere of future deathsport is a real selling-point for this game. Basic gameplay involves escorting groups of bots to the enemy's base while preventing the enemy from doing the same. Variant maps change up this formula to some degree.

MNC is often compared to TF2; this is a inaccurate comparison.  While both are class-based team shooters with a lot of zaniness, that's about where the similarities end. Basically, if you like TF2, you'll probably like MNC, but don't expect the same old gameplay.  Definitely worth your time.

If you like 4X games such as Civilization 5, play this. Really polished, smooth gameplay, and has extras that I would love to see in other 4x games.
Big one being, regions. In games like Civ, if you colonise an area, some AI can come along and plant a city practically right next to yours, and there's nothing you can do about it but declare war and raze it. In Endless Legend each region can only have ONE city. So you build a city and get exclusive rights to all the resources of that area, nobody else can colonise it.
I can't express enough how that one change alone makes for a much more interesting game.

This is a very good example of an amateur, yet very solid game! I was happy to play it, and it doesn't have too much that's wrong with it, which is surprising, as many people tend to ignore crucial details. This game does not.
However, it doesn't add anything to the genre, and while it's a solid game, it pains me how similar it is to Jamestown! In the credits, the developer says the game has been slowly "baked" in 4 years, and looking at his youtube channel, there were prototypes as far back as 2010, so it doesn't seem to me like a rip-off.
Perhaps it's just bad luck, but it's impossible to recommend this over
, since that adds a lot more to the genre, and is generally much bigger in scale and options.
Regardless of that fact, I enjoyed playing this, and I'll review it by its own merits.
The
style of this game reminds me a lot of an higher-res version of SNES games. The color-palette, especially, reminds of of A Link to the Past. It's colorful, but has a sort of
, with more passive colors.

The Boss visual design is also pretty cool. Won't blow your mind, but they're cool. There could be a bit more work into their details, but overall, I liked it.
One problem people might have with it, is that it's very bare-bones. Levels have some motion to them, but not a lot. Not many details that I saw either. No particle or lighting effects or anything of the sort. It's very basic and somewhat static, but other than that, I think it looks really cool! Very
looking.
Now, the
related to the visuals.
First off, the bullets' colors are too varied. That's a bad thing, because it makes it harder to balance the backgrounds with the bullets, and you're very likely to get hit by something you didn't see.
Related to this problem, is how the background has buildings which you never know if you'll get hit by or not. This makes dodging bullets a nightmare, and you're also trying to avoid everything. This is partially solved, with an option they introduced. You can "mute" and "darken" the backgrounds. This helps significantly with the backgrounds' distinction, but not a lot with the bullets. Especially when some bullets are very dark themselves.
Also,
. It's really annoying, in harder levels.
Other than these problems (which aren't too major, and the developer tried to give us options to deal with them), the visuals are fine. A bit too basic for some people, but they're well done!
Now, on to the
!
The sound-effects were a mixed bag. Some aspects I liked, others not so much. The positives outweigh the negatives, though.
When you destroy enemies, they explode with a loud boom. A
boom, I should say! They chose the sound well -- the downside is, when you destroy many enemies at once (there's a specific point in the game where this happens, otherwise it's totally fine) where the sounds just play exactly at once, which seems to up the volume a lot. The sound then gets overly loud and distorted. It's a very minor thing, but it happens everytime, so I thought I should mention it.
The other problem, is the gun sounds. It sounds like you're shooting rubber bullets. (There are some Bomb enemies that "pop" when they die, a very toy-like sound that does not, in any way, sound like a bomb)
I really like when the weapons sound like freakin' cannons (War Thunder and Blue Flamingo had spot on sounds for this!), and shooting rubber bullets sound a bit underwhelming. I'm aware that bullet sound often sound annoying when repeatedly shooting, and this was certainly a measure to solve that problem, but I'm not too keen on this "solution".

Moving on to the
. As I said before, it was inspired by Grieg. You probably know
, at least. Anyway, expect classical music! On the victory screens in sound almost like military march-music. I think it fits.

The difficulty affects the damage you deal, that you take, and also some enemies' shooting patterns. The levels don't change significantly (aside from the same enemies being more powerful), but it's not a matter of "more is harder!".
Every difficulty is available from the start.
The levels start locked, and you need to unlock them by beating the previous one. I think this was slightly bugged. When you start Hard mode, you're also locking the Easy and Normal levels, strangely enough. Not a big problem, but hey, it's there.
The mechanics are very simple. Your ship has a primary fire, and a secondary, more powerful weapon, instead of a Bomb. Your
has 3 states. It fires 1, 2 and then 3 bullets. You get cogs when you destroy enemies, which fills your weapon bar. I'm not sure if there are linear damage changes to the weapon, or whether it's a simple matter of being at different levels.
The
is a torpedo "barrage" -- this is too powerful of a word, though. You need to hold a button to charge it, and then launch them, doing significant damage. This plays a big part in the game's tactic, I believe. Knowing when to use them (as they're limited), and which enemies drop them is important to succeed, especially if you're not a very skilled player (*discreetly whistling*).
Other than that, if have a health-bar and lives. When your life-bar depletes, you lose a life. There are periods of invincibility.
Each level has a different theme, both visually, and in regards to enemies and hazards. If you're not good, you'll need to learn the levels before doing being able to beat the game all in one go.
is surprisingly high! I wasn't expecting that at all. Usually, these indie games tend to make the most out of a few enemies and combinations. This game, however, introduces several enemies in each level, and they behave significantly different. It's quite impressive, honestly.
The
are also really cool. They're all multi-phased, with patterns you'll need to learn. You usually have to destroy their weapons before going for the "big kill". It's good!
There's only one ship. And it's a very basic one, without any interesting feature. It's unfortunate. In a game with such a rich enemy variety, one would expect more in terms of arsenal.
As I've mentioned, there are some issues with the distinction between background and foreground -- it's dampenned, but not completely solved. And it caused me many deaths.
The biggest thing of all, is that it doesn't bring anything new, really. It's a solid game, almost

The setting, music... it's too similar to one of the best of the genre, and it's unfortunate, since it pales in comparison.
Unless you
to play a more casual 'shmup, there isn't a big reason for you to try this.

game, and a very solid one at that!

I had a hard time figuring out what direction to take this review in.
As a game, Steam & Metal is a typical, one might even say derivative bullet hell shooter, but as a larger whole I can’t quite decide where it falls on the line between shallow replication and intentional self parody.
Set in a 19th century world on the brink of a steam-powered renaissance, you take up the mantle of your late grandfather, genius inventor and creator of a machine of unstoppable power for which the blueprints have been stolen. All that was left behind is your flying machine and mechanically inclined mind, which are all that stands between you and the dastardly scoundrels who intend to turn your grandfather’s work against the world.
Its writing is so representative of a base starting point of steampunk as a genre that I wasn’t sure if I was intended to laugh at the cliche ridden dialogue and premise, or cringe at the excessively articulated speeches of its characters and their tendency to jump between societal commentary and poking fun at the meaninglessness of the plot they’d been stuck in.
But that in itself begins to disrupt the idea that Steam & Metal is anything but a poorly told retreading of every tired element of steampunk literature. Its attempts at self awareness only make it harder to swallow, pouring out line after line in such painful earnestly that I wanted to tell the game to stop shut up for its own sake.
But when it decides to stop talking its soulless gameplay left me lost as to even know where to begin to describe it. It’s a bullet hell shooter, only with few projectiles and more room to maneuver than usual. The screen quickly fills with the chaotic frenzy of your enemies, but it all feels pointless and existing without reason. There was no satisfaction in destroying enemy ships, no excitement from nimbly dodging through an onslaught of cannonfire, no pleasure to be found surpassing a difficult stage or defeating a tricky boss.
If I felt anything playing Steam & Metal it was that there was nothing especially wrong with the game, it just had nothing to offer me over almost any other bullet hell shooter out there. It’s a model of acceptable mediocrity; a project that seems proud of itself, but never find a way to project its enthusiasm outward. Instead it goes on, fully convinced it’s the coolest thing ever no matter how disinterested the player becomes. I guess that’s better than nothing.

This shooter is more hits than misses with some nice boss battles and a narrative to add some character. However, it should be noted that the game is over in just over an hour with only 3 difficulty settings and leaderboards as an incentive to keep playing.
The game opens up with a brief introduction to its universe complete with a motive and an exaggerated do-gooder protagonist. Steam and Metal is not afraid to be silly (steampunk jokes and all) and its lofty writing is smirk inducing. The hand drawn slides area nice touch to give the game some character. The in game graphics and sound are pretty average, but the game certainly tries to leave an impression with its story.
The gameplay mechanics are standard but tight. You have a health bar and limited lives. Running out of lives will send you back to restart the level, however your score/pick ups will carry over to the next level so there is a strong incentive to stay alive. Pick ups include the usual suspects: health, extra missiles, extra lives, and bonus scores, but your firepower is based on picking up gears or bullets with each tier adding another stream of bullets. Some of the level designs are well made with death riddled mazes and telegraphed danger. The boss fights feel demanding at times and keep the player on their toes. However, this game will not appeal to everyone.
Compared to other shooters Steam and Metal felt a bit sluggish at times. The weapons are also very average: you fire a single stream of bullets at first, then as you collect gears you can add up to two more streams of bullets to total at three. Your missiles require you to hold down your button for a short amount of time before they can be released (they can be held while firing), which does force you to choose your targets carefully. Given the lack of weapon variety, and little strategy (in other games you have to juggle a shield or your speed increases when not firing, only one standard single player campaign etc.) this game is on the lighter side, especially when coupled with the brief campaign length.
Steam and Metal really is a score driven top down shooter. Your ship can take a limited number of hits (depending on difficulty), but you can receive a bonus for not being hit at all. Accuracy, enemies killed, missles used, etc. all factor into your final score. Given that there are only 6 levels and 3 difficulty levels, the realy meat of the game will probably come through multiple plays in order to carve your name on the leader boards.
Clocking in at a little more than an hour (with most of the achievements thrown in) this is a top down shoot 'em up that is overall enjoyable. This game is lacking in a few areas (like variety and depth), so those that are already knee deep in shoot 'em ups and bullet hells may want to look elsewhere for their fix. However this is a neat experience for those who are in the market for a streamlined and brief experience. This game boasts dynamic boss battles, solid game play, a short campaign, and a neat little narrative mixed in the middle of all the bullets, but I would recommend waiting for a sale/bundle.

If you like girls, and hack and slash action RPGs, and having animal companions, and top notch OSTs, and also girls loving each other.... then you'll like this game a lot.
I came into Nights of Azure blind only hearing about the yuri aspects of it (ofc), but I found myself loving it the more I played. The controls can be a bit clunky (it took a bit of messing around with it to map the controller) and the combos aren't especially extraordinary for a hack and slash game, but I felt these were only minor setbacks in comparison to its good points.
For a new IP, Gust does a lot to keep it interesting. Players take control of Arnice, a holy knight tasked with protecting her childhood friend Lilysse, the Saint to be sacrificed to protect the world. It's hard not to get attached to them as they further develop their relationship, and feelings for one another, as the eternal night draws nearer. Overall, the plot manages to keep you on your toes, while not overstaying its welcome, leading to an enjoyable action RPG experience.
As for gameplay, those familiar with hack and slash games shouldn't have any trouble. The most notable feature unique to Nights of Azure is the Servans, companions loyal to Arnice that assist her in combat. Players can use a number of different servans, each with their own unique abilities, leading to different combat strategies. These also tie in to another unique feature, Arnice's transformations in battle. Though the combos may not be very versatile compared to other hack and slash games, there are other aspects to combat that still make it pretty enjoyable.
Overall, Nights of Azure was a very pleasant surprise. It's a great RPG for a new IP, with memorable characters, excellent yuri, and fun combat, and it's something I'll definitely be playing again in the future.

In terms of population and demographics, Victoria II is one of the most detailed games I've ever played. It is set from 1836 to 1936, with a dynamic economy and politics. It represents the Victorian Era (And the years shortly after) quite well, modeling imperialism and the rise of Liberalism. There are many political decisions you can make while ruling a country if the conditions are met, based on the current ruling party. Something I quite like about this is that there can be several parties with the same ideologies (Fascism, Marxists, Reactionaries, etc.), but different policies, splitting votes. Some parties will also form coalitions with other parties and win more votes. The population is simulated, down to the very person. There are also several nice "easter eggs" hidden in the game. Despite this however, I highly recommend you only get the game WITH the dlc, they have lots of improvements. Overall, I'd rate it a 9.5/10, because towards the end of the game, rebellions begin becoming a bit ridiculous and unrealistic, but that can be easily fixed with mods.
While short, this game has a ton of replayability, and is so much fun that I can't help but to reinstall it and play it once in a while. The mods add so much more to the already great experience.

With just shy of 2 hours under my belt, I'm already enjoying the heck out of Evoland. The game starts with 8-bit retro-Gameboy-spinach-green graphics and allowing you to only walk right. That's it.  And from that point on it's up to you to evolve through gaming history in terms of features, sound, graphics, and gaming styles to make your way. The game makes me think, 'what will the next unlockable be?' as I explore and find chests that could hold the next upgrade, whether it be a new feature, an upgrade in graphics, or sound. Heck, a recent one allowed me to break jars finally with my sword. You'll also be taken through various RPG battle styles, keeping things a bit more fresh when on one moment you're battle 8/16-bit Zelda style, and next you're doing random encounters and battle menus like Final Fantasy. If you're a RPG fan, or a gaming fan in general, do yourself a favor and give Evoland a shot.

I don't normally write reviews, but this piece of mindless drivel has raised me from my review embargo. NOTE: There will be some vague spoilers to puzzle solutions. No plot spoilers, however.
UPDATE Aug 25, 11:32 PM: Added 2 more negatives (darkness and text boxes)
UPDATE Nove 24, 11:14 AM: I nominated this for worst Free to Play because it's actually one of the worst games I've ever played. I urge you to join me.
I'll start with the positives as the list there is far shorter and will require no elaboration from me.
- It runs.
- The graphics are nice.
I'm done being optimistic about this game. Let's look at some negatives, shall we?
- The voice acting is mediocre at best, and didn't ever seem to be at the same volume level. The voice coming from the radio was cool for all of 5 seconds until you realized that if you were in another part of the room it was next to impossible to hear the radio, and he usually spouted something at least vaguely useful to solving the puzzle at hand.
- Speaking of vaguely useful, some of the puzzles are asinine. Specifically: puzzles in the house are ridiculous and seem to have no logical basis. It baffles me that there are people who actually tried (and succeded) in finding some way to solve these puzzles and make a walkthrough. They deserve a commendation and free medical help for the inevitable brain damage the puzzles in this game must have caused.
- "But wait!" I can hear you say through my computer monitor. "If you had waited long enough you too could have solved the problems!" And I suppose yes, you're right. But I guess the nonsensicality of the puzzles is matched only by the frustrating checkpoint system. If you can even call it that. The game never makes you aware that you're in a different zone, your only indication is the... escape menu (more on that later). Some zones are hilariously long, and it's pretty fantastic when you're 3 stories up and 4 rooms away and you pull a lever and see a light... and get shot and die. Those 3 stories of progress and exploration? Yeah do that again. Beyond the fact that that the game does not make you aware that the light indicates people coming to kill you. No you need to figure that out by trial and error, meaning if you didn't read this review or a walkthrough, you likely died there and had to do that exploration again.
- The escape menu.  No it is most definitely not a pause menu. How do you make a menu that appears when you push escape, appears for all intents and purposes to be a pause menu, but that doesn't actually pause the game? How do I know it doesn't pause, you ask? Because at one point you need to spam a key to survive, and you still need to spam it if your escape menu is up. Brilliant time I had there.
- Jumping is a nightmare. There is an entire level based around jumping that will inevitably cause you to curse the existence of the space bar before you set forward to try "just one more time." Let me tell you how much of a nightmare jumping is: You push space to jump. Logical. Hold space to jump longer. Also logical. So far so good, right? Well now try jumping forward. Seems fine, until you realize that letting go of space doesn't let you keep your forward momentum. Oh no. You just plummet almost straight down as soon as you let go of space. Physics was not invited to this party, it just weeps outside while Anthony enters.
- Another strange occurance: there is a jumping puzzle, as I said before. Near the end you start getting powerups to boost your jump height. After one of these is a checkpoint, which is nice I suppose. Until you realize that you get a powerup right before that checkpoint, and respawning after dying resets your jump height. That boost you had before the checkpoint? Gone. The rest of the level is now impossible. You have to exit to the main menu and start that little section over if that happens.
- The story. I won't say too much about it, but if you think "the writer was on drugs while writing this" while you play... you're not far off, I'm sure.
- Collision detection is wonky. Like Willy Wonka wonky. Certain objects seem to not exist beyond looking like they're there. And a word of advice? When you come out of the lake (you'll know when) DO NOT TURN LEFT. You'll be able to walk through a nice looking piece of brush before discovering that somehow the devloper borked it so much that you can't come back through the same brush. You are now trapped. Exit to main menu and start the level again.
- Gamma levels are non existant. A dark house is nearly pitch black. While nice when you're trying to emulate a house (I suppose?) it makes seeing anything basically impossible. I had my brightness to full just to see where the hell I was going. For a game so dependent on puzzles and puzzle solving, it's really rather befuddling that they'd make it impossible to see what you're solving.
- The continue from where you picked up is lackluster. Just give me an ability to save and I'll be fine. Instead the game goes for the whole retro "put in a password to get to a level" method. Ok fair enough. But there's no text box to type in the password. You just get to that screen and start typing, unable to see what you've typed. Also unable to submit, it just automagically goes when you're typed the whole thing. Coupled with the previous point, it's almost like I don't even need eyes to play this game!
- Finally: achievements are broken all to hell. And by broken all to hell, I mean as of right now I've successfully recieved... none of them. Including the one for finishing the game.
UPDATE: After testing again, they're still broken as heck.
I might be missing some flaws, but rest assured I'll return to fill them in if necessary.
I wanted to like this game. The graphics really are nice, and I almost felt something emotoinal in the park scene... until it went and told me I was talking to a clock. Really? Flipping really? Broke what little immersion I had. The problems I listed above alone would not kill a game. But put them together and... well you get this. It's like a brick in the shape of a triangualr prism. Yes it's a brick, but hell if it'll do anything correctly.
So let's wrap up shall we? It's good for about nothing. You can get through it in 2 hours with an occasional glance at a walkthrough (as I did), but without, good luck getting in that time. Some people out there disagree with me, I'm sure. Everyone's entitled to their opnion, and their's is just as valid as mine. And see, in the end, I actually almost enjoyed this game. Why? Because I streamed it to my friend and we laughed at how absolutely horrendous it is. That's what it's good for I suppose.
Let's be honest, numerical ratings are hilariously arbitrary, but for the numberphiles out there who made it this far, I'll give it a 3/10. At least it runs right?

An ARPG centered around a lesbian romance?
had my name written all over it.
This was one of the first games that attracted me to the PlayStation 4, a console that still eludes me to this day -- HDMI only in a mostly analog home leaves me with few options, none of which come at a reasonable price.
But I digress; my interest in this game came and went, forgotten for months... until the PC port came to be.
How *is* the port exactly?
Well, it works... to some extent. Full-screen is wonky; expect some alt-tabbing to get it right. The built-in MSAA doesn't work at all, either, nor does forcing it at a driver level. Nvidia DSR is a no-go considering max resolution (without a registry edit that breaks the DoF effects) caps at 1920x1080. Driver level FXAA and forced 16x anisotropic do help, however.
In short: it could be worse, excusable were
a diamond in the rough.
Unfortunately it is not. Terrible? No. Mediocre? Very, lush music and atmosphere wasted on significantly missed potential.
As someone that writes love stories for a living, the overarching narrative is... bland, pacing and structure questionable at best. Cutscenes pointlessly interrupt with no real rhyme or reason beyond pitiful fluff. Even the average
game isn't this bad about it.
Beyond Arnice -- the player character -- there's little of interest in the cast, her relative complexity lost, wasted on a world full of cardboard cutout stereotypes. That's not to say tropes are bad by nature; it's all in execution, and that's where
fails. What a conflicted bad♥♥♥♥♥like Arnice sees in a naive, accident-prone child like Lilysse? I have no idea. Someone at Gust desperately needs a lesson in character chemistry.
Visually the game looks fine courtesy to some excellent art design. Arnice looks wonderful, as do the adorable monster designs and surrounding scenery. Technically impressive? Hardly, but for a low budget project, there's nothing here to legitimately complain about.
The unnecessary focus on certain... assets of Arnice and Lilysse are another story. For something like
that embraces the absurdity in supremely self-aware parody, it works, but
's more serious tone? Just no; another victim of teenage boy mindset nonsense.
The gameplay itself is a mixed bag of good ideas and poor execution. The Servan system is interesting, but done better in other, older games (
on PlayStation 3 comes to mind). Combat from Arnice's perspective lacks weight, impact; I'd question if I was even hitting anything were it not for the chain meter, more so considering the lack of target focus on her moveset.
Both Arnice and her Servans can be equipped with non-visible accessories to boost varying stats/add bonus effects. The difference, however, is unfortunately negligible in practice, futile. I'd gladly trade it in exchange for some much-needed visual customization.
How to squander potential -- that's the lesson we can learn from
. A sequel that improves upon all of the above flaws, though? I'd give it a go.

I played this game on the ps4 and I am very close to plat it, but doing 300 quests is proving too tedious. I bought it here because it was bundled with Atelier Sophie, to support Gust's games on PC and because the anti-aliasing in the ps4 version, in the habit of jrpgs there is $hit.
This  project, which is an action rpg though, which is a fresh take on their approach for game development for Gust, who are famous for their long-running and adorable Atelier series.
I was really wary and hesitant for a long time before buying it due to reading mixed reviews about this game and because I am a Gust and Atelier fan, I decided to take the plunge.
Story: As I felt with Sophie, the story is serviceable, it is a platonic love between the two main female leads. It's nothing revolutionary or innovative but it manages to keep one's interest.
Characters: The cast is fine; I really like Arnice and her protective, gallant tendency to protect her weak friend, which in turn is mainly a fan-service damsel-in-distress type. The other characters are just there for the ride to give a sense that that world is populated but I found them mildly interesting.
Graphics: The graphics look fine for an anime rpg; they are almost Atelier level as in Sophie, not the ps3 and vita ones. However, for plot reasons they are always dark but beautiful.
Game play mechanics: You need to do a ton of quests, 300 to be exact to unlock one of the trophies. Basically, you leave the hotel to follow a certain scenario, you choose your destination on the world map and you go there for a specified amount of time that you can't exceed, for plot reasons again. This can feel like a rinse-and-repeat approach, but the game is not too long to overstay its welcome, sans the extensive grinding if you want to feel overpowered in your rpgs as I do.
The game has a pokemon-esque mechanic in which your recruit monsters to fight alongside you by getting certain item drops or buying the necessary parts to 'Actualise' them by paying with blue blood, which is also required for leveling up the main character, so you would always feel that you don't have enough of it unless you spend too much grinding and farming like I did. The main character also assumes some powerful forms depending on the type of monsters you choose to use and their affinities.
Battles: They are fun and the hits seem to have an impact. I would say the game is on the easy side, but I did lots of grinding. Although the battle system may seem barebones to many, I was OK with that because I am not a fan of unnecessarily complicated battle systems and I normally prefer turn-based jrpg's anyway.
Music: The music was very good and memorable and they suited the atmosphere of each dungeon really well for the most part.
Voice acting: I really like the voice acting but mind you it is all dubbed in Japanese. On the plus side, all dialogue is dubbed.
Extra features: the game doesn't have a difficulty setting but it does have a new game plus mode to make your life easier should you decide to replay it. It is also easy to platinum even for people who are not trophy hunters normally like myself.
Overall, I do recommend this game to Gust and Atelier fans or lovers of Jrpgs in general as I really liked it in general.

This game isn't bad, but it's not good either.  Graphically gorgeous, great setting, but the combats gets super repetitive.  And that makes the game unfun.
Part of the problem here is that they made this glorious execution system, but then (a) require you to purchase new executions with XP, and (b) hide most of the other execution forms under other stances.  (b) is especially bad because there is once stance which pretty much grants you a full health bar all the time.   And so fighting in any mode other than that one is purposely gimping yourself.
This means that combat becomes, Y,X,X,Y,X,X,RT,X,Y,X.  Repeat.  Sometimes block.  And you'll get treated to a slow-mo arm hacking off with every enemy downed.  Which is really cool the first time you see it.  And then because it's the same few animations (see above) it gets pretty old.
Comparing this to other brawler type games, Batman or Shadows of Mordor... There's no open world.  No real side quests (other than picking up scrolls along the way).  No vehicle.  No real climbing.  No setup to combal.  No puzzle type levels.  No stealth.
The story line is interesting and dramatic, but that's just not enough for my recommendation.

The core combat mechanics are neither innovative, nor particularly interesting, and become quite formulaic once you figure out how to defeat each enemy type (of which there are about 5). The combat system follows a very Arkham-esque formula, but with little variety and none of the charm. Executions come in the form of quicktime events, which do look good, but get incredibly tedious.
Despite this, I found the game to be fairly enjoyable. Some segments have you commanding legionarries in testudo formation from the front line, which was interesting even if incredibly easy.
I felt that the story was surprisingly good, as we see a soldier of Rome climb through the ranks of the Roman military across several years. The game is quite short though, and it took me only 5 hours to complete on my first playthrough (normal difficulty).
Graphically, this game is possibly the best looking game currently available. The cinematography during cinematics, the lighting during gameplay and just the general look and feel of the game is astounding.
I do recommend this game, but not with particular enthusiasm and it definitely wouldnt be my first thought when asked what to recommend someone.
If you are a fan of Roman history, combat games and this game is on sale then check it out, but I wouldn't recommend this game at full price.

One may be a bit suspicious that the game advertises so many features, but it does execute them very well.
First off, I recommend reading the only english speaking guide as a good primer on what settings make a good beginner game. Also, sell your starting shields (if your ship has any) because they are complete crap that takes up too much space at the beginning. Shields in this game only block percent damage, and starting shields block next to nothing. Missiles/frag cannons are very good weapons early to mid, though missiles must be manually reloaded. Finally, find a pirate base and join them for a free, VERY good ship. It doesn't matter if you don't want to go pirate, you can always go grab the ship and just fight dominaors for pirate favor/backstab them and hunt them down. Ironically the one segment of the game that is the most obviously advertised, space combat, is also the most infuriatingly obtuse to figure out without the help of a guide or google.
Starting tips aside, the trading in this game is dynamic and well done. Planets each start with governments/econmies that are geared towards importing/exporting certain goods, and events such as famines, pandemics, or a change of government will occur that shake up prices. One can make a fairly good amount of money by keeping check of the news and moving large quantities of goods in a freigher. you can own multiple ships, so if you have a fancy fighter you can just park it on the planet.
Speaking of which, in the lower left tab quests, assets, and any news blurbs you flagged are kept there for your future reference, making it easy to keep track of assets you store on different planets/stations, or where you were supposed to ship your cargo hold full of medical supplies.
Quests are offered at government centers on each planet, and are by and large FedEx delivery missions. Asking for easier/harder missions only affects the amount you earn and the amount of time to complete the delivery. You are paid whenever you complete a delivery, making it very easy to simply FedEx you way into riches (if you have the patience)
Some quests end up turning into text adventures (and are usually indicated rather obviously as not your standard delivery). Judging by the ones I've played, the text adventures are rather well done and fair. In the event of player death or failure, you are rerolled back in time to try again/give up whenever you want.
The RTS segments are somewhat simplistic, with the complexity coming in purely through how you choose to build your combat units. Simplistic doesn't mean bad however, and for the most part they were rather fun. With the glaring exception of several missions that are hellishly difficult.
What I find most attractive about the game is its sense of immersion. Events happen around the player, and it is up to them how to respond. The Coalition, Pirates, and Dominators will all launch attacks/defend star systems, other Space Rangers will fly around doing their thing, more Rangers will be recruited to expand/replace losses. Research into better technology will happen (and can be funded by the player), militaries will build new ships/garrison systems (can also be funded), and overall it gives of a good sense of "Hey, you aren't the only hoshot out there getting things done". Heck, on the easier difficulties, the Coalition (the rather obvious good guys) can very well defeat both their enemies without any player intervention. (It will be a VERY long game, with the player doing absolutely nothing in the mean time)

Compared to Onikakushi (which works as a standalone story), Watanagashi is less about personal psychological horror and more about digging into the mystery of Hinamizawa. The ending on its own is unsatisfying, but taken as part of a series, it's clearly leading up to a reveal that will cast the events in a new light on a second reading. Avoid if you haven't read Onikakushi and/or don't intend on reading the rest of Higurashi, but otherwise recommended.

Although Watanagashi can be played first or even as a stand-alone novel (much of the information revealed in Onikakushi is presented here as well), this is a comparative review. So, to lay out the pros and cons in relation to Ch1:
Pros (aka. the reason why I do recommend this):
- The beginning doesn't feel as slow, and it's also a little more entertaining.
- You get to understand some characters' intentions a little better (I'm looking at you, Ooishi).
- The sound during creepy/suspense moments is soooo much better.
- More of the history of Hinamizawa.
- In case you like Mion as much as I do, you get to see plenty of her backstory here as well.
Cons (aka. critique time! May be a little long and spoilery, so be warned):
- It feels like this had a "broader"/more general point of view, focusing on what's going on with everybody and having Keiichi try to find out what happened to other people in these larger-scale incidents, making this more about mystery than psychological horror. Onikakushi, on the other hand, focused on both Rena's and Keiichi's mental breakdowns. The narrative had you at the edge of your seat much more often than Watanagashi. After all, it
have a bigger impact when you read first-person descriptions of somebody stalking and trying to kill you than when you read a character talking about some other people who died.
- Keiichi's character in this also made the end really lukewarm, in my opinion. His unconditional acceptance and near-blind trust in Mion made the horrible things at the end seem much more distant than his constant paranoia and fear of Rena (his development in both chapters is understandable, however).
- The emphasis on gender roles and stereotypes for the first half of the game is SO ANNOYING.
Also, a little tip: you may think the "after party" is just a little extra, but I do recommend reading it. Characters get together as if they were actors just playing their roles and discuss the story, which may help you mull it over as well. I admit I had found the end to be incredibly underwhelming (especially in comparison to Onikakushi), but the after party shed light on some things I hadn't considered. I guess the generic writing at the start of each chapter really had me underestimating the writers...

Watanagashi is like a different author writing a slightly altered version of Onikakushi, with the focus of much of the story on Mion instead of Rena. It has the same plodding pace in the first 4 or so chapters, same low budget get's-the-job-done backgrounds, and adds a single character. For the most part this can be "played" on its own, but many of the nuances of the characters, as well as a few references in the opening chapters and music changes (every time the music stops, that creeping dread comes in...). There is much more plot resolution in this chapter than in the previous one, but also raises a lot of questions (it took me about 2 hours to read the final chapter, and it just keeps throwing stuff at you).
Ultimately, I highly recommend this second chapter. It feels to be more informational than mysterious, as with the first chapter, and provides a lot of background information, especially about Mion. If you haven't tried the first chapter, I suggest grabbing that one first as it will make the experience of this chapter more thrilling, but this one can be read right away without becoming lost.

Although, there were a few different locations that were seen in this novel, but apart from that; the way the characters were drawn are the same.
Again, the story starts off very slow and gradually picks up around chapter 10. This time, the main culprit is actually shown and told in a very obvious manner (It’s pretty obvious once you get some ideas within the story). This ruined the mystery for me once I found out who the culprit was as the main character was still ‘not accepting’ the ‘person’, it got a little frustrating. Although, it is a still a great read, but I do prefer the first novel.
Apart from a few different soundtracks here and there, it does borrow the same soundtrack heard from the first novel. They did not improve it in any way of form, but they also didn’t change it too drastically that it would mismatch the novel.
Same deal with the first novel, you get the exact same options. In addition, there were no translation errors that I spotted which is a plus. However, as with the first novel the game crashed a few times, so make to save often to avoid losing progress.
With a base price of £5.59 it is worth significantly more than the first novel for nearly the same length. That’s not to say that this is not worth reading, this is a really good visual novel that is worth picking up if you want to read the 2nd chapter of the series.

Well, Metal Gear Solid is back on PC and even BETTER yet, it is on Steam! For the first time ever the stealth genre has hit Steam with a quality port that never ceases too impress. After playing over 25 hours on my PS3 I can safely say this is a pretty big improvement. Majorly increased Draw Distance and a multiplied number of light sources this game is great to stare at alone. Game play is another thing, after almost 16 years of 3D Metal Gear Solid I love how they continue to shake things up with new gameplay mechanics and now it is shifting into an open world map. Ground Zeroes feels fresher than ever. Overall, I'm pretty content with what the game offered, however, it has its problems.
After a while, combos get extremely boring, especially with the Hammer, and especially when you're not dishing out a lot of damage to finish off enemies. You can unlock a skill that lets you continue your combos by quickly switching to a different weapon, but it requires you to use the D-Pad for that and I often found myself forgetting that I could do it.
The game's not really a grind until you hit levels 7-11, as your main method of leveling up is almost like Dark Souls: using blood you've collective through your battles and visiting an Alter. You don't find the best Servan (imo) until, literally, the final room before the final boss of the main storyline and you have to buy him and he costs a hefty amount of Blood. Luckly, the place where you do buy him is the best place to farm Blood. It got really grindy after that, since I had to level him up to 11 from 1.
There are side quests, but there aren't any achievements related to them nor do you get any specific items that'll help you in battle once you've completed them. There is a quest that gives you a pretty sweet sword, but it wasn't until right before the final boss that I realized that the quest was available. Not sure if I wouldn't call it a side quest, though, as I was stuck on level 8 for so long and it wasn't until I did this quest that allowed me to level up again, despite having the appropriate amount of Blood.
Story-wise: It wasn't really memorable. Some funny moments in there, but ultimately, I fell out over trying to keep up with it. I just wanted to fight bosses, to be honest. There is some stuff to do after you beat the main storyline, however, I haven't finished the extra stuff yet.
It has a wonderful soundtrack, though. Sometimes I would start up the game and just sit in the lobby of the hotel and listen to the music, same with cutscenes - just let the music play without advancing.
It's a "sit back and chill" sort of game. Nothing really stressfull about it. I never really died until I equipped an item that pretty much made me one shot. It was for an achievement, though. And I also died when I first encounted the final boss, as I was stuck on level 8, as I mentioned, so I was most likely underleveled.
I recommend you pick it up when it's on sale. 7.4 / 10

I find this game's love/hate is defined by two groups: people who hate cursing and abstract puzzles with very subtle hints at best, and people who love an undeniably unique atmosphere paired with exceptional vocal performances.
Only If plays like the Talos Principle as designed by an OG beatnik.  Trapped in an oddly beautiful and deeply psychological universe you're constantly taunted by a foul-mouthed stranger who serves as a powerful and genre-bending contrast to a backdrop of gigantic roman pillars, floating amethysts, antique wardrobes, a gorgeous park, and more vases than a single house should ever contain.
Only If's presentation is a one-of-a-kind experience backed by consistently good voice acting, particularly from the exasperated main character who just wants to get the hell out of there.  The puzzles weren't as hard as many of the reviews seem to suggest, provided you take everything your seemingly mad companion says into account.  The only time I got really stuck was in the park.  Just remember that you can type answers to yes/no questions (with a couple of exceptions).
I've only taken the white pawn path thus far, and I'm definitely going to go for the second one as things evidently change a lot.
If you want a unique dreamlike experience, or the concept of an adult Boondocks style Alice in Wonderland story intrigues you, then go for it.  I wasn't disappointed.

Full disclosure, I love Yuri. One lookt hrough my steam library will tell you that mutch. I recommend this game for any lover of yuri out there. Especially for those like me that are sick and ♥♥♥♥ing tired of sub text. There aint no sub text here. Our two main characters love each other. That's all there is to it.
Personally, I'm happy we have a game that's not a visual novel that focuses on yuri. As much as I love Yuri, I've longed for a yuri focused game that's actually...a game. There's gameplay here, even if it's not  the best, it's still gameplay. Anywho, i'll write an in depth review based on my experience with the game, yuri in general, and other games with similar gameplay.
Gameplay in Nights of Azure takes the form of a third person hack-n-slash. You control Arnice, and use her arenseal of weapons, servens (more on this later), and overal combat prowess to mow down many demons. In terms of controlling Arnice, it feels like Dynasty Warriors trying to mimic Devil May Cary. This doesn't exactly turn out the best, but it's forgiveable, as i've certainly played games like this with a lot worse controls and mechanics.
As mentioned, you also have Servens. These are basically summonable creatures that help you in battle. They can do many different things, from helping you attack, healing, defending, buffing, debuffing, and finding items. You summon Servens using SP, which is used for Arnice's special attacks. It's kinda like pokemon in the sense that you can find fetishes for different Servens, which allow you to summon and collect all of them. Generally though, you'll find your core party and stick with them trhough most of the game.
We also have RPG mechanics in the game. Enemies drop blood when you kill them, which is used to lvel up in a ridiculously skimpy mannor. (I'll touch on this later in the review.) Leveling up gives you access to new weapons and skills. Sevens level up as well at the end of every mission out as well. You use skill points to aqquire skills, which cpme from daytime activities. All missions take place during the night, and at the end of every mission, you ahve day time activities. You don't interract with these in any way, but they're neccessary to gain skills.
Overall, gameplay is solid, but not pretty. Like a jagged rock. Gameplay is good, but it's not exactly groundbreaking or new in any department. I probably would hav eliked this more if it did play exactly like DMC and used servens as combo assits rather then summons.
The story is...meh. It's not new, but it's not boring. By far the best thing about this game is the genuine love shared between Arnice and the Saint she ahs to guard, Lillysee. As i mentioned above, there is no subtext, no beating around the bush, no acting like it's not normal to like the same gender. They love each other, and there's no doubt in anyone's midn that's played the game. Anyone who say's it's just subtext has never played the game past the three hour mark.
Male chracters are in the game as well, but they play a purely supllemental role and can be ignored with ease.
I'm gonna come right out and say it, I hate the charcter design. Especially for Arnice and Lilysee. Let me be clear that i'm not against breasts, and that artists shoudl create what theyw ant to create; but chracter design just simply doesn't mesh with the serious story their trying to tell. It's so...for lack of a better word, weird to see a badass character like Arnice cutting down swaths of demons and looking like Dante doing it, tehn going to level up and seeing her wearing lingerie. The justification is MGS V levels of pathetic. "She breathes through her skin" and "When offering blood, you want to wear as least as possible" both sound like artists trying to justify putting♥♥♥♥♥♥in their game for the 13 year old boys, which is, from what i can tell, NOt the target audience for this game. It's meant for mature adults formw hat I can tell.
Developers, if you want♥♥♥♥♥♥in your game, just say it. Don't offer a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ justification for it. I'll respect it more that way.
Music is AMAZING. Whoever worked on the OST deserves a helluva lot of recognition. The music here invoked memories of castlevania, with symphonic rock taking the place of most of the fights, or just plain classical in certain places that go amazingly with the settings. And I know I harped on the elveling up before for it's uneccesary skimpiness, but that place has one of the best tracks in the game. When you ge tthere, just sit and listen for awhile. An excellent 4X turn-based strategy, set in pre-apocalyptic fantasy (or is it fantasy..?) world. Your planet, Auriga is dying, with winters steadily getting longer and harsher, and threatening to kill all life on the planet. But relics left by the ancient race, the Endless may hold key to saving Auriga, or some other means to survive the coming cataclysm. But other factions have their own plans on how to survive the disaster – and some just happily fight for territory heedless of approaching doom, so you may have to conquer the world in order to save it.
Gameplay-wise, Endless Legend is 4X turn-based strategy with tactical battles and some RPG elements. The main focus is strategy, particularly expanding your empire and developing your cities. As the cities control the whole regions they are built in, and as expansion is limited in early game (partially due to increasing disapproval among your citizens if you expand too much, and partially due to high for early game settler cost), you have to plan which regions to colonize first. And as your cities’ population grows, you can build up your cities, visibly expanding them from small settlements into megapolises that cover entire regions they are in.
Tactical combat isn’t as good as in some other games that focus more on it, but still decent enough. Interesting aspect of it is that while units act in turn in combat, all orders are given in the beginning of each combat turn, without knowing how enemies will act, which can make combat unpredictable. Whether it is a good or bad thing depends on whether you enjoy an extra challenge or get frustrated by randomness of battles. If you don’t want to engage in tactical battle, the game allows automatic resolution for all battles, often with quite satisfactory results.
And finally, as for RPG elements, Endless Legend allows you to recruit heroes from a very large list that can either serve as cities’ governors or command armies (and in addition to granting bonuses to an army, fighting in combat themselves as well). As might be expected, the heroes level up as they fight or govern cities, increasing not only their combat stats but allowing you to choose their level-up bonuses, with each faction’s heroes having unique set of skills to choose from.
I fully recommend Endless Legend to anyone who likes 4X turn-based strategies or want to give this genre a try, especially if they want to enjoy a pretty good story to go with the game.

Once again, Hideo Kojima is responsible for bringing us perhaps one of the most solid and beautifully crafted games to ever hit the market.
MGS exceeds all expectations for graphics. They are beyond amazing. Between the detailed models and textures, the world is created meticulously. Nothing is placed without purpose. The level of detail put into every single artifact in the game (and the new Fox Engine), as far as I'm concerned, exceeds almost (if not) every game that has preceded it. Not to mention, every lighting, water and other peripheral effects is just taking it to a whole new level cinenmatic gameplay. If you have a good card, this game will literally make you scream with agony when your pants can't support the tent you are going to make, male or female.
The gameplay/stealth is addictively fun. You are not ever forced into a waiting game without putting yourself there. Completely in control of how you approach a situation, the replayability of a single part of is absolutely immense. Not to mention the controls, while enormous in their various actions are fluid and easy to become acquainted with. I believe there is truly a high skill ceiling in this game. This gameplay possesses so much potential for multiplayer as did MGS4 which did an amazing job combing stealth, action, and shooter in a way that didn't feel clunky or cheap and was COMPLETELY original. You truly feel like Big Boss in all his expertise and bad-assery.
The only thing I'd say is wrong is that normal mode is very easy when it comes to shooting everyone in the head and sprinting around the map unseen; however, that is explained by the in-game stormy weather; plus, you can also turn up the difficulty. I'm just saying, enemy detection needs some tweaking.
Also, if passive-stealth gameplay not your style, then not a problem! If you just want to run and gun, be our guest. It may not be the traditonal nor the easiest way, but it can absolutely be done. That's right. There's absolutely, no single way to play this game.
3-7 Hours for first playthrough
15-20 hours of replayability (total)
Sooo, not terrible for the price considering the quality.
Sure, MGS can be a bit convoluted with all the different names, historical dates, and acronyms for a trillion different organizations, but if that's what you're into, you will absolutely LOVE this story. The story is weaved together intricately, balancing realism and drama without compromising any of the fun of playing the game simply to maintain story. The characters don't feel like they were snipped out of 60's-70's mystery/romance novels either for once. So coming to like and become attached to a character you can identify with is not uncommon in this game. They are people, with motives that stick to that. The conviction of the characters to their roles and how they go about being that person is flawless.
Now that I'm older since the original MGS games, I find myself totally engrossed in the story in such a way that makes this amazing game all the more personal for me. If you like story, even if the gameplay wasn't so solid, you'll find yourself immersed in the world of MGS. The voice-acting is also not shabby. I mean, you can totally hear an actor reading the line in a lot of games, but in this, it's just who it is. The acting is nothing special, but it doesn't break your immersion.
While yes, it is definitely very short, this is just a way to support Hideo Kojima before they release The Phantom Pain in a few months. How this receieved 79/100 on meta is beyond me. I know they're avoiding being too biased with a high rating due to MGS's cult following, but there is absolutely nothing so flawed about the game that it deserves anything less than a High B.
10/10 (if you don't mind the price)
8.9/10 (for $20 for a short game)

This game is great, and as everyone has pointed out, not nearly enough people play it. I remember when I bought it back when it was in alpha, and after testing it, was really pumped for it's release. The game itself did not disappoint at all, it's the most unique and fun 2D shooter I've ever played. What really got to me was how very few people play it and the servers were all dead, besides the occasional Wave Survival match. Still, while this game has insane potential for competitive multiplayer gameplay, the Singleplayer campaign alone makes it worth it : it's big, long, action-packed, full of secrets, and with a real sense of progression as you discover new areas and find more weapons to add to your collection. Classic Survival is, in my opinion, also a blast to play by yourself, and there's always the possibility to play local multiplayer. Of course, this requires you to gather a bunch of friends and some controllers, and us PC gamers may not always have many controllers available. If you do, however, then you'll have a ton of fun, because local multiplayer is really well-polished and one of the main features of the game, in fact.
Also, I should add that you will need a controller to properly play the game, and not just a cheap SNES replica, but a modern, full-featured controller. I personally use a Nintendo Switch pro controller because that's what I have available, you can also use Xbox controllers, PlayStation controllers, or if you don't have any of those, you can pick up a Logitech f310 for pretty cheap depending on where you live and it'll do the job just fine. If you don't have one and don't want to buy any hardware, then I guess you CAN survive on a keyboard, but it'll feel much, much better with a controller.
The game officially came out a year ago and never took off so I hardly believe the multiplayer situation will change much ; but while online gameplay is pretty much absent, there is an active community of modders and map-makers (because, by the way, the game includes a full-featured level design tool which is very powerful and probably what the devs used themselves) so in a way the game is not COMPLETELY dead.
Basically, get this game if you're interested in singleplayer or local multiplayer, make some awesome maps and share them if you want to, don't get your hopes up for online multiplayer since it's often empty or only a couple of gamemodes have people playing them.

It pains me to give this a bad review; the graphics are mindblowing. Watching the trailer and seeing the hype made me want to like this game SOOO badly. Unfortunately for this game, the graphics weren't enough to make up for its shortcommings. If only graphics mattered, this would be a movie.
Since I mensioned it, let's start with graphics. My computer is powerful enough to run Battlefield 4 and Tomb Raider on ultra without a problem. Ryse runs like a handicapped child trying to escaped a burning building... Not well at all.
So, without graphics the game gets pointless really quick. The acting's great, the sound design is great, but again this is not a movie. The story is half-baked, illogical, and has an anitclimax that will make you want to shoot a puppy. Besides just being a dumb story, the characters' motives are completely alien. Marius sees injustice all around him, and it doesn't change who he fights for or what he does. The idea that he is so strongly dug in to being a soldier when imperialism at its worst is the thing he's fighting for, makes me think that the writers would be okay if another superpower tried to take over the world. I have the next big game idea for you guys... Nazi: Son of Germany.
Levels and battles are entirely contrived. You don't have the ability to go anywhere, or do anything but the tasks set out before you. Run here, fight, run here, fight, all the while upgrading your character for reasons that don't seem to be that helpful. Sure you get more health or focus, but the battles are so systematic and reaction driven, that health doesn't matter all that much anyway. To top it all off, you can upgrade your character after he dies. This is nnnnnnnuts to me, because it does nothing good for gameplay, and it creates an intentional lack of continuity.
The battle system is an enigma in concept. It is a system that commits to pushing players to SYSTEMATICALLY destroy enemies. They give you different means to kill enemies(javelin, focus, etc.) but disable those abilities when they would serve you creatively in combat, forcing you back into the system. Often, in boss fights, unblockable moves are repeated by enemies, like a button masher in Mortal Kombat, forcing you to dodge until you get to finally play the game again. An especially uninspired fight, that follows this pattern, is with Boutica at the 98% mark. Boutica, in phase one of the battle has two moves she does continuously. You roll, wait, strike, and repeat FOREVER. Then, once you've done that, you fight her at full health again. She gains two moves that do not change combat style at all, so you find yourself just grinding again... Sigh... This is what they thought would be good in a climax.
As if this game couldn't get worse, the story playtime is like 7 hours. Yeah, I dare you to buy this at full price and feel good about that little fact.
I'm super glad that I got a discount on this game, because otherwise I would be much more disapointed.  It's fairly obvious that the dev team spent no time at all on historical accuracy, game play, concept. It looks like a cookie-cutter roman drama, which got a bloated animation budget.

The story is still good, and the game itself is as enchanting as the console versions - but the partial controller support is a big pain in the butt.
